who financed the setting up costs of the production.

The Volunteer Firewood Gang for both their financial assistance and their willingness

to offer encouragement.

The staff of Tauranga City Library for their technical assistance in association with the

microfiche copies of the BOP Times they hold.

The BOP Times and the Bay Sun newspapers for their publicity leading up to the Centennial celebrations.

And especially to Sharyn Cooke of Pukeko Print & Design Ltd for her professional expertise, her artistic insight, her patience, and her

personal financial contribution by way of significantly discounting

the setting up costs of producing this book.

Reference has been made to the books “A Centennial History of Tauranga” by W.H. Gifford

and H. Bradney Williams and to “Golf in New Zealand - A Centennial History” by G.M. Kelly.

title: The book and its contributors · p. 3
text:
FOREWORD

I take great pleasure in writing this foreword to “Pars from the Past”, a comprehensive History of Golf in Tauranga over the past 110 years.

In terms of European settlement Tauranga is a very young city in a young country. Early British settlers brought much of their heritage to New Zealand, and the game of golf was established in Dunedin as early as 1871. This was almost 20 years earlier than the first American Golf Club was established. Golf in Tauranga owed it’s early beginnings to the arrival of Dr Brown from Dunedin who was instrumental in developing our first course on the Domain /Sulphur Point area of the town in 1904. That course proved to be less than ideal and, in 1913, the first overtures were made to the Trustees of the Racecourse Reserve to see if it was feasible to establish a course on the reserve at Greerton. To those people who had the vision to realise that an ideal golf course could be established on what may not at first sight have appeared the best available site, we owe an enormous debt of gratitude. The course established so early in the twentieth century has been continually developed and improved over the succeeding 100 years so as to provide an enjoyable, yet challenging, course for hundreds of players through the past, the present and, we can be confident, many years into the future.

Miss Joan Mirrielees, a daughter of one of the true pioneers of golf in Tauranga, AJ Mirrielees, was the early historian to the club and her work was continued by Mrs Deidre Hartley and finally completed by long time member David Mowat. This history contains a record of the development of the original course in central Tauranga, the first course on the Racecourse Reserve that extended into the Racecourse oval, and the course as it is played today. While that record is important, this history is most notably a history of the people who have made the club what it is today. The stories of their selfless work over the course of the century, the personal anecdotes that show the human side of their personalities, these are the features of this work that will stand out for many readers.

While club members have contributed richly to our History, so too have the many visitors who have graced our course over the years.  In this context the memorable visits of Professional players from around the world who featured in the Spalding Masters and the PGA Championships staged on the course in earlier years added much to the rich tapestry of our History.

David Mowat has captured the spirit of the people who make up our Club’s History in a manner that only a person with a true love of the game and its participants could have done. A member for over sixty years David was an ideal choice to take on the task of compiling this comprehensive, entertaining, and invaluable history of our Club.

On behalf of the Board of Management and of all past, present and future members, I thank David for this contribution to us all.

Graham Cathie – Board Chairman

title: The book and its contributors · p. 4
text:
INTRODUCTION

The gestation period of this Centennial history has been a long one. The early history of the Club was first compiled by the late Miss Joan Mirrielees in preparation for the Golden Jubilee of the club in 1961 but was not published owing to a lack of funding. Miss Mirrielees was a long time Club member, a teacher and an historian. Following that earlier compilation Miss Mirrielees wrote to the 1974 committee offering to prepare a ‘complete history of the club’. This offer was accepted with enthusiasm, especially in view of the fact that the club was believed to be approaching its Diamond Jubilee year. The celebration of that milestone in 1986 seemed to cement the year 1911 as the foundation year of the club though there was evidence of a Golf Club in the town somewhat earlier. The move to the present course did not take place until 1914 when the existing club decided to take up an available lease on a portion of the Racecourse Reserve. 1911 appears to have been chosen from a perusal of the original championship honours boards, as this was the first year in which a club champion was officially recognised. Perhaps this represented a sensible compromise although it has now become clear that the club does indeed date back to 1904. Incidentally the honour of winning that first championship belonged to Mr A Matheson who repeated the feat the following year, and again in 1921 and 1927.

The major difficulty facing Miss Mirrielees and subsequent researchers has been a serious lack of documented and minuted history. At some time in the decade of the Forties the club secretary also acted as secretary to a local authority and rumour has it that there was a problem related to the funds of that authority and the said gentleman left town in undue haste, though not before taking the time to destroy significant records of both organisations. As it is impossible to substantiate these rumours so long after the event it may be best to leave the suspect unnamed.  Whatever the truth of the matter no minute books recording the first thirty years or so of our history have been discovered. Fortunately Miss

Mirrielees was able to contact a number of older residents and members who were able to recall some of the earlier history. Reference material gleaned from copies of the BOP Times held by the Tauranga City Library yielded further vital information.

As an indication of the difficulties faced in researching relevant material it was not until 1985 that the President was able to report to committee that Miss Mirrielees had made significant progress on the task. This enabled the President, Dr Eric Hutcheson, to give an interesting after dinner address on the early history of the club during the Diamond Jubilee celebrations held in 1986.

Miss Mirrielees died in 1989 without the satisfaction of seeing her work go to print .She did however leave a considerable amount of valuable material she had collected from a variety of sources. In time this material was passed on to Mrs Deidre Hartley who, in 1992, expressed the desire to produce a booklet in time for the 90th anniversary planned for June 2001. Over a period Deidre added both to the research and to the developing written text. In this endeavour members of the Ladies’ committee assisted Deidre by preparing and distributing questionnaires to members, and by checking through old documents. A notable addition to the historical record was achieved when Deidre was able to interview Jack Bateman, one of the truly outstanding players of earlier years and a senior championship

title: The book and its contributors · p. 5
text:
winner as early as 1934. Jack was able to recall precise details of the original course laid out on the Racecourse Reserve as he had himself played it on many occasions. Much of the detail of that layout has been included in this publication as the result of the information obtained from those interviews. Sadly Deidre’s health began to deteriorate before she was able to achieve as much as she would have wished in furthering the evolution of this history. Subsequently I was presented with the material that had been assembled to that date in the hope that I could use it to put together a coherent record of the first one hundred years of golf in Tauranga.

I soon realised that a great deal remained to be done. For example nothing had been done to document the deeds of the many outstanding visiting golfers who had competed in tournaments, professional and amateur, male and female, on our course. World-class performers, including winners of ‘Majors’ such as the British and US Opens, had graced our links and deserved their place in our history. The supposed Centennial in 2011 was rapidly approaching and a great deal of material still had to be collected, analysed, and organised into coherent form. Fortunately the deadline was extended forward by three years when further research proved the Club dated back to 1904.

A great many people have contributed richly to the development of the Tauranga Golf Club and I have endeavoured to give them credit for that. Unfortunately this could only be done from memory and from the meagre documentation that does exist. There will be many unsung heroes whom I have not been able to acknowledge and to them I apologise. They will have had the deep satisfaction of knowing that they helped develop and improve a vital asset to pass on to future generations. To those stalwarts of the past that would have been reward enough. My grateful thanks go to all those who have made a contribution to this history by way of oral or written material, by donating photographs, or by collecting information. Without them it would have been impossible to produce more than a basic outline of our colourful history.

Finally, though I have endeavoured to report facts in an impartial manner, it has been impossible to refrain from allowing some personal opinion to creep into this narrative. For that I make no apology. The relationship between the Mowat family and the Tauranga Golf Club since my father took up the role of Professional in 1936 dictates that it could never be otherwise.

title: Setting the scene · p. 6
text:
CHAPTER ONE

SETTING THE SCENE

title: Setting the scene · p. 7
text:
The earliest written record of Tauranga is attributed to Judge Wilson who served as Commissioner of Lands for the Tauranga District in the latter years of the 19th Century. In his ‘Sketches of Ancient Maori Life and History’ he records that when the canoe Takitimu, part of the first group of canoes to arrive from Hawaiki, called at Tauranga the newcomers found the district to be occupied by two tribes of aboriginal people known as the Purukapenga and the Ngamaramas. Purukapenga may be translated as ‘Full Net’ and so is in accord with James Cook’s observation that this was a place of abundant resources. Despite the obvious attractions of the area the immigrants aboard Takitimu decided it would be wise to sail further south in search of less populated land. Nearly 600 years then passed prior to the arrival of the first European missionaries during which time numerous tribal battles were waged in attempts, both successful and unsuccessful, to lay claim to this most desirable of locations.  Those early missionary newcomers were very soon supported by a strong contingent of British military forces and the stage was set for the commencement of the wide range of activities that these people from the other side of the world brought with them.

Construction of ‘The Elms’ Mission House began in 1838 and was completed in 1847. This was the home of Archdeacon Alfred Nesbit Brown who lived there until his death in 1884. In 1878 he wrote to a friend in London suggesting to him that he would barely recognise the town since he visited some years earlier. “We now have two large wharves, four weekly steamers, a large public office building, two well-built Banks, three churches, and three hotels. Land values have risen to prices that would astonish you. A quarter acre on the beach recently sold for £1670, he wrote.”

Living today in this modern, rapidly growing city of Tauranga it is difficult to imagine what the district was like at the beginning of the 20th century. Because of the poorly formed un-metalled roads the town was isolated. Access was mainly by steamer from Auckland. Even so there was considerable development as described by the Archdeacon above. The Strand and Devonport Road were thriving shopping and business centres, though life remained sufficiently relaxed that it was not unusual to find ‘gone fishing’ notices posted on shop and office doors. If business was urgent the proprietors were only too happy to be summoned from the waterfront.

The importance of horse-drawn transport was highlighted by the presence of Lane’s livery stables on the corner of Spring Street and Grey Street, where the National Bank now stands, and by the Grey Street Smithy where Arthur Rolfe plied his trade. That same Blacksmith’s shop was still operating in the 1950s with Charlie Haua at the forge. The now demolished Town Hall was built in 1913 where the City Council offices now stand and no less than four hotels, complete with water troughs and hitching rails, competed for custom in the down town area. The Fire Brigade Headquarters, Mechanics Institute, Hammond’s Bakery, and the Bay of Plenty Times Office were prominent buildings in the centre of the township. Cameron Road was a narrow strip, dusty in summer, muddy in winter, flanked by grassy verges where cows grazed.

The earliest European settlers must have included many far-sighted people for they dedicated areas for sport and recreation well before the turn of the century. By that time the Domain boasted six grass

title: Setting the scene · p. 8
text:
tennis courts and two croquet greens while the bowling club was established on the Domain in 1906. The rugby football ground alongside was also in active use while a cricket club had been established as early as 1873. The Tauranga Boating Club, involving both Rowing and Yachting, followed soon after in 1878. By 1880 prosperity and stability were beginning to develop and Tauranga was becoming much more than ‘an old soldiers settlement’. In 1882 Tauranga gained status as a Borough under the Municipalities Act. This allowed it to raise loans to finance the provision of public infrastructure such as roads and water supply, each being desperately needed. The first Mayor was George Vesey Stewart, an immigration agent from Ireland who had been largely responsible for arranging settlement of immigrants from Britain into the Western Bay of Plenty. He is especially honoured as the founder of Katikati while Te Puke also owes its origins to him. His faithfully restored home, Athenree House, has become an important historic landmark on the road to Waihi Beach.

Wise forethought by the early settlers ensured that an area of 200 acres comprising sections 22-25 of the Parish of Te Papa was reserved from sale in order to preserve it for future use as a racecourse and recreation reserve. This was gazetted on 10th of October 1878 and the area became known as the Racecourse Reserve. Thus the stage was set for people further ahead in time to develop the Reserve as a permanent asset to the developing township.

While the origins of the game of Golf are widely debated credit for the establishment of officially organised golf must lie with the ‘Honourable Company of Edinburgh Golfers’ founded in 1744. The first British ‘Open’ was held at Prestwick in 1860 and was ‘open’ only to professionals. The amateur championship of Great Britain followed in 1885. With these dates in mind it must be said that golf in this part of the World got off to an early start as Royal Adelaide, the first Australian Golf Club was founded in 1870. The Dunedin Golf Club followed just one year later. Surprisingly the first Club in the USA, Oakhurst in Virginia, was not established until 1885. John Reid, who founded the Saint Andrews Club at Yonkers in New York in 1888, is regarded as the father of golf in the USA as it was he who provided the initial stimulus that popularised the game there. Though the first United States Open was not held until as late as 1895, the growth of the game throughout America was such that by 1900 over 1000 courses had been established there. In that same year the A G Spalding and Brothers Sporting Goods Company contracted the immortal English Professional Harry Vardon to participate in a barnstorming exhibition tour of the USA to promote their new Gutta Percha ball, the Vardon Flyer. The exhibitions during this ten-month tour attracted thousands of spectators, including many who had had no previous exposure to the great game. The spark that John Reid had struck was fanned into raging flames by the Vardon

tour. By the time it was over more than one hundred new courses were planned or under construction and the development of American Golf was in overdrive. In view of these facts it is significant that Golf had such an early start in the small, isolated settlement of Tauranga. Charles Richie Howden was the New Zealand equivalent of America’s John Reid. He arrived in Dunedin from Edinburgh in 1861 at the age of 23. He became the first Captain of the Dunedin Golf Club in 1871 where the subscription is recorded as having been set at one guinea. A guinea was 21 shillings designed to include the commission payable in the pound on livestock sales. Racehorse sales in New Zealand were still being quoted in guineas almost up to the time of decimal currency. Besides being

title: Setting the scene · p. 9
text:
recognised as the father of New Zealand Golf Charles Howden founded The New Zealand Distilling Company to produce whisky in Dunedin. Howden left New Zealand in 1881 and, with his departure, the Dunedin Golf Club appears to have expired after its short ten-year life. Eight years later Howden returned to Dunedin and, in 1889, was instrumental in setting up the Otago Golf Club at Balmacewan. That club continues as a major club today. Notable in the list of inaugural members of the original Dunedin Golf Club was a Dr W. M. Brown who later served on the committee of the club that succeeded it, the Otago Golf Club.

Development of the game in New Zealand was very rapid and by the outbreak of World War Two Tauranga was just one of some eighty clubs affiliated to the New Zealand Golf Association that had been established in 1910. Even more rapid expansion followed the cessation of war in 1918 and by 1929 the number of clubs had swelled to 159. Today it is claimed we boast more clubs per head of population than any other country with the possible exception of Scotland where it all began. Certainly the game here is available and affordable to almost all who wish to play, something not true in most parts of the World. On the subject of costs a 1928 edition of New Zealand Golf Illustrated published an average annual golfing budget for the guidance of those contemplating taking up the game. The total cost per year was estimated at £16/2/6 made up of club fees (£6/10/0), balls (£5), repairs (£1), and refreshments (£3/12/6). This annual cost would perhaps be less than some would now spend on a single afternoon at the club. While no comment was made on the cost of equipment to get you started we can be confident that £10 would have done you proud. Based on these figures refreshments represented about 22% of a player’s annual expenditure. I wonder what proportion of the average member’s annual expenditure is now represented by the cost of refreshments.

Over the years there have been many holes in one, some more unusual than others. Perhaps Harry Jeffreys began it all in the early days when the fifth tee was located inside the Racecourse oval. The green was where the grandstand now stands. Harry made a mighty heave at the ball only succeeding in topping it so that it never became truly airborne. In spite of this it scrambled across the racetrack, hit a tree trunk, straightened up after striking a fence post, trickled up the hill onto the green, and finally dribbled exhausted into the cup. The perfect shot!

Perhaps a more notable hole in one was that scored by Miss Rachell Baker in October 1940 when she holed her tee shot at the notorious Knoll. Apart from the personal thrill associated with the perfect stroke Miss Baker had the distinction of being the first woman to achieve the feat on the course. To commemorate her achievement the Ladies of the Club presented Miss Baker with an engraved silver goblet. I wonder where that goblet is today

title: The first tee · p. 10
text:
CHAPTER TWO

THE FIRST TEE

title: The first tee · p. 11
text:
Dr. W M Brown when he arrived from Dunedin in 1903, most probably by Coastal Steamer, carried with him the seed from which the Tauranga Golf Club grew. While it is uncertain if this Dr Brown and the Dr. William M Brown mentioned above as an inaugural member of the Dunedin Golf Club were one and the same it does seem extremely likely. Both were surgeons hailing from Dunedin, each man had an abiding interest in the game of golf, and the timing fits such a scenario. The earliest written evidence of golf in Tauranga can be found in the Archives of The Bay of Plenty Times dated 20th April 1904 where it is recorded that a Golf Club had been, or was being, formed in Tauranga. On June 20th that same year the Times reported: ‘an interesting golf match was played here yesterday afternoon between members of the club for a clique (Sic) presented by Dr. Brown’. Mr. J Bull won this valuable trophy.1

Although the year 1911 has long been recognised as the foundation year of the Tauranga Golf Club it is clear the Club can trace its existence back to 1904. This is evidenced by a report in the BOP Times of 17th May 1905 in which it was observed:

‘The Tauranga Golf Club has started operations for the present season, and several of the members can be seen on the links at all hours of the day energetically practising. At the annual meeting held on Saturday evening Dr Brown and Mr J Bull were re-elected Captain and Secretary respectively’.

Clearly the club had been in existence prior to that meeting. That Dr. Brown was the inspiration behind the birth of the fledgling club is confirmed by the recollections of early residents who credited Dr. Brown with being instrumental in forming the club and in laying out nine holes based on the present Domain area in central Tauranga.2

Foundation in 1904 is further supported by documentary evidence to be found in archived material from the Bay of Plenty Times dated 18th of June 1906. In that edition there is a report of ‘a merry gathering at the Masonic Hotel when the past Mayor of Tauranga, Dr. W Brown, was entertained at dinner by the members of the Tauranga Golf and kindred clubs. Mr W Commons, Mayor, occupied the chair and, in proposing a toast to the guest of honour, he said all would regret that they were about to say farewell to Dr. Brown. It was not often that a town of this size had the services of one of such a high profession

Editor’s note: The correct name for the club presented by Dr. Brown is a cleek, a steep faced driving iron, though the BOP Times reporter of the day could be forgiven his lack of knowledge of the game and its implements. [Editor’s Note. The year 1911, upon which the 50th and 75th jubilee celebrations of 1961 and 1986 were based, appears to have been recognised as the Club’s foundation year based on evidence sourced from old Honours Boards. These commenced with the championship victory of Mr. A Matheson in that year of 1911. It is now clear that the club was founded in 1904 and moved to the present course at the Racecourse Reserve in 1914. The Board of Management in 2009 decided not to proceed with Centennial celebrations in 2011 but instead to celebrate 100 years of golf at the Gate Pa links in 2014. Thereafter it is expected that the Club will recognise 1904 as the foundation year upon which to base significant milestones in the future.

title: The first tee · p. 12
text:
of skill as Dr. Brown. He, the mayor, had expected Dr. Brown to be here for many years and he had no right to give up the mayoralty and throw it upon him (the speaker). Dr. Brown had been a member of the Racecourse Domain Board and had given that role great and successful attention. On the School Committee he had proved himself a tower of strength and had helped them along in a way that no one else could have done. He had taken great interest in Golf and this had been the salvation of many of them. He hoped interest would be kept up. The Mayor then presented the Doctor with a small token of their esteem in the form of a case of pipes, cigar and cigarette holders. In reply Dr. Brown said it took his breath away to hear the nice things that had been said of him. In presenting him with pipes they were simply pandering to his weakness. They must have noticed his pipes were very shabby. He expressed regret at leaving Tauranga. He and his wife both liked the town and he had hoped to spend the rest of his days here but stress of circumstances was too much for them. He commented on the grand climate of Tauranga and the beautiful scenery and stressed the need for municipal enterprise. Tauranga needed a water supply and other facilities and Mr. Commons, after viewing some municipalities at home in Britain, had come back full of enterprise and go. With an enterprising Mayor and a live Council Tauranga was bound to go ahead. He said Tauranga was a town without peer in New Zealand. It had a splendid harbour that should be the Port for the Bay and for the Waikato. When he returned he hoped to find a railway station, the town lighted with gas or electricity, and a library built. On the medical side he was leaving in his place Dr. Gault, an excellent man of high professional attainments, high character, and a good fellow. He hoped they would extend the same right-handed fellowship to him as they had done to the speaker during the two or three years he had been here. Mr Semadini then read a farewell ode written by a ‘Bunkered Poet’.

The poem, while perhaps not of any great literary merit, bears reprinting here as a graphic commentary on those times and the influence Dr. Brown had on the developing community during his short residence in Tauranga. From the poem it becomes apparent that the game of Bridge, as with Golf, owes its origins in the town to the initiative and enthusiasm of Dr Brown.

FAREWELL ODE

By a “Bunkered Poet” We are gathered here this evening,

For a farewell Korero, With our guest the good old Doctor Brown,

But ‘white’ as we all know.

Since he came into our midst,

About two years ago, He’s taught us Bridge, He’s taught us Golf,

And Things we didn’t know. He showed to us the strokes of Golf,

title: The first tee · p. 13
text:
With the patience of a Job, But the adjectives came naturally When we failed to hit the ‘Globe’.

He taught us how to tee a ball,

And from a bunker get; But he did not teach us stymie,

As it just is not etiquette.

And when we thought the game was done,

And finished for the day,

We had his innovation- The nineteenth hole to play.

Now the nineteenth hole is not a hole,

We never called out ‘Fore!’ But we always liked a halved one, And sometimes played ‘one more’.

We’ll think of him when he is gone,

And is miles and miles away. We’ll drink his health and happiness,

When the nineteenth hole we play.

He taught us how to Double Hearts,

Hold four aces, get a slam, And if we happened to revoke,

Why, he never used a damn.

There’ll be no such thing as Doubled Spades,

And Golf will ne’er be seen, And the little bird will build a nest,

In the hole on the putting green.

We will keep the Golf Balls snowy white,

And the Golf Clubs clean we’ll scrub,

In honour of the father of, The Tauranga Golfing Club.

We wish to him and Mrs. Brown,

Long life where’re they roam, But the best of wishes we can wish,

Is good health and safely home.

title: The first tee · p. 14
text:
As no other claimants have come forward, or are ever likely to do so, we are happy to recognise Dr. Brown as the founder of golf in Tauranga and to give to him the honour of opening proceedings by driving the first ball to commence the first one hundred years of golf in the region.

A report of the AGM of 1910 was printed in the BOP Times of 27th April of that year. The meeting was held in the office of Mr. Phillips who was elected Captain, while Messrs. Sharp, Bull, and McKenzie were elected to the committee. The position of Secretary-Treasurer was not filled and it was left to the committee to fill the vacancy. Misses E and M Wrigley were welcomed as new members along with Messrs. D Selby, A Tudhope, J A McLeod, and G L Cook.

The name Wrigley was well known in the Town in earlier years as 16th Avenue was known as Wrigley Street until some ‘progressive’ council decided to destroy so much of Tauranga’s history by dropping many original Street names and replacing them with rather uninspired numbered Avenues. The Avenues originally did not go beyond 11th Avenue. The intersection of that street with Cameron Road was known as Faulkner’s Corner in recognition of the General Store run by the pioneer Faulkner family. Mr Wrigley himself was a well-known local merchant who owned cutters that ran a regular service between Auckland and Tauranga. He also served a term as Mayor of the township. The names Sharp and Tudhope remained prominent in the City more than a century later in the Legal Partnership of that name.

In addition to the names mentioned above the original list of members who played at the Domain course included W H Clemson, R Stubbing, F Cramer-Roberts, W M Darley, J A McKenzie, H B Mountfort and ET Baker. The subscription for men rose to one pound and for women just five shillings. Dr Brown arrived at golf in a two-wheel gig driven by Arthur Faulkner whose family were to have a significant influence on trading and transport in the district for many years into the future. The good doctor’s bag contained just four hickory-shafted clubs: a driver/brassie, a cleek, a lofter and a putter. His driving club was somewhat between a 1 and a 2 wood, the cleek was akin to a 2 or 3 iron while the lofter would be a little like a modern sand iron. The responsibility of transporting this burden around the course was delegated to his caddie, one Ossie Daines, who received a shiny sixpence for his trouble. Other players may well have had a more extensive range of equipment including the mid-iron, mashie, mashie niblick, and niblick, corresponding more or less to the 3, 5, 7, and 9 irons of today. The fairway woods called Brassie and Spoon (3 wood) would hardly be required given the length of the holes they played. The 1911 balance sheet of the club showed just one asset, a hand mower valued at thirty shillings.

There were no employees to be paid and probably no shortage of volunteers when and as required.

The course laid out by Dr Brown and based at the Domain was bounded to the North by Brown Street, to the East by Cameron Road, to the South by McLean Street, and to the West by the sea. It started from the South West corner of the Wharepai Domain, the first green being located where the Band Rotunda used to stand at the top of the rise near the entrance to the Tennis Courts and behind the Bowling Green The second hole then ran through the present Rugby ground into the Domain extension which was first designated as High School reserve land. The course then ran through swampy ground below The Elms Mission House before moving down on to Sulphur Point. There must have been some

title: The first tee · p. 15
text:
unusual hazards including that of having to play around, or perhaps through, rugby games in progress. Narrow trenches crossed the fairway on the High School Reserve. These were the aftermath of the European camp constructed during the Maori Wars. These trenches and some other fortifications, made beautiful by masses of white and blue flag lilies, made an unusual form of bunker. One tee was by Waimarie Guest House on McLean Street and the ‘fairway’ was an unformed road to a green by the gates of the Mission Chapel. The next hole was played from a high tee on the Northeast corner of the Domain extension down to an Island green surrounded by water at high tide - shades of modern USA course design perhaps. This green was located where Odlin’s Timber Mill was later located. The land is now the site of the Trinity Hotel. Access to the green was by way of a few tussocky stepping- stones, particularly challenging to ladies wearing long skirts, as was the regulation golf attire of the day. The men were more appropriately turned out in knickerbockers. It was somewhat later that fashion conscious men turned to plus fours for added comfort and style.

The next hole extended eastwards along the flat towards the Military Cemetery. There were no roads, houses or railway, to impede progress, only a large frog pond in the middle of the fairway. The longest hole, ‘The Camp’, was some 420 yards and rated a bogey 6, bogey having the meaning that par has today. There were some unusual bogey ratings, the sixth and seventh holes being rated 3.5 and 4.5 respectively. Other than these two and the bogey-six second hole there was one bogey 5, four bogey

4s, and a single bogey 3, the final hole of only 105 yards. The bogey 5 eighth was only 210 yards so we have to presume it had to be negotiated in a double dog-leg pattern. The course of only 1860 yards (1690m) in length was rated bogey 38, a very generous rating by the standards of today. In spite of its lack of length the course must have represented a true challenge to the best of players considering the equipment available and the hazards encountered. After completing the first five holes the course returned along almost the same route it followed on the way out - reminiscent of the ‘R and A’ but perhaps not quite in the same class. The final hole finished where it began at the ‘Clubhouse’, a tin shed shared by rugby players beneath huge pines on the Southern boundary of Wharepai Domain.

A card from that original Club was discovered in the archives held by the City Library and the names of holes recall some of the early history of the town. In order those names were Bowler, The Camp, End of the World, Dynamite, Railway, The Straight, The Cliff, Anzac, and Home. The origin of many of these names is obvious. Bowler confirms the bowling club was already in existence while Dynamite no doubt refers to the dangerous goods store that was on Sulphur Point. Anzac however is a mystery as this acronym supposedly originated from the Gallipoli campaign of World War 1. That surely came later than the date this card was printed.

In very early times Dominic Corrigan claimed he could drive a ball off his gold watch. When challenged he demonstrated this talent before a large and interested gallery on the first tee. The spectators were witness only to the total destruction of a very good watch.

title: The first tee · p. 16
text:
The local rules recorded on the card give some insight into the conditions faced by our pioneer players. They include:

1.	 Out of Bounds - Mr Rowe’s Property. Through the fence to the right of the course from the eighth tee. 2.	 In driving from the third tee should a ball fall into and remain in the water or sand adjoining the hole it may be lifted and dropped further away from the hole without penalty. 3.	 If a ball lands in the sea from the drive off at hole 3 the player may lift and drop the same an equal distance from the hole without penalty. 4.	 A ball lying in hoof marks or cattle tracks may be lifted and dropped behind without penalty. This does not apply to a ball in a hazard. 5.	 All ditches on the course are hazards. 6.	 A ball lying on an intermediate putting green must be lifted and dropped off the green from a height of six inches without penalty at any point not more than two club lengths from the edge of the green, but not nearer to the hole to which it is being played. 7.	 A ball lying on or touching horse or cow dung may be lifted and dropped not more than a club length behind without penalty. If in a hazard the ball shall be dropped in the hazard. 8.	 Parties playing odd holes have no standing on the green. 9.	 On medal and match days parties not playing in the medal or match competition must give way to those who are playing. 10.	On Saturday afternoons gentlemen may pass ladies on any part of the course. 11.	On Saturdays players shall not be permitted to play odd holes on Findlay’s paddock unless they have completed two rounds.

Another point of interest gleaned from this card is that the recognised competitions of the day were Medal, Match, and Bogey (Par). The ubiquitous Stableford system had yet to be invented by Dr Frank Stableford, an English gentleman searching for a way to overcome the problem of one bad hole ruining his round. It was at Wallasley Golf Club near Liverpool in 1931 that this plus handicapper first suggested the system be adopted and it spread rapidly around the golfing world, perhaps to the detriment of the more demanding formats. It is also interesting to note that the longest hole on the old Domain course was the number one/two stroke hole while the shortest was stroke seventeen/eighteen.

Jack Rowe, who lived in ‘Waimarie’ on the corner of Cameron Road and Brown Street, recalled that his father, Bert Rowe, somewhat reluctantly took up the game after much urging from his golfing friends.

After just six weeks of play he entered and won the championship and promptly gave the game away to return to bowls after declaring that golf was ‘just a kid’s game’. It would seem few others found the game, or perhaps the course and its unusual hazards, quite so easy. A report on the results of a mixed foursomes competition in 1904 record the winning pair of Mr. Sharp and Miss Bull as finishing five down on bogey (now par). Dr. Brown and Mrs. Corbett were eight down, while the remaining eight pairs finished either ten down or twelve down.

Initially no golf was played on Sundays in deference to the puritanical views of the Landlady of ‘The Elms’. When she sold all her sections Sunday golf became standard practice.

title: The first tee · p. 17
text:
Following the 1905 report of an Annual General Meeting in the BOP Times the Club does not appear to have again been mentioned in that journal until June 10th 1908 when a report was carried of the AGM. This was held in the Orderly Room of Tauranga Mounted Rifles, with Mr Bull being elected Captain and Mr Ward Honorary Secretary/Treasurer. Reporting on the finances of the Club Mr Bull stated that the “annual expenses of maintenance had averaged about five pounds”. Some dozen new members were elected including four ladies. It was resolved to hold a 16-hole singles tournament under medal play format, an entrance fee of one shilling being made to cover prizes. Players were to be handicapped and a handicapping committee of Messrs Bull, McKenzie, and Shackleford was appointed. Two rounds of the then eight hole course would need to be completed during the one afternoon and proper cards were to be kept with the card showing ‘each stroke played for each hole, and the total for the same’. Perhaps one hole had been lost to the sea at the time so reducing the course to 8 holes.

The BOP Times issue of 17th May 1909 reported the election of Mr. J Bull as Captain, Mr. G A Ward as Secretary-Treasurer, and Messrs. H A Sharp, A Matheson, and H Phillips, as committee members. Mr. J A McKenzie presided over the meeting at which it was reported the Balance Sheet was in credit to the tune of 2/6d. Subscriptions were set at 10s for gentlemen, 5s for ladies, and 2/6d for juniors under 18. As Mr. Matheson, soon to be recognised as the first club champion, was welcomed as a new member to this meeting it is apparent that there was no great competition for positions on the committee. The Secretary reported that an order for £2.10.6d worth of balls had been placed but they had not yet been received.

Bill Darley, Secretary to the Club in 1951-53, used to enjoy relating a story from play on the old Domain course. A certain gentleman had the bad habit of playing up on the group ahead. There was a short hole played from the northern end of the Domain, across a small harbour inlet, to Sulphur Point. While Bill was putting out a ball landed on the edge of the green. The offender was at it again! Bill took out his Brassie and smote the ball a couple of hundred yards into the estuary. Bill was on the next green when the said gentleman arrived and asked if anyone had seen his ball. Like the man he was Bill promptly owned up. “Yes, you played onto us and I hope your ball is now well on its way to the open sea somewhere near the Mount.”

title: More distant fairways · p. 21
text:
CHAPTER THREE

MORE DISTANT FAIRWAYS

title: More distant fairways · p. 22
text:
The obvious deficiencies of the Domain course and the increasing pressure of Rugby and other sports on the grounds would have encouraged members to seek an alternative location and in 1914 the decision was made to take up an available lease at the Racecourse Reserve. This was done in spite of the fact that the early portents for the land were far from encouraging. The area was described as bleak, treeless, and open to all the winds of heaven, especially the Westerlies that appear to have been more prevalent in those days. The President of the time termed it “the coldest place within 20 miles of Tauranga.”

The history of the Racecourse Reserve dates back to 1878 when it was Gazetted that the Governor of the then Colony of New Zealand had reserved from sale that parcel of land containing 200 acres known as the Racecourse Reserve, the land to be designated for ‘a recreation ground and racecourse’. An addition to The Act of 1880 provided that all sums of money received in respect of the lands were to be applied, after deducting costs and expenses, in improving the lands in respect of which the money was received. This provision has continued to apply throughout the history of the Reserve with the lessee clubs being the beneficiaries of the rentals they pay. Initially Trustees appointed by, and responsible to, the Minister of Crown Lands administered the Reserve. These trustees were elected by the public every seven years and it was not unusual for a degree of lobbying to be undertaken prior to the election in order to ensure particular interests were catered to. In this regard the members of the Golf Club appear to have been somewhat slow to protect their interests. As a result the Racing Club had the right to park vehicles on the 8th, 9th, and 10th fairways each Race Day, and to allow traffic coming from the south to enter via the gate behind the 14th green and to then travel across the golf course to reach those parking areas. This even happened on wet winter days with the expected damage to fairways. In those earlier times attendance at race meetings was much greater than is generally the case now and it was not unusual for all three fairways to be covered in cars.  By the end of a race day the Golf Club fairways were usually littered with discarded tickets, lunch wrappings, chicken bones and the like, while on wet days they suffered badly as the soft ground became cut up by vehicles driving across them. Consequently relationships between the two neighbouring Clubs were often severely strained.

The situation improved during the Fifties when some effective lobbying by Golf Club representatives resulted in the election of Domain Board Trustees more sympathetic to the interests of golfers. Several years of negotiations eventually led to an amicable agreement being reached in 1961. Life Member and Honorary Solicitor J C (John) Hare was chiefly instrumental in achieving this agreement which covered a number of contentious issues. None the less, just one year later Secretary Noel Hockin wrote to the Racing Club expressing dismay that the Racing Club proposed breaking the agreement on parking and traffic movement for the scheduled Race Meeting to be held on the 14th of April 1962. In spite of his objection 250 cars entered via the 13th fairway. On this occasion the steward in charge of parking cut the chain locking the gate behind the 14th green with bolt cutters. Even as late as June 1965, the Golf Club committee minutes record that it was still deemed necessary to secure that gate with chain and padlock should weather conditions be adverse. This was in spite of the fact that the right to park on the fairways had supposedly been rescinded in 1960.

Relationships between the two Clubs appeared to improve dramatically from the early Seventies. A

title: More distant fairways · p. 23
text:
number of factors probably contributed to this. For some time there had been agitation from some elements of the Greerton Community who claimed they were not able to derive much benefit from the ‘Park in their backyard’. This was in spite of the fact that many local residents did use the Reserve to jog, to walk, or to attend activities. A meeting of the combined committees of Golf and Racing, meeting under the auspices of the Domain Board, negotiated an agreement whereby the Golf Club would transfer the lease they had long held over McKinlay’s paddock and one quarter of the inner oval to the Racing Club. These areas, though in the Golf Club lease, had not been utilised by them since the days when the Golf course extended into the oval. In return the Racing Club undertook to make facilities available to the public so far as was possible without interfering with their own activities. Consequently the Greerton Soccer (Football) Club was granted use of land within the oval where they developed two fields. These fields remained in use until the Club moved elsewhere in 2008. Picnic facilities were developed in McKinlay’s Paddock where specimen trees were planted to provide shade and generally beautify the area. In addition the Racing Club sub-leased an area within the oval to Equestrian Interests. These measures were successful to the extent that the interests of many appeared to be satisfied, and local agitation was no longer heard. Fortunately the interests of Golf and Racing had prevailed and eventually the future of the Racecourse Reserve, and tenure in perpetuity of the Tauranga Golf Club upon it, were enshrined in legislation. Generations of the future could look forward to enjoying the game of golf on a course that had offered great playing conditions and a more than adequate challenge to

players of all levels of ability since early in the twentieth century.

The original lease term granted to the Golf Club had been for a period of just seven years. This did not confer upon the fledgling club a great measure of security of tenure. This all changed for the better in 1944 when the Crown appointed a Racecourse Domain Board to administer the area on behalf of the Crown. This Board was given the authority to lease any part of the Reserve ‘at reasonable rental and under reasonable conditions for a term not exceeding 33 years at any one time.’ This 33 year lease

term was a big step towards permanence for the Club as the original lease term of just seven years did not allow the members to outlay capital in the confidence that they would always be able to lease the area and thus continue to derive benefit from the investment they had made in developing the land and associated buildings.

In 1956 an additional area of a little more than two hectares to the side of the third fairway was purchased by the Crown and incorporated into the area leased to the Golf Club. As a result the Reserve now contains a fraction over 83 hectares of which 34 hectares is leased to Racing Tauranga, 45 hectares to the Golf Club, the remainder being Reserve land adjoining the Golf Club boundaries. A further area adjacent to the third fairway was incorporated into the Club’s lease in 2010 and the land developed as a turf nursery. In the present era 45 hectares would not be considered sufficient by some margin for the establishment of an 18-hole golf course.

The Domain Board remained our Landlord until 1989 when the Local Government Commission proposed that the function, duties and powers of the Domain Board as an administrative body be transferred to the Tauranga District Council. The Board unsuccessfully objected but did manage to get lease terms amended to provide that the rental shall, in the event of dispute, be assessed on the current market

title: More distant fairways · p. 24
text:
value of the land upon which the Lessee’s buildings are located. This replaced the earlier provision where assessment was based on the value of all the land held under the lease.

Administrators of both the Golf and Racing Clubs immediately recognised the danger that the new legislation represented. Having local Councillors replace the Minister of Crown Lands as their Landlord caused trepidation in the minds of those who could see the possibility of wider civic interests coming into play at some future date. Credit for the harmonious administrative niche that now exists is owed most particularly to Life Member E A (Ernie) Craig. Initially a subcommittee of the District Council was set up to assist Council to administer the Reserve. When this was found to be ineffective Mr. Craig lobbied for the establishment of what became known as the Racecourse Reserve Operation and Management Committee. The new committee’s terms of reference were to deal with the operation of the Domain, and to liaise with the tenants. It was empowered to ascertain the level of rentals necessary to maintain the domain and to apply these to that maintenance. Hence all rentals charged were ultimately expended in the interests of the tenants in accordance with the terms of the 1880 Act.

The new committee came into being on the first day of January 1994 and included: • Four representatives of the City Council • one representative of the Golf Club • one representative of the Racing Club • one representative of the Equestrian group • one representative of the Greerton Soccer Club. (Now discontinued).

The four members appointed by the Council included one Councillor, the other three being members of the Public. Mr. Craig, having been elected to the Domain Board during the period when the Golf Club lobbied to increase their influence, continued to serve that Body, and its successor, for more than 50 years during which time he served equally both Golf and Racing interests. In recognition of this he was elected to Life Membership of both Clubs, a unique and fitting reward for a man who gave so much to both Clubs over such a long period. Prior to his retirement from the Reserve Committee in 2004 Ernie served as its Chairman and was responsible for much of the drive that ensured the Reserve was continually developed and improved for the benefit of the Clubs and for the Community. Ernie, in the latter years of his service, was one of the four Council appointees and upon retirement was accorded a Civic farewell to allow the Council and public to formally recognise his outstanding contribution.

For the record the current lease from the Reserve Committee to the Golf Club was renewed in August 2006 and will expire in 2039. The work of Ernie Craig and those who served with him will surely have ensured that the Racecourse Reserve will continue to accommodate Racing, Golf, Equestrian Sport, and various public activities for the foreseeable future. It is a priceless asset to the City of Tauranga. In spite of those early uncertainties of tenure on the Reserve land the original Golf Club members gave their labour enthusiastically at regular working bees where they slashed gorse, erected fences to protect greens, built stiles, planted trees, and cut and rolled greens from the existing pasture. Stock belonging to a local farmer kept the fairways under some level of control. The farmer, Mr McKinlay, is

title: More distant fairways · p. 25
text:
remembered in the name McKinlay’s paddock while the eighth hole was named McKinlay’s from the earliest years. As soon as the initial work involved in developing the rudiments of a golf course was underway Mr Fred Rutter, an Auckland Professional, was engaged to lay out 18 holes utilising much of the present land together with some land lying within the racecourse oval. A description of that first course will be given in a later chapter.

Golf in New Zealand was essentially a winter game and in summer the fairways at Tauranga were devoted to the production of hay crops. In March the greens would be mown down in preparation for the new season and a single-reel, horse drawn mower would occasionally be run over the fairways to complement the work of the grazing stock.

Secretary/Treasurer Mr H B Mountfort would go around town in January/February to ask the members to pay their subscriptions, £4 at that time, so that he could engage Mr McKinlay to mow the greens in early March and have the funds to pay him.

The first ‘clubhouse’ was a corrugated iron shed located where the eleventh tee now sits. It served as the jockey’s room on race days and must have been a miserable location on wet winter race days.3

Forms for seating and a long table took up almost all the available space in the ‘Tin Shed’ while a

smaller table accommodated the primuses and kettles. Someone donated a tatty looking basket style armchair that was squeezed into the corner and the first player in for lunch would stake his claim and sit in isolated splendour while the rest sat around the table eating their paper-wrapped sandwiches and sipping their tea. Sometime later a cookhouse was built at the end of the building and an Orion stove installed. Members would collect firewood off the course and fire up the new stove so the days of the primus ended and a new age of convenience began!

At first few members owned cars and many cycled to the course with their clubs on their backs. This was quite a trip as the course was some distance from their downtown residences. A lucky few sometimes succeeded in scrounging a ride in a car or gig. Until as late as 1957 the entry road from Cameron Road was a metal surface prone to severe potholing. The first improvement was made in 1958 when sealing was laid to 1.5 car widths over the first 20 chains of road (about 400m). The final 250m was not done until 1960. The Domain Board, as it was then known, financed this roadwork from the rental received from the two tenants. Such expenditures had to be well planned and budgeted in advance. The Club owes a very real debt of gratitude to the members of the Racecourse Domain Board and its successor, the Racecourse Reserve Committee, for their insight and astute financial management over the history of our time on the Gate Pa course.

There was no clash between racegoers and golfers for no one would have dreamed of playing golf on a race day. For one thing the races were a major social occasion when the men wore their finest suits and no self-respecting lady would attend without having first visited Amy Hogg’s establishment in Devonport Road to acquire a fashionable ensemble. In any event the Racing Club had the right to park cars on the golf course and it was not until the Sixties that this ceased to be the situation.

title: More distant fairways · p. 26
text:
Relationships were established early with neighbouring clubs and tournaments and Interclub days attracted visiting players from Rotorua, Whakatane and Matamata. A Ladies’ Committee was established and they worked hard under difficult conditions to cater for such occasions. They cleaned the ‘tin shed’, peeled buckets of potatoes, cooked meats at home, cut up baths of green salads, and baked mountains of cakes and scones. We can be confident no visitor left the course hungry. Inspired by the competition met on the occasion of these visits members were keen to improve their games and to this end Mr Hood and Mr McCormack, professionals based in Rotorua, were encouraged to visit Tauranga on some weekends in order to conduct lessons. These lessons had to be held on weekends for few members could afford to take time off during the week to play golf and the grazing stock were seldom disturbed by players during week days.

The new course was for many years known as the Gate Pa course just as the Racing Club was said to race at Gate Pa even though the Reserve is more accurately located in Greerton, a mile or so South of the site of the 1864 battle of Gate Pa and the commemorative Church that now stands on that site. Greerton was named in honour of Colonel Greer who was a prominent British military leader during the battle of Gate Pa. The suburb of Greerton had its origins when it was divided into allotments that were granted to soldiers who wished to remain in the area after the cessation of hostilities.

At some time in the thirties Dr. John Mark was playing the 10th hole when ‘over the road’ was not out of bounds. Somehow his ball lodged in the roof of a small shed that was sited there. John’s companions insisted he play the lie so they assisted him onto the roof from whence he was able to knock the ball down the corrugations onto the fairway.

The Bay of Plenty Beacon was a Newspaper of the time that was published in Whakatane. The issue for July 7th 1939 carried an item naming the Tauranga team to represent the Club versus Whakatane Golf Club at Whakatane on the following Sunday. Many of those names are notable in the Club’s history and/or in the history of the town. They were: Green, Bateman, Renshaw, Randell, Lusk, Page, Bradmore, Bullock, Douglas, Roach, Hay, Sisson, Kennedy, Jordan, Morpeth, Snodgrass, Harley, Phelan, Matheson, Kirkby, Steele, Verry, Strang. No first names or initials were given. Many of these men feature elsewhere in this publication. Older readers will remember many above such as Bob Hay, who owned a Chemist Shop in the town.
