title: The original Gate Pa links · p. 32
text:
CHAPTER FOUR

THE ORIGINAL GATE PA LINKS

title: The original Gate Pa links · p. 33
text:
The layout of the course has been changed several times and no doubt there will be further changes in the future though these are likely to be minor in comparison to what has gone before. The first course designed by Fred Rutter utilised land within the circumference of the racetrack as well as much of the present leased area. We have been fortunate to obtain a description of the course as it was prior to 1934 from Mr Jack Bateman, a fine player who followed his 1934 Championship win with another three victories in the years from 1946 to 1949. In 1948 and 1949 Jack added the BOP Champion of Champions title to his club victories, an honour not previously achieved by one of our own and not matched until the Michael Nicholson era began in 1970. The following is a description of those original 18 holes as Jack recalled them.

NUMBER 1 - THE AVENUE - PAR 4

This is now the 11th hole and essentially the same as it was then. The tee was conveniently placed adjacent to the ’Jockey’s Room’ clubhouse and the large gum trees that now form the avenue were then in their infancy.

NUMBER 2- THE KNOLL - PAR 3

This has now become the 12th and is known as Tauranga’s signature hole. According to Jack it is now considerably less formidable than when he played it. The tee shot was played through an avenue of gorse to a sloping green perched on a pinnacle. This was somewhat higher than the present cone, the green having been lowered and thus enlarged at some time in the forties. There were shallow bunkers at the sides and back and the entire green was surrounded by long grass and stumpy gorse. While there was no bunker at the front a high premium was still placed on accuracy and correct club selection. When asked his opinion of this hole in 1967 commander Harris glanced briefly at it, said: “it might have been all right in 1900. Take five feet off the top and dish it.” With that he walked to the 13th tee.

NUMBER 3 - PYES PA - PAR 5

This is now the 13th and renamed the Crescent. Apart from the new greenside bunker the hole was essentially the same as it is now and followed the racecourse fence around the top turn.

NUMBER 4 - THE STABLES - PAR 4

The tee was close to where the 14th tee is now located and the stroke was played across the oval towards the now 11th fairway to a green near the straight entrance.

NUMBER 5 - THE STRAIGHT - PAR 4

This hole was played as a slight dogleg more or less following the inside running rail to a green near the winning post.

NUMBER 6 - THE TERRACE - PAR 3

Here the tee stroke was played from inside the oval to a green located south of the grandstand and behind the then first tee. This would be where overflow parking can now be found.

title: The original Gate Pa links · p. 34
text:
NUMBER 7 - THE PAVILION - PAR 4

This was played from a tee near the present tenth green to where the practice putting green now lies.

NUMBER 8 - THE PA - PAR 4

‘The Pa’ was not unlike the present first hole except that the tee was further west towards the second green. The trundler shed now covers that old tee.

NUMBER 9 - THE RIDGE - PAR 4

The ninth was the present second hole now called The Summit though these names, with exceptions such as The Knoll and The Gully, are now seldom used. The only significant changes to the hole have been to the tee, once just a narrow shelf cut into the bank, and the establishment of the alternative green to the right of the original. The ladies played from a forward tee between the first and second fairways.

NUMBER 10 - THE DROP - PAR 3

To get to this tee the players walked around the top of the slope to a tee situated west of the present seventh tee. They were then faced with a shot across a field of turnips to the present third green. It was very difficult finding a ball falling short amongst the turnips as all turnips look very much alike at close quarters and your carefully noted reference point was easily lost. Eventually one season, when the stock had eaten this fodder crop, the hole was eliminated and pine trees planted on the slope.

NUMBER 11 - THE HUMMOCKS - PAR 4

This was a tricky dogleg that was essentially the present third in reverse. The second shot was to a small green tucked into the slope below the third tee. The shape of that green can still be discerned today. It is just as well present day players do not have to drag their trundlers up the hill while playing

that hole!

NUMBER 12 - MOUNT VIEW - PAR 5

The present seventh hole played to the right hand green. As the name suggests the hole played straight towards The Mount. This landmark could be seen much more clearly before the growth of trees eliminated much of the view.

NUMBER 13 - LONE PINE - PAR 4

This hole ran towards the access road and was essentially the present eighth hole. A line of power poles was about 20 metres in from the fence line on the boundary and frequently came into play to the consternation of many a player. On one occasion after this became the eighth hole following course re-organisation a tee shot hit the first of these poles only to fly back over the player’s head and settle in the bunker beside the seventh green. The player faced a daunting second shot as no local rule allowed a replay in such situations. No one seems to recall what happened to the ‘lone pine’ after which the hole was named.

title: The original Gate Pa links · p. 35
text:
NUMBER 14 - McKINLAYS - PAR 3 This took play back into the oval from a tee over the road behind the present ninth tee to a green not far from Cameron Road.

NUMBER 15 - KAIMAI - PAR 5

This was a long and difficult hole played as it was into the cold southerlies that seemed to blow most days of the winter. The fairway followed the back straight to a green located in the oval not far from that of ‘The Crescent’. Water troughs, fences cattle and cowpats were unusual hazards encountered on what was a most unpopular hole. To add to all the other problems Out of Bounds was never far away.

NUMBER 16 – SOUTH END - PAR 3

This hole still bears the same name but is now played as the fourteenth. As with most holes there was less bunkering than is now the case, bunkers having been added from time to time throughout the course.

NUMBER 17 - WESTWARD HO - PAR 5

This hole, together with the eighteenth, are the only holes that are essentially unchanged and are still played as the same numbered holes as they were in the original layout.

NUMBER 18 - MORETON BAY - PAR 4

That fine specimen tree has stood in its commanding position on the ridge almost from the beginning. The hole has changed little and the first real clubhouse was built behind this green to give an excellent view down the length of the hole.

title: Out of the oval · p. 36
text:
CHAPTER FIVE

OUT OF THE OVAL

title: Out of the oval · p. 37
text:
In 1934, with the confidence of the new 33-year lease behind them, the Club administration was encouraged to explore new possibilities in course design and facilities. Having determined that the oval was not conducive to the development of quality golf holes the committee commissioned well-known Auckland Professional Alex Murray to advise on the layout of new holes. As part of his commission he was requested to see if it would be feasible to eliminate ‘The Drop’ and ‘The Hummocks’ holes that, quite understandably, were most unpopular with members who did not enjoy the climb back up the hill from the present third green. Anyone foolish enough not to play a provisional ball following a doubtful drive at the third hole today will readily appreciate the point. As a result of Alex Murray’s review the five holes that utilised the oval were discontinued along with the old 7th, 10th, and 11th holes. To replace them the present 3rd, 4th, 6th, 9th, 10th, 15th, and 16th were developed and they remain in much the same form today. The remaining ten original holes were retained but renumbered to accommodate the very different sequence of holes necessitated by the changes. Below is an outline of the holes as they are now played with a brief summary of their individual history.

NUMBER 1 - THE PA - PAR 4

This was first played as the 8th hole and featured a slight dogleg to the right from a tee west of the present position. A large gum on the ridge some 50m from the green was a prominent feature. Those driving past the gum were inordinately proud of the achievement. As has been the case with other prominent gum trees this one was lost to high winds. Gums are not especially long lived in our conditions.

NUMBER 2 - THE SUMMIT - PAR 4

This was the ninth hole and originally named ‘The Ridge’. The men’s tee consisted of two shallow terraces cut into the hillock forming the present tee. The women played from a tee near the gum tree on the ridge. The right hand green was developed in the sixties in order to enable the main green to be rested. It continues to be used on a regular basis, perhaps over-used. NUMBER 3 - JUDEA - PAR 4 This was developed preparatory to the move out of the oval. Recent developments in equipment now allow quite ordinary players to ‘take on the corner’. Few, if any amongst club members, were able to achieve this feat when using the old wound ball.

NUMBER 4 - THE GULLY - PAR 3

Another hole developed to replace those in the oval. This is a classical short par three where the green and surrounds have remained in their original form. Extended tees are considered by some to add to the challenge offered while others see them as defeating the intention of the original design. The causeway was built up in the Fifties to provide a much easier passage across the gully. The pond is our one water feature though hardly considered a hazard to most players. It has served its intended purpose of draining the area at the bottom of the driving range.

title: Out of the oval · p. 38
text:
NUMBER 5 - THE SPUR - PAR 3

The fifth hole proved to be a problem from the start and has perhaps remained so up to the present time. The hole has undergone significant changes, most recently in 2003 when the green was extensively remodelled. The original hole designed by Mr Murray was named ‘The Spur’ and was played from a raised tee, still discernible in the trees to the left of the fourth green, to a small green located where the new 7th green now lies.  There was a difficult bunker with quite a steep face immediately in front of this green.  This was a rather weak par three. Perhaps its only redeeming feature was that it minimised the amount of walking required to go from the 4th green to the 6th tee. Some time later the green was relocated to its present position with no change in tee placement so that the hole remained a short par three with the tee shot being played over trees just short of the green. Generally you could not see the base of the pin from the tee.

In the days of the Invitation Tournament it was suggested that a more challenging hole could be provided for the professionals and top amateurs by building a tee in the area where it is now located so that the hole could be played parallel to the 7th fairway. This did prove to be more challenging and so the hole was retained for club play despite the extra walk required moving to the tee.

NUMBER 6 - MIRRIELEES - PAR 5

This was another hole developed when the club moved out of the oval. The excellent background provided to this hole by the positioning of the clubhouse on its present site was a welcome advantage of that siting. The hole is an excellent par five, if a shade short for the best players. It is notable for the Albatross twos scored by Norm Ducker, Ken Carter and Peg Copestake.

NUMBER 7 - MOUNT VIEW - PAR 5

This was the 12th hole and boasted a commanding view of Mount Maunganui before tree growth screened that out. Tree removal in the new Century restored the view. Several changes have been made to both tee and green and some would doubt the present design is the best that could be developed. It has long been a goal to establish a more equitable landing zone for the second shot or to find some other way to solve the problem of balls running off the side of the hill but this goal has proved elusive.

NUMBER 8 - McKINLAY’S - PAR 4 This was originally played as the 13th hole and known as ‘Lone Pine’. No one now seems to remember the tree for which it was named. McKinlay’s Paddock has long been the name of that part of the reserve North of the Racecourse so it was felt appropriate to retain the name for a hole in that area when the original ‘McKinlay’s’, a hole played into the racecourse, was discontinued.

NUMBER 9 - THE DIP - PAR 3

This new hole was named for the shallow dip that originally featured between tee and green when the tee was across the road at the top of the ridge overlooking McKinlay’s paddock. On race days players had a good view of the action should a race be taking place at the time they were on the tee. This was possible only after parking was discontinued on our fairways.

title: Out of the oval · p. 39
text:
The increasing regularity of Race Days, Show Days, Orange Festival Parades and similar activities led to players becoming increasingly frustrated as streams of traffic flowed in front of them as they awaited a break so they could tee off. Consequently a new tee was constructed across the road, trees planted behind it to lessen the distraction of passing traffic, and the green extended toward the tenth fairway. One result is the hole no longer has the ‘dipping’ profile that gave it its name but the hole has lost little of its challenge.

NUMBER 10 - K D PAGE - PAR 4

Keith Page no doubt earned the right to have his name perpetuated as a result of the selfless efforts he made to produce the green at this hole. While a green did exist previously in this area it was not suitable for the newly designed tenth hole and was abandoned when play moved from the oval.

NUMBER 11 - THE AVENUE - PAR 4

This was the original opening hole.  The stables have now been replaced further from the action, the three bunkers near the beginning of the practise area are no more, and bunkers have been created and removed beside the green. None-the-less the hole remains essentially the same today as when the course was established in 1914.

NUMBER 12 - THE KNOLL - PAR 3

This was originally the second hole and is as memorable now as it was when first played in 1914 in spite of the reduction in height and consequent increase in green size.

NUMBER 13 – THE CRESCENT - PAR 5

This was originally the third hole and named Pyes Pa. It was considered the most testing hole on the course and well deserved its number one stroke rating. When the new 15th and 16th holes were developed to replace those in the oval it was considered more appropriate to name one of these Pyes Pa and the thirteenth hole was renamed to fit its physical shape.

NUMBER 14 – SOUTH END - PAR 3

This was originally played as the sixteenth hole. It remains essentially the same as it then was although the massive pines behind the green that once provided welcome shelter from the strong Southerly winds that exert such an influence on the playing length of this particular hole are no longer there. There is an old adage that he who wins the fourteenth hole wins the match. This does seem to be the

case quite frequently.

NUMBER 15 - KAHAROA - PAR 4

Of all the holes on the course this one appears to play the longest for its carded length. Some translate the name Kaharoa as ‘long strength’, others as ‘long net’. The former is especially appropriate. The hole requires strength and stamina in order for it to be negotiated successfully. The ‘long net’ might also refer to the ability of this hole to trap the unwary. Michael Nicholson used to say that the final four holes on the course were those that separated the men from the boys. We realise how appropriate

title: Out of the oval · p. 40
text:
that comment is when we reflect upon the number of matches, and stroke play events, that have been decided over those very holes. Kaharoa begins that sequence.

NUMBER 16 - PYES PA - PAR 3

Like the fifteenth this hole was developed to replace those made obsolete following the move from the oval. It has stood the test of time and remains challenge enough for club players of all levels of ability. That test is precisely what we should look for when considering hole design on a course such as our own.

NUMBER 17 - WESTWARD HO - PAR 5

As stated earlier this hole, and the eighteenth, are essentially unchanged and are still played as the same numbered holes as they were in the original layout. The seventeenth has undergone a number of remakes over the years and I do not doubt that some future committee will make another some day. Committees over the years have not been able to agree on whether it warrants the label par 4 or par 5 for men. In its earlier years, given the equipment of the day, even quality players found difficulty reaching the green in two strokes. Now they achieve this with ease. It remains below the length normally defined as being the upper limit for par fours.

NUMBER 18 - MORETON BAY - PAR 4

The tree from which the hole derives its name has created controversy from time to time because of the difficulties it does create for clubhouse maintenance. In this case the pluses appear to exceed the minuses and the tree will likely be there for many a year to come. The hole has changed little over the years and the first real clubhouse was built behind this green to give an excellent view down the length of the hole.

The old stables that once stood to the left of the eleventh hole often came into play and something was lost from the character of the hole when they were demolished. The new stables are set a little further back from our boundary and do not have the same physical or psychological presence as did their predecessors. Many were the tee shots that found their way back to the fairway as a result of striking the roof or walls of the original buildings. One windy day a player was expecting just such a result as his ‘duck hook’ streaked towards a stable door. Just as the ball was about to strike the door a gust of wind blew the door open and the ball disappeared inside. To add insult to injury the door then blew shut as if to ensure the ball remained securely swallowed. Such are the vicissitudes of this game of golf.

title: Out of the oval · p. 41
text:
The move from the oval was a dramatic development in the history of the club. It signalled a growing maturity whereby players would no longer be satisfied with makeshift fairways and greens. The time had come to develop the property into a course that all could be proud of. The year 1936 was seen as being especially significant in foreshadowing a new era in the Club’s development. Quoting from the BOP Times of March 30th that year:

“A disability which the Club has suffered from in the past has been that its ground staff have not had experience in golf green keeping and have been at a disadvantage in not knowing just what they should work for to afford the best conditions for play. The committee has accordingly engaged an experienced greenkeeper, Mr. W H Coles, formerly greenkeeper to the Napier Golf Club and a foundation member and member of the executive of the New Zealand Greenkeepers’ Association. Mr. Coles takes over his duties today and, with the benefit of his experience, should do much to produce and keep good greens and fairways on the course.

The Club is also fortunate in that it has been able to obtain the services of Mr. Jas. Mowat to serve as its Professional. Mr. Mowat has for some years been Professional to the Poverty Bay Golf Club and is a member of the Executive Committee of the New Zealand Professional Golfers’ Association. He has had experience both in Scotland and in the United States of America, and comes to the Club with first class recommendations, both as a player and as a teacher. For young players and learners there is a tremendous advantage in being kept to the right style until the game is consolidated. For the more experienced golfer there is much to be gained from having an expert on hand to locate and cure the inevitable faults that creep into the swing. Under Mr. Mowat’s guidance it is to be hoped that there will be an all round improvement in the standard of the game in Tauranga. Mr. Mowat has already arrived and takes up his duties forthwith”.

The next significant development in the evolution of the course came in 1967 when noted British Golf Architect, Commander John Harris, was invited to visit the course and advise on possible improvements that could be made. Commander Harris was in New Zealand under contract to the Government owned Tourist Corporation of New Zealand that was at the time developing the Wairakei Resort Course near Taupo. He was free to make himself available to clubs such as ours who sought his assistance. His charge to visit Tauranga for a day and make a detailed report covering ten pages was £75, a truly bargain price for world-class advice. Commander Harris, Greens Chairman Alan Davidson, and Greens Superintendent Grant Silvester walked the course with Alan and Grant hanging on every word spoken

by the designer.  Grant later commented: “That man seems to have a built in spirit level and chain measure as, when I carried out his recommendations, I found the levels and distances to be exactly as he described them. I found his plans for alterations so clear and precise that any contractor or green keeper could carry them through with utmost expediency.” Alan made comprehensive notes from which, together with the Harris report, he was able to construct Pleistocene models depicting each of the holes as Commander Harris had envisaged them. These models were used by Grant and his staff, greatly assisted by the earth moving and contracting skills of Garth Renner, to faithfully complete the process of converting the Harris report from paper, through Pleistocene model, to completed golf holes, over the next few years. This entire process was continually supervised and monitored by Mr Davidson

title: Out of the oval · p. 42
text:
who spent an enormous number of hours on this voluntary work. Knowing Alan it can be certain that his reward came from the satisfaction of knowing that the course was so much the better upon the completion of the program. The changes made under the Harris plan were not major, nor particularly dramatic. Commander Harris recognised the course for what it is, an ideal club course offering variety and challenge to the vast majority of those who play it. He did not see it as a championship course as it lacked both the length, and the potential to extend that length, to achieve championship status. Consequently his suggested changes involved defining preferred lines of play for optimum results and to assist players to ‘navigate’ their way around the course. This was achieved by incorporating subtle bunkering and mounding on many of the existing holes. These changes were nowhere major, nor unduly expensive, yet there is no doubt that adoption of the Harris plan had a major, and lasting, influence on the level of enjoyment experienced by members and visitors alike when playing the course.

Commander Harris, in association with Michael Wolveridge and Peter Thomson, developed Wairakei to be arguably the best course in the country at that time and today it remains in the very top echelon of New Zealand courses. Commander Harris was involved in the development of some thirty courses worldwide and Tauranga was most fortunate to obtain his expert advice. It is perhaps regrettable that subsequent administrations have, for a variety of reasons, seen fit to nullify some of the improvements made as a result of his visit. Fortunately this tendency has been relatively limited and the course continues to enjoy many of the Harris subtleties incorporated in those years. As shown by many an International course sound design survives the test of time even in the face of technological advances. While the super stars may require greater length and difficulty in the face of these advances golf offers challenge enough to the vast majority of players on the courses they play on a regular basis. Improvement in the quality of playing conditions offered on courses such as our own will do more to enhance the golfing experience for the average club member than will continued fine tuning of design. Improvement in playing conditions has been made possible through the development of machinery specifically designed for golf course maintenance, through research into the soil environment, disease control, turf species, water application, and many other aspects of turf management. In particular the comprehensive training of staff has enabled them to make the best use of these advances. Tauranga has been fortunate to have all these factors adopted with skill and enthusiasm by our staff over many years.

Public interest in golf surged in New Zealand in the Sixties and Seventies driven by such television series as Big Three Golf and Challenge Golf featuring Arnold Palmer, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and other greats. This was before the days of Sky TV and the public had long been able only to read of the exploits of such giants of the game. Now they were able to see them in action and people from all walks of life were keen to see if they could emulate some of the inspiring golf they were able to watch in their living rooms each week. As a result clubs around the country welcomed a surge in membership and the pattern of play changed so that courses had to stand up to more concentrated play and to an extended season that soon stretched to a full twelve months as new members became full time golfers rather than going off to bowls, cricket, boating, or other activities in summer. Tauranga was not left out in this surge of interest and membership had to be closed for a time to those seeking full seven day a

title: Out of the oval · p. 43
text:
week membership. There were simply not the tee times available to accommodate all who wished to play. While this was unpopular with those placed on waiting lists it was the only practical solution to a problem that could not have been envisaged by earlier administrators. Since the club’s inception those administrators had been intent on building membership, not restricting it.

Surveys of course usage at the peak of demand over this period found that weekly play often exceeded 1000 rounds and few flat periods were seen through the week or through the year. This made it very difficult for the Greens Staff, still only two full time men, to maintain the quality of the greens. In response to this pressure the committee introduced a policy of trying to provide an alternate green, or at least an enlarged green, at each hole where it was practical to do so.

Under this policy the 1st, 2nd, and 15th greens were enlarged while alternate greens were formed at the 3rd, 4th, 11th, and 17th holes. Only that at the 4th hole survives, the others proving both unpopular and difficult to maintain. Later developments saw enlargements to the 5th, 8th, 9th, 10th, and 17th greens while the fortuitous retention of the old 7th green proved to be a wise decision prior to its later abandonment.

While this policy did not achieve as much as had been hoped it did relieve the pressure for a time. The advent of a vastly improved irrigation system allied to continued improvements in green keeping techniques, especially the introduction of sanding following coring, led to very much improved surfaces that are better able to withstand the constant pressure of players and machinery. These advances reduced the need for alternate greens. It is sobering to contemplate that wherever one goes in sport, as in other human activities, there are always ‘experts’ eager to give the benefit of their advice to the professionals employed to do the job. At one stage, there was a tremendous campaign launched by a group of members outside committee to have coring discontinued on the grounds that so much material was being removed, and so little replaced, that the greens were rapidly becoming sunken saucers. Usually all that such critics achieve is to prove themselves blind to the facts. In the case of coring and sanding the advantages are obvious to anyone who has played the course continually through recent years. This is because good drainage, soil aeration, and the soil environment developed under coring provide conditions that suit the growth of fine leaved grasses.  In our case Browntop and Chewings Fescue are the species used to produce quality greens. As for saucer shaped greens resulting from our coring program some may wish it had happened as the hole could then be cut in the centre of the green and all putts would find their way there!

Following the establishment of a Board of Management to administer the financial and amenity functions of club management a course improvement group was empowered to consider possible changes to the course and to establish priorities for this work. As a consequence of their deliberations quite radical changes were made to the 5th, 7th, and 17th holes, together with minor changes to the 10th, 11th and 13th holes. It would be fair to say that the most radical of these changes have not been met with universal approval by members. While the intention has clearly been to challenge the more able players the result may have been to make these holes too difficult for those members, both men and

title: Out of the oval · p. 44
text:
women, who appreciate the more user friendly nature of traditional golf at Tauranga.

While physical changes to the design of the links have had a significant influence on both the challenge and the enjoyment of playing the course they have been overshadowed by aspects of course management that have evolved over the years. In those first years after the Club moved to the Racecourse Reserve there were no defined fairways and grazing animals made up most of the ‘greens staff’. Fences surrounded the greens. The greens were the only areas mown regularly, and that perhaps just once each week. The Bay of Plenty Times of March 30th 1936 reported that the course was open for play, that the fairways would be mown from April 1st in accordance with the club’s arrangement with the tenant, and that the fences surrounding the greens would be removed. Clearly the stock would also be removed. As can be imagined playing conditions would have been very much inferior to those enjoyed by members today. The greens, following a summer of uncontrolled growth, would suddenly be cut back thus producing slow stubbly surfaces that would gradually improve with regular mowing. The rest of the course would get an occasional mowing with Mr McKinlay’s horse drawn hay mower.

Soon after the above item appeared in the ‘Times’ four groups of members representing Bankers, Commercial Travellers, Loan and Mercantile, and Insurance Brokers undertook to enlarge and remake certain greens and an intense competition was soon underway as to who would prove to have the best techniques and achieve the best results. This was perhaps not the way to get a set of greens that played consistently throughout the course but was a big step forward in the evolution of the course.

Keith Page heard that Tom Bloor had purchased a 5hp rotary hoe, the first to be demonstrated in Tauranga, so he pressured Tom into rotary hoeing his green, the 10th. This hole was subsequently named ‘K D Page’ in Keith’s honour. It was claimed that Keith practically slept beside his green to ensure everything went to plan.

The other teams were initially disadvantaged in that they had to dig over their greens with spades. Loan and Mercantile, represented by Cyril Jordan and Ron Mirrielees were claimed to have an unfair advantage because of their superior agricultural knowledge and access to fertiliser and other requirements for their green, the 16th. Perhaps the claim was true for the 16th remains an excellent green and has suffered no serious problem from disease or burnout in spite of being at the most distant corner of the course and amongst the last to receive a reliable water supply. The K D Page green on the other hand became something of a mystery as, for many years it was a ‘green of two halves’, the front being almost pure paspalum which was very green and provided quite a good playing surface in summer, while the rear half was the standard browntop/fescue mix. Perhaps only Keith knew how this came to be. It was interesting to see how the paspalum gradually disappeared to be replaced by the finer grasses under the influence of modern cultural techniques without the need to kill it off with herbicides. Such experiences vividly demonstrate the way the soil environment influences the species that grow in it.

During the Second World War the course was reduced to nine holes with the eighth, ninth, and tenth fairways being put to the plough and crops of potatoes planted as part of the war effort. On other parts

title: Out of the oval · p. 45
text:
of the course the grass was allowed to grow freely and hay crops were harvested. Until recently the ninth fairway still showed evidence of the plough’s passage down the centre. Disposal of corings from the greens over a couple of seasons has now eradicated that reminder of days gone by. During those war years nine holes were retained and kept in remarkably good order by the sole green keeper, Mr Reeves, an outstanding man who worked under very difficult conditions with limited equipment. The racecourse and its buildings were headquarters for the National Reserve and many members underwent training there. Some found the training exhausting but not so Ted Bartlett, the oldest man in camp, or Bob Gray, each of whom would run around the race track before Reveille each morning. Years later I enjoyed playing some rounds with Ted when he was quite an elderly gentleman and I can testify that he was still very fit and a real pleasure to play with. He had genuine zest and enthusiasm for the game. I especially appreciated the manner in which Ted accepted myself and other juniors as fellow players on an equal footing with himself in the days when junior members were considered by many others to be an unnecessary evil on the course. Ted loved to hit the ball hard and appeared not to change his approach as age caught up with him.

Des Roberts some 50 years back played from the third tee only to see a lad come out of the trees, pick up his ball, and head towards the stream from which we now get our irrigation water. Giving chase Des ran the lad down then marched him back to the green where he made him drop the ball. Des then two putted for a hard earned ‘Birdie three’.

Full marks for energy and enterprise if not for strict adherence to the rules.

His golfing friends fondly knew Frank Willoughby as the ‘Sand Shoe Champion’. One day Frank used a similarly free rule interpretation after hooking his ball from the 14th tee onto the lawn in front of the County Council Building. Armed with his trusty wedge Frank scaled the fence, crossed the road, played a lovely shot across the traffic to the heart of the green, holed the putt, and claimed a par. He definitely deserved one.

title: Post war revitalisation · p. 52
text:
CHAPTER SIX

POST WAR REVITALISATION

title: Post war revitalisation · p. 53
text:
After the war the returning service men and women were very enthusiastic in their desire to return to the pleasures of peacetime life as rapidly as possible and golf rated highly amongst those pleasures. As a result there was a concerted desire to restore the course to its full eighteen holes and, aided by a healthy increase in membership, this was soon achieved. By 1951, only six years after the cessation of hostilities, membership had grown to the unprecedented figure of 416. The old clubhouse soon proved woefully inadequate to cater for such a large and active membership and plans were made to finance a new brick building to be sited adjacent to the first tee. Four hundred debentures at £10 each were sold and a building committee of Alan Davidson, Dave Cambie, and Lionel Smith was empowered to supervise construction that was to be achieved at a cost not to exceed £5,700. The contract was let to a club member, Mr Beck, at what was considered the bargain price of £1/8/6 ($2.85) per square foot. This would be $20.54 per square metre in today’s units. This price allowed the project to be completed under budget to the great satisfaction, and no doubt relief, of the building committee. The old wooden building was advertised for sale at a price of £500 but when it was found it could not be moved in one piece the buyer negotiated a reduction and the building was moved to Pyes Pa where it again became a domestic home. The new clubhouse was opened in 1954. While the final outcome was widely admired the project, like most projects run for the benefit of a large group of members, had not been free of controversy. Chief amongst these was the siting of the building. There was a strong move to utilise the area to the west of the putting green on the rise where the right-hand third tee is now located. This would have provided a more panoramic view of the course and left the Moreton Bay to command the area behind the first tee. Apart from the problems this tree now causes by dropping litter on the clubhouse and surrounds it is probably true that the right location was chosen. The latest incarnation of the clubhouse, built upon the foundations of the 1954 building, provides a much better view of the course and surrounding landscape than was ever previously evident.

The new clubhouse was but one factor in the continued growth of membership and club usage. The exposure of the game on television, the advent of a healthy professional tournament circuit in New Zealand, and the rapid improvement in golf course maintenance led by the Turf Research Institute of New Zealand all contributed to the development of the game nation-wide. For the Tauranga Golf Club this renewed interest reached its peak in the sixties and seventies when player pressure became so great that membership had to be restricted. Full men’s membership was capped at 335 with just five discretionary places available for players arriving from out of town with national handicaps of 4 or less. The Club’s Bank manager or the CEO of our neighbour, the Racing Club, would also gain membership under these discretionary places.

While this restricted membership was a necessity, if play was not to become so congested as to be unpleasant for all, it was very unpopular with keen players transferring to Tauranga from other parts of New Zealand, a trend that was occurring at an ever-accelerating rate and continues into the 21st Century. In an attempt to create opportunities for prospective members to obtain some form of membership new categories of male membership were introduced. Older, less active members were encouraged to move to the new B category that allowed play on six days a week excluding Saturdays. A significant number of existing members took up this option and the reduced subscription that went

title: Post war revitalisation · p. 54
text:
with it. This enabled the committee to accept new A category members up to the 335 limit. B category was restricted to 100 members and a further category C was introduced providing for midweek golf only. This category came to be seen as a waiting room for A category and at one stage that waiting time stretched to as much as five years. Sometimes a player would move from C to B as a stepping-stone to the A membership he really wanted. Ultimately priority was given to such B members to move up to full membership. Pressure for membership within the women’s section at no time reached the stage where a waiting list had to be instituted. This sometimes caused problems when a wife would gain membership while her husband languished in frustration on the sidelines.

In December 1969 the membership committee reported the following figures: Men’s A - 337 (limit 335 + 5), Men’s B - 58 (limit 100), Men’s C - 50 (no limit), Ladies’ A - 282 (limit 300), Ladies’ B - 27 (limit 50). In addition there were 69 non-playing members, while 31 men and 21 women were listed as awaiting membership and 11 men sought a change of category. The reason 21 women were waiting upon membership was because they would accept membership only if and when their husbands gained admittance. At this time the priority for acceptance was to those seeking an upgrade followed by those holding National handicaps of four or better.

The limitation on membership continued through until 1985 when the committee were concerned over a down turn in membership figures following subscription renewals for the new season. As a result there were now vacancies for 23 male members. In response to this trend that was still apparent the following year the committee moved to increase the number of places available and to endeavour to attract new members. Category limits were consequently increased to allow up to 375 men in A category plus 25 discretionary places, up to 125 B category men, and up to 350 women in total over categories A and B, no more than 50 of those to be B category. Shortly thereafter it was realised that category limits were no longer necessary and they have not been found to be necessary since. Quite the reverse has applied. Subsequent committees have actively campaigned to attract new members in order to ensure the financial viability of the Club. Two factors have had a strongly positive influence on maintaining membership levels. These have been the growth of Nine Hole Golf amongst women players, and the attraction of the game to the growing population of Asian Immigrants arriving in Tauranga.

Reg Ellis was about to tee off at the first when a rabbit shot across the tee with a weasel on its back. Reg made a swipe with his club, a much quicker swing than his trademark slow rhythmic golf swing, and killed them both. He then teed off and scored a three. Can anyone else claim to have scored a rabbit, a weasel, and a birdie at the same hole? Well perhaps not but Des Shiel can lay claim to the weasel. As Judge Ian Thomas was about to play his tee stroke on the first tee a few years ago another weasel ran across the tee. Ian had no idea what was going on as people shouted for someone to ‘get it’. Several swung clubs at the weasel but, after chasing it out from a hole under the Moreton Bay tree, it was Des who proved himself the successful hunter.
