BEFORE

and AFTER

title: Men’s golf · p. 59
text:
CHAPTER SEVEN

MENS GOLF

title: Men’s golf · p. 60
text:
From the earliest days, when the Club based itself at the Domain, Saturday afternoon was competition time for those men who wished to exercise their competitive instincts. So it has remained although the growth in membership in the second half of the Twentieth Century resulted in competition play soon occupying Saturday mornings as well as afternoons throughout the playing season. The season has gradually been extended from an original eight or nine months until competition golf is now held almost throughout the year.

At first competition was rather informal with the Secretary or Captain deciding on the day what form the competition would take. The choice lay between Medal, Par, and Match Play, with some variation by way of playing singly or in pairs. Foursomes, including mixed foursomes, were popular. From the beginning match play, including the ubiquitous haggle, was the most popular form of competition. The Stableford scoring system had not then been invented. It was not until 1931 that Dr Frank Stableford of the Wallasley Golf Club near Liverpool developed the system, perhaps in response to his habit of destroying a good Stroke Play round with one or two bad holes. In doing so he gave new hope to generations of players afflicted with the same unfortunate habit.

As the Club membership grew a variety of trophies were donated. This was often to introduce a new competition or to encourage its adoption. Consequently the Club program grew larger as the years went by and it became increasingly difficult to fit everything in. At one time in the 1960s and 70s some competitions were designated as Sunday competitions to alleviate that problem. While this proved popular with some there were many who found it difficult, or impossible, to play both days of the weekend because of family or work commitments and the change was eventually reversed.

While competition within the Club flourished Tauranga men made little impact at Provincial or National level. Perhaps N P (Norman) Green who won the Tauranga Open Championship against all comers in 1938, 39, and 40 was the first Club member to achieve significant victories against outside opposition.

For those who find the Knoll difficult, bear in mind that Joan Mirrielees and Maurice Bradmore each aced the hole on two separate occasions. Some claim Brownie Carnachan did even better by scoring three ones on that hole in the one day. During the Labour Weekend Tournament one year he holed in one at the Knoll in the morning round then amassed an 11 in the afternoon!

On occasion even the very best can make a real mess of The Knoll. In one Spalding Masters Tournament Kel Nagle moved from winning contention after scoring no less than seven at the hole. I believe a sand fly got into his eye at the precise moment when he was attempting to recover from down the side of the green though Kel was never one to seek

an excuse for such a lapse.

title: Men’s golf · p. 61
text:
Norman and his wife Nancy came to the Club in 1936 after experiencing golfing success at Dannevirke, Napier and Stratford before moving to Tauranga. Norman’s lowest handicap was 2 yet he played with a rudimentary set of five clubs: a brassie (2 wood), a 3 iron, a niblick (5 iron), a mashie (8/9 iron), and a putter. Norman never managed to win the Tauranga Club Championship to add to his successes at previous Clubs indicating that the standard of local play was showing marked improvement. The two outstanding players of the period were H J (Jack) Bateman and F W (Fred) Ward. These two won the Tauranga Open Championship in six of the seven years from 1946 to 1953. Fred won again in 1958.

Jack Bateman, in addition to his Open successes, won the Club Championship in 1934, and then three more times in the four years from 1946 to 1949. To highlight his career he won the inaugural Bay of Plenty Champion of Champions title held at Whakatane in 1948, successfully defending it at Tauranga the following year. Further success came the way of Tauranga with victory in the Bay of Plenty District Golf Association (BOPDGA) Senior Inter Club Shield in 1951. Jack and Fred were vital members of the winning team. This shield was the forerunner of the BOP Championship Pennant Series. It was to be another 23 years before Tauranga were again able to hold the shield aloft, winning it three years in a row from 1974. Fred Ward’s many golfing exploits have been included in a later chapter. His influence, both as

competitor and as administrator, projected far into the future of the Club.

Prior to 1948 five men were honoured with Life Membership of the Club. They were E T Baker, Denis Ivory, R T (Bert) Goulding, A J Mirrielees, and P H Roach. While we know that Denis Ivory (1936-39) served as Club President little is known of the service these men gave to the Club other than in the case of Mr Mirrielees whose contribution is recorded elsewhere. Mr Roach won the Senior Championship in 1919 and Bert Goulding won the same championship in 1933. We can be sure that each of these men together with Mr Baker made outstanding contributions to the growth and development of the Club and to the course at Gate Pa. Life Membership would not have been granted lightly, especially in those times when members were more intimately involved in Club and Course management than they are today.

In the final year or two of the Forties C Steedman, H B Lusk, and Arthur Towsey were next to be honoured with Life Membership. Arthur’s long service as a member of the committee and as voluntary Keeper of the Bar has been well documented. He was a superb ‘Mine Host’ over a lengthy period during which he ruled his domain with a somewhat flexible ‘Rod of Iron’. Mr Lusk was intimately involved in the early design of the course when the Club first made the move to the Racecourse Reserve while memories of “Steedy” appear to have faded with the passing of his contemporaries.

S G (George) Wilcock will be remembered each year when the Intermediate men compete for the Wilcock Cup, a handicap Match Play event. George, who served as President from 1950-52 following his years as a member of the committee, was elected to Life membership in 1949. One year later George was elected Vice President of the BOPDGA

title: Men’s golf · p. 62
text:
A W (Warwick) Nicol was the Accountant of the BNZ in Tauranga. He was a committee member and Vice President before being elected President in 1958-59. From 1954-56 he was Vice President of the BOPDGA and President in 1957-58. For many of those years he held the post of Men’s handicapper at Tauranga. He was made a Life Member of the Tauranga Golf Club in 1958 before retiring to Tirau.

H J W (Harry) Bradmore who was honoured with Life Membership in 1958 was not one to seek the limelight. He, along with his son Maurice, was very active behind the scenes. They followed on from the work of Mr Mirrielees in planting trees and nurturing their early growth. By doing so they made a valuable contribution to the development of the excellent conditions we now enjoy. Mr Bradmore presented the Alan Bradmore Memorial Trophy in remembrance of another son, Alan, who was killed in the Second World War. That trophy is contested annually over two Stableford rounds as part of the regular Saturday programme.

R J (Dick) Phelan was elected to Life Membership in 1963. Details of Dick’s contribution to Veterans’ Golf and of his long competitive career have been documented elsewhere in this publication. That he was able to feature in the final of the Junior Championship 47 years after his Senior Championship victory in 1930 bears testimony to his unprecedented longevity in the game he so obviously loved. It is unfortunate that complete records of committee personnel prior to 1953 have not been uncovered

so it is not possible to document the service records of men of that era. We can be confident that Dick Phelan did more than his share to see that the Club advanced in the right direction.

A L (Alan) Davidson was elected to Life Membership in 1964. There could be no more worthy recipient than ‘Zuke’ as he became known for reasons lost in time. Much of Alan’s contribution to the Club he loved has been well documented elsewhere in this History. For the record Alan was Vice President in 1953 when our full records began and he progressed to the Presidency in 1956-58. There is no doubt his committee work began earlier than that. He returned again to the committee in 1966 serving a second term of Presidency from 1968-70. During this phase Alan did much of his most significant work particularly in relation to course development and the incorporation of the ‘Harris Plan’ into the design of specific holes.

Many a match committee member of today would be amazed at the amount of work that was once done to achieve the same result that now happens automatically as computer data are projected onto the clubhouse screen to show individual scores. For example prior to the Tauranga Open 28 hole event all competitor names would have been meticulously hand printed on cardboard strips that were then slotted into metal runners on wooden score boards. In the course of the day all the tournament details would be appended by hand following manual checking of all cards. For years Alan, Des Wilson, Jim Reid, Keith Frith and others would forgo the opportunity to participate in the day in order to ensure that all this documentation was completed quickly and efficiently so that prize giving could be held as soon as possible following play. For some years the first two mentioned above sponsored that particular tournament.

title: Men’s golf · p. 63
text:
As a player Alan won the Junior Championship in 1946 and went on to play to single figures, his best round being a 69. Alan served in the Second World War as crew in Bomber raids over Germany. On one occasion his plane having been hit by Anti Aircraft fire Alan, believing the plane to be doomed, prepared to bail out. On his way to the escape hatch he touched the Rear Gunners shoulder saying: “the plane is going down. We have to get out”. A few seconds after they cleared the plane it exploded with the loss of the rest of the crew. Alan made it to ground but was captured by German troops and became a prisoner of war. The Tauranga Golf Club was indeed fortunate that Alan survived to tell the tale. For many years Alan owned and managed the Business known as Davidson’s in Spring Street where many a fashion conscious lady member of the Golf Club bought her ensembles.

Keith Nattrass was first elected to the committee in 1957 joining an especially strong group made up of A L Davidson, A W Nicol, D Coutts, A Towsey, J Mowat, N H E Hockin, F Cassin, and S Randell. Colin Evitt was then the Honorary Secretary. Keith’s administrative abilities were immediately recognised and he was elected Vice President a year later and served as President from 1960-63. At District level Keith served as President of the BOPDGA in 1961-62. The high point of Keith’s golf administration came in 1969 when he assumed the position of North Island Vice President of the NZGA, a position bringing credit both to Keith and to the Tauranga Club. In 1973 Keith was awarded the highest honour available to Golf Club members, that of Life Membership.

J C (John) Hare has been mentioned elsewhere in connection with his work in reconciling differences between the Racing Club and the Golf Club in relation to various privileges each might exercise in their use of the Reserve. He became a member of the Racecourse Domain Board, as it then was, in 1952. He later became its Chairman. John refrained from taking office in either of the tenant clubs in order to avoid any possible conflict of interest though he did serve the Golf Club in the role of honorary solicitor. For many years he acted as timekeeper for the Racing Club. His ‘apprentice’ in that capacity was Keith Frith who carried on the role following John’s death. John was a partner in the law firm of Maltby, Hare and Willoughby with offices in Wharf Street. The firm later merged with Holland, Beckett and Partners to form Hobec, one of the leading Law Partnerships in the city. John was an enthusiastic golfer whose invaluable contribution to establishing and protecting the Club’s rights on the Reserve were recognised by the award of Life Membership in 1980.

Keith Frith will be remembered as ‘Captain Extraordinaire’. Keith joined the committee in 1971 as Vice Captain before assuming the role of Captain in 1973. Where it had been the custom for men to serve in this demanding role for two years Keith broke the mould by continuing in the post for seven years before accepting the position of Vice President for a further three years. Never one to relish the limelight Keith was reluctantly persuaded to accept the Presidency in 1983, an honour he richly deserved. Never really comfortable in the role of President Keith handed over the reins after just one year but it was not long before he returned to the committee. In 1985 D Cotterall was elected Captain but did not take up the role. Keith stepped into the breach to help the Club out and served another two

title: Men’s golf · p. 64
text:
years. In recognition of his dedicated service over so many years the Club were delighted to honour him with Life Membership in 1985.

Keith had his moments as a golfer as well as an administrator. In 1979 Keith contested the final of the Junior Championship and, to the delight of all, he was successful against Kevin Moynahan who was generally well ahead of Keith on the drive. Kevin was almost as pleased as everyone else to have Keith enjoy this success on the course where his Match Committee work had enabled so many others to enjoy their competitions over the years. In 1968 Keith won the Nicoll Cup. On the first Saturday of this 36-hole par competition Keith shot 84- 21-63 to be 7 up on par. On the second Saturday Keith’s daughter was to be married and Keith had not intended playing golf. His friend and wedding guest Vince O’Connor persuaded him they should play at dawn on the Saturday and still have ample time to prepare for the wedding. And so they did with Keith this time scoring an 86 to be 5 up on par. Is there anyone else who has bettered 12 up against par over 36 holes? When the horror of Parkinson’s disease caught up with him Keith had to give up playing the game he so enjoyed but it did not end his association with the Club. For many years he continued to arrive prior to midday on Saturday to start the afternoon field. His extensive knowledge of the organisation of Saturday competition play was frequently called upon, and greatly appreciated, by successive match

committees. Keith’s unobtrusive manner, his wisdom and experience, and his unfailing loyalty to his Club and to his colleagues made him an exceptional member.

Alex Gallagher joined the Club in 1938 and remained a member for more than 60 years. In 1972 he was elected Vice President, progressing to the Chair in 1974, filling that position for three years. In the days of manual score boards Alex’ special skills were much in demand. A surveyor by profession, Alex produced scoreboards that were works of art. His calligraphic skills became legend in the Club. As co-ordinator of scoring information from around the course during the Spalding Masters, the PGA Championship, and the Russell Grace Inter Provincial Tournament, Alex was unsurpassed. It never crossed anyone’s mind that anyone other than Alex would fill that role when important tournaments were held.

Alex won the Junior Championship in 1989. There was a certain irony in the victory. The previous season Mark Mangos joined the Club shortly before the championship qualifying rounds were due to be held. Mark had been on a 7 handicap previously but had been out of the game for a few years and his handicap had lapsed. Keen to play in the championships Mark got in three quick rounds. These qualified him for a 17 handicap and thus a place in the Junior Championship field. Mark, knowing he was better than that, requested a handicap that would allow him to play in the Intermediate division. His pleas fell on the deaf ears of handicapper Alex Gallagher and so Mark qualified for the Junior Championship. Making easy work of the early rounds he met none other than Alex in the final and prevailed with little trouble. He was possibly the most able winner of that title in its history. Perhaps it was poetic justice when Alex gained his success the following year. Earlier in 1988 Alex won the Junior Stroke Play Championship. Alex was elected to Life Membership in 1988.

title: Men’s golf · p. 65
text:
M W (Maurice) White was the son in law of Jimmy Mowat, our first Professional. Maurice was first elected to the committee in 1971. He was elected Vice President in 1974 and President in 1977, filling that role for two years. Maurice returned to the committee in 1988 and remained a committee member until the advent of the Board of Management in 1994. For the majority of his time on committee Maurice chaired the Finance Committee, sometimes as its sole member. Maurice was an early advocate of the Board form of management and was active in promoting the concept and in assisting in setting up the constitutional details to enable it to function. For his contribution to Club administration over a lengthy period Maurice was elected to Life Membership in 1991. Noel Copestake joined the Club in 1960. Few have given as much to the Club in the course of our history as has Noel. First elected to the committee in 1985 Noel remained there in various roles until the advent of the Board in 1994. Noel assumed the Vice Captaincy in 1989, and the Captaincy a year later. Following three years as Club Captain Noel was elected President in 1993, an honour he held for two years. In the last of these he took his place on the Board in its inaugural year, the constitution providing for the President to be an automatic Board member. Noel’s contribution to the Club through his promotion of Twilight Golf, and his leadership of the ‘Wednesday Firewood Gang’ further evidenced his dedication to the Club.

In 1984 Noel won the Junior Championship. He has had a long association with the selection and management of Pennant teams over the years. In recognition of his work in the interests of Golf Noel was elected to the Bay of Plenty Eagles Golfing Society in 1995, later becoming their Secretary/ Treasurer.

Noel was elected to Life Membership of the Tauranga Golf Club in 1997, soon to be joined in that elite company by his wife Peg. These two appointments represented a remarkable and unique achievement, one that would have been applauded by every member who had been privileged to experience the service these two gave to the Club over so many years.

Bernie Child came to the Club from the Manawatu where he had worked as a contractor using heavy machinery in his work. A very practical man it was behind the scenes where Bernie flourished. He was project organiser for the ‘Vets’ for a number of years and, organiser or not, he was ever to the fore when work required to be done. Few who have not had the experience of working at some of the many projects Bernie and his peers have completed over the years would appreciate just how valuable

Bernie’s contributions have been. The Club is much the richer for his contribution. We enjoyed his little plaque on the drinking fountain behind the first tee: ‘A fountain of youth built by a child’. The fountain was his idea and entirely his own work. It stands as an indication of the commitment Bernie has to his fellow members. He became involved in administration as a member of the Veterans’ Golfing Society. In 1995 he was honoured with the Presidency of that organisation, a job he did with his characteristic dedication. In recognition of his commitment to his Club, and to his selfless contributions of time and energy over many years, Bernie Child was elected to Life Membership in 1997.

title: Men’s golf · p. 66
text:
K D (Keith) Dawkins was an excellent cricketer who rapidly adapted to golf despite a grip that the experts frowned upon. Natural talent can overcome a lot. Keith was in his prime years as a golfer when he won the Senior Championship on four occasions during the five years from 1963 to 1967. Only Doug Furrie intervened to prevent Keith sweeping five in a row. In 1972 and 73 Keith had a taste of committee work as Vice Captain to Keith Frith. This was a most useful apprenticeship in Match Committee work. In 1983 Keith again got the call and completed another year as Vice Captain to Bob Allen before taking on the Captaincy in 1984. Again in 1995 when it became difficult to find anyone to stand as Captain Keith volunteered to fill the position. As would be expected he led the Match Committee through another successful season. In his half-century and more of membership Keith served the Club with distinction in his own quiet manner. A member of the Eagles Golfing Society Keith was elected to Life Membership of the Tauranga Golf Club in 2000.

E A (Ernie) Craig was elected to Life Membership in 2007. The vital role played by Ernie in ensuring that the administration of the Racecourse Reserve continued to serve the interests of the two primary tenants has been detailed in Chapter 3. While it is difficult to visualise what may have happened had Ernie not been so diligent in pursuing his plans for the future administration of the Reserve we can be confident that the Club would have found themselves in a much less secure position than it now holds.

The Racing Club also honoured Ernie with Life Membership in recognition of his work in the interests of the Reserve. D G S (David) Mowat has been a Club member for well over 50 years. He was first elected to the committee in 1967 and served as Captain in 1969 and 70, as Vice President in 1971, and as President in 1972 and 73. In 1989 he was again elected to committee, serving until the Board became a reality in 1994. Four years later he was encouraged to stand for one of the elected positions on the Board. In 1999 David was appointed to the Board Chairmanship, a position he held for 3 years.

In recognition of his contribution to Club administration over an extended period David was honoured with Life Membership in 2006. In over 100 years 23 men have been made Life Members of the Club. While all of these men have richly deserved the honour bestowed upon them by a grateful Club there are many others who have contributed much over the years. The names of many of these will be found scattered throughout this history. Below we pay homage to a selection of those whose service added real value to their Club over the years and we apologise to those many others who must, for one reason or another, go unrecorded, though not unappreciated.

C W (Colin) Johnstone joined the committee as Vice Captain in 1956, graduating to Captain in 1958. Elected Vice President in 1960 Colin assumed the Presidency in 1963. For one period in our history there was a tendency for committee members to follow a progressive path, spending two years in each of the executive positions before stepping up. This had the advantage of providing continuity from one

title: Men’s golf · p. 67
text:
year to the next and each officer would be well versed in the requirements of the new position when he reached it. Colin was the first to follow such a path. The advantages of such a progression were obvious. As the trailblazer Colin proved well versed and efficient in all that he did for the Club over a lengthy period.

R G (Roy) Bathgate followed Colin through the ranks. Roy was an accountant by profession and brought much of the meticulous nature of that discipline to his work on committee. Serving as Vice Captain in 1958 Roy progressed to the Presidency in 1965. Through no fault of his own Roy served just one year as President before being defeated in a ‘bloodless coup’. Other members of the committee went down with him, some voluntarily withdrawing in protest at what they considered to be an unjustifiable vendetta. For some reason that 1966 Annual Meeting was held at the ‘Down Under’ Coffee Lounge in Central Tauranga. Those present will long remember the meeting for the currents that stirred beneath the surface. In retrospect the break in committee continuity that followed that evening did not make for a happy and settled Club over the next two or three years.

Jim Reid and his wife Jean were very well known members who began their golf at the old Te Puna Golf Club. It is believed that some members of Te Puna formed the nucleus of what became the Otumoetai Golf Club. The details appear lost in the mists of time. Both Jim and Jean were very supportive of Tauranga Golf Club through the fifties, sixties, and into the seventies. Jean took on the catering role during the fifties and was admired for the quality service she provided. A very keen Intermediate level golfer Jim was known for his advocacy of the ‘corkscrew grip and the K address’. Jim survived the 1966 coup to continue in his role as Captain but it was not until 1970 that he was finally elected President, an honour he had probably earned some years previously. Jim’s golfing wisdom was recognised on a wider level through his services to Bay of Plenty Golf. There he rose through the ranks to assume the Presidency from 1971-73. Jim was elected to Life Membership of that organisation in 1985 in deserved recognition of his service over many years.

Dr R S (Rod) Rowe was a member of the committee when Bruce Cunningham, at that time Town Clerk to the Mt Maunganui Borough Council, initiated a move to establish a new Golf Club on land adjacent to the Tauranga Airport. There were restrictions on heights and buildings on the area owing to Airport activities. These caused Bruce to believe a golf course might well be the ideal solution. Coincidentally this was at a time in the early Seventies when membership of the two existing courses was at a premium and another course was seen to be a virtual necessity. In 1971 a committee made up of representatives

of the Tauranga and Mt Maunganui clubs was formed to promote the concept. Rod Rowe took a special interest in this and selflessly ignored the prospect of almost certain progression through the committee ranks at Tauranga in order to see the Omanu Golf Club successfully established. He was ultimately to be rewarded with election to the Presidency of the new club.

D M (Des) Wilson joined the committee as Vice Captain to Sol Kanapu in 1969. It was a period when committee posts were turning over rapidly. Des was to move up to Captaincy the following year and to Presidency one year later. Des was not one to be very happy as a ‘Back Bencher’ in any organisation

title: Men’s golf · p. 68
text:
he belonged to and, after two years as President, he became active in the Bay of Plenty District Golf Association where he assumed the Presidency from 1977-79. From there he went on to represent the Bay as their Councillor on the New Zealand Golf Association (now NZ Golf). In recognition of his service to BOP Golf Des was made a Life Member of the BOPDGA in 1988.

R B (Bob) Eaton joined the Club in 1963. First elected to the committee in 1977 Bob took on the Vice Captaincy in 1978 before filling the Captaincy for three years. Vice President to Keith Frith, Bob moved into the President’s chair in 1983 when Keith moved aside with a sigh of relief. Later, when the Board of Management was in operation, Bob’s experience was again called upon and he was elected to serve a term there. It is probable that the high point of Bob’s golfing career came in 1987 when he was a member of the Junior Pennant team that won the Bay of Plenty final at Lake View.

D W (Dan) Dougherty was elected to the committee in 1989. Following a rather more low key coup than that of 1966 Dan made a rather meteoric rise to become President just a year later, serving in that capacity for three years. During his years as President the Club dramatically improved the quality and range of equipment available to the Greens Staff. For this Dan deserves a lot of credit. The purchase of up to the minute equipment to mow greens, fairways, and surrounds, immediately improved the efficiency of the staff and the appearance and quality of the course. It was a bold step as it meant the Club was forced to borrow heavily to finance purchases but in retrospect it was the right move. While present and future members continue to carry a burden of debt they also benefit from the better course conditions now prevailing. In the new Millennium Dan became heavily involved in the administrative side of Bay of Plenty Golf as a Selector, Team Manager, and eventually President. He was active during the period when Bay of Plenty became the predominant competitive Province in New Zealand Men’s Golf. Many believe Dan was instrumental in inculcating a spirit of commitment amongst team members that overcame a previous over-emphasis on the social aspects of Tournament golf. This lead to continuing success for Bay teams at National level. Fittingly Dan was made a Life Member of Bay of Plenty Golf, the organisation that arose out of the amalgamation of Men and Women’s golf in the Bay.

Gary Baker joined us from the Manawatu Golf Club. An ideas man, who was prepared to put in the effort to see that many of these came to fruition, Gary was elected to the Vice Captaincy in 1990. He and Noel Copestake made a strong and innovative team heading the Match Committee. When Noel accepted the President’s chair in 1993 Gary took over as Captain, serving two years in that role. With the advent of the Board of Management he took a brief break from committee work until returning as Vice President in 1997. A year later he was elected President, a position he held for the next three years. As President he was automatically a member of the Board over that period. Gary’s contribution to the initial launch of Business House Golf is detailed elsewhere but it is clear that his influence was pivotal to its success. In the realm of Thursday ‘Ball in the Bucket’ golf Gary was much to the fore through his organisation and his innovative ideas.

title: Men’s golf · p. 69
text:
MEN’S REPRESENTATIVE GOLF

As mentioned earlier Tauranga won the BOP Senior Inter Club Shield in 1951 with the help of two outstanding players in Jack Bateman and Fred Ward. It was not until the Michael Nicholson era beginning in the Seventies that Tauranga again enjoyed success at that level, annexing the Shield in 1974, 75, and 76, before becoming the first winners of the Championship Pennant Series in 1978. During this period a talented team of ‘Young Guns’ supported Michael. The team included John Ward, Jim Lancaster, and Noel Johnson. All these represented the Bay of Plenty with distinction at Inter Provincial level. Through the Eighties Mt. Maunganui reigned virtually unchallenged in the Championship Pennant Series so Tauranga had to wait until 1993 to again taste success. Further wins followed in 1994, 96, and 99. In addition to the four mentioned above prominent team members involved in those wins included Bruce Burbery, Eddie Burgess, Jay Carter, Blair Murdock, and Gavan MacFarlane. The victorious 1996 team were Runners Up in the Johnnie Walker National Inter Club Championship held in Wellington. That team comprised Mike Cannell, Martin Hall, Andrew McNair, Eddie Burgess, Mike Nicholson, and Blair Murdock. Stuart Browne managed the team throughout the season. This Wellington visit may well have been the last occasion on which a Tauranga team was outfitted in our official Club blazers. These had to be borrowed from a group of older Club members, as few, if any, more recent members now owned them.

Further success at BOP Senior Championship level came in 2006 and 2008 featuring new players including Michael Melling, Andre Arthur, George Kinghorn, Scott Trebilco, Jared Pender, Matt Moorehead, Kevin Smith, and Toby Pudney. Eddie Burgess added his experience to this mix.  2011 proved to be a vintage year for our Senior Pennant players with both the Championship, and the Senior A teams winning their BOP finals. For the Championship team the precocious talents of Sam Davis, David Feeney, Karl Knedler, and Ben Shanly were reinforced by the experience of Eddie Burgess, Blair Murdock, George Kinghorn and John Waretini. Karl’s father Peter ably managed the team throughout the season.

A judicious mix of youth and experience also featured in the Senior A team where Jason Ornberg and John Laing provided the experience, James Cannon, Jin Hwang, Oliver and Will Coxhead, the youth. John Laing, a one-time stalwart of Kaiangaroa golf managed this team together with playing for it.

At Intermediate and Junior Pennant level Tauranga have been much less successful. During the 19 years of Shield competition Tauranga failed to win at Intermediate level. It was not until 1980, 30 years after BOP Inter Club competition began, that a Tauranga Intermediate team was successful. Under the system prevailing prior to the present Zone structure Tauranga met Opotiki in the final at Omanu. This day was so memorable in our history it is worthy of further comment. Captained by Norm Robson, the team included Syd Carswell, Ashley Norman, Peter Chadwick, and David Mowat. The Tauranga team became very concerned when Ashley had not appeared half an hour or so prior to tee off. Someone got on the phone only to wake up a somewhat hungover Ashley who flew into his clothes before breaking all records in driving from Otumoetai to Omanu. Norm Robson, teeing off one group ahead of Ashley, caused a delay by stopping near his ball on the first fairway and beginning a search for his car keys that he claimed to have lost. When he sighted Ashley hurrying from his car Norm fortunately ‘found

title: Men’s golf · p. 70
text:
the keys’. The delay was enough though Ashley’s early progress seemed to indicate it was all rather pointless. Four down in almost as many holes Ashley suddenly came alive to win comfortably with holes to spare. Elsewhere the standard of golf was very high for Intermediate players, most having to shoot close to, or under, 80 to succeed. As the final match approached the 18th green Peter Chadwick’s approach finished to the right of the green with a set of gang mowers intervening on his line of play. When no relief was offered the rest of his team dragged the offending mowers aside and Peter chipped successfully to remain square. With two wins, two halves, and two losses the teams finished tied on three points each so a sudden death play off was required. Team members looked at one another, most none too keen to carry the responsibility. Finally someone said: ‘Norm’s the man for the job’. And so he was. There would be few more competitive players at that level than was Norman Robson. His nerve held as he calmly parred the first extra hole while Johnny Tai, of Opotiki, three putted from well away from the pin. The final chapter in the story came when Norm, arriving at the Tauranga Clubhouse to proudly present the hard earned Pennant, found he did not have it. Eventually it transpired he had placed it on top of his car while he loaded his clubs at Omanu before driving off. It was never found and another had to be obtained from BOP administrators.

It was to be another 18 years before an Intermediate team was again successful. A team for which Ray Pittams, Mike Sherratt, Colin Gray, Ralph Bills, Steve Stephens, Gary Baker, Brent Hickisey, Chris Best,

Alan Bush, Nigel Rose, and Andrew Reid all appeared at some time throughout the pennant season won the final played at Te Puke in 1998. The team was player-managed by Bruce Simister, a man who gave much to the encouragement and management of pennant teams over many years. Further success followed in 2003 when Tauranga scored the trifecta with success at Senior Championship, Intermediate, and Junior level, an epic achievement in our history. Members of the Intermediate team were Robbie Aitken, Ralph Bills, Jim Costello, Colin Gray, Ian Humble, Chris McAlpine, Klaus Niermann, Mike Sherratt, and Paul Smith. The Junior team that year included Alan Brown, Roger Craw, Graham

Fowler, Ian Given, David Hermitage, Roy MacGregor, Ernie Pratt, and Bernie Priestley.

Junior teams were successful four times in the old Inter-Club Shield years, bringing home the trophy the first year it was held in 1950 and again in 1955, 56, and 1965. Since the Pennant format was introduced in 1971 they have been victorious in 1983, 87, and 2003. The 1983 team were successful in the final at Whakatane in the last year before the Zone system began. The Tauranga team included a number of ‘grey haired gentleman’ including Bill Good and Jack Hill. At the presentation someone made the observation that Tauranga had at last won their first Junior Pennant since the series began. A wag at the back called out: ‘it looks as though the same team has been trying all those years’. Junior golfers do not get many opportunities to compete in a team contest over a full weekend so the BOP Pennant finals provide a memorable occasion for them. This was certainly the case for the 1987 Junior team who competed against the other Zone winners in the final at Lake View. Tauranga team members were Peter Brown, Bob Eaton, Kevin Moynahan, John Robinson, Neville Robinson, and David Mowat. Gary Hardaker had been an important member earlier in the season before his handicap moved down a division.

title: Men’s golf · p. 71
text:
Staying together at the Ngongataha Hotel enabled great team spirit to develop and, having seen off the challenges of Waiotapu and Kaingaroa on the Saturday, it was only necessary to take two wins from the highly rated Opotiki team on the Sunday to secure the Pennant. Although the top pair from Opotiki played exceptional golf to go through the weekend undefeated our other four came through to gain the win. Neville Robinson memorably summed up the weekend when he commented: “This tournament has been my Freyberg Rose Bowl. I will never reach that level of play but being a member of a team at my own level, and helping that team succeed, has been the highlight of my golfing life”. He spoke for all the team. THE LABOUR WEEKEND TOURNAMENT The Tauranga Open Championship was first played in 1934. From the start it was a three-day event played over Labour Weekend. The Saturday play featured two rounds of stroke play. These served as qualifying rounds to sort the field into groups of 16 to contest match play over the following two days. The first sixteen qualified on gross to form the championship division, the remainder on nett scores. All contestants were assured two matches while those defeated on the Sunday afternoon round could play in a Stableford competition on the Monday morning should they so wish. For many years the second sixteen became the ‘Calcutta’ flight with spirited bidding taking place on the Saturday evening as individuals and syndicates vied with one another to secure the most favoured ‘horses’. In later years it became apparent that some players were setting themselves to qualify in this second sixteen in order to be in a position to lay bids upon themselves. Consequently the organisers altered the conditions so that a draw was made after the qualifying rounds to establish which of groups two or three would form the Calcutta group. This partially thwarted those ‘setting’ themselves to profit from a sudden show of form beyond that which their handicap indicated they were prone to display.

Labour weekend had long had the reputation of featuring severely inclement weather so competitors had to be prepared for wind and rain, especially during the qualifying rounds on the Saturday. The weather could generally be expected to improve on the latter days, the finals almost invariably being played in glorious conditions. One year in the early seventies visitors and locals alike arrived on the course early on Saturday morning to find it virtually unplayable owing to very heavy overnight rain that continued to fall. Auckland players in particular, accustomed as they were to their courses being closed for days on end following such rainfall, suggested that they might as well return to their hotels as there would be no play that day. “Stay” we assured them. “The rain will stop shortly and the course

will dry out rapidly. We will then start after lunch and reduce qualifying to just one round”. They looked at us as though we were several shillings short of the full quid, they looked at the lakes of water on the eleventh and eighteenth fairways, they looked at one another and they shook their heads in the certain knowledge there would be no play today. How wrong they were. By eleven am the sun was out, by noon the field was away from the first tee, and all signs of water had gone from the worst affected fairways by the time they were reached. From that year on the format of the tournament never again featured two rounds on the Saturday. The single qualifying round later in the day proved very popular, especially amongst those who were enabled to travel from their homes that morning and thus save a night’s accommodation.

title: Men’s golf · p. 72
text:
H D (Harold) Brinsden won that first Tauranga Open, following up with a further three successive wins before local man Norman Green, who also won three in a row, broke his dominance. Multiple winners were a feature of the tournament over the succeeding years, Fred Ward winning six times, Don Boone five, Noel Johnson, Owen Kendall, and Michael Nicholson each four times. These were all outstanding players who each represented the Bay of Plenty with distinction on many occasions. Noel Johnson, who learnt his golf in Tauranga before moving to Whakatane, fashioned a remarkable record by winning his fourth title in 1999 twenty-five years after winning his first.

While outstanding championship winners make for an interesting history of the tournament it is often the ‘bit-part’ players who confer upon the event its special quality. This was certainly true of the Labour Weekend Tournament. From the start it attracted an enthusiastic field from a wide range of clubs from Auckland, The Waikato, The King Country, and The Bay of Plenty. The Maungakiekie club of Auckland built their representation in the event to as many as twenty-five over the years, with the same faces appearing year after year. Who from that time would forget the likes of Nick Burmaz, Ian (Mouse) McKendry, Dick Talyancich, Auctioneer supreme Peter McCullough, and their ilk?

The tiny Matiere club from the King Country came in such force that almost their entire male membership must at times have been entrants. The rapport between that club and our own grew to the point where a summer fixture was established with reciprocal visits being organised to play cricket and golf matches between members of the two clubs, the hosts billeting their guests and families for the occasion. Noel Copestake was instrumental in initiating these exchanges. They will be remembered with much pleasure, not least by the children of our members. The children were usually billeted separately from their parents and enjoyed the novel experience of life on a farm and perhaps the freedom from parental supervision.

The Labour Weekend Tournament flourished in an age when life was more relaxed. People seemed to have more leisure time and a greater willingness to travel away from home in order to participate in organised events. Whole families came on these trips, the wives getting together to enjoy their own activities while the men played golf. Social activity involving the men and their wives (the concept of partners being little considered at that time) was catered for in the clubhouse in the evenings.

Calcutta Sweeps, though illegal, were exceptionally popular and usually built into large prize pools. Sometimes it was necessary to advise the likes of Jim Rossiter, Russell Christie, or Bill Graham,

Norman Ducker, Ken Carter, and Peg Copestake all have the distinction of having scored an albatross at the sixth hole. Though the American commentators insist on calling this a double eagle we like the original, more descriptive, term. In any event the feat is a rare and meritorious achievement. Each of these three-under-par scores was recorded using the old equipment and they are especially notable for that reason alone.

title: Men’s golf · p. 73
text:
policemen members all, that it would be wise of them to leave for home at a certain point of the evening. This they did without demur and the clandestine operation was able to get underway. Before liquor licences were granted to Sports Clubs these operated illegal bars and club members who were policemen found it appropriate to turn a blind eye so they could enjoy the same after match social hour as did their playing partners. The law is indeed an ass in certain situations. It was a relief to all when enlightened legislation allowed responsible clubs such as our own to legitimise their activities. Though it is now possible to run a Calcutta Sweep legally it is ironic that their attraction has long since passed. This may be because people find a legal activity less attractive though a more likely explanation is that there is such a plethora of gambling opportunities now available that Calcuttas attract little bidding in comparison to days gone by. Certainly they were well past their ‘use by’ date before they were finally put to rest in our club environment.

Something similar happened to the Labour Weekend Tournament. From the days when you almost had to put your name down for the next year’s tournament at the closure of the current one participation steadily declined until, in the nineties, it became uneconomic to continue to promote the tournament. The attraction of other activities, the extension of weekend trade, the reluctance of people to travel and accommodate themselves away from home, all these and more contributed to the demise of the tournament. Several attempts were made to revive it without success. These included offering

competition for women and alternative formats but nothing came of these initiatives. Perhaps those who remember the ‘old days’ with affectionate nostalgia have a genuine basis for such feelings. Life does appear to have been more relaxed in earlier years and the Labour Weekend Tournament is but one of the casualties of the high-pressure age we have inherited.

THURSDAY GOLF

At our Club Thursday afternoon vies with Saturday afternoon as the most important day in the realm of Men’s Golf. It was not always so. The first mention of any semblance of organised golf on a Thursday comes from the recorded history of the Tauranga Veteran Golfing Society. Shortly after the Second World War a small group of elderly golfers began meeting on both Tuesday and Thursday afternoons to enjoy informal fourballs.  Gradually every second Tuesday developed into a day when an informal draw was made and from this the Veteran Golfers Society evolved in the early fifties. Tuesday remained as Veteran’s day until 1957 when Thursday was adopted as their official day. Gradually other members began to seek a mid-week game and these called themselves Businessmen to distinguish themselves from the Vets. As their numbers increased the ‘Businessmen’ became more assertive and it was not long before the first few grumbles about ‘those old buggers in front’ began to surface. Eventually the Vets decided to adhere to the old adage that discretion is the better part of valour and gracefully reverted to their original Tuesday afternoon draw. Naturally there were those amongst the older players who decided they wanted to continue their Thursday golf and thus a group of these continue to precede the ‘Ball in the Bucket’ brigade each Thursday afternoon, even to the present day. It was not until well into the new century that satisfactory terms were established so that a lasting truce could be established between the two groups. Under mutual agreement those not participating in the ball in the bucket draw

title: Men’s golf · p. 74
text:
still play off at the head of the field as part of the overall draw so that the field flows as well as can be expected under a multiple tee start involving the large number of participants the day attracts.

The life of any living system is subject to the process of evolution. The game of golf may not be considered to be a living system and yet it does display many of the characteristics of life. Those early veteran golfers first decided to satisfy their mid-week craving for a bit of competition by playing simple ‘haggles’ or ‘Nassaus’ as the Americans call them. These would usually be played for a maximum of  ‘a bob, a bob, a bob’. As weekends merged into the working week the attraction of a break in the normal Monday to Friday routine became more and more attractive to a wider range of working people. Consequently those who could do so began to ‘put a line through’ Thursday afternoon appointment diaries in order to be free to head for the greener acres of the golf course.

In the mid-eighties Bruce Simister became one of these as he found running a retail business left little opportunity to enjoy golf on a Saturday. On joining play on Thursday afternoons Bruce was disappointed to find that those participating did so in regular fours that played together week after week. Nothing wrong with that perhaps but would it not be a good opportunity to meet new people and discuss some of the issues that might arise in business? It did seem that more could be made of the afternoon. The idea began to spread until there were a dozen or so who were keen to  form drawn fours and have a

little competition between the groups so established. At first the winning team would receive $20 from each of the losing teams. This was fine when there were only two or three teams but as the concept became more popular the reality that one team got $100 or more while the rest got nothing became a little difficult to accept with good grace. Consequently a scale of reward based on the number of teams in the competition was instigated. Someone then found a 10-litre paint tin in the locker room and knocked a hole in the top so each potential participant could place his named ball in this bucket.  Prior to tee off these would be drawn in groups of four from the bucket and away the teams would go from

midday onward. So began the ‘Ball in the Bucket’ brigade, the same system, and perhaps the same bucket still being used today.

To add variety to the team competition a mathematical formula was instigated with fresh combinations being employed from one week to the next. Everything is based on Stableford points earned at each hole. One week the formula might require the first two scores to be added, the result then multiplied by the third. On another occasion the first and second scores are added, likewise the third and fourth, the two sums then being multiplied together. The variations are endless and often challenge the mathematically impaired. There have been those who swear that multiplying one by zero gives a different result from that obtained by multiplying zero by one, while the ‘order of operations’ rule taught to every third form student is a great unknown to many a successful businessman.

While the team entry remains at $20 the potential financial wins and losses have escalated as the variety of ‘extras’ within the group has expanded. The basic ‘Nassau’ became $5, $5, $5, while a range of ‘Stars’ gradually evolved. Gaining a star added 50c to the pair’s total earnings. These stars included the usual birdies, weasels, and nearies, and in addition such exotic creatures as gritties, fannies, and jesneys. To the uninitiated it might well seem as though he had arrived on an alien planet where the

title: Men’s golf · p. 75
text:
game of golf had evolved along a different path. Very likely the same ingénue would be astounded by the amount of money required from him to settle all of these at the table afterwards. Of course he would then find that all the money that changed hands would stay on the table to cover the cost of the required refreshments. He might also find himself receiving his share of a team prize. The Professional also runs an individual competition in conjunction with the team competition where a two, a good Stableford score, or a well-played ‘hidden hole’ might also produce a handsome reward. GLOSSARY Weasel - A shot holed from off the green. Nearie - Nearest the pin on a par three provided the ball is on the green. Grittie  - Par following a bunker stroke. Fannie - A tee stroke failing to reach the Women’s tee. Jesney – Nearies are carried forward if no one is on the green with their tee shot. If these have not been settled by the time the final hole is played the nearest the pin after three shots on the 18th wins the accumulated stars.

An extension to the Ball in the Bucket Brigade evolved as the ‘Baker’s Dozen’.  A small group from within the regular Thursday players decided to make an out of town trip to enjoy courses they had not played. The first such trip was planned for Napier in 1991. Gary Baker was supposed to be one of the touring group but had to pull out at the last moment. Though there were never a dozen Gary was somehow thought of as the extra loaf and so the name came into being. Ten players made that initial trip, travelling together in a mini-van and staying at Ormly Lodge alongside the Napier Golf Club course at Maraenui. Since that initial adventure trips have been organised each year. The destinations have included the Manawatu, Dunedin, Christchurch, and even the Gold Coast. The travelling party eventually reached a head count of 32 and many the tales that are told, or often not told, of these memorable tours. Those intending to travel make voluntary weekly contributions to the pool, while a three putt results in a compulsory contribution.

In the middle years of the first decade of the new Century another Thursday group became established. Utilising the same ‘ball in the bucket’ draw technology this group assembles prior to 8am and tees off from the first and seventh tees. The entry fee at time of writing stands at $2, the stakes are set at one, one, two, and first prize is a golf ball and a small chocolate bar. Depending on the number of entries the next several accumulators of Stableford points receive one golf ball each. The group early voted to

not reward twos in order to allow for more balls to be available to those scoring good Stableford scores. Naturally a number of regulars recall scoring a two the week following their vote being recorded against rewarding this particular feat.

title: Men’s golf · p. 76
text:
OUTSTANDING TAURANGA CLUB PLAYERS

M N (MICHAEL) NICHOLSON Michael began playing golf following a Football (Soccer) accident when he was 14. A promising footballer Michael took up golf in an attempt to put power back into his damaged wrist. Football’s loss proved to be Golf’s gain with Michael reducing his handicap to 1 within two years and never returning to his promising football career. Michael was unusual in his approach to practice as he spent untold hours on the tiny practice fairway between the 11th and 18th fairways hitting wedge shots. After some time his wedge had virtually no grooves left on its face. Somehow the timing and power he learned to put into playing these wedge shots carried over to the longer clubs, even to the driver. Throughout his competitive career Michael’s ability to play recovery shots was legend. Where he learned to play these is a bit of a mystery but learn them he clearly did. A great strength of his game was the ability to visualise the way the ball would behave in unusual situations. Michael stands supreme amongst those who have represented both the Tauranga Club and the Bay of Plenty. At Club level he won our Senior Championship on 12 occasions and headed our Pennant team for at least 25 years. While based in Whakatane he won their Senior Match play Championship in 1978, 79, and 80. He added the Whakatane Stroke Play title in 1977, 78, and 79. To further demonstrate his command of the Whakatane course Michael won the Bay of Plenty Open there in 1970, 74, 77, and 82. At Bay of Plenty level Michael set a record of 20 consecutive appearances in the National Inter-Provincial Championship variously known as the Freyberg Rose Bowl, The Government Life Tournament, and later The Tower Tournament when Government Life was renamed Tower Insurance. Michael’s first appearance in the team was in 1970 when he was just 16 years old, his last in 1989. In all he played 136 matches winning 64. In the great majority of these matches he was playing at number one and therefore meeting the best golfers each rival team put forward. In all Bay of Plenty representative fixtures Michael played 260 individual matches. At National Championship level Michael’s record reads: 1971	 NZ Under 18 Champion. 1972	 NZ Boys Champion. Under 23 Men’s NZ Champion. 1973	 NZ Amateur Champion - also Top Qualifier. NZ Foursomes. 1974	 North Island Amateur Champion. 1977	 North Island Amateur Champion. NZ Foursomes. 1984	 NZ Mixed Foursomes. At International level Michael was selected for the New Zealand Junior Team in 1971 and 73. In 1974 he represented NZ at the Eisenhower Tournament held in the Dominican Republic, and in 1975 he was a member of the NZ team that contested the R and A Trophy at Royal Durban Golf Club in South Africa. Further National honours came in 1975 with selection in the Sloan Morpeth team to play Australia. Michael ended his long association with the Tauranga Golf Club when he joined the Professional ranks, not as a player, but as a Club Professional with the Mount Maunganui Club.  After some years at Mount Maunganui Michael moved to Australia late in 2009 where he joined the Brosnan Group as Manager of their Golf World Branch in Kawana in Queensland.  All those who were associated with Michael during his time in Tauranga will long remember him with respect and admiration.

title: Men’s golf · p. 77
text:
NOEL JOHNSON

Noel was another good young player who was a contemporary of John Ward, Michael Nicholson, and Jim Lancaster.  Like them Noel was selected to represent Bay of Plenty Freyberg Rose Bowl teams of the Seventies and Eighties. Like Michael Noel spent some years in Whakatane where he won the Stroke Play Championship in 1987 and the Bay of Plenty Open in 1984. Noel was a multiple winner of the Tauranga Open played at Labour weekend.

E A (EDDIE) BURGESS

Eddie came to Tauranga with his family from Wellington when still at Primary School. He had already set himself the goal of becoming a top golfer before joining Tauranga and emulated Michael Nicholson by spending many an hour hitting wedge shots on our small practice fairway. Surprisingly Eddie won our Senior Championship on just the one occasion, his reputation tending to be built in other tournaments.

Misunderstanding the rules has cost many a golfer dearly. Our most infamous incident arose in the 1983 Senior Championship final between Brian Roderick and Michael Nicholson. Playing the 13th hole in the afternoon round Michael was on the green in three while Brian, having been out of bounds, was alongside the green in five. As Brian’s caddy moved towards the flagstick Brian made a gesture that Michael interpreted to mean Brian was conceding the hole.

When Michael lifted his ball Brian asked him why he had done so. In subsequent discussion Brian stated he had been asking his caddy to remove the flagstick. Bob Allen, the Captain, was refereeing the match. Bob was not a qualified referee and he awarded the hole to Brian though Michael should have replaced his ball under penalty of one stroke. Had this happened it is probable Michael would have won the hole and perhaps gone on to win the match. We will never know. The incident left Michael three down rather than one down. Michael showed his fighting spirit to square the match at the 18th, only to lose at the third extra hole.

Many opinions were expressed in relation to the incident. The facts may be summarised as follows. First it is unlikely that Brian would concede before chipping. Had he holed out he would have forced Michael to get down in two putts to win the hole. Secondly Michael should not have accepted Brian’s gesture before seeking confirmation of its meaning. Vague concessions are often made and it is wise to seek confirmation. Thirdly had Michael known the rules he could have put his case with a good chance of success. The incident highlighted the need for trained people to referee important matches and other fixtures. Fortunately since courses for Referees were instigated in 1986 our Club has had an enthusiastic core of qualified people available. In a follow up to the above incident Michael was playing an Inter-Provincial match for Bay of Plenty when he marked and lifted his ball from the fringe of the green in the belief it was on the green. Realising his mistake he notified his opponent that he had incurred a penalty. The opponent claimed Michael had lost the hole. A referee, who happened to be a prominent Auckland administrator, was called. He agreed with the opponent that Michael had lost the hole whereupon Michael protested that he had been in the situation previously and requested the referee to consult the Rule Book before making a binding decision. The official did so and, somewhat shamefacedly, ruled in Michael’s favour.

title: Men’s golf · p. 78
text:
At pennant level Eddie was an automatic choice in the strong and successful Championship Teams of the 1990s. At Schoolboy and Under 23 level he had an enviable record in local tournaments, winning both the Spalding Masters and Davidson Cup Match Play titles on more than one occasion, the former five times. In 1993 Eddie represented New Zealand at under-18 level versus Australia, having played in the Clare Hingston Trophy fixture in Christchurch the year before. In 2000 Eddie reached the pinnacle of his career by winning the New Zealand Amateur Championship. Soon afterwards he turned Professional with the intention of playing the Asian Circuit but was frustrated by a lack of opportunities. Gaining tournament entries proved extremely difficult and Eddie eventually applied for reinstatement as an amateur.

JAY CARTER

Jay has been associated with the club from a young age. His father Jack has served both the Club and the Bay of Plenty Association in administrative roles while his Grandfather George was a popular member in an earlier age. After reaching high standards as a Junior that culminated in his selection in the New Zealand under 18 team to Australia in 1995 Jay spent a year developing his game under the tutelage of Mal Tongue at Manor Park in Wellington. He then returned to Tauranga where he and his father took on the contract to run the Pro Shop business at the Club. The business initially employed Doug Milne, previously professional at Whakatane, to allow Jay to serve his apprenticeship under a PGA Professional and so qualify as a fully-fledged PGA Professional himself. The service provided by Jack, Jay, and their associates has been outstanding.

BRUCE BURBERY

Bruce joined the Club as a junior in the years before there was much encouragement to juniors from many senior members. Juniors were often regarded more as a nuisance than as an asset by a number of those members. With no background in the game Bruce gripped the club in a way that felt natural to him with his left hand below his right. With this grip he was soon able to hit the ball a very long way. The subtleties of the game seemed of little interest to him at that stage. When playing with his school friends he was mainly concerned with how far he could hit the tee shot. After that he was inclined to head for the next tee, the finer arts of chipping and putting holding little interest for him. Once when playing with Ken Fraser, donor of the Fraser Cup for the Schoolboy Championship, and myself Bruce was persuaded to try the ‘proper’ right hand down grip as we attempted to convince him that there was little future for him in the game unless he changed. After trying the new grip with mixed success he

stood on the 18th tee saying: ‘I have had enough of that. I’ll hit one my way.’ With that he launched a drive to the foot of the hill, a very long drive in that era of the wound ball and laminated-wooden headed driver. We complimented his effort before suggesting he hit another ball using our suggested grip. He did so and the ball finished about 40m ahead of the first. From that day onward he stuck to the new grip and was rewarded with both length and accuracy.

Always a threat to anyone in Match Play Bruce was not to win the Senior Championship until the year 2000. He then claimed to have been trying to win it for 40 years. He was a very proud and deserving winner. He repeated that victory ten years later in 2010. A very valuable member of our Senior Pennant

title: Men’s golf · p. 79
text:
teams over the years Bruce had great success in Police and Inter-Services Golf where he won the latter New Zealand Championship on more than one occasion. For the Police he represented New Zealand in ‘Test Matches’ versus Australia.

JIM LANCASTER

Jim Lancaster lived adjacent to Pemberton Park. As a boy he was employed to cut Margaret Mowat’s lawn. One day he asked her if he could have an old golf club he saw in the garage. Margaret said she thought she could do better than that and gave him a couple of better clubs that she had. With these he started hitting balls around the Park outside his fence, probably against local by-laws. One day I noticed he used the ‘left hand down’ grip. He said he had only seen Bruce Burbery hit a ball and that was what Bruce did. Jim soon adjusted to a conventional style and in 1969 became the youngest winner of the Senior Championship before Michael Nicholson took that record away from him just one year later. In that same year of 1970 both Jim and Michael were selected in the Bay of Plenty Freyberg Rose Bowl team to compete in Invercargill, pioneers in a trend that saw representative golf teams getting younger and younger in average age.

At Club level Jim won the Senior Championship again in 1978 and 1988. At one stage he turned Professional in order to run a business at the 9-hole course and Practise Range that operated at Te Maunga opposite Bay Park during the seventies and eighties. Having soon regained his amateur status he continues to play quality golf to this day

MARTIN HALL

Martin was another junior who learnt his golf in Tauranga before making his mark further afield when winning the New Zealand Maori Championship in 1998.

GAVAN MacFARLANE Another quality player to come through the junior ranks at Tauranga Gavan had a golden run in the early nineties, winning the Senior Championship in three of the four years from 1992 to 1995. Gavan represented New Zealand at under-18 level versus Australia in 1994. In 1992 he placed third in the World Junior Stroke Play Championship in Aberdeen, Scotland. Partially as a result he was elected BOP Sportsman of the year. Later he joined the Professional ranks, serving an apprenticeship at the Hamilton Golf Club. Gavan’s father Ian was, for some years, the Manager/Selector of our Senior Pennant team.

JOSH GEARY

Josh learned his early golf at Otumoetai before holding joint membership at Tauranga where, as a fifteen year old in 2001, he contested the final of the Senior Championship. On that occasion the experience of Gavin Smillie proved just a little too much for the young man who, even then, showed much of the quality play that would eventually take him to the Professional ranks. After joining the Mount Maunganui Club Josh continued to demonstrate his liking for the Tauranga course when achieving spectacular success in under-23 events and in the Carrus Tournament held on the course.

title: Men’s golf · p. 80
text:
JARED PENDER

Jared is the son of Jim Pender, a racehorse trainer based on the course next door. Jared spent much of his time on the adjacent fairways while growing up. An independent personality Jared seemed reluctant to accept advice during his early years and perhaps this hindered his golfing development.  As he matured and his game developed to a standard where he became an automatic selection in Bay of Plenty teams the difficulties of the past were left well behind. A strong young man with an excellent swing and the ability to hit the ball a very long way Jared earned New Zealand selection in the Eisenhower team that played in Melbourne in 2008. Soon afterward he turned Professional but, like Eddie Burgess before him, he found opportunities hard to come by. The developing American players have a huge advantage in being able to temper their games in the fiery cauldron of competitive College Golf. Our own young players might well consider the advantages of emulating Sir Bob Charles and getting much more experience courtesy of New Zealand Golf before attempting the move to Professional competition.

KEVIN SMITH

Kevin was already a low handicap player when he moved here from England. During his time in Tauranga he experienced success when representing both his club and his province before attracting the attention of the National selectors and consequently being selected to represent New Zealand at senior level. He featured with distinction on a number of occasions when playing the Carrus Tournament against the professionals and leading amateurs on his home course. Kevin moved to Melbourne early

in the new century.

Ron Holden was popular around the Club over many years. His standard stroke stayed close to the ground and moved in a comparatively sharp curve to the left. To see him start the ball out some 45 degrees right of the target line and have it curve back to the green was a sight to treasure. On occasion the ball refused to swing back to the left and that led to some fine entertainment for Ron’s playing partners. In the days when the practice range to the right of the 4th hole was still a scrub-covered swamp this would occasionally happen to Ron’s tee stroke on that hole. To see a ball aimed for the middle of the swamp sail unerringly there was enough to reduce even the kindest of companions to helpless laughter. It was always best to have the honour there in case that should happen. Ron is the only player known to have hit a ball out of bounds into the Bus Depot when playing the 10th hole. On that occasion his low flying tee shot struck the Ladies’ tee marker, flew straight back past him, ran right across the 8th fairway and through the fence.
