title: Women’s golf · p. 89
text: Women’s golf

title: Women’s golf · p. 90
text:
Women, or Ladies as they were then known, were accepted as members from the earliest years of the Club. The initial subscription of 5/- was half that of male members and remained at a discount until the 1990s when it was moved that all senior members, men and women, should pay the same subscription. From the beginning the Club was run by men, for men. In common with worldwide practise the course design was intended to cater for the way men played the game and women had simply to make the best of it by playing from forward tees. Nothing much has changed in that regard although recent club and ball developments have meant that some of the original design features of our courses offer a more appropriate challenge to the women players of today than they once did.

Life Member Rennie Wallis (nee Daines) told a story from the earliest days of golf at Gate Pa that perhaps illustrates the standing of women in the club at the time. The women, ever inclined to be more innovative and adventurous in their competitions than were the men, decided to hold a Flag Match for their Saturday competition. At the time their club day was on the Saturday prior to the men’s starting times. Rennie described the event as follows: “there were about a dozen of us and we were each told to bring along a flag in our bags. We did this and each of us planted our flag at the point where our handicap strokes ran out. A sea of waving flags greeted the first men as they approached the final green at the end of their rounds. On entering the clubhouse these men told us in no uncertain terms what we could do with our flags! Our Captain dashed out red-faced to remove the offending obstructions”.

Rennie recalled some of those early Lady Members: Mrs. Cook (Margaret Wrigley), Mrs. Wickham (Nan Daines), Mrs. Maltby (Violet Carr), Mrs. Hanna (Elsie Sweet), Mrs. Heald, Mrs. Jordan, Mrs. Saunders, Mrs. Ripley, Miss Phyllis Bateman, Miss Lynn Moller, Miss Nancy Snodgrass, Miss May Cameron, the three Goodyear sisters (Frances, Annie, and Eva), Miss Samuels, Miss Nora Wallis, and Miss Ivy Litten. Ladies Championships were at first played in two grades irrespective of handicaps. The first sixteen qualifiers were designated as the seniors, the second sixteen as juniors.

TITBITS FROM THE LADIES CLUB MINUTES

1937: There was a discussion on the separation of the Men and Ladies’ sections of the Club. It was unanimously decided that it would be unsuitable to change at this time.

1940: The first sub-committee was formed. It was to be responsible for the cleanliness and tidiness of the clubhouse. (Women clearly knew their place in the scheme of things). The Lady members were active in supporting the War effort by raising funds for the Patriotic Shop.

1944: The competition fee was set at 5/-.

1946: The services of a woman were secured to attend to Afternoon Teas on Wednesdays and Saturdays. The Businesswomen requested permission to play their competitions on Saturday afternoons. (It is not recorded what the reaction of the men was to this request!).

title: Women’s golf · p. 91
text:
1947: A recommendation from the AGM that three starting tees be used in turn by the three grades was discussed. (At the time the Ladies were always drawn in their own handicap grades). A secret ballot was held to decide which day was favoured as Match day. The size of the Ladies’ Committee was increased to thirteen. (How did they ever reach an agreed decision?) 1948: A new Local Rule was adopted for the Fourth Hole: ‘if a player from the tee plays her first ball from the gully she has the option of playing it or picking it up. If she decides to play the first ball, and takes a stroke, she must hole out with that ball’. (Was this a product of a committee of thirteen? Thankfully we now have better worded local rules - comprehending this one must have been more difficult than playing the hole).

1950: Competition fees were raised to 15/- for the season. Locker fees were set at 10/- pa. Another Local Rule was adopted for the troublesome Fourth Hole: “a ball played from the tee failing to reach cut fairway is Out of Bounds. Play second shot from the tee and, in the event of the first ball passing through the rough grass at the top bank, first ball is in play”.  (Was this really considered to be an improvement?).

1952: There was a Special General Meeting called to discuss the notice of motion that starting times on Club day (Wednesday) be from 12.00 to 12.45. This was not agreed to. A Ways and Means Committee was to be established to raise funds for the Building program planned to alter and enlarge the clubhouse. The hole-in-one fund fee was 1/- pa reducing to 6d the following year if not collected. (Anyone successful was awarded the entire pool with which to ‘shout’. On occasion someone would be unfortunate enough to hole out soon after another had done so only to find the ‘cupboard was bare’).

1953: It was determined that the results of Ladies’ competitions and other Club news should be published in the BOP Times.

1954: The hole-in-one fund fee was increased to 1/6d. A new Local Rule was adopted for play of the Eighth Hole. It read: “should the tee shot hit the second power pole the tee shot may be replayed. In addition if any pole interfere with the line to the green the ball may be moved away to a safe position no nearer the hole”. A vote established Club day as being Wednesday. 1955: Dr. Jean Reading established a competition for Girls of school age in order to encourage wider participation by them. The BOP/TV Ladies’ Association split from the Waikato/King Country Association. It was suggested that the social side of competition day was being lost with the system of morning and afternoon start times. A three-tee start at 10.30 was promoted as a way of rectifying the problem.

1956: The Saturday Ladies’ start time had been agreed to from 9.30 to 10.30am. There had not been enough interest to continue with Jean Reading’s School Age competitions.

title: Women’s golf · p. 92
text:
1957: Mary Shanks started golf this season and reduced her handicap to 26, winning the Junior Championship, the Junior Jubilee, and the trophy for the most improved player. It was suggested that Senior players should assist and guide this promising young player and see that she have the opportunity to play with low handicap players. (Traditionally low handicap players did not get drawn with those on longer handicaps). The Club cardigan colour was to be Navy Blue.

1958: There was another request to change the colour of the cardigan as Rotorua, Matamata and Te Puke already have Navy Blue as their club colour. 1960: Advice was received from LGU Executive member Anne Mark that from June 1st. it would no longer be necessary for any player to sign an extra-day Score.

1961: It was reported that Mrs. Rennie Gordon was assisting in compiling a History of the Club that would be published and issued as a souvenir booklet at a price of 30/-. (This presumably refers to the proposed publication first worked upon by Joan Mirrielees that was not published owing to lack of funding. Some of the material collected then has been incorporated into this publication).

1962: A proposal to allow the wearing of shorts on the course did not find favour. 1965: The resolution to start C-Graders on Tuesdays was rescinded. (C-Graders were players who had not yet earned a handicap of 36). It was determined to trial new start times for Wednesday play. Approximately six groups of handicapped players would commence play from tee 7 from 9am. C-Graders were to follow them. All others were to start from number one tee at 9.30am.

1966: The membership limits were eased to allow for 300 A-Category and 50 B-Category Women.

B-Category was to be accorded priority as vacancies arose. The Ladies’ AGM voted to have separate Club days for Junior and C-graders on Tuesday, and for Senior and Intermediate players on Wednesday. (This was probably greeted with relief by members of both groups, especially the C-Graders who were always under pressure from the more Senior players behind them, and understandably did not find the Seventh the most welcoming of starting holes. They would not be the only members to hold that sentiment.)

1969: The Club committee requested that in future the Ladies use the profits from their tournaments to meet their own expenses. (Unbiased opinion would readily concede that over the years the women have husbanded their financial resources better than have the men.)

1970: Bermuda Shorts were to be permitted on the course but not in the Clubhouse.

1971: The dress regulations were again extended to allow the wearing of Slacks on the course, but only Slack Suits would be acceptable in the Lounge. (Presumably the sky had not fallen the previous year when the first few brave souls wore shorts).

title: Women’s golf · p. 93
text:
1974: Nen Sim became the first woman ever to be elected to the Club Executive.

1977: It was proposed to provide for a nine-hole handicap for Veteran Lady members who found it difficult to complete full rounds. Play was to be from the Eleventh to the First hole inclusive. This was seen as a means of encouraging these members to continue their membership rather than retire, or move away to less hilly courses as some had done in the past.

In this regard Tauranga led the way when introducing this abbreviated form of the game prior to its widespread adoption by NZ Golf. Later we were to become one of the first Clubs to promote Nine Hole

Golf to younger players in addition to this group of older women.

The power poles on the left hand side of the 8th fairway caused many a player to lose a stroke or two and a collective sigh of relief went up when, in the Fifties, these unwelcome obstructions were removed. Local rules did not normally allow for a replay should you be unfortunate enough to strike a pole. Why the 1954 rule referred to in the minutes quoted above only applied to the second pole is a mystery. Balls were as likely as not to ricochet out of bounds after striking a pole and Murphy’s Law ensured that seldom was a ricochet favourable to the player. Perhaps the most spectacular happening was when one player’s drive struck the pole nearest the tee, flew back over his head, and disappeared into the bunker that then bordered the 7th green. Though his playing partners were amused the player was not. A bunker shot over trees to the fairway was certainly daunting. He would have been better to have declared it unplayable and gone forward to play again from the tee though some ‘expert’ would probably have told him he couldn’t do that. (Incidentally a correctly worded local rule would not allow an optional replay. If a replay was to be allowed it would need to be compulsory.)

title: Women’s golf · p. 94
text:
PROMINENT WOMEN PERSONALITIES

The following profiles are of a random assortment of women members who have made a mark through the years. They are not in any particular order, chronologically or otherwise. They are simply memories and anecdotes that came to mind to recent or present members who were asked for their suggestions. All those recognised below have made an indelible impression upon our history in their own particular way, some in competitive play, some in administration, some in each of these fields. All have been recognised by their fellow members as having contributed greatly to the very life-blood of their Club. We salute them all.

MISS ANNE MARK

Miss Mark joined the Club in 1935. She recalled that sheep then grazed the course and most greens were fenced. The course was the original layout that included holes in the racecourse oval. The ‘Hummocks’ and the ‘Drop’, both in the area of the present third, were difficult but exciting holes quite fondly remembered. Miss Mark tells her own story: “My first experience in helping Mrs. Hanna with the catering was in finding sticks to use as kindling to get the fire lit in the enormous Range in the Racing Club kitchen, and then cutting firewood to satisfy

its insatiable appetite. I first served the Ladies’ Committee as Handicap Manager in 1938, and from then on periodically until 1954. I held every office except President. I didn’t think I was the type for that. I think I won the Championship six times. We did not play it during the war years”. (Miss Mark did win the Championship on six occasions but would almost certainly have been successful in those ‘no competition’ years of 1941, 42, and 43, as she had been the winner in 1940, and again in 1944 and 1945. The other successes came in 1950 and finally in 1953 immediately before the ‘Wickham era’ began.)

Miss Mark continued: “In 1954 we formed the Bay of Plenty Ladies’ Golf Association and I was its President for three years. I then captained the Bay of Plenty/Thames Valley Russell Grace team until 1963. During that time we won the Cup three times and were runner-up once.

In 1955 I was elected to the LGU Council. The Ladies’ Golf Union was the National governing body at that time. It has now amalgamated with the Men’s governing body to form Golf New Zealand. I remained a member of the LGU Council until 1963, being honoured with the Presidency for the final two years. (It seems I overcame the aversion to accepting that role). In 1963 I had the wonderful experience of serving as non-playing Captain of the New Zealand team to the Commonwealth Tournament in Melbourne. In that same year the Tauranga Golf Club elected me to Life Membership. Despite all my previous experiences I rate that award as the most moving experience of my career in golf”. An exceptional sportswoman, an efficient, knowledgeable administrator ever ready to help those who sought her advice, Anne Mark’s sense of humour and special capabilities set her apart. She was further

title: Women’s golf · p. 95
text:
honoured when made a Vice-President of the British LGU, and a Life Vice-President of the NZLGU. Anne died at Tauranga in November 1983. She has been sorely missed.

MISS UNA WICKHAM

Una Wickham was born in Tauranga and began playing at a young age on a small nine-hole course. Armed with just one club and a putter Una followed in the wake of her parents. Her father was a very keen cricketer and encouraged Una to take an active part in that game and in all other sports she may have had access to. As a result Una excelled in tennis, hockey, and cricket as a boarder at Sacred Heart Girls’ School in Auckland where she was a student from 1937-39. In 1940 Una enrolled at Auckland Teachers’ Training College. On graduating from there she was appointed Sports Mistress at Diocesan Girls’ School. One year later she graduated with a Diploma of Physical Education from Otago University. About the same time she started to play golf seriously and quickly demonstrated her considerable talent. As a member of The Grange Club she had reduced to a handicap of four by 1948 and eventually played to a low of plus two.

On a trip to England in 1953 Una was contacted by the Manager of a New Zealand representative team that was in England at the time. One of the team had been forced to return to New Zealand on account of illness and, in Una’s words: “by the greatest of good fortune I was asked to fill the gap”.

Una played with distinction even though equipped with “the wickedest set of clubs ever seen at that level. Two woods, three irons, a bunker club, a putter, and a borrowed eight iron”. In that same year she played in the British Open at Troon, and again at Portland the following year. In both years she claimed she was “early eliminated”. Not without a fight we would warrant. One aftermath of the exposure New Zealand women were then having to International competition was the call for longer, tougher courses in this country to better prepare the top women players for these contests. It was clear that our short and open courses fell well short of the standard required to extend our most promising players so as to condition them to compete with the best overseas. Calls for the simple remedy that these top women should regularly play from the men’s tees were generally ignored. In addition club committees, dominated as they were by men, were not much interested in redesigning courses to suit women members. The best Una was able to do on her home course was to see some of the forward tees eliminated. Consequently those on the 2nd, 6th, 7th, and 16th were eliminated though that on the 7th has since been reinstated. Seldom do the best women players get to play from the back tees at holes

like the 3rd, 11th and 13th.

Una first joined the Tauranga Club in 1954 and was selected that year to represent Bay of Plenty (later Bay of Plenty/Thames Valley) in the Russell Grace Inter- provincial Tournament. That year the team won the tournament and by 1956 Una had been selected as number one, a position she retained for twenty years. The team followed the 1954 win with further wins in 1955, 59, 64, 66, and 75. At National level Miss Wickham represented New Zealand on eight occasions including Tasman Trophy and Commonwealth contests. In 1959 and 69 she won the Amateur Championship of New Zealand and in 1968, in a tribute to her longevity in the game, won the Mellsop Cup - the New Zealand Amateur

title: Women’s golf · p. 96
text:
Stroke Play Championship. Her unparalleled sporting abilities were showcased by her selection to represent New Zealand in Cricket.  Una also represented Auckland at hockey while in tennis she won the Championship at Sacred Heart (now Barradene College) in three successive years. Has any athlete, man or woman, equalled or surpassed such a record?

Dress was much more conventional and officialdom much more hidebound in Una’s heyday. Nancy Hare recalled that when Una returned from England where she had been living she was selected to make her Russell Grace debut and having suffered a spell of ill health she opted to wear black slacks when the weather turned nasty on the first morning. Not only were the LGU officials scandalised but influential Herald Sports writer Terry Mclean saw fit to write half a column the next day deploring the “dreadful attire” of this newcomer, and claiming that such garments were quite out of place on any golf course, let alone at an event of National significance. This was not the only time Una ran into controversy on the issue. One year she featured in the New Zealand Championship final and requested permission of the LGU to play in Slacks as the weather was cold and unpleasant, conditions that adversely affected her health. Permission was refused.

At Club level Una won the Tauranga Senior Championship on no less than sixteen occasions, the first seven in succession starting in that first year of joining in 1954. Olga Johnson (5 times), Pat Kidd (three times), Peg Copestake (twice), and Kath Johnstone (once) interrupted Una’s winning streak over the succeeding years until Una’s final triumph in 1980.

In 1975 Una was honoured with election to the executive of the Ladies’ Golf Union of New Zealand (LGU). There she excelled in her administrative role, especially in the area of recognising and developing potential talent amongst young players. This was an interest she had exercised during her time as a teacher at Tauranga Intermediate School where she had encouraged John Ward, Noel Johnston, and others to start the game at a young age. Both John and Noel went on to represent Bay of Plenty in the Freyberg Rosebowl as the Inter-provincial Championship was then known. When the inaugural New Zealand Mixed Foursomes Championship was scheduled to be held in Wellington in 1973 Una suggested to the young Noel that they should try their luck as a team in the event. Noel accepted with enthusiasm and the pair annexed the title in style, winning their preliminary matches by the convincing margins of 6/5, 4/3, and 5/4, on the way to a convincing 3/2 win over a Wellington pairing in the final. In her self-effacing style Una had nothing but praise for the form shown by her young partner.

Una’s untimely death in 1983 was a shock to all in the golfing fraternity. Her memory was celebrated through the institution of the prestigious Una Wickham Memorial Match Play Tournament that was held at Tauranga for many years.

MISS JOAN MIRRIELEES

Miss Mirrielees was the first to undertake a compilation of the history of the Tauranga Golf Club, beginning the research for this as early as 1974, and presenting an incomplete and unpublished version in time for the Jubilee celebrations of 1986.

title: Women’s golf · p. 97
text:
Born in 1903, Joan came to Tauranga with her family in 1910. Her father, A J Mirrielees, was a pharmacist in the town and a very active member of the original club based at the Tauranga Domain. He maintained his interest when the Club moved out to the Racecourse Reserve in 1914 and was largely responsible for the planting of a great variety of trees on the Reserve. Many of these survive to this day adding both beauty and strategic difficulty to the golf course. Joan was encouraged by her father to take up the game from an early age. Joan maintained this interest throughout her life, so much so that she was able to achieve victory in the Rotorua Ladies’ Golf Club Annual Veterans’ Tourney in 1965, shooting a meritorious 89 to annex the title.

Joan graduated as a teacher in 1924 and taught at all levels in schools throughout the North Island. In 1938 Joan went to Bradford in Yorkshire, England, as an Exchange teacher, later moving on to Lytham St. Anne’s, well known to New Zealanders as the scene of Bob Charles’ Open victory in 1963.

Back home in New Zealand Joan was active on a number of fronts including a stint as the hostess of the Women’s Hour and Shopping Report on local radio 1ZD (now BOP 95 FM) in 1959 and the early sixties. For many years she filled the role of editor of the Tauranga Historical Society Journal, researching and publishing many invaluable articles about the early history of the district. In 1984 Joan’s contribution in this sphere was recognised with the Societies’ Heritage award. Another special honour came Joan’s way when she was presented with the Key to the City in 1975. Credit for the early work done on this history goes to Miss Mirrielees. She would have loved to see her efforts culminate in a published version but, sadly, that was not to be achieved in her time.

MRS EVELYN SIM. (NEN)

In 1974 Nen Sim became the first women member to be elected to the Executive of the Club. In later years other women members served on the committee following a successful resolution to allow for a representative from the Women’s committee to join the Executive. Nen, on the other hand, was a pioneer, being elected in open competition with male nominees. No better pioneer in the role could have been found. Nen had considerable experience on the Women’s committee having served as handicapper and for many years she had written a weekly column of Ladies’ Golf News in the Bay of Plenty Times under the pseudonym ‘Bunkered’. Contrary to the fears of some on the ‘Men’s Committee’ Nen did not play the part of a militant feminist upon joining the committee. Instead it soon became apparent that she was there for one purpose only, to look after the interests of all members of the Club,

both male and female. In her quiet and pleasant manner Nen did much over the next eight years to change the mind set of those members of the committee who still retained some of the old concepts of the club being run by the men for the benefit of the men. Nen has a logical mind and her contributions to discussion were always to the point and frequently indicated the best path to follow. During Nen’s time on the committee the social life of the Club experienced a period of enhanced activity with successful dinner/dance evenings complementing the regular Opening and Closing day highlights.  In 1985 Nen

was honoured with Life Membership of the Club. Few could be more worthy of the honour.

MRS. ELSIE HANNA came to Tauranga in 1922. She won the Senior Championship in 1924 and 1926. She served on the Ladies’ committee from 1926 to 1939. In 1937 it was recorded that she presided

title: Women’s golf · p. 98
text:
over an Annual General Meeting at which the following were in attendance: Mesdames Maltby, Mowat, Mayfield, Page, Auld, Kirkby, Ronayne, Sinclair and Jervis together with the Misses Humphries, Mark, Gillanders, F, A, and E Goodyear. Interestingly the meeting was held in the Tauranga Council Chambers, the clubhouse facilities being quite inadequate for an evening meeting. Mrs. Hanna was a pioneer in catering for such events as Inter-club fixtures when water had to be heated in an outside bath and small spirit burners were utilised for boiling kettles. Mrs. Hanna was elected to Life membership at some time prior to 1948 and was the first woman to be so honoured by the club.

MISS FRANCES GOODYEAR became a member with her two sisters, Annie and Eva in 1927. Membership was small in those years and all members became actively involved and worked hard for the good of the Club. The sisters were no exception. Frances was a schoolteacher and it was not unusual to see her dismiss her class a few minutes early on certain golfing afternoons. Grateful pupils were happy to polish her clubs, clean balls, and put water in the radiator of her Ford motorcar. Frances recalled interclub matches being arranged with players coming from Rotorua, Whakatane, Thames, Te Puke, Waihi, Matamata, Cambridge, and Paeroa.

MISS EVA GOODYEAR was interviewed on tape in 1993 when she was well into her eighties and provided us with some of the earliest memories of golf in Tauranga in those pioneering years. She

recalled the old Links at the Domain with the blue Irises and the Flag Lilies though she was obviously not then a golfer. Her father Canon William Goodyear had come to Tauranga in 1896 having been appointed by the Church Mission Society to serve as Supervising Maori Missioner for the Bay of Plenty. He had arrived in New Zealand in 1878 and was canonised in 1913 to recognise his sterling work for the Mission.

PHYLL, DAWN and HELEN HARTLEY were another group of three sisters who were early members of the Club. They joined in 1929 and Dawn would sometimes accompany Mr Mirrielees when he was planting trees. She recalled his criteria for spacing the trees was to ‘hit a ball, plant a tree’. Dawn remembered the wires around the greens to keep the sheep out. She was forever ruining her stockings clambering over them. The accepted mode of dress for a young lady on the course was grey pullover, grey culottes, and grey stockings. Rather a contrast to the young women glamorising the courses of today. Dawn remembered Kit Hardy and Alison Wilcox from those early days.

PHYLL BATEMAN joined the Club in 1931. Both she and her brother Jack were devoted to the sport and were dedicated Club members. Phyll served on committee from 1947-49. Her recollections of the early days included committee meetings held at night in hired rooms and having to hit over the road into the racecourse when playing McKinleys. Personalities Phyll recalled included top visiting players Bessie Gaisford (twice New Zealand Ladies’ Amateur Champion), Ruth Hodgeman, and Elsie Heald. Rennie Daines, Hannah Bartlett, Mrs. Page, Mrs Sanders (wife of a Colonel, but not the Colonel), Claire Mayfield, Audrey Gamman, and promising junior Kathy Moloney were some fellow Club members of whom Phyll had pleasant memories.

MARGARET MOWAT joined in 1936 when her husband arrived from Gisborne to take the position of

title: Women’s golf · p. 99
text:
resident Professional to the Club. Margaret learned her golf on the family sheep and cattle Station at Ngatapa where the family laid out a nine-hole course on the area surrounding the homestead. She was rather proud of the fact that when she first played the Poverty Bay Golf Club’s Awapuni Links she gained her official handicap, thus proving that the play at home had enabled her to develop a swing that stood up to the standards of the Town players.

Soon after arriving in Tauranga Margaret was asked to take on the Secretarial role with the Ladies’ Committee which she did. She recalled that they met at Violet Maltby’s home in 13th. Avenue. Claire Mayfield was the Captain and “dear old Elsie Hanna” was President. Margaret recalled the era as a happy time with the Ladies working together to put on wonderful spreads when hosting visiting teams. Mrs. Hanna was famed for the wonderful Potato salads she produced and no one could make and add the dressing quite like her. Myrtle Ripley was especially instrumental in the drive to establish a new clubhouse in 1938. Margaret was still playing regularly two or three times a week, and to a very creditable level, until well into her eighties. Throughout she pulled her own clubs and she and her regular Monday group of similarly aged ladies played at a pace that would outstrip many younger players of today. In 1978 Anne Mark and Rennie Wallis nominated Margaret for Life Membership. The committee sought further information and nothing eventually came of the nomination.

RENNIE DAINES will best be remembered as Mrs Rennie Gordon while much later in life she became Mrs Wallis. As Miss Daines Rennie won the Ladies’ Championship three times in succession from 1920 to 1922. She served three years as Captain in the Nineteen Forties at which time she also became Mrs Gordon. Some ten years later she served a three-year term as Ladies’ President. A strong supporter of the Club from its early years at Gate Pa Rennie continued her association with, and support of, the Club throughout her life.  She was the second Woman to be elected to Life Membership following the election of Elsie Hanna.

NELL SILSON joined the Club in the thirties. She lived at Katikati and drove to golf and home again after the day’s play. Club competitions were then held on Saturday afternoons. The road to Katikati was rough and particularly treacherous in winter. Driving home on dark winter evenings must have been a real challenge yet Nell seldom missed her Club Day.

JOYCE CARNACHAN joined in 1931 and served on committee for many years during which she

organised the catering. She served the Women’s committee as Captain and later as President. Joyce was a selector for the Russell Grace Teams and in 1963 was elected to the executive committee of the TVBOP Ladies Golf Association, serving as Vice President until 1967. In 1972 the Tauranga Golf Club elected Joyce to Life Membership in recognition of her service to the Club over many years. Those who played with Joyce remembered her with affection and with not a little envy for her special touch with the putter.

AMY SMITH joined in 1936 and moved away from town two years later. In 1948 she returned and began a long association with the Club, retaining membership until 1999. A committee member for two

title: Women’s golf · p. 100
text:
years Amy won many competitions, represented the Club at Pennant level, and was chosen to play for TVBOP against the Waikato/King Country team. One year an epic contest developed for the Elsie Hanna Cup. The original conditions stipulated an 18 hole replay if the match was square after the 18th. Amy and Jean Ellis played three rounds before Jean won! The conditions of competition were promptly changed so that a decision would be reached at the first time of asking.

BERNICE WILLOUGHBY was a member from 1939 until 1999. She was another to win many competitions in her time. Bernice was a member early enough to remember the original clubhouse shared with the jockeys. Sometimes bales of hay were stored at one end. Occasionally these served as extra seating. Bernice fondly recalled scoring eagles at the sixth and fifteenth. Golf bags were much lighter then. Slung over the shoulder, as was the custom, they were more than heavy enough, especially towards the latter stages of a round. She remembered preferring the Bromford golf ball costing 1/9d. Bernice recalled Junior players always showing due deference to their elders in those times, perhaps implying that things were not quite the same today.

ANN BRANCH was a member from 1939 until 1991. She was a committee member in 1941. Her husband A J (Bronco) Branch owned a Sporting Goods store in the town that still operates under the name ‘Broncos’. Ann was one of the first members to wear slacks when playing, a trend much frowned upon by the more traditional of members, and certainly one that had long met with the disapproval of the hidebound members of the LGU hierarchy. What would they have thought of the on-course fashion of the young women players of today?

Bronco was a fine teaching Professional who gave lessons to Tauranga members, and others, over many years. His pupils were recognised for the slow tempo of their swings, and for the distinctive pause at the top of the backswing. Some felt his methods led to somewhat mechanical swings as opposed to more free flowing ‘natural’ swings. Whatever the rights or wrongs of these opinions there could be no denying the success enjoyed by his pupils. Notable amongst the more recent of these has been Peg Copestake, twice winner of our Senior Championship.

PEG COPESTAKE joined the club in 1961 having been introduced to the game by Edna Galbally. Peg soon gained her handicap and then was offered a course of lessons by Bronco Branch. Responding to

Peggy Turner, playing the knoll one day, pitched short of the bunker. The ball leaped the bunker, bounced between bunker and green, and ran unerringly into the hole. Ray Hay may have upstaged this. Ray was an unusual golfer who tended to mishit a series of three Iron strokes until close to the green when he was prone to finally hit one over the green. On one occasion Ray’s tee shot at the fifth flew low and fast before striking a tree behind the green. From there it bounced back across a bunker onto the green and into the hole. These things happen in golf yet many an excellent player goes through life without being able to claim a single ace.

title: Women’s golf · p. 101
text:
the opportunity Peg spent many hours practising after her school-teaching day was completed. She recalled Bronco’s methods did not involve hitting a ball for the first lesson or two, and new pupils were not allowed near a golf course for at least three months. This could be very frustrating to the keen beginner. The season following these sessions with Bronco saw Peg’s handicap down to single figures, a level she was able to maintain for many years. Although playing to one’s age is a not an uncommon feat amongst male players Peg is one of the few women we know to have achieved this. A strong commitment to the encouragement of junior players saw Peg an early disciple of the ‘Gillian Bannan’ method of introducing youngsters to the game. Consequently she travelled to local schools with a trailer load of clubs, hoops, mats, buckets and flags, to teach groups of about twenty children the rudiments of golf. Peg served on the executive committee of the club and in 2000 became the first woman to be elected Club President, an honour very much deserved following years of involvement in so many aspects of both the Club and the game itself. Notable amongst these have been her commitment to spreading the word on the Rules of Golf and, along with husband Noel, to the organisation of Twilight Golf.

To recognise her outstanding service Peg was elected to Life Membership in 2005. In joining husband Noel in receiving this distinction they became the only married couple to have been so honoured. Sadly Peg passed away in December 2011 within days of her return from a much anticipated trip to Melbourne to follow the fortunes of the players competing in the President’s Cup. It was wonderful that she was able to enjoy every day of that great event featuring the American team versus the rest of the World, excluding Europe.

EDNA GALBALLY joined the Club in 1943 having arrived in Tauranga the previous year to take up a teaching appointment in the two Primary Schools at Otumoetai. As Committee member, Secretary, Handicapper, and Saturday Supervisor Edna spent 23 years as an officer of the Tauranga Ladies’ Golf Club. Her quiet efficiency, her wealth of golfing knowledge, and her encouragement both to committee members and players made her a greatly valued member of the Ladies’ Club. For her services over so many years she was elected to Life Membership in 1994.

NANCY HARE joined the Club in 1946. She served the Ladies’ Committee as Vice Captain, Captain, and President. Nancy won the Junior Championship soon after joining and, in 1975, reached the final of the Senior Championship where she met Una Wickham who was in her usual matchless form.

Women golfing personalities especially recalled by Nancy included Doreen Blundell (Juno) of the Mount Maunganui Club, Linda Caruthers, Joyce Carnachan, Merle Carter, Cookie Grant, Ruby Poynter and Rennie Gordon. OLGA JOHNSON came to Tauranga from South Africa in the 1950s. She and husband Eric were members for 34 years before joining the Mount Club when Eric found our hills rather too difficult to negotiate. During their time at Tauranga they were wonderful Club members, both fully involved in all aspects of club life. Even after resigning they were regular contestants in the Friday night Twilight competitions where it was not necessary for Eric to play the hilly first six holes. Olga was an exceptional

title: Women’s golf · p. 102
text:
Sportswoman who excelled at Golf, winning the Club Senior Championship in 1961,63, 64, and again in 1970. At National level she and Una Wickham combined to win the 1959 National Foursomes, and in 1962 Olga tied with Susan Grigg of Christchurch in the New Zealand Stroke Play Championship for the Mellsop Cup. Olga was a member of the BOPTV Russell Grace teams of 1964, 68, and 70, and in 1964 she won the BOPTV Senior Championship. In 1976 she shared the same title with Miss E Fleming and Mrs. V Fraher. In later years Olga further demonstrated her sporting prowess with considerable success in Veterans’ swimming events.

NAN  WEBSTER became a member in 1952 and was active for many years. She particularly remembered early golfing partners in Cookie Grant, Pat Kidd, Dos Green, Vera Park, Freda White, Ruby Strang, and Maisey Hardy. Her own personal highlight was holing an Iron shot for an eagle two at the tenth hole. In earlier days members took their own cut lunches to golf and it was a pleasant innovation when professional catering was introduced. She enjoyed especially the services provided by Mrs. Polley and later, by Mrs. Anderson. Both these ladies made an indelible impression on those who were members in that period.

JOYCE WATERWORTH joined the Club in 1954 and was competitive at senior level over many years. She represented the BOPTV team at Russell Grace Inter-provincial Tournaments in 1957, 58, 59, and 61. She recalled that there were seven members of the team at that time with no set reserve so one member had to be left out each time. When Anne Mark was the Manager of the team she did not enjoy telling anyone they would not be playing the following day. To overcome that problem Anne would get the message across while the team relaxed in the Motel hot pool by pinching the unlucky one on her bare bottom. Joyce knew because it happened to her once.

MARY PARKINSON (Nee Shanks) and her sister JO DAWKINS began playing golf in 1957 at which time their father Arnold was still an active player. Harry Bradmore, ever one to encourage the young player, gave Mary a book on Golf for Ladies. This must have set her in the right direction for she went on to win both the Junior and Senior Club Championships and, in 1982, the Senior BOP Champion of Champions title. While Mary and Terry resided in Northland she added the Mt. Denby Senior Championship title to her tally. During her competitive career Mary represented both Bay Of Plenty and

Northland at Inter- Provincial level.

JOYCE EDWARDS joined the Club with husband Roy in the mid-fifties and soon became involved in many facets of club life. She was a committee member as early as 1957 and took on the secretaryship one year later. In 1958 Joyce became Vice-Captain and Handicapper, served as Captain from 1961 to 63 and as President from 1964 to 68. In that final year of Presidency her administrative talents were recognised further afield and she was elected Northern Delegate to the BOPTV Association in 1968, 69, and 70. From 1972-77 she was Vice-President of the Association and served as its President in 1978-79.

title: Women’s golf · p. 103
text:
In 1980 Joyce was elected to Life Membership of the Tauranga Golf Club and was still enjoying a few holes well into the new Millennium. Many wondered how Joyce managed to retain so youthful an appearance as the years went by. I am sure it was a reflection of her positive outlook, her interest in those around her, and her general zest for life. The game of golf does seem to keep a lot of participants in good health and spirit longer than is the case with many other people.

ALISON FAULKNER, who joined in 1960, recalled with pleasure the stricter etiquette that prevailed in an earlier age. Dress requirements were quite rigid. The initial Club uniform comprised grey skirts and navy cardigans. Subsequently a uniform featuring green skirts, a cream jersey, and a navy blouse replaced this. Another change meant the ladies all had to get Air Force blue skirts and jumpers with the Club insignia if they wanted to be up to date. Alison remembered Mrs. Robertson, Mrs Wagstaff, and Noeline Leech as caterers who went out of their way to ensure their service was to the satisfaction of all members. Alison recalled Nen Sim’s overseer role of the Social and House side of Club activities as being exemplary.

SHIRLEY EATON joined in 1963. In 1978 Shirley was the Ladies’ Club Captain and remembered that a highlight in the competitive history of the Club occurred that year when a team made up of Una Wickham, Val Hemingway, and Susan Harkin won the Bay of Plenty section of the Peter Stuyvesant National Team Championship played at Omanu. The team was made up of the three Club champions at Senior, Intermediate, and Junior levels. The sponsors then flew the team to Wellington, all expenses paid, to contest the National final at Heretaunga. The team did well to finish in fourth place out of a field of thirteen teams. Peter Stuyvesant was a popular brand of cigarette and tobacco companies were very active sponsors of a wide range of sporting events at that time. They sponsored a similar team event for male golfers.

NOELINE SHIEL joined the Club in 1972. In 1987 she was elected to the Club Committee and continued to serve that committee until 1994 when the Board of Management was instituted. In that same year Noeline was elected Vice-President, the first woman ever to occupy that position. Noeline was an outstanding Chairperson of the Social Committee putting an enormous amount of time, energy, and imagination into the role. With husband Des providing unstinting support and assistance Noeline did much to foster club spirit at a time when counter attractions in other spheres made it more difficult to encourage members to support Club activities. The work Noeline and Des did in facilitating Friday night Twilight golf was truly appreciated by those who enjoyed that activity over many happy years.

DOROTHY GARLAND came to Tauranga from Reporoa in 1973. She served the Ladies’ Club as both Captain and Vice-Captain and also served as President of the BOPTV Association for four years during which time Jocelyn Glen assisted her in the role of Secretary.

ROSEMARY CLARK joined in 1981 and made an immediate impact on the competitive Club scene. At the end of that first year she annexed the Senior Championship. From 1991 to 1997 she won the title on another five occasions. Another four successive championships fell to Rosemary from 2001 - 2004. Her ten championship victories are second only to Una’s sixteen. Rosemary was the Club Stroke Play

title: Women’s golf · p. 104
text:
Champion in 1991,92, 93, 94, and again in 97. Inter-Provincial honours came Rosemary’s way in 1981, 82, 83, 86, 87, and in 1991. LYN GOODHEW began her golfing career in 1982 at the Springfield Club in Rotorua before moving back to Tauranga a year later. Within two years she was elected Ladies Vice-Captain, a position she held for two years before moving up to Captain for the following two years. In the established tradition that had ensured continuity of policy over many years Lyn went on to serve as Ladies President for the two years ending in November 2001. Ever willing to serve she substituted for President Robyn Anderson when the latter was absent for a part of the following year.

In 2003 Lyn became actively involved with Nine-hole golf by assisting new players to understand the Rules and etiquette of the game following on from the clinics provided to them by the Club professionals. In 2008 she began serving as assistant to Alison Holdem in the administration of the Nine-hole section of Women’s Golf.

ALISON HOLDEM learned to play the game in 1983 at the Ngawaro Club on Hugh and Biddy McCarroll’s sheep and cattle farm at Pyes Pa. Alison held the position of Club Captain at Ngawaro and won the senior championship there in 1991. The Ngawaro Club was established by Hugh and existed for a considerable number of years before the property was sold and the new owners were not prepared to continue the course. Many members moved to the new Renner Park course that had then become established in Oropi Road. Alison joined Tauranga in 1985 while still retaining membership at Ngawaro and soon moved onto the committee, being elected Vice-captain in November 1993, Captain in 1995, and President in 1997. Almost immediately upon completing these six years of service to the Women’s committee Alison was elected to represent the Central Zone on the BOP/TV Association. She completed a six-year term in that role in 2006. Alison became involved in the Nine-hole program with Phyll Sandlant from 1998 to 2008 before taking over as Nine-hole Convenor when Phyll retired from that position. In addition to her work for Women’s golf Alison served a term as a member of the Board of Management.

ANNA BRABYN grew up in a farming district east of Whanganui called Mangamahu where there was a country course of just twelve holes and featuring the usual small fenced greens. These were a bit trickier than those usually encountered on such courses as they were electrified and hence extra caution was

required near them. The course was sometimes closed when necessary farming operations were being performed as the course was laid out on a private farm. Both Anna’s father and his sister represented New Zealand and won National titles so it was inevitable that Anna should follow them in playing the game. She was a member at Mangamahu from 1971 until 1994 winning the Senior championship on 18 occasions. While still a member there she joined Whanganui’s Belmont Golf Club in 1977 in order to further her game. There she won the championship on a number of occasions and also furthered her administrative experience through Club Captaincy and a term of four years on the Board of Management. Belmont had moved into that form of management

title: Women’s golf · p. 105
text:
structure somewhat earlier than had the majority of clubs. Representative honours followed with Anna appearing in Russell Grace teams for Manawatu/Whanganui for ten years. In the following three years she represented the same District in the Masters team before moving to Tauranga in 1995. Anna has been a member of Tauranga Golf Club since 1996 winning the Senior Championship on three occasions with perhaps more yet to come. Anna’s talents were immediately recognised in her new District where she represented the Bay of Plenty at Master’s level for a further twelve years. In her fifteen years of Master’s golf Anna was on the winning side on seven occasions, a remarkable record. During this period Anna was asked to serve as a selector for New Zealand Women’s Golf becoming convenor of selectors soon afterward. Management of National teams followed involving a number of overseas trips to tournaments such as the Queen Sirikit Tournament, the Espirito Santo World Cup, the Tasman Cup, and a number of Asian tournaments. In 2005 Anna was elected President of the Tauranga Golf Club and continued in that role to become easily its longest serving President. As President she was automatically a member of the Board of Management where her wide experience and her wisdom proven invaluable.

HAZEL CASEY learned to play golf as an eleven year old on a farm course at Waiotahi near Opotiki. Her uncle Jack Carter taught her the game. He was the father of Tauranga members George and Doug Carter, and thus the grandfather and great-grandfather respectively of the men of Golf Fusion, Jack and Jay. The greens at Waiotahi were fenced and the cows kept the fairways to a reasonable height. Hazel was armed with just three clubs, a wood, an iron, and a putter. Her first “subscription’ took the form of five large fruit tins. These were required to line the five holes the course boasted. Hazel had difficulty finding these as few families could afford large tins of fruit in the difficult years of the early thirties. A couple of years later the family moved the short distance to Nukuhau North where the sub. was five shillings, quite a lot for a schoolgirl to find at the time. After marrying during the war Hazel and Bill later moved to Tauranga where they joined the Mt. Maunganui club in 1963. In 1970 application was made to join Tauranga where membership was restricted and ‘B’ membership only available at the time. Forty one years later Hazel was still an active member. Early on Hazel became involved in assisting Adrienne Coad with helping the 36+ ladies to learn the rudiments of the game and gain their handicaps. Later Ali Smit took over from Adrienne. No professional lessons were offered the beginners so Ali and Hazel did the best they could to inculcate good swing habits into the group. When Ali left Hazel took over as the 36+ supervisor. She loved the role and took great pleasure in seeing “her girls” progress and become competent and valued members of the Club. To cover the cost of some

During the 2007 Carrus Tournament Emily Perry of Lochiel recorded the best round (65) ever by a woman player on our course. Playing off the blue tees Emily scored birdies at the first; second, fifth, seventh and seventeenth holes, together with an eagle three at the sixth. Her only blemish came at the fourteenth.

title: Women’s golf · p. 106
text:
Professional tuition Hazel organised raffles and the resulting lessons with Rick proved very valuable to the women. Not satisfied with the great job she was doing with the beginning ladies Hazel became involved teaching school children to play. In this she was helped by Joyce Paris and Fay O’Neill. When Nine Hole golf got underway Hazel was asked to look after the Saturday morning group. She loved doing this and continued as long as she was able to do so. She wanted to place on record her appreciation for the help and advice that Rick Barker gave to her in getting the new ladies started and on their way to earning their handicaps. For her dedicated service to ‘her girls’ over many years Hazel Casey was elected to Life Membership of the club in 2000.

NINE HOLE GOLF

The 1977 move by the Club to institute a nine hole handicap for women in order to cater for the needs of an older group of members who were finding it difficult to complete full 18 hole rounds on our demanding course proved to be the successful forerunner of a movement that was to have a major impact in later years. Perhaps inspired by the success of One-Day Cricket, administrators of New Zealand Golf began a campaign to institute Nine Hole Golf on a National scale. At the time NZGolf recognised that the wave of interest in the game that had flowed through New Zealand during the Sixties and Seventies had now ebbed and they were searching for ways to encourage more people to take up the game and join clubs. Nine hole golf was seen as a game that would appeal to younger working people, and to mothers with young families, as it would not commit them to as much time away from the responsibilities of modern life as did the Eighteen hole game.

Tauranga Golf Club officials were quick to see the potential of Nine-hole Golf and the Women’s Committee immediately began to actively pursue the concept. Phyll Sandlant was an early volunteer to step forward and offer to lead the promotion. Her report on the evolution of this new form of the game follows. Phyll Sandlant reports: “In February 1998 Tauranga advertised for women who would like to ‘have a go’ at Nine Hole Golf. We intended to start a group at Tauranga, the first in the Bay of Plenty. Professional coaching was offered and it was hoped the idea would appeal to young mothers, working mothers, and perhaps

grandmothers. It is, after all, a game for life.

We were overwhelmed with the response when 96 women registered on the first call. With the invaluable assistance of our Professional, Rick Barker, coaching groups were organised. When each clinic finished the beginners would play a few holes accompanied by members of a wonderful group of volunteers who would walk with them to encourage and assist them in following Rick’s instructions. At the same time these volunteers would ensure the newcomers learnt aspects of etiquette and course management. Later we introduced the women to the mysteries of Match Play, Stroke Play, Stableford and Par competition.

title: Women’s golf · p. 107
text:
The inaugural BOPTV Honda Nine Hole Tournament was held at Tauranga in 1999, thus recognising the lead that Tauranga had assumed in promoting this form of the game.

Women’s Nine Hole Golf is now an integral and important sector of our Club. A full program of organised competition on Tuesday mornings caters to a full field of members in the category.  The game is here to stay. The popularity of this form of the game is obvious and it appears there will be no diminution of interest from beginners and older members alike”.

(While nine-hole membership is also available to men there has not been the same response from them. This may be that men are better able to find the time to devote most of a day to their game, or perhaps a more likely explanation is that there has been much less encouragement provided to them. The dedication to the cause of Women’s Nine Hole Golf shown by Phyll Sandlant and her team, and by those such as Alison Holdem and Lynn Goodhew who followed, has clearly been the vital ingredient in the success of the program. In is also clear that the establishment of Nine Hole Golf represented a significant financial bonus to the Club as it provided additional income at a time when clubs throughout New Zealand were finding it difficult to balance their books.)

In recognition of her outstanding contribution to Women’s Golf as Captain, President, and pioneer promoter of Nine Hole Golf, Phyll was elected a Life Member of the Club in 2006.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 117
text:
The Tauranga Veterans’ Golfing Society was officially launched in 1952. John McKenzie was the inaugural President with Dick Phelan as his Secretary. To celebrate the Silver Jubilee of the Society in 1977 the then President, G A (Bill) Sanders, and Past President, K C (Ken) McIntyre, produced a history of those first 25 years. I can do no better than to print their history as they presented it to their members at that time and then move on to cover the succeeding 44 years during which the Society has flourished in a manner that would be a revelation and a source of great pleasure and pride to the founding members. In Bill Sander’s words in his preface to their document: “We hope that all who read this History will be caught up in the spirit of our founders and those who followed them over the past 25 years”. Here then is the history of those first 25 years as compiled by Bill Sanders and Ken McIntyre.

THE BEGINNING

Like most beginnings, what was to become our Veterans’ Society started in a very small and somewhat obscure way. Shortly after World War Two a small group of elderly golfers began meeting by arrangement on Tuesdays and Thursdays to make up friendly Four-balls so as to enjoy some easy going and pleasant golf. Under these idyllic golfing conditions the ranks of those originals began to grow and, with growth, the natural corollary was organisation. Attendance became more regular and someone soon decided that every second Tuesday a draw would be made at 12:45 pm. All who wished to play were asked to report prior to that time. Shades of the past were beginning to cast future shadows! At this point it is appropriate to ask who were those old timers who started it all. Names start to emerge including Dick Phelan, Gavin Wallace, Tom Long, George Munroe, Harry Bradmore, John McKenzie, Ron Galloway, George Willcock, Len Belk, Jimmy Mowat, Arthur Towsey, and Johnny Walker. Doubtless there were others but if the written record fails how can the best of memories make up for that? Many of those mentioned had served the Golf Club well and four of them, Phelan, Towsey, Bradmore, and Willcock, were made Life Members. We salute those original few who started something that has given such joy and golfing pleasure to so many veterans of the future.

Like Topsy, what was to become our Veterans’ Society, grew slowly but surely. In late 1952 the first records began to appear and a group organised themselves into the Veterans’ Association with John

During his time as professional to the Club Greg Holst scored an ace, and five successive twos at the par three fifth hole. Some years earlier, when the hole was much shorter and played from a tee in the North West corner across a row of trees, Robert Mowat claimed thirteen twos in fifteen consecutive rounds.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 118
text:
Above:   A happy group in the renovated lounge in the nineties.  The No-Smoking signs were now prominent. Marge Kirk,  Dorothy Garland,  Amy Smith , Nan Webster,  Joyce Waterworth, Bernice Willoughy

Above:    Prominent Veteran golfers during the seventies and eighties.

left - right:  Bill Johns,  Bill Saunders,  John Farmer, Alan Davidson

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 119
text:
Mckenzie as President and Dick Phelan as Secretary. With a great deal of courage the fledgling association decided, in 1953, to stage a five-day tournament from the 9th to the 13th of November that year. At the time the Association boasted just 23 members of which eight were on the committee. This was not unusual in many an organisation of the time. In any event the tournament must have proven to be a success as it was to be the forerunner of 24 annual tournaments to come.

During the first five years John McKenzie and Dick Phelan continued in office with their committee and Annual General Meetings would number no more than twelve to fifteen members. Play continued along the original lines until 1957 when Veterans’ day was changed to Thursday. This was not a problem as there were no Weekday Starting Sheets though sometimes a ball shoot was used. Thursday also gradually evolved into Businessman’s day and as their numbers increased so did the mutterings about ‘the old buggers in front’. Diplomacy finally came into it somewhere and ‘the old buggers’ changed their day to Tuesday where it has remained to this day.

Another change took place in the mid fifties when the Veterans’ Association renamed itself the Veterans’ Society in order to distinguish it from the NZ Veteran Golfers’ Association. Early members were never loath to dip into their own pockets to support the Society. For example we find that on the 4th of April 1957 when £3.15.0 was due to the NZVGA four members paid £1 each to meet the bill. It is not recorded what became of the extra five shillings. As early as 1955 the Vets had organised a summer competition known as the ‘Angus Plate’. The donor was Gavin Wallace who was often referred to as ‘Angus’. His trophy was awarded to the player with the best three nett medal rounds out of five nominated by the committee. About this same time trophies were donated by Dick Phelan and George Willcock for annual competition and these, together with one later donated by Frank Macklow, are still contested on our annual calendar. Dick and George each embellished their trophies with prizes that the winners could keep. The winners were instructed to make their own purchase and send the account to the donor. In the following year a winner, assuming incorrectly that he could do the same, sent off a bill to Dick Phelan who promptly forwarded it to the committee. The committee did accept responsibility for the payment but made it clear the donors had not undertaken to supply the prize on an annual basis. The committee also wrote a letter of apology to Mr Phelan.

Membership of the Society remained fairly static until as late as 1965 when Ken McIntyre can recall reporting to Jack Babington outside the Pro Shop where Jack was busily engaged in scribbling names on the back of an old envelope. Those who had reported were given a numbered disc and these were later drawn from a hat. On that day four were sent off the 7th tee, four off the 3rd, and two fours off the first. That was it and the field, about the standard number for that time, were away.

THE ANNUAL TOURNAMENT

In organising their first five-day tournament in 1953 the Executive were assisted by Miss Anne Mark and Mrs Rennie Gordon (Later Wallis). The Society reported a credit balance of £13.8.9 that, the

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 120
text:
secretary reported, would be adequate for preliminary expenses. At that time few clubs held such tournaments and those tournaments that were held appear to have been given NZ status for the ‘principal event’. Thus at our first tournament 56 starters competed in four Match Play flights for: (1) The NZ Premiership - the first 16 gross qualifiers. Won by V Mortenson of Te Puke. (2) The BOP Handicap - the first 16 nett qualifiers. Won by R H Phelan of Tauranga. (3) The Tauranga Handicap - the second 16 nett qualifiers. Won by A Sharpe of Northcote. (4) Gate Pa Handicap. Won by G Willcock of Tauranga.

The tournament was operated from the old cottage style clubhouse behind the 18th green. First prize for the ‘NZ Premiership’ was a magnificent dinner set donated by Johnny Walker. It caused some consternation because of its value, especially relative to other division prizes. Later such problems were sorted out and the amount spent in each division became more or less equal.

For the 1954 tournament Ron Galloway and John McKenzie donated Cups, Gavin Wallace a Silver Plate, and Johnny Walker a Rose Bowl. In doing so they set the pattern under which the tournament was run over future years. In 1958 Ted Bartlett donated the Honours Board that still hangs in the clubhouse. In the same year, and again in 1959, Galloway, McKenzie, Wallace, and Walker all gave money to be used to provide personal awards to the winners of their respective trophies while George Willcock provided the prize for the final day Stableford. During the same year D C (David) Collins donated the Plate that is still in use for the National Vets’ Championship. David was a winner of that championship and had earlier captained the New Zealand Cricket team long before it became known as the ‘Black Caps’. He and Ron Galloway had also given trophies to our local Veterans’ Society for competition in a ‘Yankee Tournament’.

In contemplating all of the foregoing one cannot help but be impressed by the way in which this handful of enthusiasts did all in their power to stimulate the interest of players of their day. As the number of entrants in the Five Day Tournament grew other trophies were presented. These include Dr John Mark’s Trophy (1966), George Mole’s Trophy (1973), Cliff Colson’s Salver (1974), and Basil Coxhead’s Salver (1977). The names of our trophies bring back memories of so many wonderful personalities who gave so much to the development of the Society and to the Golf Club itself.

In 1959 we held our first New Zealand Veteran Championships, the winner of the main event being W J (Billy) Castell, a member of our own Club. Almost every day for many years Billy would head for the Golf Course right after closing his shoe store on The Strand. He would then play two balls over as many holes as he could fit in, rarely having to move more than five or ten paces between the two balls. Maurice White was once scheduled to play Billy in the final of the Intermediate Club Championship. Maurice asked Jim Paterson the day before how Jimmy thought the match would go. “He will beat you by whatever margin he thinks appropriate” was the candid, if undiplomatic response. So it proved the following day.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 121
text:
In 1964 Tauranga were again hosts to the New Zealand Championship with Frank Macklow of our Club the winner on that occasion. The last time the Championship had been held here was in 1959 with E S Toogood of Poverty Bay the winner and Frank Macklow runner-up.

A perusal of some entries in the old Minute Books can be full of interest. Take for instance the financial summary following the initial tournament in 1953. It reads: Entry fees were £85.10.0 and a donation made total receipts £90. Trophies cost £60.0.4, Printing £7.15.6, Petty Cash and Secretary’s Expenses £7.1.9, Lime Juice £3.16.6, Tauranga Golf Club Green Fees £5, which left a balance of £6.5.11 profit. Also of interest is a list of the Secretary’s purchases of victuals for the 1961 tournament covering the Cocktail Party and lunches. Here they are. Cocktail Party: 6 Whisky, 3 Gin, 1 Brandy, 1 Sherry, 12 Beer (Dozens presumably), 15 dozen sandwiches, 15 dozen savouries, 6 bags potato chips and 2 lbs. of salted peanuts. Lunches:  6 quarts milk, 4 cut loaves, 4 dozen cakes, 2 dozen scones, 3 dozen Cottage Pies, 6 lbs. Blade Steak, 6 Kidneys, 2lbs. tea, 8lbs. sugar, 2lbs. ham, 3lbs. tomatoes, 12 lbs. potatoes, 1 bottle tomato sauce, 1lb. cheese, 1 pkt. Gravyquick, 2lbs. onions, 2 large pkts. of frozen peas.

All this was just part of the Secretary’s job. No wonder it was a difficult post to fill. Those of our members

who have served on the Veterans’ Committee know that the job is no sinecure, particularly when it comes to tournament time. The planning, the need for detail, the frustrations, and all the general organisation required in order to present a successful tournament call for a great deal of expertise. How fortunate then that we have had the splendid assistance of Anne Mark and Rennie Gordon (Wallis) over these past 25 years. Together these two performed all the clerical work involved in the tournament until the early Sixties when Miss Mark took over on her own. In the minutes of the meeting following that first 1951 tournament it is recorded that “our thanks are due to Miss Anne Mark and Mrs Rennie Gordon

for the smooth and capable running of the tournament”. Every successive committee has echoed the same sentiment over the past 24 years. It is noteworthy that both ladies were made Life Members of the Tauranga Golf Club.

After work one afternoon I was getting my clubs from the Trundler shed ready to do some practise. It was during Veterans’ week. An elderly gentleman came in dragging his clubs slowly behind him. “My goodness” I said. “You do look as though you have had a hard day out there”. “Hard day” he said. “You have no idea. These old buggers are really tough. The one I played today was eight under his handicap. I had to go to the 22nd hole to beat him”. He did not seem to register where this explanation might have positioned him in relation to his own performance.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 122
text:
At the Society’s 25th Jubilee Tournament Prize Giving the 1977 President, Bill Sanders, presented Miss Mark with a Silver Coffee Pot in recognition of her 25 years of wonderful service as Tournament Secretary. All living Past Presidents subscribed to this handsome gift. This thoughtful and generous act is worthy of record and in Chronological order those who contributed were Past Presidents Ken McIntyre, Kevin Thomson, Eric Blomfield, Ossie Simmonds, Cliff Colson, Len Woods, and Ken Golden. During the presentation Club President Alex Gallagher also paid tribute to Miss Mark and she replied to all those present in her usual charming and eloquent manner.

Regular Old Timers attending our tournaments have been Barney Barnett (Waikato), Eddie Edwards (Christchurch), Jim Forbes (Mirimar), and Alf Sharpe (Auckland). The latter played his last Tauranga tournament at the age of ninety. Over the years many a character has played in our Tournament and some very amusing incidents have arisen but time and space prevent us delving too deeply into these. However one Old Timer who wished to remain anonymous sent in the following anecdote that we felt may prove useful to present day veterans. We Quote: “From the third tee this player drove his ball straight into the scrub which then extended across much of the hill and was very difficult to extricate a ball from. He then played a provisional ball that was a screamer right between the two pines at the bottom, one of which is now defunct. This left a short Iron to the green. A search for the original was made and his ball located. The player did some quick thinking. He would require one stroke, or even two, to get in the clear, then another towards the gap with no guarantee of success. His silent conclusion: I can’t better my provisional and might do worse. His response followed in seconds. “That is not my ball. Can’t hold up the field. Let’s press on.” So saying he played to the green, sunk the putt and halved the hole in fives. His opponent, of course, was up one good Dunlop 65. Little wonder so many of us found it difficult to make the grade in Veteran’s Tournaments!

THE OLD TIMERS

In our earlier text we made mention of those men who founded our Society and, as there were so many interesting characters amongst them, no history would be complete without some short biographical details of them, and of those who followed in their footsteps.

JOHN McKENZIE Our first President, John was a recent arrival from Scotland. He was liable to suddenly appear quite

unexpectedly in full Highland Dress. He was President from 1953-56, again in 1960 and 1964, and yet again in 1967, seven times in all. A golfing stylist John hit a good, straight ball with a minimum of effort. As a raconteur of no mean talent he loved the telling of a tale. His mellifluous Scottish accent had undoubted appeal and his training as a Minister in the Church of Scotland ensured his delivery commanded attention. John was one of the first Vets Ken McIntyre played with upon first joining the Society and he recalls John addressing him all day as “young Man”. Ken was then 58 years old! In later years John lived alone and when asked how he fared in the kitchen his response was: “My boy, I have many friends upon whom I call not long before dinner, but early enough to allow them time to put another potato in the pot. Never the less, when forced into providing for myself, I always manage

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 123
text:
a five-course dinner. I have two Whiskeys, a boiled egg, then two more whiskeys”. John was one of the original Broadlands Finance Directors and many a veteran made good investments in Broadlands on the strength of his advice. Broadlands for many years donated a handsome trophy for our annual tournament while the McKenzie Cup is one of John’s personal donations.

DICK PHELAN

Dick was made a Life Member of the Golf Club and served as Secretary to the Tauranga Veteran Golfers’ Association, as it was then known, from its inception in 1952 until 1956 after which he continued to serve on committee. Dick donated the Phelan trophy for which we still compete. A fine golfer he retained a single figure handicap for many years. It is recalled that one Saturday after holing his final putt on the 18th green he quietly remarked: “Well, I have played to my age”. He was 76 at the time. An indication of Dick’s skill and longevity as a player is evident from the fact that he won the Senior Championship in 1930 and, 47 years later, was runner-up in the Junior Championship to then 16-year old Robbie Meyer. That 1976 Finals Day was one of the very rare occasions when the weather has been unkind to the finalists with wet, cold, and windy conditions prevailing throughout most of the day. In spite of that, or of the disparity of sixty years in the ages of the two, it was not until the 35th hole that Dick finally succumbed to his young rival.

Dick objected strongly to the term ‘Die-hards’ that was used to identify the over 70 division in most Veterans’ Tournaments and it is for that reason that we still use the term ‘Veteran of Veterans’ in our Tournament.

GEORGE WILLCOCK

George was a kindly and enthusiastic gentleman in the true sense of the word. A past President of the Golf Club, George was made a life member for his services over many years, especially his work in the

role of Honorary Secretary during the War years. The Willcock name is commemorated in the playing of the popular Intermediate Handicap Match Play event for the Willcock Cup as part of the Saturday Club Programme.

One day Grant Silvester said to me: “Keep your eyes open for green tees on the fairways”. I asked what on earth he meant. “Well it is Veteran’s week and there is a placing rule” I was told. I indeed found green tees on some fairways. It seems some of the old chaps had perfected the technique of palming a green tee as they lifted the ball prior to placing it. At the end of the process the ball would be perched on a tee, not resting on the grass. Having played the stroke they would not want to give the game away by bending to retrieve the tee. Holes such as the 11th, the 15th, and the 16th became reachable with a second stroke when played with ‘brassie’ from a teed lie. Little wonder it was hard to beat these wily characters.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 124
text:
ARTHUR TOWSEY

Arthur was another whose services the Club recognised by conferring Life Membership upon him. He is best remembered for his efficient management of the Bar over a long period dating back to the days of the old Clubhouse behind the 18th green. A martinet in his domain, woe betides anyone who overstepped the bounds of propriety. For many years a six o’clock closure was the rule despite the fact that the entire operation was outside the law applying at that time. Many a member narrowly avoided losing a finger or two as the shutter came down precisely on the hour. Fortunately the stairs then ran down at the back of the Bar and, if you were in the know, and Arthur was in a good mood, you might just grab a quick one on your way out from the back door of the lounge where it opened onto the stairs. Whilst on the subject of the ‘Nineteenth Hole’ it seems that the Veterans’ must have been a ‘dry’ society for, in 1960, a subcommittee waited upon the Club Committee to ask if Bar facilities could be made available on Tuesdays and Thursdays. This was granted much to the relief of many a member.

Dr JOHN MARK Johnny was perhaps the most dedicated of all who served the Veterans’ Society. He was President for five years after previously serving on committee. For two years John served as both President and Secretary and, as he himself put it, general factotum. This was occasioned by the fact that no one at the Annual General Meeting was willing to accept the role of Secretary so it was left to the committee to fill the post. This they never did so Johnny simply carried on. Possibly the task of running the Tournament was beginning to look formidable enough to discourage potential Secretaries and, when Harry Du Faur resigned in 1965 after three terms in the job no one was anxious to succeed him. Harry had established a very efficient Secretarial Management System which few felt they could emulate.

John Mark and his sister Anne developed the Tournament draw system we use so that a player does not play with his opponent until he meets him in a match. When John died in 1967 the Mount and Tauranga Veterans began playing for the Mark Memorial Shield to recognise his work for Veterans’ golf. In 1965 George Mole and Ron Horman presented this shield for competition between the two clubs. In 1966 Dr Mark presented a trophy for our annual Tournament and it was fitting that this was presented to the winner by his sister Anne following the Jubilee year Tournament in 1977.

HARRY BRADMORE

Harry was another to be honoured with Life Membership of the Golf Club. A foundation member of the Veterans he continued a program of planting and care of the trees on the course that had been initiated

by Mr Mirrielees in the first years of course development. In this Harry was assisted by his son Maurice, another keen golfer with a real interest in improving the aesthetics of the course. Another son, Alan, was a victim of World War Two. Alan is remembered through the Alan Bradmore Memorial Trophy that is contested in the Saturday Programme.

GAVIN WALLACE

Gavin was our second President and also served as Treasurer for a number of years. He stimulated a lot of interest in Veteran activities and retained a lively interest in the society beyond his playing days. He donated a number of trophies during his membership.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 125
text:
JIMMY MOWAT

Born in Scotland Jimmy was the first Professional appointed to the Club in 1936. He was a foundation member of the Veterans and a regular Tuesday/Thursday participant from the earliest beginnings. Long after his reinstatement to the amateur ranks members, both male and female, would seek his advice on the finer points of the game. His interest in course development served the developing club well over a long period of time. When Jim and his wife Margaret sold their property, which is now the Tauranga Girls’ College, the turf on their tennis court was rolled up and delivered to the eleventh green where Grant Silvester laid it. It provided an excellent surface from the beginning and continues to do so today. Margaret was also an enthusiastic golfer and active participant in club affairs. She made a great job of catering for our first Veterans’ Tournament in 1953.

FRANK MACKLOW

Frank has only recently had to give up golf. A perfectionist the slightest deviation from a straight shot down the fairway would see him on the practise fairway ironing out the problem prior to heading home. On the committee in his first year of joining the Vets he later served five years as Treasurer. Frank twice won the New Zealand Veterans’ Championship, first at Tauranga in 1964 and again in 1965 at the Hutt Club where he defeated Harold Black. In 1969 Frank was runner-up in the Championship.

SYD RANDELL

Syd, along with others, claimed responsibility for the lone pine tree between the 13th and 17th fairways. Originally there were three but two were removed after careful analysis revealed the one reprieved caught the most balls. Syd served the Tauranga Golf Club as President from 1954-56.

OTHER PERSONALITIES

There was the dignified ex school master Noel Gibson whose greatest profanity was “oh drat it”. A noisy opponent, caddie, or fellow competitor would immediately be quelled by a single look cast down from his full height of six feet.
