He was one of four to be given a presentation upon achieving the age of eighty, a tradition that still survives in the society. The other three were Harry Bradmore, Percy Maude, and Johnny Walker. Percy will be remembered for his home made trundler, and for his tees made from sections of milking inflations cut to different lengths and strung together with an old boot lace. Following Percy could be something of an ordeal as he was prone to shed tees, pieces of trundler, and articles of clothing as he went along his way.

Harry Smith contributed much towards the new Clubhouse built in 1954.  When it was undergoing its first alteration Harry claimed: “they can knock down those walls but they will need a bulldozer for that corner. I laid those bricks myself”. They did in fact survive that first alteration but not the next.

Where do we stop? There are so many that could be mentioned. Men like Les Woods, Frank McFadyen, and Bob Innis, all served on our committee and are still with us in 1977. Later we will attempt to cover events and people from 1970 onwards. In the meantime all veterans salute and thank the ‘Old Stalwarts’ who pushed the boat out on its first days of a successful and rewarding voyage.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 126
text:
THE LADIES

Our association with the Ladies’ Club goes back as many years as we have existed, as far back in fact as to our earliest Tournaments when Margaret Mowat volunteered to handle the catering before any sort of regular canteen existed. The Ladies always helped at the tournaments with afternoon teas and Mrs Wardrop will be remembered for her kindness in providing baskets of goodies for our midweek games, and also for the wonderful floral arrangements she set up in the clubhouse.

The first organised matches between the ladies and ourselves were played for a shield that still resides somewhere in the clubhouse. The ladies could not find a way to register a win for the shield and the contest gradually faded away. In those early times the two groups alternated the supply of afternoon tea and the results were impressive. As a fuller catering service became available at the Club it became inappropriate to continue the self catering and those marvellous afternoon teas became a distant memory.

More recently we have established ‘Melbourne Cup Day’ when the Vets entertain the Ladies at a golf match held on Cup Day, the first Tuesday in November. The Ladies compete for a Cup presented by Mr and Mrs Tom Dick. The Ladies have christened it the ‘Fillies Cup’, while the men play for a tankard engraved ‘Co-operation 1972’. This was given to the Vets by the Ladies in appreciation of the

assistance given to them during the staging of the Russell Grace Inter Provincial Tournament held in Tauranga that year. The day is an important one in our calendar and involves sweepstakes on the Cup and a social afternoon culminating in a live showing of the big race. As a measure of appreciation for the co-operation shown the Vets by the Ladies Club we presented them with a tray for competition amongst themselves. Each year we send a cheque to provide a personal prize for the winner. This spirit of co-operation engendered so many years ago is still as vibrant today. As an example we relinquish a Tuesday so the Ladies can stage their Championships and, a few weeks later, they give up one of their days so that we can stage the Mark Trophy fixture with the Mount Maunganui Vets. May such happy associations long continue.

Editor’s Note: This arrangement no longer applies as circumstances changed in 2013 so as to make it untenable.

THE PRESENT

From 1970, when Ken McIntyre was President, the Society began to grow dramatically and this growth was indisputably tied to the general influx of retirees to the Tauranga area and to the reputation and popularity of Veterans’ golf at the Tauranga Golf Club. In three years our numbers increased from 50 to 100 and the old starting board disc system, designed for just 48 people, became taxed to its limit. Eventually our members became frustrated with starting delays and waiting times of up to two hours before they were able to tee off. When membership reached 120 there was no choice but to institute an advance weekly starting sheet. Many members disliked this system feeling it might destroy the friendly social atmosphere that arose when everyone arrived and left together. Fortunately this did not prove to be the case.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 127
text:
Up until this Jubilee year Veterans have been accepted from age 55 but in an endeavour to contain our numbers to a manageable level that limit has now been raised to 60 years. Our roll now stands at 130 plus. All the trophies presented years ago by some of the founding members are still regular features of our annual programme. A notable addition to the trophy list came in 1976 when Colin Cathie gave the Society the Cornelius Cup, named for his very successful racehorse of that name. This fine cup is contested as a Match Play event with the final being held on Club Finals Day. This has become recognised as the major award contested by our members over the season. In addition to presenting the cup Colin arranged for a debenture, the annual interest from which would provide funds for a personal prize to be awarded the winner. This was a most pleasing and generous gesture by Colin.

A notable achievement of recent times was the feat of one of our members, Bill Johns, to hold a single figure handicap for 50 consecutive years. Bill, or “Dummy “ Johns as he has been affectionately known for many years was honoured by the Tauranga Golf Club with the presentation of a silver salver to commemorate this remarkable feat, most of which was achieved prior to his moving to Tauranga.

Cliff Colson, President of our Society in 1974, has done an enormous amount of work for Veterans’ golf over recent years. He has been a committeeman, Treasurer, Secretary, and President. His work has been recognised by his current appointment as Vice President of the NZ Veterans’ Association. It is

hoped that this will lead to the Presidency in 1978.

The story of our Society has so far been one of men who have been prepared to give generously of their time, their talents, and their material resources. As the Society has grown it has required a high level of organisational expertise and we have never lacked for volunteers with the necessary skills. It has not been possible to cover all aspects of our history in this publication, nor to pay personal tribute to all those many people whose ideas and practical assistance have contributed so much

to the success of the Society over the past 25 years. What has been done has been achieved in a wonderful spirit of friendship and camaraderie that would be hard to match elsewhere. The solid base that has been established over the first 25 years augurs well for the years ahead. We hope that in telling this story we have rekindled some of the wonderful spirit of the past so that the ideals of our founders may burn brightly into the future.

So ended the History of the first 25 years of organised Veteran Golf in Tauranga as compiled by Bill Sanders and Ken McIntyre.

THE SUCCEEDING YEARS

When Bernie Baker became President of the Society in 1993 he inherited a number of papers relating to past happenings within the Society. These included a copy of the above history of the first 25 years and, upon reading it, Bernie was prompted to initiate the production of an album to record the Officers and activities of the Society on a year-by-year basis. This album commenced in 1974 as this was the earliest year for which full committee details could be discovered. In his preface to the album Bernie recorded that, in 1985, the committee of the Society approached the Golf Club committee with the proposition: “That the Vets carry out projects, mutually agreed, that will benefit the course and

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 128
text:
members. In return the Club management will not charge the Vets course fees for their annual five day tournament”. This proposal was agreed to and, although the five day tournament is now consigned to history, the Vets have continued to support the Club through a wide variety of projects and services right through to the present day.

Peter Steward warrants special appreciation for his immaculate calligraphy and fine photography that grace the pages of the album from its birth in 1993 until 2004 when Peter’s failing eyesight made it impossible for him to continue the work. His back-dating of the album over the 20 years prior to 1993 must have required many hours of meticulous work before the album was ready for presentation to the Society. It is to be hoped that the album will be updated from 2004, and continue to be maintained as an invaluable record of the activities and administration of the society.

While many individual veteran members had provided voluntary services to the Club over earlier years it was not until 1985 that official projects began as a routine part of the Society’s year. In that year the following projects were successfully undertaken under the leadership of President Phill Johnston: • Provision of a new Golf Club flag • Overhaul and maintenance of the ball washers on the tees • Improvements to the first tee surrounds

• Repainting of the Men’s locker room • Stripping and repainting the walls in the Dining Room.

Phill Johnston, a fine sportsman who played both golf and tennis until very late in life, probably holds the record for the longest continual membership of Tauranga Golf Club. This was commemorated through the planting of a Pohutukawa tree to the left of the 14th green. An accompanying plaque records that Phill was a member from 1936   until 1996.

In 1986 President Wally Calver saw the following projects to fruition:

• Construction of a brick entranceway adjacent to the 10th green. This was to commemorate the 75th anniversary of the Club. The bricklaying expertise of Andy Graham was especially valuable in this undertaking, the bricks being chosen to blend with those featured on the Club House at the time. Unfortunately those bricks are no longer discernible, having been plastered over presumably to match the Club House. • Replacing stolen and vandalised bunker rakes. • Painting 11th tee shelter. • Painting trundler shed interior. • Assisting with sweeping and removing cores from greens. This assistance continued twice yearly until 2008 when machinery was hired to do the job. Walter Tombleson and Peter Baveystock come to mind as two who participated in this work at virtually every coring throughout the period.

In 1987 under President Noel Payne the Society:

• Provided the Club with a Walkie Talkie set to enable communication with the starter on tee 11. • Rebuilt the surrounds of the first tee.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 129
text:
• Assisted with the design and construction of the new 9th green. • Purchased and installed eight additional ball washers.

In 1988 Bert Krause was in the Chair and the Society: • Purchased and installed an additional six ball washers. • Provided a new blade attachment for the Toro mower. • Regraded the route to the fifth green and constructed a trundler park at the same hole. • Repaired and sealed the area by the Pro Shop. • Built bark gardens with mowing strips by tenth tee and beside trundler shed. • Assisted the staff to spray paspalum in eradication program.

In 1989 under President George Mason the Society: • Built a new bark garden adjacent to the eleventh green. • Built an observation tower forward of seventh tee. •  Upgraded the first tee. This included installing a block wall. • Assisted staff in cleaning around bunkers prior to Finals Day. • Erected new tee marker boards. • Felled and removed dead trees. • Cleared the old garden in front of the Club House. • Repaired and rebuilt block work on the sixth tee.

In 1990 under President Bill Vinnecombe the Society: • Erected a wind screen along the fifteenth hole boundary. • Planted new trees, particularly on fifteenth hole and behind fourteenth green. •  Removed trees felled by storm. • Erected new tee marker boards. • Cleaned and painted trundler shed exterior and Club House veranda. • Assisted staff in spraying for eradication of Cape Daisy. • Improved drainage around 5th and 7th greens and 8th fairway by installing soak holes. • Constructed a pathway to the side and rear of the 7th green.

In 1991 under President Merv Kelly the Society: • Completed ground works around 7th green and 8th tee area. • Rebuilt and repainted the fence behind 8th green and 9th tee. • Supplied and erected pipe rail to ladies 3rd tee. • Maintained gardens, an ongoing project. • Erected new club sign at Cameron Road entrance. • Maintained ball washers, another ongoing project. • Purchased new blue tee markers. • Supplied material and constructed steps to the 2nd tee. • Installed pipe and chain fences on path to Club House.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 130
text:
In 1992 under President John Newman the Society: • Built a set of steps and laid a path from the 3rd green to 4th tee. • Laid a path from the 11th tee to fairway. • Laid a path from the17th green to 18th tee. • Continued planting and development of “Vets’ Dell” below 3rd tee - now somewhat neglected. • Installed a plaque at the 11th tee entrance gate. In 1993 under President Bernie Baker the Society: • Installed a garden and steps at the 5th tee. • Supplied and installed a second flagpole on Club House. • Assisted in remodelling several bunkers in association with the Greens Staff. • Replaced stolen or vandalised tee markers. • Provided and installed fairway distance markers.

In 1994 under President Paul Munn the Society: • Painted all the seats around the course. • Refurbished the starting sheet display cabinet. • Installed gauge to indicate water level in reservoir.

In 1995 under President Bernie Child the Society: • Repainted the car park lines. • Financed and constructed new practice nets beside the reservoir. • Assisted in the installation of new course irrigation system’ • Trimmed the skirts of most trees that come into play. • Cut up firewood for sale. • Installed the David Coates memorial seat at the 10th tee.

The reference to firewood and skirt trimming above suggests that the Noel Copestake led group of Wednesday volunteers was initiated around that time. There has been a hard core of regulars on that team since, the core changing only as the years take their toll and new volunteers step forward. It would be interesting to know just how much the Club has gained from the activities of this group, both in terms of actual cash provided to specific projects, and in the amount saved in the costs of removing dead trees, trimming trees, tidying up fallen branches, and supplying firewood to the Club House. It would be difficult indeed to estimate the value gained from ‘Dads’ Army’, as the group is known, since

its inception. While the group as an entity deserve the accolades of us all some inevitably stand out. Without Noel’s enthusiastic example it is very doubtful the group would have survived more than a year or two, or perhaps even got started. Deserving of special mention would be Jim Swainson. Jim’s expertise with a chain saw has made a huge impact on the overall health, appearance, and ‘playability’ of the trees on the course. President in that year of 1995, Bernie Child, continues to lead projects as late as 2008 even though he retired as project manager in 1999. Bernie’s ability to design, develop, and maintain equipment has been a revelation to all who have worked with him. The Club recognised his immense contribution over many years by conferring Life Membership upon him.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 131
text:
In 1996 Ron Holden was President of the Society.

• One major project highlighted Ron’s year. This was the construction of a Caddie Car shed abutted to the Greenkeeper’s building beside the practise range. The Society provided the materials, then designed and constructed the building. • On-going activities included the maintenance projects mentioned earlier.

In 1997 under President Ted Otway the Society: • Painted the Course Managers Staff facility. • Painted the distance marker blocks. • Repaired paving at the first tee. • Repaired the path to 5th tee with bitumen seal. • Laid rubber matting on the above path. • Fixed new Colour Steel cladding, gifted by Longrun Industries, to the inside of the Clubhouse fascia. • Realigned and relaid a path from 17th green to 18th tee, including new timber railing. • Poured concrete storm water channel beside 18th tee. • Poured concrete to form a storm water catchment off the car park. Redrilled the existing soak hole to a depth of 8m. • Installed irrigation to serve the shrubbery on the path to the 18th tee and to the bank of the 2nd tee. • Purchased a new fairway irrigator and associated hoses. • Fabricated a 1.8m wide steel roller for use behind the greens mower.

In 1998 under President Matt Sproule the Society: • Laid a storm water channel along the pathway over the causeway. • Resurfaced paths on the 4th, 5th, and 11th holes. • Arranged and financed drilling and piping of soak holes at a number of locations. • Financed and constructed the erection of pipe railing beside the roadway past the10th green.

In 1999 under President Joe Loughlin the Society:

• Completed projects commenced in 1998 including the design and installation of a sliding roof over the sand-storage bin in the implement shed area. • Maintained the car park lines and garden areas.

In 2000 under President George Riley the Society:

• Donated $6000 to be used to finance an upgrade of the path at the 1st tee and that from the 3rd green to the 4th tee. • Purchased and installed a compressor and air pressure cylinder in the implement shed. • Installed piping to wash down area for golf carts. • Maintained paint work on pipe fencing and car park lines. • Contributed funds to Ladies’ shrub planting project.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 132
text:
In 2001 under President Ross Ellison the Society: • Donated $4500 towards purchase of fairway irrigator and the support of Junior Golf. • Installed drinking fountain by 1st tee. The “Fountain of Youth” built by a Child. This project was an independent Bernie Child enterprise.

In 2002 under President Peter Walker the Society:

• Donated $12 000 to the Club. All but $400 of this came from the firewood team.

In 2003 under President John Turnbull the Society: • Carried out regular maintenance work. Mike Champion’s work in maintaining ball washers was especially noteworthy. • Assisted the Club program to replace trees around the course by donating $200 from Society funds. A number of individual veterans contributed independently to that programme.

In 2004 under President Mike Sandlant the Society:

• Provided funds for the construction of an appropriate lectern for use in the clubhouse. Joe Carr voluntarily did the actual woodworking to bring this to fruition. • Improved the surrounds of the toilet block beside the 13th tee.

In 2005 under President Ian Anderson the Society:

• allocated $2000 for the purpose of sealing the path from the 11th tee to the fairway. • painted the rails indicating out of bounds on the 10th hole.

In 2006 under President Bob Diprose the Society:

• assisted in tidying the course prior to the Carrus tournament. • assisted in the coring program by sweeping and removing corings - a regular project.

In 2007 under President Hugh Boughtwood the Society:

• laid a new sealed path from the 5th green to the 6th tee incorporating reconstruction and resealing of all sealed areas around the 6th tee/8th tee complex. This was jointly financed with the firewood team, and supervised by Denis Smith. Peter Bourne was involved in the planning while a number of members provided their labour. • relaid the path alongside the 15th tee by removing invading tree roots and surfacing with

crusher dust.

In 2008 under President Jim Miller the Society: • allocated $2000 for the renovation of the practice nets. This work was carried out in 2009.

In 2009 under President Phill Simpson the Society: • allocated $3000 for an upgrade planned for the 15th tee and surrounds.

title: Veteran men’s golf · p. 133
text:
In 2010 under President Ross Fletcher the Society: • provided finance for the connection of the water supply from Cameron Road to the fountain at the 13th green. • Contributed $4000 towards the establishment of the turf nursery developed beyond the third fairway. • Veteran volunteers helped in laying Windsor Green stolons on the 18th fairway and the turf nursery – a full day project.

Cliff Horsburgh was playing the eleventh hole one day in the company of a gentleman who was claimed to have been the Captain of a Club in the Manawatu. Cliff’s tee stroke was seen to ricochet from the roof of the stable out onto the fairway. As Cliff set off down the path towards it the visitor enquired if perhaps he should play another. Upon Cliff asking why he would do that he was informed his ball was out of bounds. “No. It is in the fairway” protested Cliff. “Yes but it has struck something out of bounds so that is what counts” was the response. After Cliff gained support from the other two in the group the visitor grudgingly conceded the point with the statement: “Well, that is not how it would be handled at our Club”.

Ray Pittams Ray heads the list of those members who have achieved the feat of playing to or below their age on a number of occasions.  While other multiple winners include Pat Kendall, Clive Sheerin and Cliff Breeds, none approach Ray’s record. During the Spring of 2013 Ray played his fiftieth such round and followed that up within days with his fifty first. Ray retired from farming in the Waipa Valley of the King Country and moved to Tauranga in 1977. Having been a regular visitor to our Labour weekend tournament Ray had a soft spot for the Club and sought membership only to be told membership was closed to all but those boasting a National Handicap. Consequently Ray joined Omanu and was admitted to Tauranga as a restricted B category member in 1980 before finally gaining full membership.   Ray first played to his age at the age of 71 in 1996 and has achieved the feat each year since with the exception of 1999 when he was 74.   Ray became a valuable member of our Intermediate Pennant team and featured in the winning team of 1998.  To cap his membership at Tauranga he won the Intermediate Championship in 2012.

title: The women veterans’ golf club · p. 134
text: The women veterans’ golf club

title: The women veterans’ golf club · p. 135
text:
This organization was launched in 1987 under the enthusiastic instigation of Jean Mack and Phyl Carter, the latter being recognised as the first president. Phyl and her husband Reg were wonderful Club members who both participated fully in Club activities over many years.  When the undulations of our course became rather too much for Reg in his latter years they became members of the Omokoroa Club where they again participated very fully. Their home was adjacent to the entrance of that Club and Phyl took on the role of caterer to the Club for a number of years during which she provided a magnificent service.

Tauranga women members who were actively involved with Phyl in establishing the fledgling Lady Veterans’ Group included Hazel Casey, Marg Calver, Mona Lilly, Kath Christie, Joan Standford, Shirley Morris, and Shirley Crawford. This group were ultimately elected to form the committee when the inaugural AGM was held in November 1988, Marg Calver serving as the first elected President.

At that first meeting it was decided to request that members should make a $2 donation each year to maintain membership. A further donation of $1 was requested so that a presentation could be made to the caterer Mary Goodjohn who gave up her day-off in order to cater to the group on the one Monday each month when the veteran women held their competition day. Mary was most gratified to receive a kitchen slicer from the proceeds of this collection. Hardly a personal gift but very practical as the kitchen was, at that time, ill equipped for the functions it served.

In 1989 a tradition was established whereby members would travel by bus to Okoroire during the October coring week in order to enjoy a round of golf followed by a group luncheon at the hotel there. Twenty-nine ladies made that first trip and enjoyed a wonderful day out. The costs were interesting. The bus cost $8 per head, green fees $5, while for lunch there was a choice of an $11 buffet or a three course meal for $15.

From those early years it was established that the AGM would be held in November and take the form of a Christmas lunch preceding the meeting. Fifty-two members attended the AGM of 1989.

In July 1990 ten veteran ladies from each of the Omokoroa and Mt. Maunganui clubs were invited to participate in the monthly competition so beginning a tradition of Inter-club visitations. In November 1990 another step was made in the direction of establishing relationships with other clubs when an open Christmas Hamper Tournament was staged in association with the BOP/TV Lady Vets Association. These tournaments were organised into five zones within the District with Te Puke, Omanu, Mt. Maunganui, Otumoetai, and Tauranga members being eligible to compete in the Tauranga event. The Veterans negotiated a reduction of $100 on the $500 fee normally charged for the use of the course. One hundred and five players participated in that first event.

At this stage in the history of the Lady Vets no subscription had been required beyond the initial $2 donation upon joining. Despite this the club had been able to build a surplus as the result of raffles, the Okoroire trip, the Christmas function, and other activities. Consequently the Treasurer was able to report to the AGM of 1990 that the Bank balance was near to $400. The ladies responded to this

title: The women veterans’ golf club · p. 136
text:
healthy situation by donating $200 towards the cost of upgrading the Ladies changing room. It was further resolved to continue to hold the Christmas function on a Monday in November not designated for competition although some members were in favour of holding the meeting following a morning round of golf.

Mixed events in cooperation with the men vets proved very successful and popular with all those who participated during those earlier years. Following such an event in October 1992 the men donated three dozen balls to the lady vets to be used as prizes on their competition days. By 1993 membership had risen to 92. An informal ten holes of golf were organised to precede the Christmas luncheon and AGM that year. The Treasurer was able to report a profit of almost $600 on the year’s activities leading up to the 1994 AGM. Clearly the organization was in very good heart. Much of the profit generated was the result of the generosity of members both in donating prizes for the raffle table, and in purchasing tickets in those raffles. I wonder how often someone won the prize they had donated.

From the beginning the Lady Vets affiliated themselves to the BOP/TV Lady Veterans’ Society with members paying a joining fee of $5. The District Society organises four official tournaments each year at two-monthly intervals in addition to a ‘Home Links’ teams competition and the Christmas Hamper events held in the five zones. All these events are open to women aged 55 and over. The tournament events are run in age groups, the highest of these being for golfers of 75 years or more. Shirley Crawford represented Tauranga on the District committee for a number of years before handing over to Kath Christie, another stalwart supporter and promoter of Veteran Ladies’ Golf.

In 1994 members voted in favour of travelling to Walton rather than Okoroire for the annual bus trip. The subsequent trip proved very successful. The inclusive cost of $20 for bus transport, green fees, and lunch at the Walton Club being considered very good value indeed. This experience opened up the idea of varying the destination chosen for these trips from year to year and in 1995 the trip was made to Paeroa. Though some found that course a little too undulating for their liking the trip was voted a success by the majority who travelled there. The reaction to course steepness was intensified by a later trip to Waihi following which it was cautioned that greater care needed to be exercised in selecting future venues as members were “not as young and fit as they once had been”.

The equitable distribution of golf balls as competition prizes appears to have been a contentious issue over a number of years. A Special General Meeting was even called in 1995 to debate the issue. At the meeting a proposal to divide the competition into three groups was lost and a subsequent motion to award balls based on Stableford points in one grade was carried by a wide margin.

In 1996 the Club was requested to stage the Home Links Teams event but when the Club Management required payment of $10 per participant the event was transferred elsewhere. The Lady Vets committee did try to negotiate a better deal with Management and were very disappointed that their pleas fell on deaf ears. They felt they had been let down by their own Club as the fee sought appeared to be excessive in comparison to those charged by other clubs in the District.

title: The women veterans’ golf club · p. 137
text:
By 1999 Nine Hole members had joined the monthly competitions and were integrated into the field. Play was now organised in fours and it was reported the caterer was unhappy with this format, as the pace of play was slow in comparison to the earlier play in threes. This caused a delay in completing the round and players coming in for lunch. The committee resolved to continue with play in fours. The Players’ Committee advised that the Lady Vets should accept players on handicaps up to 54 as this was now an official handicap under the new Slope system.

By the turn of the century membership had grown to include 102 Eighteen-hole members and 23 Nine-holers, though the average attendance was seldom much over forty-five. BOP Zone tournaments catered for fields of 120 and more to show that Veteran Golf was strong throughout the District. A team from Tauranga travelled to the Tauhara course in Taupo to claim the first ever victory for the Club in the Home Links Competition. The successful team included Hazel Casey, Sybil Grant, and Fay Horan. Perhaps inspired by this success the Club voted to have more competition days with official draws being made for the first and third Monday of each month. Kath Simmonds was seen to be doing an excellent job of organising the nine-hole players on these days.

Carmel Country Estate sponsored a tournament in October 2002 that attracted a field of 102 from a wide range of clubs. While the tournament proved an unqualified success the sponsorship sadly was not continued beyond that year. Bay Radiology continued to sponsor the popular Grandmothers’ Tournament for several years until 2005 when Palmer’s Garden Centre became involved for the first time.

In 2003 it was proposed that the Lady Vets no longer be represented on the Players’ Committee. While the committee resolved to formally object to this their objection was not successful and there has been no restoration of that representation.

It appears that Veteran Lady Golfers all became Veteran Women in 2005 in keeping with other female golfers throughout the Country. In that year the President’s report noted that research had determined that the first AGM was held in 1988 with Marg Calver elected President. Prior to that it would appear that Phyl Carter had been recognised as presiding over an unofficial organization the year prior. Notable amongst the women elected to office in 1988 was Shirley Crawford who served on the committee almost continuously until 2005. Shirley was elected President for the 2002/3 years and represented the Club at District level for several years. For the record the following statistics taken during the 2006 season showed the average attendance to be 25.6 Eighteen-holers and 10.7 Nine-holers. The largest field hosted 34 of the former and 18 of the latter. Understandably most members are ‘fair weather players’ and attendance falls dramatically when rain threatens.

By 2007 accumulated funds had reached such a level that the committee voted to donate $400 to the Club with the suggestion this be used to provide decorative Planter Boxes. Total sponsorship through the season amounted to $515 with Gate Pa New World, Aussie Butcher, PaknSave, Fresh Fruit of Chapel Street, and BB’s Coffee Shop of Fraser Cove being willing supporters. The Grandmothers’ tournament attracted 92 entries, an indication of the strength of Veteran Women’s golf.

title: The women veterans’ golf club · p. 138
text:
In 2008 the group instigated an Interclub fixture where they invited veterans from Matamata and Te Puke to visit. A special general meeting the same year voted unanimously to reduce the qualifying age from 55 to 50 though a 55+ tournament was still held with Golf Fusion providing $800 worth of sponsorship, an exceptionally generous gesture indeed.

After many years of a roll-up starting system the veterans instigated a draw for their Monday competition, the change being accepted with enthusiasm by the vast majority of participants. It is nice to know where and when you are starting well in advance of teeing off.

Kathy Gregg, in announcing that she would be retiring from the presidency at the end of the 2010 season, donated a trophy to be known as the Women Veterans’ Presidents Trophy. The competition format for this would be the prerogative of the serving President each year.

Club funds had again reached a healthy profit and the sum of $500 was donated to the Golf Club with the suggestion that a rail be installed to assist descent from the sixth tee. This had not appeared by 2011.

The 2010 tournament was open to players 50 years and over and again attracted a strong field of some 90 players. Sponsorship of $1000 from Althorpe Village ensured the success of the tournament. Greerton Lotto meantime had established an on-going sponsorship involving $30 vouchers and three golf balls per month while Artisan Jewellers sponsored the Pairs tournament.

In 2010 Connie Breeds retired from organising the summer golf programme, a job she had done with enthusiasm and efficiency for a number of years. Beryl Smith and Adrienne Coad volunteered to continue the work so ensuring this successful initiative would continue. Over the years Women’s golf has not suffered from any lack of well qualified, enthusiastic volunteers to take on the many roles that need to be filled in providing for the administration of both the playing and the social side of golf. Trophies played for during the season include the Jean Mack trophy over three rounds of Stableford play for women of 65 years and over, the Birdie and Founder’s Trophies, each presented by Phyl Carter, the Joan Standford Memorial tray awarded to the player scoring most Stableford points on the day of the Club Birthday in June, and the Val Western Putting Trophy. The Grandmothers’ Trophy for the best Stableford was donated by Tom and Edna Dick who also donated the Fillies Cup awarded to the woman recording the best Stableford score on Melbourne Cup day when the Veteran men invite the Ladies to join them for golf and sociability.

title: Administration · p. 139
text:
CHAPTER ELEVEN

ADMINISTRATION

title: Administration · p. 140
text:
In 1904 it was a Man’s World run by men for the benefit of men. In the realm of golf this was possibly even more pronounced than it was elsewhere. At the original Club based at the Domain women were welcome so long as they did not interfere with the ‘proper playing of the game’ as practised by the men. This is evidenced from Local Rule 9 of the card that read: “ On Saturday afternoons Gentlemen may pass Ladies on any part of the course”. Rennie Wallis’ recollection of a Flag Match played by the Ladies on a Saturday in the early years of golf at Gate Pa, as described in Chapter 11, further emphasises the position women golfers held in the Club hierarchy. The Club Committee, which controlled all things related to the course, the finances, the clubhouse, social activity, employment, and men’s competition golf, was made up entirely of men until the election of 1974. That year marked the emancipation of women golfers at Tauranga. Evelyn (Nen) Sim, backed by the strong support of a large contingent of women members, threw her hat into the ring for election to the ‘Men’s Committee’. Nen’s election was never in doubt and she proved to be a wise choice to represent the women of the Club and an invaluable member of the committee over a significant period.

The constitution had never stood in the way of women serving on the committee and, had the women wished it, their voting strength could easily have seen women elected at any time prior to Nen’s pioneering success. Under the constitution women could have been elected to any position on the committee, even that of Men’s Captain! Possibly they were perfectly happy to run their own affairs during the week and let the men get on with the complexities of maintaining the course and facilities. Women did have full voting rights at annual meetings and could thus influence major issues should they so wish. We can also be sure that many a committeeman listened carefully to what his wife had to say before casting his vote on certain contentious issues. The women members were very efficient in the organisation of their own affairs. Their competition programming, their handicapping, their social activities, were all organised with enthusiasm and expertise. In many of these respects they could have shown the men a thing or two, and probably sometimes did.

For four years Nen Sim carried the women’s banner on the Club Committee until 1979 when joined by Loeta Hutcheson. At the AGM in August 1978 the women members moved to have a woman member appointed to the General Committee annually. The motion was eventually carried on a show of hands after the voice vote had proved indeterminate. Some of the opposition to the move came from the fact that the opportunity already existed for women to have adequate representation. Hadn’t Nen Sim already demonstrated that? Loeta Hutcheson was subsequently appointed to the position and was

followed by Peg Cross in 1980. From then until the advent of the Board there were usually two women on committee, one elected and one appointed. Noeline Shiel was an elected member from 1987 through to 1994, a record term for a woman member. Later in 1994 when the Board became a reality Noeline was elected Vice President. Perhaps this paved the way for Peg Copestake who became the first woman to be elected Club President when she succeeded Gary Baker in 2000, a landmark event for the new Millennium. It had taken nearly 100 years but now the emancipation of women within the Club was complete with a woman being elected to the highest office. It was not long before Anna Brabyn was to continue the trend by assuming the Presidential chair.

title: Administration · p. 141
text:
At the fifth hole one summer morning Noel Hockin, then Secretary Manager, holed in one during a round that started before 6 am. This was the day after the Races and punters, as was normal in earlier years, had been parked on the 8th and 9th fairways the previous day. First of his Sunday morning four to climb up to the elevated tee Noel discovered that someone had been “caught short” the previous day and deposited human waste in the centre of the tee. Feeling duty bound to clean up this disgusting mess Noel did so before teeing up and playing the perfect shot which duly reached the bottom of the hole for Noel’s first and only hole in one in 45 years of playing the game. That day must have proven to be an awfully long one for Noel who was never one to shy away from a celebratory drink or three.

The advent of the Board of Management in 1994 inevitably resulted in the committee becoming redundant in the form under which it had existed over the previous ninety years. This made little difference to the administration of specific groups such as the Women, the Veterans, or the Thursday players. It did have quite a profound influence on the administration of Men’s competition golf. Where previously a Match Committee, the members of which were drawn from the Club Committee, had supported the Captain and his Deputy they now became part of a stand-alone group with restricted responsibilities. Further these officers had once been part of a strong committee responsible for all aspects of Club management. Now they had responsibilities essentially limited to managing Men’s competition golf including representative golf. This appeared to make the job less attractive and it became difficult to find people willing to stand for positions on the Men’s Committee. In addition life styles had changed and many members, through work and family commitments, could not find the time to make themselves available for committee work. Those who did step forward often stayed for only a year or two with the result that continuity was tenuous at best. This was an unfortunate and unexpected disadvantage arising from the introduction of the Board system of Club governance. Gradually the problem resolved itself as the Saturday men came to realise the importance of consistent leadership and a level of continuity began to flow through their administrative structure once more.

The concept of a Board of Management to control the financial aspects of the Club began to be discussed seriously in the early nineties as other Golf Clubs around New Zealand began to adopt this form of management. An informal investigative group consisting of Ted Bold, Rex Edmonds, Barry Jensen, and Bruce Simister reported to Committee in August 1994. They recommended that a Board of Management be established to handle the business aspects of Club management with a separate committee to control the playing and social aspects of club life. Maurice White and David Mowat were appointed to join that group which would then prepare a final document to present to a Special General Meeting of the Club. Honorary Solicitor Bruce Gordon was of immense value in assisting the group to draft the appropriate wording that would be needed both to present the concept to Club members, and to amend Club rules appropriately in the event the proposals should be adopted. Ultimately 187 members signed the attendance register when the proposals were presented, and adopted, on the 17th

title: Administration · p. 142
text:
of October 1994. At the AGM a month later Bruce Partridge and Joyce Paris became the first elected members of the Board. Club President Noel Copestake and Player’s Representative Paul Munn joined them to form the nucleus of the new Board. In accordance with the new rules these four then invited Ian Cross and Jackie McDonald to fill the remaining positions Inaugural Chairman Bruce Partridge had a difficult two-year term as the Board strove to establish itself in a club environment that was not entirely supportive. In spite of the democratic process by which the Board came into being there were those who lamented the demise of the previous committee system. To their mind the Board had too much power, the players and their committees too little. The Players Committee suggested they should act as the Greens Committee in addition to their other responsibilities. The roles of Board, Committee, and General Manager were clearly not yet established in the minds of all participants. Attitudes changed as successive Boards began to convince Club members that the Club was able to make real progress under the new management structure. The financial position, a problem for as long as anyone could remember, improved under Board management, the clubhouse was virtually rebuilt, the Pro Shop was enlarged and made more attractive and, most importantly, the course showed continual improvement in appearance and playing quality. While some would claim these improvements would have been made equally quickly under the old committee system it is difficult to believe that to be true. Progress under the old system had been stalled for far too long. Aylene McGregor, who had done an excellent job in a role she had taken on with some reluctance, continued to act as Manager during 1995 though she was unwilling to take on the more onerous responsibilities associated with the role now envisaged for the General Manager. The Board subsequently appointed Chris Linn to fill the position. He took up the new role in October 1995. The work of the inaugural Board was made more difficult as a result of this selection as the new manager proved somewhat less than satisfactory and after three years a replacement was sought. In December 1996 Bruce Partridge stood down from the Chair, citing pressure of work. Bruce remained on the Board until the AGM of November 97 when the Board elected Joyce Paris to fill the Chair. Jackie McDonald stood down in 1996 and was replaced by Barbara Glynn who, soon afterward, was appointed Chairperson. By November 1997 Barbara had a new look Board to Chair with Bruce Simister and David Mowat as the elected members, Michael Sandlant and Noelene Shiel as President and Player Representative respectively, while Barbara and Ian Cross continued as the invited members.  The first task of the new Board was to appoint a General Manager to replace Chris Linn. Barbara led the panel that recommended the appointment of Grant Scoones who took office in March 1998. The two proved to work very well together. Barbara was a strong Chairperson who established excellent procedures for future Boards to follow. At one stage of her term the Trustees of the Golf Club Trust were expressing doubts as to

the ability of the Board to run the affairs of the Club. These were powerful personalities who wanted to impose conditions upon the Board before they were willing to loosen the purse strings by which they held the Trust funds. As an accountant Barbara had sound financial skills and was able to approach these people and convince them that both she and the rest of the Board had both the wisdom and the expertise required to utilise the funds in a responsible manner. In the end the Trustees were pleased to wind up the Trust and make the funds available to the Board to be used in the Clubhouse rebuild. The willingness of the trustees was made especially evident when Avon Carpenter, a long-standing Trustee, seconded the motion to proceed with the clubhouse redevelopment program. In doing so Avon assured the AGM attendees of June 2000 that the Trustees were unanimous that the decision to wind up the

title: Administration · p. 143
text:
Trust and make the funds available specifically for the clubhouse project was in the best interests of the long term future of the club. Without Trust funds of $230 000 being made available it is doubtful the project would have been completed.

In October 1998 Grant Scoones presented the Board with a Business Plan for the years 1999 to 2004. In this plan the Mission Statement read: “To provide a quality golf experience for all players in surroundings of excellence”. A month later he presented a second paper entitled: “Club Leadership Guide”. In this he states: “Board members must provide leadership. They must be as good at their job as they expect the General Manager to be. The GM must be the Chief Executive Officer, and seen to be that. The Board must give the GM and the Club strategic direction. The Board must formulate policy and empower and enable the GM to implement that policy. The Board’s mission is to achieve the objectives of the membership. The Players Committee is to be responsible for the playing and social aspects of Club life and is to report to the Board via the General Manager”.

Current and future Boards might do well to study these two papers and note the concepts they outline. Together they provide much of what might best serve the needs of an evolving membership.

Barbara Glynn completed her term as Chairperson of the Board following the 1999 AGM of the Club. Barbara could be well proud of the progress made during her term. She was chiefly responsible for guiding the Board through the difficult period of uncertainty that precedes the wisdom of maturity. The dramatically remodelled and modernised clubhouse stands as a monument to her endeavours. Though building did not commence on the project during Barbara’s term in office the initial concept was developed, and the funding put in place, during those years.

The new Board elected David Mowat to the Chair and invited Jim Verran and Alison Holdem to serve as invited members. President Gary Baker, Player Representative Peg Copestake, and elected member Tony Gallagher completed the Board of six. Two major projects occupied the Board at the time. These were ensuring that the best possible result was obtained from the clubhouse redevelopment and that the condition of the fairways be improved. The story of clubhouse development is told elsewhere in this History.

Two options appeared to be available to improve the playing quality of our fairways. The first would involve a major commitment to developing a comprehensive fairway watering system, the second to

introduce fairway grasses that would thrive during our driest summers without the need for additional watering. Estimates at the time suggested it would cost $300 000 to $500 000 to set up full fairway watering, plus another $50 000 per annum in running costs. There was no guarantee that the required volume of water would be available in perpetuity.

David Ormsby, our advisor from Turf Research, was invited to meet with Club representatives to present the case for establishing a suitable Cynodon cultivar on our fairways. Windsor Green was considered to be the most suitable of those available. This grass had been successfully introduced to a number of Northern Clubs, notably Gulf Harbour where the World Cup had been staged within twelve months

title: Administration · p. 144
text:
of establishment. David gave estimated costs of $7000 to $10 000 per fairway using imported turf. A decision was made to trial Windsor Green on the 11th and 13th fairways and the contractor supplied and planted stolons into these in November 2001. This experimental planting was made possible by a grant of $25 000 from Renner’s Bar and Pub Charity. Members of the Board waited anxiously as the new turf slowly established itself and spread across the bare ground. Meanwhile Club members were dubious about the prospects for the turf and unhappy with the inconvenience of lifting balls from the developing areas. Many were critical and vociferous in their claims that the Board had made a very unwise decision. The eventual success of the fairway conversion program will be told later in this story.

Following the AGM of 2001 the new Board consisted of elected representatives David Mowat and Bob Birch, invited members Margot McCool and Richard Cashmore, President Peg Copestake, and Player Representative John Roberts. It was noted that the objective of increasing membership had seen some degree of success with total membership increasing from a low of 855 in 1997 to a healthier 1109 in 2002. These figures do not tell the full story though as senior membership, not total membership, is the important factor in relation to Club finances.

The Board determined that it was not logical that the President should continue to chair General Meetings of the Club as the Board were the body responsible for the Financial and Administrative functions of the Club and consequently the Board Chairperson was best positioned to conduct such meetings. The Club adopted this policy.

David Mowat completed his three years as Board Chairman in November 2002 and was replaced by Richard Cashmore.  David was elected to the Presidency and so remained on the Board. Bruce Calderwood and Tony Reynish were newly elected Board members. One of this Board’s first responsibilities was to appoint a Greens Superintendent to replace Murray Clark who had decided to step down in order to reduce his responsibilities. Brendan Allen was appointed and he made an immediate and significant impact in the role. It was unfortunate that he was induced to move to bigger things in Auckland before he had time to fully develop his ideas for our course.

The Board had long recognised the difficulties that were associated with the Financial and Membership years being significantly different. Consequently plans were made to align these in order to facilitate budgeting and other issues of financial management. Changes were adopted by the AGM of 2003 with the result that the financial year now concludes on January 31st with the AGM required to be held before

April 30th. The opportunity was taken at this meeting to present a major upgrade of Club rules. This was adopted without serious opposition.

During the period of this Board a number of major alterations to the course were made. The 5th, 7th, 10th, 13th and 17th holes were altered significantly, while minor alterations were made elsewhere. Opinion on the value of these to the playing quality of the course will differ from one player to the next but it would be true to say that not all such alterations have been widely accepted as being positive steps forward.

title: Administration · p. 145
text:
It was interesting to note in the Board minutes of June 2003 that the Board directed their Chairman to attend the next meeting of the Men’s Committee in order to stress to them the importance of that committee focusing their energies on the responsibilities allocated to them through Club rules. These were to attend to the needs of Men’s competitive golf.  The Board was concerned that the Men’s Committee appeared to concentrate much of their energy on matters relevant to the Board and Management, and that the direction of much of this was negative. This was an example of the difficulty some individuals and groups found in adapting to the new management structure of Board and Committees. Gradually the structure has been accepted as the benefits it confers have been recognised and most groups have learned to concentrate their efforts in furthering the interests of their own members. The Men’s Committee has understandably had the most difficulty with adapting to its role as for some 90 years their members had effectively managed all aspects of the Club’s affairs through their various sub-committees.

Included with the August 2003 Board minutes is a paper entitled ‘Where are we Heading’?  This was presented to the Board by President David Mowat and discusses a number of aspects of Course and Club development that continue to be relevant to future planning. Over the years Committees and Boards have discussed many topics and put forward many ideas worthy of consideration by those who follow them. An occasional perusal of these ideas from the past might well prove a rewarding exercise for future administrations.

The 2004 Board received a report from David Ormsby of the NZ Turf Research Institute in which he recommended the Club concentrate on encouraging Browntop in the greens. While Poa annua may be seen to dominate over the winter months the Browntop would prevail from September through May and so provide an excellent playing surface over most of the year. To encourage Browntop more aeration and deep root encouragement was needed. The greens should be oversown with Browntop following each renovation. This represented a throwback to earlier times in the fifties and sixties when grooving and seeding with Browntop was a standard annual procedure on our greens. Sometimes progress is made in a circular fashion. Other recommendations harking back to an earlier age were to keep the pH (acidity) level low between 4.9 and 5.3. Nitrogen levels were to be moderate and Potassium level low (below 3%). I have to wonder when, and why, we got off the Browntop track that had previously proved so successful. Mr Ormsby also stressed that the Cynodon fairways would require careful thatch management to provide the best possible playing surface. This has proved only too true.   Opinion throughout the Club on the merits of Cynodon fairways was at this time still divided though the Board

was united on the need to push forward with the program. Brendan Allen and David Ormsby presented a summary of the main points for and against the contending strategies of Cynodon versus full fairway watering to the Board in 2004. The following points were made.

Water requirement Full irrigation would require 1020 cubic metres of water per day. The club had resource consent for only 200 cubic metres per day from the stream and was unlikely to be granted additional rights.

title: Administration · p. 146
text:
Town water supply would be prohibitively expensive. Bore water availability is questionable at best, and expensive. The Racing Club bored to 1500ft to get 75cubic metres per day at a temperature of 40ºC.

Reticulation Cost estimate for full irrigation to fairways was $446 000 plus GST or $500 000 if the greens and tees reticulation was to be upgraded in conjunction. Maintenance costs Current maintenance costs on the two Windsor Green fairways was approximately $3500/ha/annum. The other fairways with travelling irrigators cost approximately $3000/ha/annum. Over time this difference would disappear as the cost of controlling Poa annua on the Windsor Green fairways reduced. Extra cost of maintaining irrigated fairways Irrigated fairway does not mean perfect fairway. Additionally there is a cost spiral involving extra fertiliser, extra use of fungicides and insecticides, extra system maintenance and extra mowing. This extra mowing means an increase in costs through additional fuel, staffing, and machinery maintenance and replacement costs. Without major drainage and regular renovation work the fairways would become very wet in winter. All this meant the additional costs associated with irrigated fairways were conservatively estimated at $40 000 per annum plus another staff member at $25 000 minimum. This estimate was in line with what had been found at other courses. Comparative playing surface Compared to the existing fairways Windsor Green is

1)	 Far superior from January to April, 2)	 Superior in May, June, November and December, 3)	 Similar from July through to October.

Their conclusion Developing Windsor Green is a far superior strategy for the Tauranga Golf Club to adopt than that of irrigating existing fairways. It will be cheaper to introduce, no more costly to maintain, and will give

better playing surfaces longer term.

Faced with information such as this, and with the evidence developed from the first two trial fairways, the Board had no difficulty in adopting a policy to convert all fairways to Windsor Green (a Cynodon variety) as rapidly as resources would allow. While this variety does show winter dormancy in line with other warm weather grasses it still provides an adequate playing surface through the dormancy period. Over the following years improved techniques were developed to convert fairways using stolons harvested from our existing fairways. While keeping costs down there were disadvantages associated with this as conversion was piecemeal and members were inconvenienced as individual fairways were

title: Administration · p. 147
text:
taken out of play for varying periods. Even so this was less intrusive than would have been the case had the course been closed completely while all fairways were converted simultaneously.

On leaving the Club in 2006 Brendan Allen provided the Club with a summary of some of his thoughts for the future of the course. He was strongly in favour of the Windsor Green introduction, gave pointers as to the management techniques he had found most successful with it, and felt that the fairways would continue to improve over several years as the Windsor Green dominates and weed invasion by Poa annua and other species is reduced. He was also supportive of the strategic development plan provided earlier by Alex Glasgow and adopted by the Club in General Meeting as a blueprint for future development. Brendan stated that the plan was sensibly aimed at meeting the needs of the mid to longer handicapped player, the emphasis of the plan being on modernisation rather than development. The message was to make the most of what we have, not aim for something we cannot be.   In the context of Brendan’s comments it is interesting to note that George Kinghorn, one of our ‘young guns’, wrote to the Board in 2004 to suggest he felt the Board should concentrate on providing better course conditions rather than attempting to provide additional length and difficulty. George felt that the present course design provided a great environment and a good test of golfing prowess for Club members and visitors alike. Many a Club member would endorse those sentiments with enthusiasm.

Bunkers on the course were a topic of much official debate at this time. They have probably been the topic of many an unofficial debate throughout the history of the Club. Brendan was of the opinion that the feature bunker on the Knoll should be eliminated for a number of reasons, most important of which was that it was a danger to staff when operating machines. Eventually the bunker was remodelled and now appears to be destined to survive as an important visual feature on this signature hole even though it is the destroyer of many a promising round. One of the justifiable criticisms of this bunker is that it severely penalises the poorer player amongst us while having virtually no impact at all upon the play of the more talented. This is in conflict with the valid theory that hazards should be placed so as to penalise the good player who strays rather than the poorer player who is well capable of penalising himself without the need for course intervention. The visual nature and the strategic position of this particular bunker probably determine that it remain as ‘the exception that proves the rule’.

Brendan’s parting shot was to the effect that the bunker upgrade program formulated by the Course Development Group should be put into action immediately as “further member input will only unnecessarily delay the process”. Most of the program was proceeded with though not to the satisfaction of all.

While bunkers do add considerably to the workload of the Greens staff they also serve a number of important roles.  Commander Harris claimed they could be placed so as to act as lighthouses guiding the safe route to the fairway or green. A number of those he designated to serve that purpose have been removed, presumably because they were considered to serve no useful purpose and added to the cost of course upkeep. Not all would believe their removal was justified or beneficial. The role of bunkers as hazards is often poorly understood, perhaps because of the pristine condition of most seen on Television, and because the extremely talented players seen there have so little trouble recovering from them. In spite of this bunkers have proven to be a very efficient and fair way of providing a means

title: Administration · p. 148
text:
by which a wayward stroke might be penalised. The Board that was elected in 2005 had a new look about it. The members were Richard Cashmore as Chairman, Anna Brabyn (President), Kevin Steward (Captain), Bruce Calderwood, Murray Goodhue, and Margot McCool. Now that a very successful clubhouse upgrade had been completed this Board turned its attention to the Pro Shop. This was seen to provide an important first impression to newcomers to the Club and its condition at the time was not in keeping with the standards the Board aspired to. Plans for the upgrade were prepared in 2004 and the new-look facility was completed in time for ‘Golf Fusion’ to move in during February 2006. The new operation headed by Jack and Jay Carter introduced a new standard of service to members and visitors alike. ‘Golf Fusion’ was required to operate under a new agreement that required them to extend the role to one considerably wider than had previously been the case. This they have done with the result that the level of service provided to members and to visitors alike would surely not be exceeded elsewhere in this country.

The 2006 Board appointed Graeme Duncan, previously based at Inglewood, and a native of Scotland, to the vital post of Greens Superintendent. Graeme proved his worth quickly and the course continued to develop as it had done in recent years through the skill and application of men of the ilk of Brendan Allen and Murray Clark.

Richard Cashmore retired from the Board in 2007 and was replaced as Chairman by Murray Goodhue who unfortunately served for just that one year. Consequently the Board of 2009 had something of a new look about it with new members Richard Craven and Michael Smith joining Anna Brabyn, Bruce Calderwood, Murray Goodhue and Margot McCool.

Richard Craven was thrust into the Chairman’s role rather sooner than he may have anticipated when the 2010 elections saw Graham Cathie and Bob Diprose elected to join the President and Captain. These four invited Richard and Margot to continue in their roles. Richard stood down from the Chairmanship after just the one year so adding to the instability that is inevitable when management roles turn over too quickly. Following the 2011 AGM Graham Cathie was appointed to the chair after just the one year on the Board. Michelle Towersey and Evan McKain were invited to join the sitting members.

SECRETARIES AND MANAGERS

Any organisation whether commercial, charitable, public or private is very dependent upon one particular person to act as the hub upon which the business of the organisation revolves. In the first years of our Golf Club that person was the Secretary, a role filled by Mr John Bull until he was elected Captain. The job was then elevated to Honorary Secretary/Treasurer and filled by Mr G A Ward though the honorarium, if any, must have been very small based on the level of expenses quoted in the BOP Times of the day. Perhaps Mr H B Mountfort, who was said to chase about the Township to collect subscriptions in order to be able to pay to have the Gate Pa Links mown ready for the new season, was the first to really get the Club established on a more secure financial basis. At one time the firm of H B Mountfort and Company was very prominent in the town. It was an Agricultural and Horticultural Supply

title: Administration · p. 149
text:
Company headquartered in Harington Street where a Produce Market now trades. Later the company moved to the corner of Cameron Road and 12th Avenue before being taken over by Dalgety’s who continued to trade there until themselves merging and fading into history under the Wrightson banner.

Colin Evitt was possibly the first professional to take on the job of Secretary/Treasurer following on from a series of Club members who had served in an honorary capacity. Col, as he was known, was a partner in an accountancy practise in the town. Though Col only held the job for a couple of years before moving to Hawkes Bay he established procedures that were to serve the Club well into the future. When Col vacated the job in 1957 he was replaced by N H E (Noel) Hockin, a colleague who had moved to Tauranga from Whakatane. A keen sportsman Noel had been active in cricket and golf at Whakatane, both in the playing side and in administration. From 1951-53 he had been President of the Bay of Plenty District Golf Association. First appointed Secretary/Treasurer to the Club in 1957 Noel was promoted to the newly created post of Secretary Manager shortly afterward and became involved full time at the Club before retiring in 1967. With his background in sport and his professional qualifications in accounting Noel was a real asset to the Club. He was strong on public relations, a genial and friendly host, and a true gentleman in the old-fashioned sense of the word. His appointment was an inspired one and set the standard for those who were to follow.

As the job moved from Secretary to Secretary Manager and finally to Manager three men stand out as having brought something special to the role. A number of others came and went without leaving a lasting legacy in their wake. Noel Hockin was the first of the memorable trio. The next was R J (Royce) Lahood.

Royce Lahood was recruited from Inglewood where he and his brother Sonny owned a Snooker Parlour and a Dry Cleaning business. Like Noel, Royce was active in both golf and cricket as both player and administrator. At Inglewood Royce had not been averse to active involvement in pitch and ground preparation for cricket, nor in voluntary work at the Golf Course as required. Appointed to the Secretary Management job at Tauranga in 1970 Royce filled that role until 1983 when he retired. Royce was exceptional in the field of public relations. He knew every member by name and greeted each with warmth and enthusiasm thus giving him or her the impression that they were both respected and valued as Club members. Even more impressive was his ability to recall the names of those visitors who came once a year to play in the Labour Weekend Tournament. These would be visibly surprised and delighted to be welcomed back by first name. Even green fee players who visited only occasionally

were sometimes surprised to be greeted by name.

The role of Club Manager is not an easy one to fill. In addition to good public relations the Manager is expected to be an expert Financial Manager, a good communicator, a convivial host, an excellent Personnel Manager, a promoter of the Club, a Tournament organiser. If in addition the incumbent should have an understanding of the game of golf including course management and player psychology this would certainly help him or her to better fill the role. To expect to find all this in one person is to expect the near impossible. Royce was no exception. His weakness was in the office side of the job where, were it not for the assistance of Henry Becker and others, Royce would have had difficulty in keeping

title: Administration · p. 150
text:
everything up to the standard required. Henry was a retired Post Master who took up golf only upon his retirement. Late to the game he became a true enthusiast claiming to find a new secret, and even a new swing, each time he went out to hit practise balls. Henry served not only as assistant to Royce but also at one stage took on the job of Secretary to the BOPDGA.

Those who worked with Royce will remember him with great respect and admiration. During his nearly 14 years as Manager the Club was involved in a high level of activity. On the competition side the Men’s North Island Championship and the Women’s Inter Provincial (Russell Grace) Tournament were each held. These were additional to the regular Amateur tournaments, and to the Spalding Masters and PGA Tournaments. Major clubhouse extensions were undertaken and irrigation installed to tees and greens. Water was sourced from the Kopurereroa stream for the first time. Social activity reached a peak with Twilight Tournaments and Friday night meals proving popular. The pool table was at the height of its popularity, which added to the conviviality throughout the Club. Bar trading remained outside the law and application had to be made for a new Booth license to cover each special occasion. Under cover of this a large supply of liquor would be purchased to meet future needs up to a year ahead.

The third member of the ‘Great Triumvirate’ was appointed in 1998. Grant Scoones served in the New Zealand Air Force before taking on Sports Management. Before his appointment to Tauranga Grant managed the Port Nicholson Yacht Club and was CEO of Squash New Zealand. Grant was the first to truly serve the management role in the Club. He had the vision to see what needed to be done in order to set the Club on a sound financial base and the drive to lead the Board towards that goal. The major weakness in the financial management of the Club had been a failure to set subscriptions sufficiently high enough to enable course and clubhouse development to progress at the level most members would consider desirable. From the very beginning subscriptions had been set at a level to cover little more than annual running costs. No provision had been made for machinery replacement or course improvement. Staffing was kept at minimal levels. Any expenditure beyond this had to be borrowed against the hope that future members would eventually repay the debt. Whilst it is perfectly reasonable to expect future members to cover a share of development costs it is not reasonable to expect them to cover daily operating costs. This failure to maintain subscriptions at such a level as to cover annual operating costs and also provide for the replacement of plant and machinery had placed a burden upon the Club’s resources throughout much of its history. Many an AGM featured long discussions on the question of subscription increases. Successive committees were frustrated as they presented thoroughly researched documentation to justify subscription increases that would enable them to meet

current costs and also put aside funds for the future only to have these voted down or substantially reduced. The 1970 AGM will probably best be remembered for an amendment by Mr Fookes to the motion calling for a $5 increase in subscriptions. The amendment was to limit all subscription increases to a maximum of $3. The said gentleman (a banker) was thereafter known as “Three dollar Fookes”. The Club still suffered under the same burden of debt resultant upon this type of thinking twenty-three years later. The 1993 AGM received a proposal from the committee to increase subscriptions by $20 per member. It was claimed from the floor that adopting this proposal would result in a serious fall in membership. An amendment was then put to reduce subscriptions by $30 on the basis that this would encourage new members to join. When this was defeated another amendment to the effect that no

title: Administration · p. 151
text:
increase be made was carried and another committee was frustrated in their desire to move the Club forward.

Nothing much had changed by the time Grant Scoones was appointed in 1999. The previous manager had been asked what he intended to do to prevent the Club running up deficits. His answer was that he would resign if the Club ran at a deficit the following year. There was a deficit, of course, though whether he honoured his pledge or was encouraged to move on is a moot point.

It has to be said that the Club environment was in a state of change at the time Grant Scoones came onto the scene. These changes were conducive to the Club moving forward in a manner that had not proved possible in the past. Central to this was the fact that the Board of Management was now firmly established, Board members understood their role and the Board was slowly gaining the confidence of a majority of the membership. The strength of the Board style of management lies in the restricted role the Board has. It is responsible for providing the best Course and Clubhouse facilities possible under prevailing circumstances. It must do this while ensuring that Club finances, staffing, and forward planning satisfy membership requirements as far as is reasonably possible. The Board was not to be concerned with running competition golf, with promoting social activities, nor with the numerous, and often trivial matters, that committees of the past often found themselves involved with. Consequently Board members were expected to devote their energies to a concentrated sector of Club governance with the expectation that this would lead to better husbandry of financial resources. Similarly the General Manager was not contracted to involve himself in the organization of competitive golf. This was to remain the responsibility of the sectional committees. Inevitably there were areas related to competition where the Manager did become involved. These mainly related to major events such as the Five Course Classic and the Carrus Tournament, not to normal Club competition.

Another change related to the attitude of members. Who, even ten years before, would have believed that the Club would vote in General Meeting to raise women’s subscriptions to the same level as men’s? Further who would have believed that the Club would vote to allow the Board to raise subscriptions by up to 5% without reference to members? These changes were made in the first few years following the introduction of the Board and were symptomatic of changing attitudes. Where once sectional groups would lobby their members to attend AGMs and vote against progressive moves there was now wide recognition of the need to consider the greater good of all members, both present and future. It may well have been thought that those attitudes that had previously stifled Club progress had now been

relegated to the past. In that regard judgement must remain suspended as subscription levels at the end of the first decade of the twenty-first Century remain at levels below those many administrators would consider necessary if the twin goals of covering current costs and building reserves against future capital needs are to be met. In order to facilitate its role the Board appoints a General Manager to implement the policies it decides upon. In addition the General Manager is expected to bring forward ideas for the Board’s consideration. Grant Scoones enjoyed the advantage of moving into a more responsive environment than did his predecessors. Equally importantly he was the right man for the time. With no background in golf,

title: Administration · p. 152
text:
and no desire to spend very much time socialising in the lounge, Grant was able to apply all of his energy and enthusiasm to the task of improving the Club’s financial status and its facilities. In this he was certainly successful. He was instrumental in driving the building project that gave the Club an excellent clubhouse at a very competitive cost. His organisation of Cafeteria and Bar facilities, and his employment and supervision of the staff to run them, have provided members with outstanding service. The service provided by Jack and Jay Carter and their team in the Pro Shop has been a revelation. As each year goes by the golf course, the most important aspect of the Club, looks more and more the sort of course any golfer would be keen to play. Green fee players invariably give the course the thumbs up. Yes, there will always be critics but members with open minds will have no difficulty recognising the progress that has been made over recent years. It is no coincidence that progress in terms of course and clubhouse facilities, staffing, and financial stability has been most pronounced since Grant Scoones was appointed in 1999. It was unfortunate that Grant decided he was not willing to extend his term of service beyond 2011. In his fourteen years as General Manager he achieved a great deal on behalf of the Club. He had proven to be the right man for the role at a time when it was vitally important that the Club move positively towards a sound financial future. His legacy is likely to gain even greater recognition as we move forward from the base he established.
