The new look Board that was installed in 2011 employed an outside consultant, Peter Dale, one time CEO of NZGolf, to advise them on an appropriate management structure to serve the Club’s future needs. It is too early to comment on the success or otherwise of the new directions the Board resolved to follow.

Jim Paterson told a few stories in his time. Some may have come from a lively imagination but there always seemed to be a ring of authenticity to them. Once he told us of a visiting American player who came into the shop one morning, paid his green fee, and spent some time discussing the characteristics of the different brands of balls Jim had available. After due consideration he settled upon a dozen Dunlop 65s and headed for the first tee. Jim went out to wave him on his way. After some limbering exercises and a few practise swings our man teed up and took a lusty swing, missing the ball by a narrow margin. Two air shots later he stowed his club and ball in his bag, turned to Jim saying “It is not much of a golf course anyway” and headed back to the car park.

title: Administration · p. 153
text:
GLEANINGS FROM THE CLUB MINUTE BOOKS

As noted earlier no Minute Books from the first 40 years or so exist to this day. Perhaps this is not the serious problem that it might seem to be at first glance. I say this because, having pored over dusty minutes from as far back as possible, the overwhelming impression has been one of the enormous amount of trivia that has occupied the time of committee members throughout the years. While this is not said to disparage the work successive committees have done it would be obvious to anyone going through the books that they do not truly reflect the value of that work. Much of the important work of a committee is done at sub-committee level and is not recorded in the full committee minutes.

The following excerpts have been selected to provide a timeline of events that have had some significance in the history of our Club. 1954: The new Clubhouse was completed in its present position at a cost of £5750. The furnishing committee raised another £1034 to purchase tables and chairs. The AGM reaffirmed that the required dress for men in the Clubhouse during the season was to include a jacket or Club blazer. The committee were to decide on the colour and style of the blazer to be adopted as the official Club blazer. 1956: £25 was allocated to assist the Greenkeeper to attend the NZ Greenkeepers’ Conference in Dunedin. Imported sand was tried in our bunkers for the first time. The Labour Weekend tournament fee was set at £1:10:0, meals not included. 1957: Noel Hockin replaced Col Evitt as Club Secretary. It was resolved that schoolboys could play in the school holidays for 2/6d per week but only if accompanied by a member. The price of the traditional meal of ‘pea, pie, and potatoes’ was to increase from 1/6d to 2/3d. 1960: Tauranga invited Te Puke and Mt. Maunganui Clubs to send two representatives each to play in our fixture with the Waikato Eagles. 1961: Subscriptions were set at £12 for men, £10 for women, and £20 for a married couple. Trials were conducted with the 1.68-inch American ball in New Zealand. It was found acceptable. 1962: USGA Handicapping system adopted. Membership was closed for the first time but reopened a month later. 1963: The causeway across the gully at the 4th hole was raised to provide a level crossing. Trials were conducted with Papamoa sea sand in the bunkers. Research was conducted on the feasibility of using water from the Judea stream. It was found to be much cheaper to remain on Borough supply. No positive results had been gained from trial drilling for water. 1964: Entry fee for Labour Weekend Tournament set at £2:10. This included three lunches at 5/- each. A profit of £70 was made. 1965: The committee approved Professional charges of £1:10 pa for club storage, £2:10 for storage and cleaning, and £3:10 if you wished to include shoe cleaning. Greens committee reported fairways had been mowed in August for the first time in 6 weeks. The BOPDGA had been advised we were concerned that some local clubs were not applying the handicapping rules properly. C G Wilson Ltd. were the successful tenderers for Clubhouse alterations, their tender being for £15 586.

title: Administration · p. 154
text:
1966: A proposal to sell draught beer was lost. One month later a draught beer trial was approved. One committee member dissented on the grounds that it would not be good for ‘the decorum of the Club’. Another thought it might conflict with the law, apparently overlooking the fact that the entire operation of the bar was outside the law of the day. One month after draught beer sales were introduced consumption was reported to have reached an average of 100 flagons a week. A new course assessment gave an SSS (Standard Scratch Score) of 69.05. It was resolved that junior players not be allowed in the lounge except on tournament days or by permission of the Secretary Manager or Club Captain. 1967: Membership closed and limits set. The power poles on the 8th fairway had now been removed. 1968: The appointment of a permanent third greenkeeper was approved. 1969: Flagon beer price was increased to 25¢ per jug. 1971: Match committee advised men’s 17th now designated a par 4 in line with the guidelines in the handicapping manual. An application was made to stage the 1973 Russell Grace Women’s Inter- provincials. 1972: Play over rule to be discontinued. A delegation from the RSA Golf committee requested that the decision to charge outside competitors in their tournament a $2 green fee be rescinded. This was unsuccessful. 1973: It was resolved to purchase a house at 1368 Cameron Road and sell the Club’s section off Hynd’s Road. An offer of $5000 was accepted for the section.  McKinlay’s Paddock made available for practise but very little used. A Pool table was purchased at a cost of $970. It was felt necessary to introduce crowd control for Finals Day on account of the large galleries being attracted. $40 000 was allocated for Clubhouse extensions. 1974: M Nicholson selected to represent NZ in Eisenhower team. BOP Association approached for a ruling re local clubs (notably Mt Maunganui) not observing handicap rules over summer. 1975: Twilight tournaments were introduced. A local rule was introduced banning attendance of the flagstick and requiring all four balls to be holed prior to retrieval. This was to protect the area surrounding the hole in winter. (This was an illegal rule in conflict with the Rules of Golf.) 1976: A plan was introduced to clean up the area to the left of the 7th hole at a cost of $12 000 for the development of a Driving Range. This was subsequently rejected by the AGM of 1977. 1977: Reciprocal agreements were negotiated with the Cronulla Club of Sydney and with the Invercargill Golf Club. Three-tee starting was tried for the first time. The tradition of honouring Life Members at Finals Day was initiated. 1978: In view of reported cases of gambling associated with Pool games it was resolved to impose

tighter controls and to deal severely with offenders. Les Hill resigned and was replaced by Lyn Gillon. As Mr Gillon did not require the house it was rented at $40 per week. Bob Burstall and Willis Faulds were reported to have surveyed and named all of the trees on the course. ’Play the Lie’ instituted. Prior to this a ‘placing’ rule had applied all season only to be lifted the week prior to the Championship qualifying rounds!  A long-term lease had finally been successfully negotiated with the Minister of Crown Lands. A water easement re the stream had been obtained and consequently a $48 000 irrigation scheme approved. 1979: The Pine trees adjacent to the car park were felled. The Gum trees beside them were given a safe life of 5-10 years. (They remain more than 30 years later). Friday night meals were proving

title: Administration · p. 155
text:
successful. Because of the uncertainty that still prevailed over the hours the bar could legally be open wine would only be available until 7pm. The minutes record there were 29 greens on the course. (I doubt this count). Warwick Nicoll gave $200 to be held in trust, the interest to cover the prize associated with the Nicoll Cup. Installation of the Harvin irrigation system was completed in June. In response to some conflict between committee members and the green keepers the chairman of the Greens Committee, Des Wilson, said this: “In no way will I, or can I, instruct the Greenkeeper in the carrying out of his duties. My job is to provide a bridge of communication between him and the committee and to assist him with his programming.” The Racing Club were keen to install a 2200m starting point. This would project into the 11th fairway. Pegs were placed to show the positioning. (Fortunately this development was not approved). Lance Bedford, an engineer, gave estimates relating to the Driving Range proposal. Earthworks were evaluated at $15 000, drainage at $2 000, and grassing at $5 000. 1980: A Special General Meeting voted to proceed with the Driving Range at a cost of $20 000. This same meeting approved the realignment of the entry road to separate Golf and racing areas. The 9th tee would move forward and the project would be at no cost to the Golf Club as the Racing Club would finance it through a raffle. 1981: The par of the 17th hole was increased to 5 with a stroke allocation of 15 on the motion of R Eaton and K Frith. A motion to allow junior members access to the Club lounge wearing Club jerseys rather than jackets was defeated. All male members using the lounge must wear jackets. Our rental doubled from $1 000 to $2 000, set for the following five years. During development, and afterward, the Driving Range area was to be classified as a ’lateral hazard”. (This was again contrary to the rules of golf as there is no such thing as a ‘lateral hazard’ in those rules). 1982: Driving range opened with Alan Snape being authorised to provide practice balls for members though members were permitted to use their own. Members who were improperly dressed were to be served from the side bar that opened to the Dining Room. The greens were now mown four times per week. 1983: The BOP Association advised that the larger ‘American’ ball would be mandatory in all competition under their jurisdiction. R Lahood attended his final meeting in June after 13.5 years service. The local rule re flagstick and four balls in the hole was rescinded. Reciprocal rights with Invercargill were discontinued. At the AGM a move to equate men and women’s subscriptions was defeated. Men’s were set at $225, women’s at $205. Long-playing membership was confirmed as applying after 40 years membership and age 65. Subscription was to be 50% of senior subscription.

Apparently the 1980 agreement with the Racing Club to finance the shift of the access road had been unsuccessful for it was now recorded that agreement had been reached on the issue. The clubs would now share the cost estimated at $10 900. 1984: The condition of the course over summer prompted 54 members to sign a petition claiming the greens were awful, the tees bad, weeds prolific, and the state of the trees unacceptable. (We had however developed some good paths during the employment of the then greenkeeper). The greens were now mown four days each week. Alan Snape requested release from his obligation to supply range balls owing to the high attrition rate. The response was to pay him $2 000 per year as Range supervisor and grant him $500 to help defray losses over the previous two years.

title: Administration · p. 156
text:
1985: Concern was expressed at the slide in membership. There were 23 vacancies in Men’s A category. New membership limits were set for 1986. These increased Men’s A to 375 with 25 discretionary places, Men’s B to 125, Ladies’ A plus B to 350. Fairway bunkers on the 8th were authorised. The requirement for men to wear a jacket in the lounge was deleted from regulations as a result of a motion to the AGM. 1992: The trimming of tree ‘skirts’ was very favourably received. The new eighth green was opened. 1993: A report from the NZ Turf Research Institute was very favourable to the condition of the course, especially the greens. This reflected very well on the work of Grant Patterson and his staff. The Championship pennant team had won the BOP Pennant for the first time in fifteen years. Michael Nicholson gave praise to the younger players in the team. The junior programme had done much to bring about this success. The Board of Management concept was first mentioned as being worthy of consideration. Lack of financial support for the Golf Club Trust was seen as a matter of some concern. 1994: It was reported that the existing irrigation system made it difficult to maintain the greens to their best potential. The system had been poorly laid with sub-standard piping having been laid too shallow resulting in frequent breakdown. An urgent upgrade was required before the course development plan could be properly instigated. The May committee meeting that year was disrupted by the breakout of a fire in the Bar. As luck would have it Neil Marson left the meeting to collect his wife Shirley from an appointment. He returned immediately to enquire why there was “steam” emanating from beneath the Bar slide. On looking out towards the Bar I said “that is not steam. Those are flames.” Rapid action followed and the fire was extinguished by using all the available extinguishers from upstairs and downstairs though not before substantial damage to the interior of the Bar had been sustained. It transpired that the women volunteering to do Bar duty that day had cleaned the ash trays by tipping the butts into a waste bin under the Bar as was usual. Unfortunately on this occasion there were apparently some incompletely extinguished butts in the trays and several hours later the bin burst into open flames. Another example of the hidden dangers of smoking!  It was fortunate the monthly committee meeting was scheduled for that Monday evening and that Neil had an errand that took him from the committee room at the critical moment. But for these circumstances the Clubhouse would certainly have been a total loss before the Fire Brigade had reached the scene. Some thought it may have been better if the clubhouse had been destroyed and a new one built under insurance. Such thoughts ignore the serious loss of Club records, cups, trophies, and other paraphernalia that would have resulted.  The minutes report that the meeting reconvened after the committee had “distinguished” the fire and the Fire Brigade had attended to check that there was no further risk. 1995: The Players Committee wrote to the Board requesting that they, the Players Committee, should

act as the Greens Committee. The Board reminded the committee that they, the Board, were responsible for ensuring that the course was presented in the best possible condition for the benefit of members. To facilitate this they had appointed a highly qualified Greens Superintendent and charged him with the responsibility of achieving this. As with other staff he would report directly to the General Manager. 1999: The AGM approved the establishment of the position of Club Captain, such elected member to chair the Players Committee and to serve on the Board. The membership category of Intermediate was also approved. The Golf Club Trust were now willing to wind up and to transfer their funds to the Board, such funds to be utilised in the proposed Clubhouse modernisation. Ismo Torvelainen and Russell Black were

title: Administration · p. 157
text:
co-opted onto the Building committee for their expertise in structural engineering and design work respectively. The Board was to seek approval to borrow up to $600 000 for the project.  This was reduced to $400 000 when the Trust indicated $230 000 was available through them. 2001: Turf advisory consultant David Ormsby met with the Board to discuss the establishment of Cynodon Fairways. 2002: Resolved that the Board Chairman, rather than the President, should chair General meetings of the Club. 2003: Plans were initiated to align the financial year with the membership subscription year. This would confer a number of advantages in budgeting and general administration of the Club. This was ratified at the AGM that year together with a comprehensive revamp of the Club Rules. Doubts were expressed in relation to the establishment of the experimental Windsor Green fairways. Climatic conditions had not been conducive to a rapid spread of stolons and some Board members were questioning the decision to proceed. Consequently the Board resolved to delay further development until more positive results were seen. 2004: David Ormsby recommended Browntop be encouraged on the greens by facilitating deeper rooting through coring and improving aeration. Greens should be over sown with Brown top at each renovation. The pH level should be low (4.9-5.3), Nitrogen levels moderate, and Potash levels low (less than 3%). Greens Superintendent Brendan Allan presented a comprehensive report on the Windsor Green fairways in which he expressed great confidence in their future under our conditions. Fairway improvement would be a continual process over several years as the Windsor Green becomes dominant over Poa annua and invasive weeds. In the same paper Brendan praised the Alex Glasgow development plan as being sensibly aimed at the mid to longer handicapped player with an emphasis on modernisation versus development. Brendan’s advice was that we should make the most of what we have, not aim to be something we cannot be. A paper on the upgrade of the Pro Shop was presented. 2005: Golf Autoscore demonstrated their computerised scoring system following a number of improvements they had made following an earlier demonstration in 2002 when several deficiencies had been evident. The Board decided to purchase the improved system at a cost of $8500 plus service fees of $200 per month. Golf Autoscore was installed in Nov. 2005. and met with immediate acceptance by members and officials alike. 2006: Brendan Allan prepared the course for the first Carrus Professional Tournament in May before

leaving for Auckland Golf Club. His parting comment was that the Club should proceed with the proposed upgrade of bunkers as further member input would only delay the process unnecessarily. His report also recommended the removal of the bunker on the Knoll as it was dangerous to staff, served no purpose other than to penalise poorer players, and was difficult to maintain. The father and son team of Jack and Jay Carter began operations from the renovated Professional Shop. 2009: The Board adopted a new Course Management Policy Document. The degree of success these strategic plans achieve will be revealed as time goes by. Judgement must be reserved at this time.

title: Administration · p. 158
text:
CLUBHOUSE REDEVELOPMENT

In February 1999 the Board established a Facilities Advisory Group (FAG). This group was tasked with the responsibility of advising the Board on the development and modernisation of the clubhouse facility to a standard more in keeping with a modern sports club providing food, beverage, and administrative services to a membership of more than 1000 together with annual visitor numbers in excess of 5000. This was in keeping with the Mission Statement adopted by the Board that reads: “To provide a quality golf experience for all players in surroundings of excellence”. The members of the group were Gary Baker and Tony Gallagher, representing the Board, Russell Black (Architectural Draftsman), Ismo Torvelainen (Engineer with Martin, McCaulay, Morton Ltd), and Grant Scoones (General Manager). Later Alan Rydings volunteered his services as a qualified Quantity Surveyor/Estimator willing to assist with the tender process and with supervision of the contract as construction developed. Both Board representatives Gary and Tony had extensive experience in the construction industry while Russell, Ismo, and Alan had proven expertise in their respective fields. While Russell and Ismo were each paid for their professional services all three attended meetings and site visits on a voluntary basis as Club members wishing to contribute to the development of their

Club’s facilities.

The Board called a Special General Meeting in July 2000 for the purpose of placing before the membership a proposal to completely redevelop the Clubhouse. The building had first been erected in 1954 and had been extensively extended and refurbished on two subsequent occasions. In spite of this the clubhouse was overdue for a further upgrade in regard to the facilities it was required to provide and to the structural integrity of the building. The roof was of particular concern in the latter context. The Board had identified a number of areas where substantial expenditure would be required in the short term should a complete rebuild not be proceeded with. These areas included the roof, the

lounge ceiling, all electrical and plumbing services, the floor coverings, the Bar and Kitchen units, and the outside decking. In view of all this necessary maintenance the Board recommended that the most appropriate solution would be to completely rebuild the structure above the existing basement level thus preserving the existing changing and storage rooms. The advantages of this approach were seen to be wide ranging. They included the urgent replacement of the roof, the creation of an appropriate and obvious front entry to the Clubhouse leading directly to the office, provision both of alternative entry points for players and much needed upstairs toilets. The provision of a committee room on a third floor level would be a welcome addition. A special attraction would be the enhanced views possible from all points of the clubhouse resulting from the installation of larger, more modern windows throughout the upper levels. The poor visibility from within the clubhouse had long been a source of frustration to many a member. The concept proposed would open up sweeping views of the course, the racecourse, and in particular the superb vista provided by the hills to the East. Ultimately the views that were revealed when the new clubhouse was opened to the membership proved to be every bit as rewarding as had been anticipated. The Board did consider the idea of building a completely new clubhouse possibly located to the West of the putting green but rejected this as being impractical owing to financial considerations. The cost of

title: Administration · p. 159
text:
such a project was estimated to lie in the region of $1.3 to $1.5 million and it was considered it would be imprudent to take on a debt of some $1m even if a loan of such magnitude could have been negotiated with our Bank.

Alternatively the cost of building over the existing basement and foundation was estimated at $630 000 of which $230 000 would be available following the wind up of the Golf Club Trust. This Trust had been set up following the sale of the house owned by the Club and located in Cameron Road near the Reserve entrance.

Concerns were expressed during the meeting that the Board should be paying off debt rather than incurring more by going ahead with the development. The General Manager was able to explain that term liabilities had totalled $440 000 in August 1998 at which point the Board had claimed that this debt would be paid off within six years. In fact all but $82 000 had been paid off by August 2000 meaning that $358 000 had been paid off in just two years. This indicated the Board’s financial policies were working and gave Board members the confidence to recommend the Club borrow the required funds to complete the proposed development. Subsequent to the presentation the Special General Meeting authorised the Board to borrow up to $400 000 to complete the proposed development. Had the Trustees not resolved to wind up the Trust and make the funds available the project would not have been viable. In addition to the $230 000 in cash provided by them the Trustees resolved to write off a loan of $130 000 owed to the Trust by the Club. This had been advanced some years previously to enable the purchase of urgently required course maintenance machinery.

Financial sustainability was the first priority of the Board when considering the proposal. They were meticulous in their planning in order to ensure the budgetary goals were both conservative and sustainable. The Club’s auditors, Murray, Crossman and Partners, were able to report that, while results might vary significantly from those forecast, these variations were likely to be positive rather than negative as a result of conservative forecasts and probable growth of membership, the latter a hopeful consequence of the proposed upgrade. Financial projections for the subsequent years indicated the level of borrowing now envisaged would have little impact on subscription levels over succeeding years with repayments being amortised so as to require both present and future members to bear the cost.

Miden Construction, the principals of which were club member brothers Denis and Michael Smith, were awarded the contract in a fully competitive and open tendering process. The majority of sub-contracts

also went to club members again in open tendering. While these were the responsibility of Miden Construction it is probably true that they “sharpened their pencils” to give their club the best possible price. For that the Club should be very grateful. For the record club member related firms or individual contractors who were involved included Stewart Browne Electrical, Tauranga Hardware and Plumbing (Brian McCord), Don Allen Painting and Decorating, and Helen Fritchley Interior Design. During construction the normal business of the Club was planned to be as free from interruption as possible. A temporary office was located adjacent to the putting green and food and beverage services relocated to the trundler shed. These arrangements proved highly satisfactory, the informality of the

title: Administration · p. 160
text:
Trundler Shed hospitality centre being well received by the majority of members. The atmosphere created in that centre owed much to the tolerance and cheerful cooperation of our caterers Peter and Tania Robb, our Bar Persons, and to our Professional Rick Barker who was required to run his business in reduced premises and was inconvenienced in a number of other ways.

When the new facility opened in April 2001 with a champagne breakfast the membership at large, including some who had been sceptical earlier, were delighted with the appearance and overall ambience of their new clubhouse. General Manager Grant Scoones who had been instrumental in developing the original concept and in driving its progress, the entire Facilities Advisory Group who had planned and monitored every step of the development, and the Board members, none of whom ever wavered in their belief in the value and viability of the new look clubhouse, could all be justly proud of the part they had played in bringing an ambitious concept to fruition.

title: Resident professionals · p. 164
text:
CHAPTER TWELVE

RESIDENT PROFESSIONALS

title: Resident professionals · p. 165
text:
JAMES MOWAT

The Rotorua based Professionals, Mr. Hood and Mr. McCormack visited Tauranga in the early years though Tauranga had no resident Professional until 1936 when James Mowat accepted appointment to the position. James was born in Montrose, Scotland in 1895. Montrose lies North of St. Andrews on the coast and is home to one of the oldest golf courses in Scotland. It was founded in 1812 and is reputed to be the ninth oldest course in the World. After playing limited golf as a boy James enlisted in the 10th. Highland Light Infantry in December 1914 and served first in France where he was twice wounded. He was drafted back to Montrose for short convalescent spells at home before returning to the Battlefield. He ended the war fighting the Turkish forces in Mesopotamia, now known as Iraq. The Battalion was on the way home after the armistice in 1918 when it was diverted to quell an uprising in the Khyber Pass. As a result James was the last of all the men from Montrose to make it home after the war.

The prospect of life as a clerk in the Railways had little appeal to James after his experiences during the war and it was not long before he set sail for the USA where he at first worked for his uncle Bob who owned a shoe business in New York. A year or so later he met up with another man from Montrose and they responded to the growing demand in America for people who had some knowledge of, and experience in, the game of golf. Men from Scotland were highly regarded in that context. Most of Jim’s work in America was involved in Golf Course design though he did fit in some teaching and playing. His reputation must have been well established as he was on one occasion invited to partner the then US Open Champion Gene Sarazen in an exhibition match in Miami against Leo Diegel (twice winner of the USPGA Championship) and Mike Brady, the latter being widely known as the Bridesmaid on account of his numerous second placings in major championships. In this match Jim scored seven birdies, his side prevailing without the need for Sarazen to contribute anything to improve their combined card.

Major Tournament winners to have played our course at some time in the past include:

Peter Thomson – Five times British Open Champion. Also placed 4th in US Open. Kel Nagle - Centennial British Open Champion. Also 2nd US Open. David Graham - US Open and PGA Champion Top five in Masters and British Open. Tony Jacklin - British and US Open Championships. Billy Casper - Twice winner US Open. Also Masters Champion and 3 times second placed in PGA Championship, 4th in British Open. Sir Bob Charles – British Open Champion. Tied 2nd PGA Championship, Twice tied 3rd in US Opens.

title: Resident professionals · p. 166
text:
James work and other experiences in America brought him into contact with a number of well known personalities including Jack Dempsey, the great heavyweight boxing champion known as the ‘Manassa Mauler’, Jack McDonald the superb sprinter termed the ‘Australian Blue Streak’, and Tommy Armour, then the most respected golf teacher in America. During Jim’s time in the Shoe Store in New York Damon Runyon, the renowned storyteller would often visit the shop to sit in a big old leather chair and ‘spin the breeze’ with Uncle Bob as the latter cobbled at his bench. Runyon’s short stories later formed the basis for the Broadway Musical ‘Guys and Dolls’.

One day an American friend who had recently returned from a trip to New Zealand said to Jim: “New Zealand is the place of the future. That is where you should go”. Soon afterward an advertisement appeared in an American publication seeking applications for the position of Professional at the Poverty Bay Golf Club. Jim applied, was duly appointed and, in 1929, he ended his nine year sojourn in the USA to set sail for a country he knew very little about. He spent seven years in Gisborne where, in 1934, he married local lass Margaret McIldowie. Soon afterward, while visiting Rotorua, he met with some Tauranga golfers who enticed Jim to move to Tauranga to take up the position of Professional there.

The Rotorua Golf Club course at Arikikapakapa was a favourite with Jimmy. On one occasion he stood on the ninth tee and said to Margaret who was caddying for him: “If I can par this hole I will be out in 30.” He promptly birdied that beautiful par three to be out in 29. We never did hear what happened in the second nine holes.

It must have been very difficult to build a business as a Club professional in those times. The great depression was still casting a long shadow over the World economy, club memberships were not large, and the course was only open for eight or nine months each year. James supplemented his income by giving lessons to Te Puke members in addition to serving his home club though the trip to Te Puke took a good deal longer than it does today. The Mowat farm and orchard, now the site of Tauranga Girls’ College, contributed further to the needs of the growing Mowat family.

In 1940, with the Second World War in full swing and less and less golf being played, James decided there was little point in persevering in the role of Professional and submitted his resignation. Soon afterward he applied to be reinstated as an Amateur. This was granted by the Golf Association on condition that he have no association with golf in any manner for a stand down period of five years, a condition much more stringent than those that prevail in this modern era. Following this enforced withdrawal, broken only by clandestine lessons in the back paddock for some of his old pupils who became desperate for guidance, James resumed life as an Amateur golfer. Along with Margaret he participated fully in club activities, including committee work, and played regularly two or three times a week.

Jimmy Mowat was one of many memorable characters to have graced our links. Renowned for the quality of his short game he holed more than his fair share of full iron shots, sometimes after asking an incredulous companion to hold the flag for him. Surprisingly he was never to score a ‘recognised’ hole in one in spite of achieving the feat several times when playing unaccompanied rounds during his time

title: Resident professionals · p. 167
text:
in America. A stickler for the etiquette of the game, a true student of its rules and history, Jimmy Mowat was a lover of all aspects of this great game. Sadly, in 1958, he succumbed to Prostate Cancer at the early age of 63. With the treatment available today he would surely have enjoyed many more years of golf. As it was he fought on longer than expected and, despite being essentially bedridden for most of two years was able to shoot a 76 in his final round, this being at a very late stage of his illness. James Mowat, professional golfer, was ahead of his time in many ways. How he would love to have contributed to, and participated in, the wave of popularity the game has enjoyed over more recent times.

JAMES A PATERSON

James A Paterson was appointed to the vacant Professional position in 1953 and served the Club in that role until 1972. Prior to his appointment members seeking professional instruction were accommodated by A J (Bronco) Branch who owned the Sports Store in Central Tauranga still known as Broncos. Bronco was never attached to the Club but was authorised to give lessons and provide equipment to any member requiring assistance.

Jim was born in England where his father was a Professional who had learned his trade in a region where Harry Vardon, one of the greatest players of all time, was located. Vardon had an enormous influence on the game throughout Britain and in the United States where his barnstorming tours in the company of fellow Jersey Islander Ted Ray were instrumental in introducing millions of Americans to the game in the early years of the Twentieth Century. The golfer of today may not recognise that when he or she locks the ‘pinkie’ of their top hand over the forefinger of their bottom hand in gripping the club they are adopting the ‘Vardon’ grip, introduced to the game by this great player and teacher and now used almost universally. An older generation of players would have been told early in their golfing education that it was essential that they adopt the ‘Vardon’ grip. Harry Vardon was to influence the senior Paterson and inevitably much of Vardon’s method and philosophy of golf was transferred to the younger Paterson in his teaching.  Few, if any, Professionals at that time could expect to make a living from tournament golf so when Jim joined the Professional ranks it was as an apprentice learning the trade. There was time to compete in some of the tournaments that were held and Jim had the thrill and the honour of winning the Dutch Open on one momentous occasion.

Another great English player with whom Jim had some association was Henry Cotton. Henry was the man who restored British golfing pride by winning the British Open for Britain after Americans had dominated the famous championship for many years. The popular Dunlop 65 golf ball that many older players will recall having played in earlier days was named for the 65 Henry posted in that famous victory. Cotton was resident in the same area of England and Jim met him in tournaments and on other occasions. One story Jim told was of playing in a tournament where no local rule had been posted to allow free relief for an embedded ball on the green or anywhere else for that matter, the embedded ball rule having not then been added to the Rule Book. Henry Cotton, having requested and been denied relief for a ball so embedded on the second green, proceeded to play a wedge stroke resulting in a large divot being removed from the green. A local rule was promptly introduced and soon afterward the Rule Book was amended to allow relief for a ball embedded both on, and through, the green.

title: Resident professionals · p. 168
text:
After learning his trade in England Jim came to New Zealand to take up the resident Professional’s position with the Wanganui Golf Club at their Belmont course. A few years later some of our members made a trip to Wanganui where they met Jim and, being impressed with his personality and teaching skills, encouraged him to apply for the position at Tauranga. This Jim did and soon he and Barbara and their two sons were on their way North. Some years later twin daughters were born to the couple.

When Jim settled into his new role at Tauranga he found the available facilities to be rather less adequate than those that prevail today. The Pro Shop was located downstairs in the Clubhouse adjacent to the Ladies’ locker room. When the new Pro Shop was opened beside the first tee the Ladies Locker Room was expanded to fill the space it now occupies. Both the Professional and the Lady members were relieved to leave behind the cramped accommodation they had been forced to share for so long. While some members found that Jim’s quiet manner and distinctive accent made it hard for them to grasp the skill concepts he was endeavouring to pass on to them others reacted very positively to his teaching. There is little doubt that his own swing was one that would serve as an ideal model for any aspiring player. One of the best lessons an observant player can have is to watch a really good golfing stylist practice. The easy rhythm, the perfect timing and the understated power tend to find their way into the observer’s own practice sessions. Jim Paterson was a very good example of a player to study in that context. His iron shots in particular had a special quality about them. The ball would start out low then climb higher towards the end of its flight before dropping quietly to the green. Unfortunately Jim’s tournament play was plagued by a nervous system that frequently did not allow him to demonstrate his true ability. In spite of that he was competitive, often finishing near the head of the field amongst those Professionals competing in New Zealand at the time. On the basis of those performances he was selected to represent New Zealand in the two-man Canada Cup team. This was the forerunner of the present day World Cup.

Employment as a Club Professional has seldom been a lucrative career in New Zealand. When Jim took over the post in Tauranga the vast majority of players were of a generation that had lived through the depression years as well as the Second World War. As a result they were cautious in their spending habits and few people in the town would have been considered wealthy in any case. To help the family income Barbara worked at Hartleys on the Strand. When Barbara died at a relatively early age some of Jim’s motivation seemed to desert him and it perhaps came as some relief to him when the committee decided it was time to seek another to fill his position.

Throughout his twenty years at the Club Jim served loyally and with cheerful dignity. He assisted with work on the course when required over the summer months and was ever willing to assist in other areas when the need arose.

GREG HOLST

G T (Greg) Holst took up the position of Professional to the Tauranga Club in November 1972. Greg made a strong impression on the subcommittee that interviewed candidates on that occasion. It would be fair to say that Greg was the outsider in a strong field of four who were short listed for the position, his short listing probably justified by the fact that no one on the committee seemed to know much about

title: Resident professionals · p. 169
text:
him. At interview he sold himself very well indeed moving to the top of the prospects as a result of the energy, enthusiasm, and progressive ideas he believed he could bring to the job.

Greg completed his schooling at St. Kentigen’s College in Auckland before signing on with a Scottish professional, Graham Gordon at the old Remuera Golf Club. On completing the apprenticeship he played the Australian Professional circuit for four years with no more than moderate success. The great Australian player and noted teacher Norman von Nida coached Greg for a period at that time.

Having never quite achieved the promise the selection committee saw in him Greg returned to Australia in 1980 to open a Sporting Goods Store, later returning across the Tasman again to take up a position with the Mount Maunganui Golf Club. He now holds the position of Professional with the Carrington Golf Club in Northland.

During his time at Tauranga Kevin Wiltshire, one of three brothers who graced our junior ranks served an apprenticeship with Greg before going on to a successful career as Professional to the Ngaruawahia Golf Club.

ALLAN SNAPE

A P (Allan) Snape was appointed to the position in 1980. Allan was very promising at a range of sports during his school days in New South Wales during which time he played at representative level in rugby, cricket, tennis, athletics, and golf. This was at a time when boys were less inclined to specialise in one sport at the expense of all else. Many would argue that the former practise tended to produce more rounded individuals than is often the case today. On leaving school Allan attended Business College where he gained an excellent grounding in salesmanship and general management skills. These were to serve him well as these are the areas that often let down those who serve as Club Professionals. For nine years the Australian Golf Company PGF employed Allan. In those years he gained invaluable insight into the finer points of Golf equipment.

A two-year working holiday to the United Kingdom and Europe followed in 1966. In the UK Allan won a prestigious Amateur tournament called the Mosely Golf Open before returning to New South Wales where he gained representative honours and won a number of tournaments including an Australian Foursomes title.

A member, who had best not be named, hooked one onto the road off the 14th tee. The club ‘slipped from his grip’ in his words and followed the ball out onto the road where it struck and broke the windscreen of a passing Holden. This created a difficult situation that required a good deal of diplomacy to keep a ‘Cap’ on possible recriminations. The same 14th tee has been the scene of several incidents including a serious one when an errant club lodged over the power lines beside the road causing a short circuit and bringing down a line. A certain ex member of the Greens staff remained subdued for some time after that incident.

title: Resident professionals · p. 170
text:
In 1969 Allan got on a ship to visit relatives in New Zealand and has been in this country ever since. He immediately hit the headlines in New Zealand winning five important Amateur titles in that first year. His only failure came in a semi-final loss to Ted McDougall in the New Zealand Amateur Championship. These successes encouraged him to try the Professional game. Consequently he served a 12-month trainee period as required in order to gain entry to the NZPGA. In 1971 Allan played with moderate success in Asia and Europe. The highlight of this trip came when Allan played in, and made the cut, in the Centennial British Open.

Allan married in 1971 and held down two jobs while trying to play in as many tournaments as possible, managing to win some 14 Pro-Ams along the way. Success in the New Zealand Club Pro Championship came on two occasions.

The pressures of this life while supporting a family of three children proved too much and, in 1978, Allan accepted the professional position at the Flaxmere Club in Hawkes Bay. Though Flaxmere proved an enjoyable experience Tauranga appeared to offer better prospects and Allan took up the position here in 1980. Disaster struck in 1986 when a major fire swept through the Pro Shop and Trundler Shed destroying the shop and stock, together with some 256 sets of members clubs. The Club held a special golf day raising substantial revenue that was presented to the Snape family to help Allan get re-established.

In 1988 Allan resigned his Tauranga position and became attached to both Omanu and the Western Bay (Omokoroa) Clubs. He also established a coaching circuit through the Coromandel, setting up shop at Whangamata through holiday periods. Allan was instrumental in getting the Golf Range developed off the end of the Omanu course. This was a private undertaking involving some business partners of Allan’s.

Some years later Allan was diagnosed with Prostate cancer. This ultimately spread to his spine. Despite this Allan determined to get back to playing golf as soon as possible. Sheer determination saw him graduate from walking with a frame, to doing so with two sticks, then unaided. Eventually he was able to stand to hit a few balls. Finally he managed to play 18 holes, even carrying a light bag to do so. By the end of 2009 deterioration of the spine was so bad that Allan lost the strength to remain on his feet and life in a wheelchair became the only option. This was a sad final phase in the life of a talented sportsman who never lost his zest for life.

Jeff Macnab must hold the record for holes in one scored on our course. During his years as a member Jeff scored five of his seven lifetime aces on our course. An excellent golfer who played representative golf at Provincial level Jeff learned to play in Scotland so he was well equipped to handle those windy days that severely test most players. Jeff may well have become known as the peripatetic golfer as he was at various times a member of Omokoroa, Omanu, and Mt Maunganui Golf Clubs in addition to his membership atTauranga. Jeff served several years as a member of our committee during the Eighties including a term as Vice- Captain.

title: Resident professionals · p. 171
text:
RICK BARKER

Rick began his golfing life in Northland at the age of ten when he became a junior member of the Helensville District Golf Club. He recalled being the only junior member at that time, an era when clubs were less welcoming of juniors than is now the case. The junior subscription at Helensville of just 10/- was no indication that juniors were unwelcome at that club however.

Rick won his first open senior event when just 14 years of age and, by age 16, was winning 72-hole open events against opposition much older and more experienced than himself. Rick’s first success at this level was a victory in the Kaipara Open where he headed a former NZ representative and National amateur champion in Bruce Stevens. At the under 18 NZ Boys’ Championship he finished in second place. At Provincial level Rick represented Northland in the Garrard Shield and Freyberg Rosebowl teams of 1975 and 76, and the Auckland Garrard Shield team in the following two years. His amateur career peaked in 1975 when he annexed the NZ Stroke Play Championship and was leading amateur in the NZ Open. Partnered with Phil Reid, Rick won the NZ Foresomes title of 1976 and later in the tournament he was beaten in the NZ Amateur Plate final.

Rick joined the Professional ranks in 1978 and won his first event, the Waikato PGA Championship, the following year. Rick then tried his luck on the Australian circuit with little success though he did manage a win in a small Pro-Am at Royal Melbourne. Following on from his Waikato PGA win in 1979 Rick won over 40 Pro-Am events throughout New Zealand and the Pacific Islands over the following eight years.

Highlights of Rick’s professional career included: • Third place in the NZ PGA Championship, • Second place in the American Samoa Open, • Third place in the Tahiti Open, • Third place in the Pacific Harbour Open, • Third place in the Raratongan Open, • Winner of the 84-hole Fijian Hotel Pro-Am. On another occasion Rick was credited with the lowest round scored in the NZ Open of that year.

By 1986 Rick had decided that he had probably gone as far as he could as a Tournament Professional and he accepted the job as resident professional at the small Otumoetai Club in Tauranga. Two years later the Tauranga position became available when Alan Snape moved to Omanu and Rick was appointed to the job. For some years he maintained the shop at Otumoetai while serving full time at Tauranga. In 2006 the Club upgraded the shop and, in conjunction with that, the Board revised the role of the Professional so that it would include extended participation in the activities of the club and its membership. Rick did not feel he wished to be involved in this extended role and did not apply for a renewal of his contract. Consequently he completed his service as the Club’s professional in 2006 to go into an unrelated business.

title: Resident professionals · p. 172
text:
JAY CARTER AND GOLF FUSION

Jay began as a junior at the Tauranga Club while still a schoolboy. He developed into a player of considerable promise and, upon leaving school, spent time in Wellington developing his game as a full time student under Mal Tongue. When the Professional contract was up for renewal at Tauranga Jay and his father decided to put in an application to run the business. The Board had made it a priority to upgrade the Pro Shop and now advertised a contract to operate the business. This contract extended the role of the Professional to an extent that had not previously been envisaged.

When the contract was awarded to the Carter team Jay was not then a member of the PGA. In order for him to become a member it was required that he serve his time under a full member. Doug Milne, previously Professional to the Whakatane Golf Club was therefore employed as the PGA Professional. This arrangement remained in place until Jay graduated to full membership of the PGA.

Members were soon able to appreciate the new services introduced by Golf Fusion as the business is known. A fleet of new Golf Carts arrived and were available for hire by members and visitors alike, the new look Pro Shop was soon stocked with a wide range of equipment, lessons were readily available, junior clinics were developed, and the Pro Shop staff acted as starters to get the field efficiently on its way. Buckets of practice balls were made available for use on the Driving Range and later the Card

Issuing machine was located in the Pro Shop for easy access by members. Staff would even accept bookings and cancellations as part of the service offered. Manufacturer demonstrations became a regular feature of the service and many a member took the opportunity to try out new clubs to see what these might do for their game.

The story of Jay Carter and Golf Fusion is still unfolding at time of writing though there is no doubt the concept has changed the nature of the services offered to our members.

Playing to your age is an achievement any golfer would be proud of. This feat is becoming more common as more players live on into their older years in robust good health. Prominent members of our Veterans Society, Pat Kendall and Clive Sheerin, maintained quite a competition between themselves as they seemingly vied to outdo the other in adding to their total number of rounds to, or under, their age. Neither of these redoubtable proponents of the game however was able to match the feat of another of the Society, George Reilly. George must have established the record for our Club as the youngest to achieve the feat when he returned a 67 at that age.

Peg Copestake, to the best of our knowledge remains the only woman member to have achieved the feat.

title: Resident professionals · p. 173
text:
Junior golfers are now given every encouragement to participate from an early age. It was not always so. Many older members, especially male members, made early pioneers in this category less than welcome. Junior girls were even fewer in number

than were the boys so the reaction the ladies may have had to them is difficult to assess. We suspect it would have been very supportive. During the Fifties Michael Cambie and Robert Mowat qualified for the Club championships only to draw objections from their seniors who claimed that as these two schoolboys did not pay full senior subscriptions they could not be eligible for such competitions. Jimmy Mowat and others took up the cudgels on behalf of the boys and eventually their arguments were upheld allowing the boys to participate.

title: Greenkeeping · p. 176
text:
CHAPTER THIRTEEN

GREENKEEPING

title: Greenkeeping · p. 177
text:
There could be no more important function in the management of a golf club than that of ensuring that the physical environment should satisfy the aspirations of the majority of members. As all who have sat in a clubhouse for any length of time will realise it is very difficult to achieve that end. The “experts” who are eager to inform all who will listen as to what is wrong with the way the course is managed are legion. In spite of this, and in spite of the difficulties presented through lack of surplus funding to achieve all that might be desired, conditions on the majority of New Zealand courses are remarkably good. In this regard Tauranga is no exception and it is probably true that members have enjoyed above average conditions compared to those prevailing elsewhere in New Zealand throughout most of our history.

In the early years green keeping was very much a matter of keeping the grass growing and regularly mown. The machinery used to achieve this was not specifically designed for golf course work with the result that greens tended to be well-grassed but slow, fairways weedy and stalky, the rough long, thick and difficult. Bunkers, where they existed, were generally unkempt and highly variable in playing characteristics. On many courses greens were mown just once a week, usually on a Friday ready for the weekend play.

While Mr Coles, Mr Reeves, and other early members of staff did a very good job with the equipment and knowledge they had at the time it was not until the appointment of Grant Silvester in 1951 that Tauranga Golf Club entered the modern era of scientific Golf Course Management. That aspect of our history, and the history of Golf Course Management in New Zealand is best presented by detailing Grant’s career in the service of the Club.

GRANT SILVESTER

Grant Silvester took over the role of head greenkeeper in 1951 and remained in the role for a further 21 years. Up until that time the role had been seen more as that of a grass cutter and general labourer than that of a manager of fine turf. The work of Sir Bruce Levy, Ernie Madden, and others, which ultimately led to the publication, in 1949, of the booklet, “The Construction, Care and renovation of the Golf Course” marked the beginning of a new era in turf culture. It is to the great credit of Grant Silvester that he very quickly recognised the value of the research that had been done, and continues to be done, through the work of the New Zealand Institute of Turf Culture. Coming to the job with no preconceived ideas Grant proved the right man in the right place at the right time. Prior to the work of Levy and his associates well meaning farmers and others had dominated Greens Committees. These men promoted grass growth through the use of lime and superphosphate, as they would have done in growing pasture. This proved to be the antithesis of what was required and greens throughout the country suffered from a host of deficiencies until staff and administrators gradually began to adopt the “acid theory” of fine turf culture identified through the research. It was the beginning of a movement that would see rapid improvement in playing conditions on courses throughout New Zealand and it is to Grant Silvester and the members of the Greens committees of the time that we owe gratitude for ensuring that Tauranga Golf Club was in the vanguard of that movement.

title: Greenkeeping · p. 178
text:
Obviously not everyone accepted the new philosophy of turf management and there were many ‘clubhouse experts’ who disagreed very vocally with what was being put into practice. Nothing has really changed has it? In desperation Grant agreed to let some of these ‘expert’ grass growers put their theories into practice. The seventeenth green was divided into four quarters, three of which were allocated to different theorists, the fourth remaining under Grant’s management. Within less than twelve months the three sections under amateur control showed poor grass cover, disease, a muddy surface, and other undesirable features. That under professional management exhibited good grass cover with healthy colour and appearance and a good putting surface. The ‘experts’ were silenced, at least temporarily. Unfortunately there was an ongoing downside to the experiment as, for some years to follow, one could look down upon the green from the ‘Knoll’ and distinguish the four separate sections. Members had to endure varied conditions on the green for quite a lengthy period.

Grant Silvester was brought up on a small farm overlooking the Waimapu estuary and caught many a flounder there. Upon leaving home he set up an orchard and glasshouse property on the part of Courtney Road now known as 22nd Avenue. It was his neighbour Jimmy Mowat who suggested to Grant that he would be ideally suited to the Greenkeeper role that had become available at the Club. After ensuring that he would have some flexibility in meeting the demands of both his orchard and the greenkeeper role Grant accepted the job with some trepidation. He accepted that he had all the

practical skills required but he had no experience of golf, golfers, or the special requirements of sports turf. Having accepted the challenge he took it upon himself to gain the necessary knowledge as quickly as possible. In doing so he became the first at Tauranga, and amongst the first Nationally, to recognise the value of the research done on turf culture. Encouraged by Alan Davidson, Jimmy Mowat and others, Grant visited other clubs to study their methods. He went to greenkeepers’ conferences, often accompanied by Greens Committee Chairman Alan Davidson, and in time became recognised as a man other greenkeepers could approach for advice in the knowledge that they would ‘get the right oil’.

Equipment in Grant’s tenure was basic to say the least. Essentially it consisted of a set of gang mowers towed behind the versatile Ferguson tractor, a set of Overgreen mowers behind which the operator would walk, and an Attco hand mower used to mow tight spots such as the edges of bunkers. An old model T Ford with a small tray served a great variety of transport requirements. This Model T had to be started with a crank handle though it was extremely reliable and generally started easily even on frosty mornings. When required Grant would bring his own Gravely tractor from his home property. The Gravely was a very versatile machine to which could be attached a number of implements including a rotary hoe, a sickle bar mower, and a rotary mower. Later Grant developed a rotary broom to sweep cores into rows for easy removal from the greens. He also adapted an old Morrison lawn mower as a grooving machine for use on the greens.

In spite of this paucity of equipment and the fact that the Green Staff consisted of the Head Greenkeeper and just one assistant the course was kept in very good order throughout the year. Initially there were significant areas of deep rough which were mown with the sickle bar mower just two or three times a year. One such area was the ridge between the first and second fairways, another along the left of the seventh. A ball in such an area was often unable to be found. Later the course began to be mown from

title: Greenkeeping · p. 179
text:
boundary to boundary and the rough became restricted to small isolated areas. Towards the end of Grant’s time at the Club he became more and more proprietorial toward the course. It was almost as though it was his private park and to some extent he resented the golfers who came daily to make a mess of it by chopping up the fairways, walking their trundlers too close to the greens and tees, and otherwise making a nuisance of themselves. There are still those of us at the club who would not dream of taking a trundler across a tee, or close to a green for fear of provoking a roar of wrath from the ghost of a greenkeeper past. One could understand Grant’s feeling that the course belonged to him as there can be no doubt that Grant Silvester put his heart and soul into producing the course in the best possible condition day by day, month by month, year by year, throughout his many years in the job. His signature remains to this day as so many of the tees, greens, bunkers, and other features of the course were reformed or developed during his tenure. He brought the course into a new age and laid the foundation for much that has followed. Grant left the Club to take on the role of Superintendent of Parks and Reserves for the Western Bay of Plenty District Council and later, with his wife Faye, retired to live in Mangonui, North Auckland, where he continued his love of fishing.

THE POST SILVESTER YEARS

Les Hill replaced Grant in 1973 and was able to maintain the rate of course improvement that members

had become accustomed to. Golf Course maintenance is like so many other aspects of life: unless you strive for improvement it seems you are doomed to go backwards. Les was enticed to join us from Rotorua by the offer of a salary of $3900 and the prospect of accommodation in a house owned by the Club. This house was located at 1368 Cameron Road almost directly opposite the entrance to the Racecourse Reserve and Mr. Hill took up residence there that year. To finance the purchase of this house the Club sold the section they owned off Hynd’s Road behind the Substation.

Les Hill was an excellent Greenkeeper, well versed in the modern concepts of Turf Management. During his tenure the course was well maintained and was further improved under his guidance. Unfortunately he pushed himself too hard in attempting to get as much done as possible. He virtually ran around the course and this self-imposed pressure could not be sustained indefinitely. In 1978 Les took up an appointment with the Pukekohe Club where he continued to produce playing conditions of which he could justifiably be proud.

Following a period during which a number of employees served short terms in charge of the course Alan Martin was enticed from Mt. Denby, the Whangarei headquarters of the Northland Golf Club. One of our members played Mt. Denby subsequent to this appointment and, upon mentioning that we now had Alan in charge of our course, the laconic response from the Mt. Denby member was to the effect that “we would now enjoy some excellent paths on our course.” Grant Patterson was appointed in 1980. Grant was a New Zealander who had been working in Australia for some years where he had considerable experience in developing golf courses from scratch. Interestingly one of his reasons for wishing to move back to New Zealand was so his children could

title: Greenkeeping · p. 180
text:
attend school here. He felt the New Zealand education system was superior to that in Australia. It is almost certainly true that the membership in general did not give Grant the credit his abilities deserved. When he began his time at Tauranga he inherited a course that, despite the best intentions of those involved, had not experienced the level of professional care that had prevailed during the Silvester/Hill period. Consequently the greens were suffering from gross mineral deficiency, the turf was weak and readily susceptible to disease, and the general state of the course was well below that which should have prevailed at the time. No Course Superintendent could have been expected to rectify those conditions over night. Grant Patterson was no exception though the evidence at the time suggested he took the correct steps to get course management back onto a sound foundation. By the time he resigned to move back to Australia in 1985 it was clear that the course was well on the road to recovery.

The next significant appointment was that of Murray Clark in 1995. Murray had been in charge of the Poverty Bay Golf Club’s Awapuni course in Gisborne. Not long before he moved north he had been responsible for preparing that course for the Freyberg Rosebowl as the Inter-provincial Men’s Team Championship was then known. During that tournament the Awapuni greens were given unusually high praise for their exceptionally good condition. I had the pleasure of playing them the week before the tournament and can truthfully say I have never experienced better greens. They were fast and very true. Some of those who were players or spectators during the tournament afterwards vouched for the extremely high standard of putting those greens promoted. Clearly Murray knew what was required to produce greens of that quality. Awapuni is near the coast and so is natural sand country that is ideal for the promotion of the fine turf grasses best suited to golf greens. Tauranga posed a different challenge, one that Murray proved, over the next few years, well able to meet. In his favour an excellent team of assistants aided him. The needs of the Club had by this time built up to the stage where it was considered that four full time assistants were required in order to groom the course to the higher standard now considered appropriate. Naturally there were members who believed this to be an unnecessarily high number but if the Club wished to satisfy the more exacting demands of the modern player then there was little choice but to supply the manpower to do the job. In contrast to earlier, more relaxed times, when greens were mowed twice weekly, fairways mowed boundary to boundary, and bunkers given an occasional tidy up, greens were now required to be mown daily, fairways contoured and more frequently mown, and bunkers and surrounds manicured regularly. All of this is labour intensive and the staff must attempt to fit everything in and around people playing the course. Collectively somewhere in the vicinity of 1000 rounds are played each week of the year.

By 2002 Murray Clark began to feel he would like to relinquish some of the responsibility he then held and an agreement was reached whereby he would step down to an assistant role if the Club were able to attract a suitably qualified Course Supervisor. An outstanding young candidate in Brendan Allen applied for the position and was duly appointed. An old student of Tauranga Boys’ College, Brendan had almost completed a Business Studies degree at Waikato University when he decided he preferred the idea of an outdoor life and joined the staff of the Hamilton Golf Club at their St. Andrews course. On completing an apprenticeship there he moved to become second in charge at the Russley Golf Club in Christchurch where he experienced quite different climatic and soil conditions thus broadening his experience and knowledge.

title: Greenkeeping · p. 181
text:
During the few short years Brendan spent as Course Supervisor at Tauranga he made a tremendous impact on all those with whom he was associated. Not only did he bring a wealth of experience disproportionate to his years, he introduced fresh ideas and methods that continued to influence course conditions and policy long after his departure. Whilst the Club administration would dearly have loved to retain Brendan’s services they were unable to compete with the resources available to the Auckland Golf Club of Middlemore who soon became aware of Brendan’s outstanding ability and made him “an offer he couldn’t refuse”. We could only wish him well and lament that we had not been able to enjoy the benefit of his expertise over a much longer period. It will be surprising if Brendan does not have a lasting impact on green keeping practise throughout the country.

In 2006 Graeme Duncan was appointed to fill the role vacated by Brendan. Graeme came to us from the home of Golf, Scotland, via Inglewood Golf Club in Taranaki. This was the same club from which we recruited Royce Lahood, a man who contributed so much to our Club while serving in the capacity of Manager from 1970 to 1983. Graeme demonstrated early in his tenure that he had clear ideas on how he wanted the course to develop under his methods and simply got on with the task of achieving those objectives. Again conditions are different here to those in Taranaki or in Scotland. None the less the principles of growing fine turf and maintaining it over extended periods do not differ markedly from place to place. As Graeme became familiar with the subtle environmental differences of our course that need to be taken into account he grew confidently into the job and soon produced course conditions right up to the expectations of the majority of members. Perhaps he will be most remembered for his bunker construction. While the reconstruction of the bunker fronting the Knoll has added greatly to the frustrations so many of our members experience when playing that hole there is nothing inherently wrong with the bunker or its construction. Any perceived problem really lies in the inadequacy of our techniques to deal with genuine hazards. Shallow bunkers with low lips, as are common on New Zealand courses, hardly constitute hazards.

The first trial of sand imported from outside the course for use in bunkers was made in 1956 when one truckload of river sand was purchased. It was not until 1963 that Papamoa beach sand was finally used in bunkers throughout the course thus relegating the fine pumice previously used to history. It was definitely an improvement though the pumice, when dry and fluffy, had been excellent to play from. Unfortunately it did not remain in that state for long. Sanding of greens was considered over many years before it was finally introduced. Grant Silvester and others had observed that those areas of the greens where players had spread sand when recovering from bunkers appeared to offer a better

environment to Browntop and Chewings Fescue than did other parts of the green. Bruce Levy and his associates had proven the value of sanding on the Hokowhitu greens but would it confer the same benefits under our very different soil and climatic conditions?  Michael Nicholson was probably the man who did most to push for the introduction of sanding on our greens. A member of the Greens Committee from 1985 to 1993 Michael had seen the value of incorporating sand into the greens on courses he played at Provincial and International level, both in New Zealand and Overseas. There was plenty of opposition however. The Club had received a report from the New Zealand Institute of Turf Culture advising that the technique would not be suitable on our greens. This was backed up by Les Hill who applied for his old job at Tauranga when Alan Martin resigned. At interview Les commented: “we would

title: Greenkeeping · p. 182
text: be wasting our time to sand greens at Tauranga”.  In spite of these and other objections Michael, then Chairman of the Greens Committee, finally got the OK from the committee to proceed with a sanding program. Surprisingly this was not to be a trial using the putting green, or some other area, for a year or two to prove the worth or otherwise of the program. The risky approach of committing all the greens to the program was instead embarked upon from the beginning. Fortunately the doubters were soon proven to be wrong and the program was here to stay with obvious on-going advantage to the course and its members. Sports Turf preparation is both an Art and a Science. Those charged with that preparation make decisions that prove advantageous at some times and not at others. Tauranga Golf Club has been fortunate that the long-term trend resulting from the totality of decisions reached has been one of steady improvement to the general benefit of both present and future members. The decision to sand greens, the installation of an adequate irrigation system, the establishment of Windsor Green fairways, and the instigation of daily mowing of greens have been amongst the most significant decisions made by the Club during its first one hundred years. While each has been made in the face of opposition, each has proven to be of enormous benefit. In March 1984 it was reported that the greens were being mown four days per week. This was a clear improvement on the twice a week schedule that had prevailed for many years. It was considered that Saturday morning mowing would be beneficial but the cost at $60 per time, or $3000 per year, was prohibitive. Sunday morning mowing would be even more costly. It was not until the 1980s that daily mowing, including weekends, was instituted. The availability of better machinery allowed this to be completed quickly and efficiently. No one would have contemplated such a program in the days of the Over-green mowers when the operator walked behind the machine. Throughout our history there have been those who disagree with the way our course has been managed. It may be difficult to appreciate that fine turf greens cannot be kept in ‘tournament condition’ 52 weeks of the year. The courses the Professionals play on the USA and European PGA Tours are brought to a peak for those events. This process may take place over several months. It is the same for the major events we stage. Turf grasses do not respond well to constant close mowing and rolling but this is what is required to produce tournament greens that are fast and true. The Greens Supervisor must temper the desire of members to experience ‘tournament conditions’ on a regular basis with the need to protect the health of the greens throughout the year. Sadly some Club officials over the years have not appreciated this and have agitated for conditions that are simply unsustainable. Should such views ever prevail the long term consequences would be serious indeed.

title: Water supply · p. 183
text:
CHAPTER FOURTEEN

WATER SUPPLY

title: Water supply · p. 184
text:
The problem of obtaining adequate water at reasonable cost exercised the minds of successive Greens Committees over many years. The first supply was sourced from the Borough Council and was piped from Cameron Road and then pumped around the course from a small pump shed located behind the 11th tee. There was no storage tank so pressure depended upon the demands placed on the Borough supply by householders. The pipe system did not reach as far as the greens at the southern end of the course so they tended to deteriorate badly in the hot dry days of summer. The sprinklers were of the garden variety fed by hoses attached to taps near the green margins. Consequently they required shifting two or three times in order to cover the entire green. Daytime watering was unpopular with members but a necessary evil. Grant Silvester was especially diligent in watering at night whenever practicable even though this meant he had to drive to the course at inconvenient times through the night in order to move sprinklers.

In 1963 the possibility of obtaining water from the Kopurereroa stream, which runs in close proximity to the western boundary of the Reserve, was first investigated. This concept was deferred indefinitely as it was considered to be a much more expensive option than continuing to utilise the Council supply. However the cost of Council water soon began to rise and it became once again imperative to seek a more permanent solution to the supply problem. In 1970 Brown Brothers from the Waikato were commissioned to investigate the prospect of obtaining water from a bore and promising sites were located near the stables on the 11th and to the west of the first tee. It was decided to sink a bore at the latter site and this initially produced adequate supplies from a depth of some 45m. In July 1971 the Club minutes record that a quote had been obtained to extend the reticulation system to cover all greens at a cost of $5000 while another $12 000 was to be spent on the bore, deep well pump, motor and accessories.  This work was proceeded with by utilising a $16 000 loan from the ANZ Bank which was guaranteed by a group of members. The terms of repayment were that $4000 was to be repaid in the first year, followed by a minimum of $1333 per year for nine years. The interest rate was fixed at 7.5%. The completed system was still very basic and still involved placing and shifting sprinklers while the teeing grounds were not yet part of the network. Furthermore the flow from the bore gradually diminished and even though the present reservoir was constructed nearby it soon became apparent that the supply was never going to keep up with the demand. Forced to look elsewhere the committee again investigated piping water from the Kopurereroa stream. Fortunately the water quality was found to be appropriate for turf irrigation and the Club was granted a Water Right. Today water can be pumped from the stream to the 100,000-gallon reservoir at the rate of 7500 gallons per hour. Initially it was planned to have a smaller reservoir but when Royce Lahood contacted the Boys’ College Mathematics

department to check the dimensions required he decided that adding an extra metre to the quoted radius would add little to the cost and be on the “safe side”. Little did Royce know what an enormous difference that 1m would make to the capacity of the reservoir but in hindsight it was a serendipitous decision on his part as the modern reticulation system the course now boasts is required to pump out a great volume of water when performing at full capacity.

The next development came in 1978 when after a long negotiation a new long-term lease was arranged with the Commissioner of Crown Lands. With renewed confidence in their long term tenancy the Club approved the expenditure of $48,000 to install full water reticulation to all tees and greens, including

title: Water supply · p. 185
text:
The Club is fortunate that incidents of interference through balls being stolen from fairways have been rare over the years but they do happen. On one occasion two visiting competitors in the 28-hole open Tournament had this happen to them on the 10th hole. Not knowing their rights under the rules they returned to the tee and played out the hole. They were of course entitled to replace the moved balls without penalty. The two strokes this cost them meant that one at least missed out on a high placing.
