Though the Match Committee was sympathetic to their plight there was nothing they could do to alter the outcome as they had ‘put another ball into play under Stroke and Distance’.

automatic sprinklers. Again the ANZ Bank approved the required finance, granting the Club another ten-year term loan to complete the project. The system was installed under the direction of a club member who, though a qualified Civil Engineer, was neither experienced nor expert in the field of water reticulation. The Club were later to learn to their regret that designing and installing a reticulation system is a job for a specialist in the field. For the next 17 years the Greens staff did their best with a system that proved more and more unreliable until it became obvious that the Club would never achieve the standard of course presentation they desired unless they “grasped the nettle” and replaced the system with a modern, professionally designed, reticulation network incorporating top quality components.

Subsequently the Greens Committee submitted a proposal to the Club for the installation of just such a system by the company known as Northern Irrigation at a cost of $196 000. Approval was gained and the system completed in April 1995. It was wonderful to see the coverage of greens, tees and surrounds that eventuated when the system was first switched on and it was not long before the benefits to the turf could be seen. The water system had finally become a major tool in enabling the staff to achieve the ideal environment to suit the growth of quality sports turf. The cost of the system remained a burden to be carried by the membership for a number of years to follow but few would argue the decision to proceed was not a wise one. There were some problems encountered as more pressure was placed upon the system, the main one being one of “hammering” in the pipes where their laying had not been up to scratch in some areas. This resulted in some blowouts and leakage that frustrated staff and imposed upon their limited labour resources. Fortunately problems became less frequent as solutions were found. The problems that were encountered illustrated once again the fallacy of cutting corners when building something that is expected to perform reliably day-by-day, year-by-year. In this case the problems encountered were probably the result of using non-specialist labour for the actual installation

Will we be extending the watering system to include fairway watering in the future? It seems unlikely from this perspective. The cost of installation would be high but not insurmountable in a more affluent future. Of more concern would be the high cost of maintenance and the probable difficulty in obtaining

title: Water supply · p. 186
text:
a sufficient quantity of water, a resource that will become increasingly scarce as Global warming and population pressures continue to develop. For these reasons the Board of Management, early this Century, initiated the development of “Windsor Green” fairways. The decision to do so was made in consultation with David Ormsby of the New Zealand Sports Turf Institute. Other Cynodon species were considered before the decision to go with Windsor Green was made. Properly managed this grass thrives under hot dry conditions without the need for any applied water. Windsor Green has obvious faults, chief of which is the period of dormancy it undergoes in winter. Even then it provides a very playable surface, something that could not be said of the drought stricken fairways encountered in many a previous summer. The wisdom of the policy to convert our fairways becomes more and more apparent as the years go by.

The first trial introduction of Windsor Green was made in 2000 when it was incorporated into the 11th and 13th fairways as a trial. The fairways were first sprayed with Roundup to eliminate all existing growth. The contracted supplier used a machine that simultaneously cut grooves, shredded the turf, and laid the shredded material in the grooves.  This was an expensive exercise, the price to the contractor alone being $17 000, while our own staff spent many hours ensuring the implants had the best chance of survival. Conditions for growth that first summer were far from ideal with the result that those who were promoting the development of these new fairways had some anxious moments as the material struggled to become established. The doubters, of whom there were many, claimed the Executive had made a serious error of judgement. Fortunately conditions improved and a solid carpet of turf was finally achieved. That was not the end of the doubts however as the staff had to learn how to manage the new turf to achieve the best playing conditions and to ensure these were maintained through the growing season. Fortunately Brendan Allen was enthusiastic about the new turf and developed a management program that was successful in achieving these ends. Cynodon species, and Windsor Green in particular, have an extremely vigorous and robust growth form and require quite severe mechanical treatment to achieve ideal fairway conditions. This meant increased mowing while regular grooving had to be implemented in order to maintain turf vigour. These requirements increased the demands upon staff resources, a factor partially offset by lower needs for fairway watering.

It was Brendan’s belief that the groovings from established fairways could be used to spread the Windsor Green to other fairways. Consequently he piled up large stacks of these with the intention of trialling this technique. Unfortunately some members of the Board were not totally convinced that the policy of introducing Windsor Green throughout the fairways had yet proven to be the correct option for

the future. While they debated the issue the stored material deteriorated and became useless much to Brendan’s disappointment. It was not until after Brendan’s departure that a trial was finally undertaken, the second fairway, and part of the sixth, being “seeded” with groovings in 2005. Though establishment was slow much was learnt from the trial and the final result was successful following a second season of growth.

In 2006 the remainder of the sixth fairway was planted. On this occasion the Pukekohe supplier delivered truckloads of turf that were then manually cut into narrow slices, an arduous job indeed. These slices were then fed by hand into grooves that had been previously cut into the fairway after the

title: Water supply · p. 187
text: existing fairway grasses had been eliminated with herbicide. Faced with a shortage of volunteers to perform this final task Manager Grant Scoones contacted local Backpacker Hostels and soon young people from many Countries including Austria, Argentina, Belgium, England, Scotland, Germany, and Italy joined the working group. These young men and women were keen to earn some cash and proved to be willing and diligent workers with the result that the job was completed within three days. While this method proved successful, and much was learnt that might have enabled subsequent plantings to be carried out more efficiently, there were obvious drawbacks. The turf alone cost $7000 while the labour requirement was very high. In view of these factors it was decided to continue the establishment program using our own material obtained by grooving our existing fairways. Unfortunately this has meant the program has progressed at the rate of just one fairway per year. At least this minimised the inconvenience to members caused by taking each treated fairway out of play for several months. The eighth and tenth fairways were successfully converted to Windsor Green in 2008 and 2009 respectively with minimum disruption to play as staff became more adept at handling this new technique. The program lapsed in 2010 before resuming in 2011 when a successful conversion of the 18th fairway was achieved. At this stage there was still much to be done to convert the remaining fairways.

title: Trees · p. 188
text:
CHAPTER FIFTEEN

TREES

title: Trees · p. 189
text:
During the depression years of the Thirties then President Mr A J Mirrielees saw an opportunity to use the Government unemployed relief worker scheme to enhance the Golf Course environment through an extensive tree planting program. Ultimately many thousands of trees were planted as shelterbelts, strategic course components, and as purely ornamental trees. Mr Mirrielees worked with those trees that were available to him at the time and in general the selection and placement of these have stood the test of time. Over the years some specimens proved less than ideal and were removed and often replaced with more suitable varieties. Others have died, become diseased, or been damaged or blown over by the strong winds that sometimes sweep the area. Controversy has arisen over almost all moves to remove any particular tree and yet, once they have gone, they are soon forgotten and people wonder what the fuss was about. The most cosseted tree on the course was perhaps the Japanese Weeping pine (Pinus patula), also known as the Waterfall pine, which once graced the ridge between the first and second fairways. The protective shelters erected around it were blown down, cows trampled it, rabbits burrowed under it, golfers occasionally struck it with ball or club, and mowers knocked bark off it. Despite all these setbacks it flourished and enhanced the ridge for many years until it finally lost a  battle with the elements during a storm in 1979.

Bruce Burbery, Murray McDonald, and occasionally others of their friends were early “golf ball entrepreneurs” on the course. As youngsters they would find balls at various popular spots and offer them to members at 1/- for a good one. At this price Dunlop 65s and Spalding Hot Dots were keenly sought. The boys had to be on the alert for, should Grant Silvester sight them, he would chase them from the course, sometimes before they had time to take their prize finds with them. In time Bruce accumulated enough 1/- pieces to purchase a new Peter Thomson driver from Jim Paterson. Jim encouraged Bruce to try his new purchase on the first tee. Jim came out of his shop to watch, knowing that he might see something spectacular from the long hitting youngster. The first drive finished Pin high left, the next right. As Bruce prepared to hit a third Noel Hocken appeared from his office. “We do not allow more than two balls from the tees in practice” said Noel in his most formal and forbidding managerial manner. While Jim looked sheepishly the other way Bruce headed up the fairway to retrieve the balls and head to the second tee. Jim, guessing Bruce would not be able to resist the challenge of driving to the second green headed across there. Grant Silvester was on his faithful ‘Fergie’ beside the green so Bruce waited for him to move away but Grant waved him to play. Bruce drove, the ball carrying far enough to strike the engine cover on the tractor leaving a considerable dent, and flying past Grant’s ducking head. Jim sneaked quietly back to his shop while Bruce anticipated a right bollocking but Grant took it all in good part.

title: Trees · p. 190
text:
Bert Goulding planted the Moreton Bay Fig beside the clubhouse around 1920. It is as fine a specimen as can be seen anywhere, including its native Australia, and, though it creates problems for the clubhouse situated alongside, few would be prepared to advocate its removal. Mr Goulding was also responsible for supplying and nurturing the two Canadian Redwoods behind the Knoll.

Joyce Carnachan donated the Jacaranda by the fourth green while Keith Lusk planted the three Kauris on the second tee during the late thirties. The latter three showed little growth until released to the light some twenty years later. The date palms that were once more prevalent on the course originated through the children of one member sneaking dates from the kitchen cupboard and throwing the stones out the window to destroy the evidence. Eventually the stones germinated, the misdemeanour was forgiven, and the young palms transplanted to the course where they flourished unless becoming victim to a misdirected sweep of the mower. Over the years many people have contributed to the planting, nurture, and ongoing care of the trees on the course. Harry and Maurice Bradmore, Fred Washer, Frank and Maisie Warnes, and Willis Faulds were especially involved during mid-century years when many strategic fairway trees were introduced. Bill Kennedy of the Tree Society, though not a golfer, donated many fine specimens. He was also the driving force behind the development of McLarens Falls Park and has been responsible for much

enhancement of the City and surrounds through the donation of trees and the encouragement given to others to become involved in planting specimen trees. Many other people have donated trees over the years and the tradition continues.  Around the turn of the new century members were given the opportunity to donate $100 to purchase suitably selected trees which were then planted, each with a small plaque recognising the donor. This project was very well supported.

Bob Burstall, an authority on trees, was based in Rotorua with the Forest Service. In 1979 he and Club

identity Willis Faulds did a thorough survey of the trees on the course during which they identified 102 different species and estimated there were over 7000 individual trees and shrubs. For some years Mr. Burstall was regularly consulted on the program for the planting, care, removal and replacement of trees. His expertise in that role was invaluable and added much to the development of the property. In recent years the “Firewood Gang”, recognised elsewhere in this publication have undertaken the task of controlling and encouraging the proper growth of trees on the course, an essential task that was sometimes neglected in the past as evidenced by the large number of multi-trunk and poorly shaped trees that we do have. The work of Jim Swainson has been particularly valuable in this context. “Arbor Care Ltd” has provided annual tree maintenance under contract funded by the Racecourse Reserve Committee. COMMEMORATIVE TREES In addition to being honoured with Life Membership of the Club a commemorative Deodar (Cedrus deodar) was planted between the sixth green and seventh tee as a permanent reminder of the contribution Mr Mirrielees made to the Club. This was the first of a number of commemorative plantings that have been made either by the Club itself, by groups within it, or by family members.

title: Trees · p. 191
text:
Beside the entrance path to the clubhouse stands a European Olive from Galatos in Greece. This was planted by members of the RSA Golf Group in memory of New Zealand men who died in the Cretan Campaign. Beside it stands a Magnolia (Michaela dolposa) planted in 1983 in memory of Una Wickham, our greatest woman golfer. Three flowering cherries were planted adjacent to the tenth tee to enhance the setting for a dedicated seat placed there in memory of David Coates by his family. The family of Norm Roberts planted a Kauri behind the fourth tee in his memory. As we walk from the fifth green behind the seventh green we pass a Kauri tree planted in memory of Jack Pattison, son of member Brian Pattison. This Kauri has since been joined by a matching Kauri donated by Tony Reynish and Jackie MacDonald. These two trees will, in time, form an imposing backdrop to the fifth green when viewed from the tee. Long serving professional Jim Paterson is commemorated by a Rimu planted near the fourteenth green by his family while close by can be seen the Pohutukawa commemorating Phill Johnston’s 60 years of membership. A fine Gingko tree was planted in memory of Henry Becker to the right of the seventeenth tee. Henry was a keen golfer in retirement, served as assistant secretary to Royce Lahood, and at one time was secretary to the BOP Golf Association. The Dorothy Garland Competition was contested by teams of committee members from the Zones of the BOPTV Golf Association. Each year Dorothy donated a Camellia to be planted in honour of the winning team. Tauranga successes can be seen in the Camellias planted beside the first tee. The

Ladies Club also planted a Camellia in the garden beside the trundler shed in memory of Peg Cross (Later Bates).

The tradition of planting a tree in commemoration of past members whose association with the club gave them special pleasure is to be encouraged though it is important that tree selection and siting need to be authorised by the Club Administration to ensure that the long term policies of the Board are not compromised. A welcome alternative to the planting of a tree would be the donation of a bench seat

beside an appropriate tee. The seat beside the 12th tee, donated in memory of Joe Loughlin by his family, provides a welcome resting spot where players can pause while they contemplate how to handle the difficulties that await them on that challenging hole. The daughters of Barbara Carlisle went a step further when they erected an elaborate shelter below the fifth tee in memory of Barbara. Golfers can sit in comfort and safety while waiting for the players ahead to complete play from the tee. This was an appropriate and most welcome addition to the facilities around the course. In earlier times Harry Butts, who played on the old Domain course and later at Gate Pa, showed his appreciation of the pleasure he had derived from membership by donating seats for every tee on the course. These were custom built seats with a fitted rubbish bin at one end and a water container at the other. On Fridays a member of the green staff would empty the rubbish and replenish the water container with clean water. Patent ball washers were unknown at the time and the water and associated cloth were well-used accessories. Mr Butts was a very well known identity in the Town, it being his custom to walk down to the Strand each morning, summer and winter to swim in the harbour. He kept this up until well into his eighties. It must have kept him in fine fettle for it was claimed he collected his BNZ superannuation longer than any other ex-employee of that venerable institution. In the World at large trees serve a wide variety of vitally important roles. This is no less true on Golf

title: Trees · p. 192
text:
Courses where they may be used to enhance the strategic design of particular holes, to provide shelter and shade, to beautify the landscape, and to encourage bird and insect life. Unfortunately many a course in New Zealand has been designed as a series of tree-lined avenues with little attempt to provide variation through the use of strategically placed bunkers, mounds, or other features. Such courses may be challenging but they do lack the variety that distinguishes those courses that provide the most stimulating golfing experience. Tauranga is not free of such holes but fortunately the topography of the course lends itself to a good measure of variety between holes and within single holes. Careful planning and wise future development are necessary if the “member friendly” character of the course is to be preserved for the benefit of future generations. Sensible selection, placement, and culture of trees will be an important aspect of those aspirations. Mistakes have been made in the past. Some trees such as the Casuarinas planted to the right of the second fairway are totally unsuited to the role for a variety of reasons. They are not attractive specimen trees, they shed acidic litter that kills the grass around their base and, as they age, they spread large shallow roots over a wide area. Similar criticism could be made of Pinus radiata, Macrocarpa, and others that are far too common on our courses. Alex Glasgow, a senior advisor with the New Zealand Sports Turf Institute said in a paper on Golf Course Tree Planting that “the only good thing about yellow macrocarpas is that they don’t live too long and most of them are now coming to the end of their lives”. The Japanese flowering cherries that attract large numbers of Tuis in Springtime unfortunately are readily spread in the droppings of those beautiful birds. As a result they threaten to become a major weed problem if that is not already the case. How much better it would have been had Kowhai and Kaka Beak been planted instead to encourage the Tuis. There are many other attractive native trees that may well have found a place on the course though hindsight is indeed a wonderful thing and perhaps Mr Mirrielees, and those who followed, had little choice but to use what was readily available and affordable at the time.

For many years any tree growing on the course appeared to be treated as though it was untouchable. This was unfortunate, as trees on a golf course primarily need to serve the needs of the game. While well placed, well groomed, trees are an important adjunct to the landscape of a golf course the course is not, nor should it be seen to be, a Botanical Garden. In many cases early specimens were allowed to grow as they wished with the result that many grew into multi-trunk specimens that cannot now be readily trained to gain pleasing shape and form though Arbor Care and our own chain saw artiste, Jim Swainson, have made valiant efforts to do so. Many of these trees, especially the less desirable conifers, are past their best days and it is to be hoped that

a continued program of removal and replacement will see an improvement in both the aesthetic, and strategic value of trees on the course.

In earlier times branches were allowed to grow down to ground level making it difficult to get under them, let alone play any form of recovery shot should you be unfortunate enough to be a few yards off line. In other situations trees close to greens and tees caused severe shading that led to weak turf subject to insect and disease damage. Happily a more enlightened approach has been taken in more recent times with real benefit to both the quality of the turf and to the enjoyment of the player. Longer standing members will remember the sense of relief that flowed through the membership when

title: Trees · p. 193
text: the skirts on most of the trees were raised during the eighties. Fashionably attired golfers, women in particular, could now expect to complete the round in something close to the sartorial state in which they commenced their round, having not been forced to crawl under low hanging branches in order to get into position to play some sort of recovery stroke.

title: Twilight golf · p. 194
text:
CHAPTER SIXTEEN

TWILIGHT GOLF

title: Twilight golf · p. 195
text:
There are few pleasures to match that of wandering over a golf course on a balmy summer evening. Should the drives be booming down the centres of the fairways and the putts nestling into the bottoms of the holes so much the better, though something less on the scale of golfing excellence will not significantly dampen our enjoyment. For this reason vast numbers of golfers throughout the Country, from raw beginner to seasoned expert, look forward to the onset of Daylight Saving and the start of Twilight Golf. Residents of Tauranga are no exception though interest has not been consistent through the years.

Twilight tournaments were introduced to Tauranga in the summer of 1974/75 when willing volunteers would organise roll up starts, simple prizes, and a light meal to follow the golf. These weekly events were rotated over different week nights in an attempt to cater for those who might have commitments on particular nights. On account of the lay out of the course, the ninth hole being well away from the clubhouse, these events were played over ten holes simply because the tenth hole finished right by the car park. The first year realised a profit of $186 thanks mainly to the splendid catering provided by a large team of volunteers led by Nen Sim. Nen kept meticulous records where she listed the income and expenditure each night together with many other relevant details including the menu, recipes, and suggestions for improvement. From these records we learn that on one night in January 1975 seventy people were served a meal. To cater for that number the menu included nine roast chickens served cold, four pounds of corned beef, and fourteen pounds of tomatoes. A potato salad included five pounds of potatoes plus a range of complementary ingredients. Cole Slaw and a bean, corn, carrot and onion salad were also available. For this sumptuous feast the princely sum of $1 was charged and yet the profit shown was more than $26. The price of a meal increased to $1.50 the following year with the objective being to build up a pool of funds from which to purchase a number of items that it was felt the kitchen lacked. This objective was successfully achieved under Nen’s efficient management. At the end of the 1976/77 season items such as a Zip Water Heater, an extra refrigerator, an electric fan, and a selection of kitchen utensils were purchased from accumulated profit. By this time the catering for Twilight Golf was a joint effort involving Nen and her volunteers together with Mrs Anderson, the Club Caterer. It was a most amenable arrangement. Though a large number of women volunteered to assist Nen those who carried most of the burden were Nen herself, Joan Frith, Mavis Ward, and Joyce Gallagher. What a wonderful job they did so willingly.

While these early events were popular with a group of loyal devotees, mainly regular club members, the concept gained additional impetus when Noel Copestake became involved. Under Noel’s leadership a small team gradually evolved a streamlined system that allowed a large field to play their ten holes, enjoy a social hour, a pleasant meal, and a generous prize table each Friday evening. All this was provided at very moderate cost and attracted Club members and visitors alike. Certain key personnel including treasurer, card checkers, bar persons, and barbecue cooks arrived each Friday to play their parts, usually sacrificing their own chance to play so as to ensure that all ran smoothly for the participants. Noel himself started the field, having developed a starting program that ensured that the field flowed freely. He was never known to play in the field himself in all the years he was involved. In addition to acting as starter Noel filled the roles of sponsorship organiser, Master of Ceremonies, and occasional bar tender or barbecue cook as required. He hardly missed an evening in all the time he

title: Twilight golf · p. 196
text:
was involved. Noel’s wife Peg was always there to lend support and it was often Peg who did much of the prior work in buying a stock of prizes from which a selection could be placed on the table each week. Of the other members of the team Joan Brown kept track of the finances, Bruce (bow tie and all) and Marge Anderson checked the cards, Ian Dale, Peter Heeney, and Steve Stephens tended the barbecue, while John Robinson, David Mowat, Des and Noeline Shiel frequently served as bar tenders. Noeline and Des never left before the clubhouse, including the bar area, was clean and tidy ready for the weekend golf. Mary Goodjohn was the caterer through most of those years and she co-operated fully in ensuring that there were ample side dishes to supplement the barbecued offerings. Later the barbecue was used on alternate weeks with Mary providing the full meal on other occasions. From small beginnings, when sixty participants would have been considered an excellent field, the popularity of twilight golf increased until fields of 100 or more were not unusual. The record attendance reached a staggering 158, rather more than could comfortably be accommodated. Since there was never any way of knowing how many might roll up between the scheduled starting period from 4.45 to 6pm the starter had to be very flexible in order to satisfy everyone. To facilitate play for such large numbers four separate courses, each with its own printed card, were developed. Course A covered holes 1-10, while course B covered the same holes but started from the 7th. tee with players moving to the 1st. tee after completing the 10th. hole. Course C covered holes 3-12 while course D played

through 11- 18, then through holes one and two. These courses all start and finish in reasonable proximity to the clubhouse and special starting sheets were developed to co-ordinate the timing so that groups passing through common tees were not inconvenienced. These proved to work very well even under the requirements of large fields.

To ensure all contestants were fairly treated regardless of the holes they played three different 10 hole cards were developed. Had the regular 18 hole card been used this would not have been so as players

would have received different numbers of strokes depending upon the particular course they played. The new cards solved that problem. While the stroke allocation initially confused some players our card checkers, Bruce and Marge, were adept at explaining the system to them. The stroke allocation on these cards followed a different principle to that used on 18 hole cards where fairness in Match Play is the aim. With abbreviated rounds and Stableford scoring the aim was to allocate low strokes to holes where it was most difficult to score Stableford points, typically long par three and four holes. This was quite the reverse of the allocation appropriate to Match Play. The heyday of Friday Evening Twilight Golf came in the Seventies and Eighties and, as with many other activities, circumstances changed and interest began to decline. Somewhat reluctantly Noel was persuaded to step aside from his involvement in order to see if others could rekindle interest. This does not appear to have been achieved despite the effort made. Perhaps it was just a case of the trend line turning inexorably downward. Has not the same thing happened with Indoor Cricket, the game of Pool, and the playing of “skinners” after golf on Saturdays?

To compensate for the decline in one form of Twilight Golf another form has arisen. Gary Baker, a prominent administrator throughout the Nineties, arrived from the Manawatu and soon began promoting the concept of Business House Golf, a development that had been particularly successful at

title: Twilight golf · p. 197
text:
Hokowhitu. With the encouragement and assistance of Noel and others Gary oversaw the instigation of a Wednesday evening competition that initially attracted fourteen teams, each consisting of four players.

The number of teams grew rapidly as the popularity of the competition became widely recognised in the Business Community and soon reached the maximum possible field of 36 teams. In spite of the large field of 144 the play flows relatively freely with everyone usually back in the clubhouse by 8pm. following the 5.30 start. The best three of the four Stableford scores of each team are counted to decide the winner of the teams match each night and also aggregated throughout the season. Team and individual prizes are awarded each evening and, at the end of the season the top teams in both Stableford and Match Play throughout the year are awarded major prizes. Once again ordinary Club cards were used in the early years of this competition until some anomalies became apparent. For example a male five handicapper starting at the sixth tee would receive all five of his strokes in the ten holes he played whereas the same player starting at the fourteenth would receive only one stroke. A new card was consequently designed so as to be as fair as possible to all participants. Two principles were considered in allocating strokes on the new card. The first was that players starting on any one of the 18 holes should receive as close to one half of their handicap as

possible. A secondary requirement was to consider the relative difficulty of scoring Stableford points on a particular hole. These two principles are not entirely compatible so compromise was a necessary part of the process.

At first no consideration was given to developing a handicapping system for twilight golf as participants were all members of Tauranga or other local Clubs and simply used their Club handicaps. As the popularity of the events grew an increasing number of participants with no Club affiliation became

involved, especially in the Business House competition. It became obvious a handicap system especially designed for Twilight Golf was needed. At first the handicapper used his discretion in dealing with those who returned particularly good scores. This soon led to dissatisfaction as real or imagined disparities arose in the way similar performances were treated. In particular there appeared to be a reluctance to allow handicaps to move outward with the result that one really good performance could render the competitor uncompetitive for the remainder of the season. A feature of Nine or Ten Hole golf is that players are often able to produce exceptional scoring which they would be unlikely to sustain through the full 18 holes. A regular club handicap is not necessarily a sound guide to a player’s likely performance over the shorter course. To overcome these problems a new system was developed using suggestions found in the NZGA Handicapping and Course Rating Booklet. This suggested that a player should score about 2.2 points per hole when playing to their handicap. On that basis 22 points was the expected score over ten holes so a buffer zone was set from 20 to 23 points inclusive where no handicap adjustment would result. Points below 20 would allow the handicap to move out one-quarter stroke to a maximum of one stroke. Points from 24 to 26 inclusive would each incur a half stroke reduction, while any points above 26 would each reduce the handicap by a further stroke. Thus someone scoring 30 points over the ten holes, as happened more often than might have been expected, would find themselves cut 5.5 strokes.

title: Twilight golf · p. 198
text:
David Mowat who would, each week, print out a new list of handicaps incorporating both the Friday- night players and the Business-House team members developed this system, and a Computer program to handle it. Non-scoring holes were counted as scoring one point when reviewing cards for handicap purposes. Peg and Kim Copestake became expert at checking and adjusting cards and isolating those that needed to be kept for the handicapper. When the Dot Golf Computer system was installed the technicians wrote and incorporated the Twilight Handicapping system onto the Club computer software. This program has saved countless volunteer hours since its introduction. Under the regular handicapping system women were at a clear disadvantage when competing against men in the Business House competition. In recognition of this they were given a bonus of two points to add to their scores. Once the Twilight Handicap system was fully operating and men and women were being treated in exactly the same way for handicapping purposes it became clear this bonus was no longer justified and it was discontinued.

Twilight Golf proved to be a winner. The Club gained through the facilities being used during evenings when they would otherwise be deserted, potential members were exposed to the attractions full membership does offer and, most importantly, a large number of people were enabled to enjoy themselves in truly pleasant surroundings.   It is to be hoped that some day a reinvigorated Friday evening Twilight program will supplement the Business-House competition.

Over the years many people have given their time to ensure the twilight programmes have run successfully and efficiently. Sometimes these have been Committee members, more often members who have simply enjoyed the opportunity to be part of a convivial group helping to provide pleasure to others and value to their Club. They deserve our admiration and our gratitude.

title: Handicapping through the years · p. 199
text:
CHAPTER SEVENTEEN

HANDICAPPING

THROUGH THE YEARS

title: Handicapping through the years · p. 200
text:
Until the advent of the modern handicapping system developed by the USGA in the sixties handicapping was in the hands of a handicapping committee that may very well have consisted of a single appointee. The committee had a poorly defined mode of operation and essentially used their best judgement as to when to cut and when to increase a player’s handicap, and by how much. These decisions were not made arbitrarily; it just seemed that way to a lot of players especially on those occasions when a cut was made. Men and women had quite different systems, the women having a much more stringent system under which their handicap was based on the best golf they played and one good round could place a player on a handicap to which they might well struggle to play for the next few months. Reviews were done at six monthly intervals and if the one good round was not repeated the player might be let out a stroke or two. Consequently players often found themselves quite uncompetitive for long periods. In addition women were required to earn their first official handicap by playing a round in not more than 36 strokes over par and many a tear was shed when a promising round was destroyed by a single really bad hole. This often happened at holes such as the Gully and the Knoll that claim many victims other than novice women. At times those bunkers at the Gully must have seemed three metres deep and the sides of the Knoll virtually insurmountable. Never the less the day would eventually arrive when that magic score of 108, or better, was achieved and the champagne could be uncorked. What a thrill and a relief it must have been!

Men on the other hand had it easy. Upon joining they were automatically placed on a 24 handicap and it was then up to them to learn to play to that, or better, in order to become competitive. It is possible that the memories of older members become confused as age creeps up on them but there are those who recall that virtually all members in those times eventually learned to play to their 24 handicap and usually improved upon it. In more modern times some seem satisfied to remain on more generous handicaps up to 36. (The slope system may result in men playing off course handicaps even higher than 36). Perhaps the challenge once offered to the 24-handicapper to become competitive is no

longer there.

The handicapper would usually be generous to the novice and allow him a degree of success before “wielding the axe”. My own experience of the system came in my first season when, after a few months, I began to play with a mild degree of success whereupon I picked up the occasional remark about “burgling”. Very politely, as then befitted the approach of a junior to a senior member, I approached the handicapper, Mr Warwick Nicoll. “Excuse me Sir”, I said, “I am starting to get a bit of gentle ribbing regarding my form. Should you not be reviewing my handicap downward”?  His response was to the effect that it would happen soon enough. “You haven’t won enough just yet”. When the axe finally descended a few weeks later it did so with a vengeance, my handicap falling by some ten strokes over a period of two months or so. Both men and women were allowed only three quarters of their handicap when playing Stableford or Bogey (now called Par) competitions, and also three quarters of the difference in handicaps when playing matches. A score of 36 points would often be sufficient to win a Stableford competition and 40 points or more was very rare. Women would have considered 36 points exceptional.

When, in 1962, the NZGA adopted the USGA system for men golfers the task of the handicapper

title: Handicapping through the years · p. 201
text:
became quite onerous. The system was based on the best 10 of your last 20 rounds and, prior to the advent of the personal computer, these records had to be kept manually for every player. As each new score was entered the oldest would be dropped and the handicap, if necessary, recalculated. Arnold Shanks took over the role of keeping track of all this as part of his many duties as Barman and House Manager. It became a common sight to see Arnold poring over cards and record books covering the entire pool table and surrounding area. A number of modifications and improvements have been made to the system since the first version was introduced but the essential basis of the best 10 of the last 20 rounds still applies ensuring that handicaps change quickly so as to more accurately represent current form. No handicapping system will ever achieve the ultimate aim of placing everyone on an equal footing because we humans are far from perfect. There will always be those seeking to gain an edge and Tauranga, like every other Club around the Country, has had its share of those who have found ways to do this. They soon become well known, if not well respected.

In 1995 a complicated system called Calculated Course Rating (CCR) was introduced in an attempt to equate scores made on different days on the same course by allowing for changing conditions. This system proved totally impractical, was widely ‘honoured in the breach’, and finally abandoned to the relief of all who attempted to operate it. The next genuine step forward was made in September 2000 with the adoption of the ‘Slope’ system, the aim of which is to allow players from different Clubs to compete on an equal footing irrespective of the course they are playing. Essentially the system measures how much more difficult a particular course is for the ‘Bogey Player’ compared to the ‘Scratch Player’. This measurement results in a theoretical slope line running between the scratch player and the “bogey” player that is then extrapolated to include players on handicaps beyond those limits. It is interesting to note that Tauranga’s Slope Ratings of 117 for men and 120 for women, as measured from the standard tees, are each slightly above the average rating of 113. The course is clearly not as “easy” as some have suggested over the years.

For many years it seemed apparent that Tauranga members were not well served by the Course rating System. Certainly the Club’s record in Bay of Plenty Intermediate and Junior Pennant fixtures supported this view. The introduction of the Slope System appears to have brought with it a more equitable comparison between the courses in the Bay, and probably beyond. The Club does seem to have been more competitive at these levels in recent years. Course ratings depend upon the subjective decisions of those appointed to do the job and are thus subject to human error so there is no way of confirming or disproving any assumption people may make about the relative fairness between ratings. There will always be discrepancies, both real and imaginary, but these will reduce as rating committees become more experienced and skilled. The combination of the USGA Handicapping System, The Slope System, and accurate Course Rating, have gone a long way towards providing a “level playing field” for all registered golfers. The amalgamation of the National organisations controlling Men’s and Women’s Golf in New Zealand has resulted in a Handicapping and Course Rating system common to both. The development and widespread adoption of computerised handicapping and card analysis has made what were onerous and time-consuming tasks quite simple. Over the course of its history Tauranga Golf Club has not been slow to adopt the

title: Handicapping through the years · p. 202
text:
latest ideas and improvements that have been developed to assist in the playing of the game and in its administration. When computerised handicapping and card reading were first introduced the Club was amongst the first to trial the available systems. Fortunately we did not jump straight into one of the first available systems, preferring to wait, correctly anticipating that improvements would inevitably follow. As a result we were able to install Golf Autoscore when it first became available. In 2005 the Board approved this installation after presentations convinced them that the deficiencies noted in 2002 had now been remedied. The cost involved a purchase price of $8500, and a monthly service fee of $200. It is arguably the best available system by a considerable margin and the administration and the membership have been well pleased with its performance.

It is possible that Tauranga was the first Club in New Zealand to have an opportunity to use computerised handicapping. During the Eighties a computer based handicapping program was written by some students and staff of Tauranga Boys’ College and demonstrated to committee members of the Club. The demonstration was successful in the sense that it accurately recalculated handicaps as new data were entered. It was even able to demonstrate that some of the records entered manually had not resulted in correct recalculation of handicaps. This was hardly surprising in view of the number of records that had to be kept, and the manual calculations that had to be made. Arnold would indeed have to be congratulated on the overall accuracy of the handicap records he kept. Obviously the College could not offer a free service so suggested that they would do a weekly input of all men’s cards for a fee of $50. After some consideration the offer was declined and computerised handicapping had to wait for a few more years before being introduced.

title: Personal experiences · p. 203
text:
CHAPTER EIGHTEEN

PERSONAL EXPERIENCES

title: Personal experiences · p. 204
text:
ARNOLD SHANKS REMINISCES

Arnold joined the club in 1948 and was active as a player until 1967 when he took over the role of club steward and bar manager, a role he filled until his retirement in 1983. Arnold’s courteous manner, his patience, his quiet efficiency, his genuine interest in members and visitors alike, all contributed a great deal to the popularity of the club. His generosity in providing beautiful floral arrangements for the lounge with flowers from his own Bethlehem property was greatly appreciated. All who enjoyed his service and his cheerful friendliness will remember Arnold with affection. Here is his story in his own words.

“I came to Tauranga from Ardglass Northern Ireland in 1927 with my golf clubs - a Mills cleek (like a short driver) and an old mashie. I played initially as a country member and enjoyed Open Tournaments. I farmed at Oropi and had to get feeding-out done a day ahead so I could be free on Saturdays between milkings. The Tauranga course was well laid out and well kept. I did not get any serious practice but played reasonably to an 18 handicap. We enjoyed our golf very much and prizes were not considered very important. At the end of the season we received a voucher covering any successes during the season and we would buy what we wanted and take it out to the Club for prize giving in November. This was all very convivial though it would be rather impractical today.

title: Personal experiences · p. 205
text:
In time the membership outgrew the rather primitive clubhouse and a bigger and brighter one was built on the present site. The facilities in the new building were good. The bar instead of being a cubby-hole was well planned and a decent size. The crates of beer were kept in a locked cupboard under the stairs. This meant they had to be carried up manually. The bar was run by Arthur Towsey, a commercial traveller, and a real personality around the club. The job was a labour of love carrying no salary. In the bar Arthur ruled. Early players would be caught as they arrived and made to do their share by carrying up crates of beer. He opened and closed when he felt like it as no one else imposed restrictions or, if they did, no one bothered with them. In earlier times each case of beer or bottle of spirits was labelled with the name of a member for “personal delivery” at the club before leaving Guiness Brothers, the suppliers. This was the method used to get around the law that had no way of licensing clubs such as ours.

As the bar was quite small there was no room for two to serve behind it so there was often a crowd waiting. The dining room was to the left and the lounge to the right. The latter was well furnished and carpeted with landscape windows giving excellent views of the 6th and 18th greens.

With better facilities inside and out the Club boomed and it was not long before the new clubhouse was too small to meet the demands placed upon it. Arthur Towsey, a bachelor up till then, was fading in his barman role and he was soon to marry his Landlady and disappear from the scene. A new man took over. He had an English name which I forget. He seemed to spend a lot of time cleaning his ear!

Noel Hockin was our secretary, a job he had done for some time on a small honorarium. He then became full time Secretary Manager on a salary. One day, talking to Noel, I said to him, mostly as a joke that had I known the Barman’s job was up for application I would have applied. Noel just laughed. It really was a joke as, not being a drinker, I did not patronise the bar and had no idea of its inner workings. By 1964 there was talk of enlarging the clubhouse again. The changing rooms were too small, Jim Paterson’s shop was much too small, and the trundler shed was only a small building rescued from the Mowat property when it became the Girls’ College. Consequently a new trundler shed was built incorporating a good-size Pro Shop and plans prepared for clubhouse extensions. The enlarged changing rooms expanded into the area previously occupied by the old Pro Shop beneath the dining room that, along with the lounge, was extended out towards the 18th fairway. The building plan was a major project for the Club and caused much discussion and controversy amongst the members with many strongly in favour and many against. With the assistance of the Club’s Bankers and a good take up of debentures by members the work was eventually completed.

There was one small hitch. The chap who was steward and barman decided it would be too much upheaval for him to cope with during the extensions and he handed in his notice. Noel Hockin informed the committee he had a solution to that problem. He rang me and said did I remember telling him I would have been interested in a job at the Club. I’d quite forgotten all about it but he said the job would only be a temporary one until the alterations were complete and everything had settled down once again. After that the plan was to appoint a married couple to handle catering and the bar. I thought it would be a nice change for a while as I was doing little apart from growing a few flowers and greenery

title: Personal experiences · p. 206
text:
for the shop run by my daughters so I said that yes, I would fill in for the short term.

It is always exciting to do something new. A temporary bar was set up in the back of the trundler shed. Fortunately there was hot water and wash up facilities but it was still pretty primitive, just a counter on trestles to serve from, a few tables each side of an old carpet runner, and enough chairs at a pinch. Knowing it was only a temporary inconvenience the arrangement was accepted in good spirit by members and there were a lot of happy times there. Jim Paterson was a great help to me at that time, always pleasant and willing to give a hand in tidying and cleaning up what was a less than ideal facility. I did enjoy the company and the change of life style. It was an interesting job. The alterations went ahead on schedule and no one was greatly inconvenienced. The new caterers took over and I went home to the life I had been leading. At the Club all was settled and going smoothly, or so I imagined. For my part I know I missed the company. As part of the official opening of the new facilities there was a social evening and dinner in the clubhouse. I did not go but later heard it had not proved to be the success anticipated. The golf day had been a success and the dinner tables very nicely set up with several quite elaborate decorations. Obviously the new husband and wife team had gone to a good deal of trouble to make a good initial impression. There was a big crowd but unfortunately the caterer was not familiar with hungry golfers. There were to be two servings but practically all the food disappeared at the first of these and many went home hungry and dissatisfied. It was a bad start but allowances had to be made for the new staff. They would improve. After all they had come with glowing credentials from an Australian firm. Things did improve for a time though there were doubts. The barman was slow with service and with giving change. I think the members missed a familiar face behind the bar and someone they could tell their golfing woes to. One day, not too long after the opening, I had another ring from Noel Hockin. Could I come out to a committee meeting at the clubhouse that evening? The House Committee were there - Noel, Arthur Bluett, Owen Evans, Jim Reid, and Frank Warnes. The new caretaker couple were leaving and they would like me to take over the Bar and Clubhouse maintenance role. The job would be full time including running the bar and cleaning the clubhouse and changing rooms, a much bigger job than I had been doing before the alterations. The committee had worked out a schedule of duties, hours of work, and pay. The hours were long and the pay not very high but I felt it would be interesting and pleasant working with people I knew. After giving the matter some thought I accepted. If it didn’t work out from my point of view or that of the committee I could always resign. At least I would have something to fill the

rather empty life that lay ahead. Everyone was pleased. The committee were free of the responsibility of advertising the job and all that would have entailed. It was intended I would start work the following Monday but even that did not go to plan. Whenever the previous barman required a day off during the week the gap had been filled by Bill Drummond, a retired engine driver. Bill was a nice quiet man who was to continue in that role on my days off. On the Friday prior to my official start I had a call from Noel. There had been an accident. From the bar storeroom there was a lift for bringing up full beer crates and other supplies and returning empties to ground level. Old Bill was lowering the lift with a load of empties when the cable somehow slipped and the cage suddenly came down, crushing Bill’s forearms and trapping him. Someone freed him and he was rushed to hospital where he stayed quite a long

title: Personal experiences · p. 207
text:
time. He never quite got over the trauma of the accident.  It turned out the cable had been too loosely wrapped around the spool and had gradually tightened, leaving some slack that eventually allowed the cage to drop suddenly.

So it was that my job began a few days earlier than planned. Noel handed me the keys of the bar and said: “This is your bar. You are in full charge”. He did have a spare key of course and I think when I was not there he would nip in for a quick one. That Saturday morning I started my new career. It was fun really, long hours but not hard work once I was organised and before the novelty began to wear off. The committee had made up a time sheet for me. Monday was cleaning up day, 4 hours. Each changing room took an hour or more, then there was cash to tally, the bar to restock, the lounge to vacuum. If there had been a Sunday tournament or function this latter took at least two hours. Flat out it was a hard four hours work. Theoretically I worked 44 hours a week and had Monday afternoon off together with a full day off on Fridays. For this I received £20/6/0 or £17/7/4 net of tax. This was in 1967. If, as occasionally happened, the course was closed as a result of bad weather I didn’t get paid for the day.

We had no liquor license so the whole set up was illegal but the law turned a blind eye. Sometimes on a Saturday or Sunday evening someone would ring to say there was a traffic officer parked down the road so everyone leaving would be extra careful. There was never a serious accident, only the occasional scrape on the way home. One chap had a minor run in with a tree on the driveway out to Cameron Road. It was difficult to get the bar closed. Even though we were illegal there was an attempt to stick to the six o’clock closing time for licensed premises but there was a hardened core of drinkers, including Noel, who would stay and stay. I often had trouble getting the slide down and it was often well after 6:30pm by the time I did.

I also said I would do the flowers, a task that had been done off and on by some of the ladies. Somehow it became part of my job as I had plenty of flowers and enjoyed seeing them in the clubhouse. Usually I had three or four large arrangements and they were always admired, even by some of the men. That chore took some time as the flowers had to be picked freshly every day but I soon got into a routine. I did all I could to keep the clubhouse clean and tidy and no one complained in the time I worked there. Much later, on an economy drive, the committee decided the staff were getting too much free service at the kitchen so we were cut back to just morning and afternoon teas. Previously I had got my lunch free, now I brought sandwiches from home. I did say: “no lunch, no flowers” but after a week I got tired of the bareness and went back to my arrangements.

Gradually conditions in the bar changed. Instead of bottled beer we changed to draught beer in flagons, then to small casks with a pressure pump. Eventually, following the next building extension, two large tanks and a proper pressure system were installed. That made the serving of drinks and the handling easier but increased the cleaning work. I carried a good stock of spirits and soft drinks and graduated from a small refrigerator to a large commercial style model.

The time passed with no special excitement. Noel’s rather casual book keeping and business supervision gradually deteriorated and the committee decided it was time for a change. Noel had been a hard

title: Personal experiences · p. 208
text:
worker for the Club, both as an honorary Secretary and as a Secretary Manager. I was sorry to see him go. He had always been very considerate to me. At the time I seriously considered throwing the job in but I didn’t. Not long after leaving Noel fell from a ladder while painting his house and died shortly after.

Curly Peters replaced Noel. Gradually my pay increased but not, I think, to the full award rate, and certainly not to reflect the work that I did. The Club membership was always growing in that period. There was talk of further additions to the clubhouse, plans were made and there was another upheaval in the offing. Curly did a good job as secretary though his assistant, Henry Becker a retired post master, did a lot more than his fair share and, upon his retirement I think that Pat Massey did the lion’s share of the work. I carried on cleaning, serving in the bar, and doing the flowers while avoiding getting involved though I could sense Pat was not too happy with her lot at times. I would sometimes have a few holes of golf during the summer months when things were quiet. I would play round to the 6th on my own, or sometimes with an occasional lone visitor. I missed playing very much. I used to stand at the window overlooking the 6th green or watch the players coming up the slope to the 18th green and wonder if I would have the chance to play again.

Eventually another round of clubhouse extensions was started. The whole upstairs area was doubled in area and a basement area excavated underneath to provide a storage room with lock up facilities for spirits, bottled beer, and the like. This meant a lot more work for me. Vacuuming the lounge and rearranging and cleaning the tables could take all morning. The committee did employ window cleaners to clean the windows both inside and out where previously I had done the inside and occasionally make a special trip to do the outside. A new social committee decided to run dinner dances, a sit down dinner and a band for dancing. That meant another big rise in the work required of me. We would borrow long tables and extra chairs from the Racing Club while all our small tables would be carried out and stacked on the veranda. I would get people to give a hand but on Sunday morning everything would have to be put back in order to be ready for the players coming in to the bar in the afternoon. Those were very long weekends, especially as some party lovers would stretch their evening out well into the small hours of Sunday morning. It was often 2 am before I got home and then it was back to clean up in the morning. The final result of the extensions was very successful. While the work was going ahead I would take home off cuts for firewood and there were often other items piled to go to the dump that were too good to waste so I would salvage those too.

Kitchen staff came and went, committees changed year-to-year, new members arrived and older ones

departed but I carried on as usual. The same Vets came to their Annual Tournament, the same players to the Labour Weekend Tournament. It was nice to see their faces year after year. The bar usually ran smoothly. I changed from the old tin box for the cash to a hand operated cash register, then to a fancy one that had me tied in knots for a time. That slowed down service until I got used to it. Getting the big gas cylinder up to the bar was a major effort. Occasionally I would manage to get one of the boys who played to help me up the stairs with it but they would dodge me if they could. I would then have to back the van up to where the suppliers had delivered the cylinder, manhandle the cylinder into the van, drive the van round to the porch end of the lounge under the Moreton Bay, get the thing out and roll it along the lounge floor and into the bar. It was quite a task. Every now and then someone would come

title: Personal experiences · p. 209
text:
to inspect the bar. There was never a complaint.

Another change and another secretary, a nice chap from Inglewood called Royce Lahood. Royce was another who was very good at delegating jobs and once again Pat Massey found herself doing most of the office work so far as I could see.

Royce was an ideal public relations man and easy to get along with. He fitted in very well and was soon right at home in the Club. One day he was doing something urgent so he brought the handicap books to me and asked if I would finish them for him. He explained the system and soon I got into the job. Royce never again did that job. It was interesting doing it but very time consuming. Any little bit of spare time I had was taken up doing handicapping. Hours of work spread over the week, masses of cards spread over the pool table, and the pins to move on the handicap board ready for weekend play.

Tuesday was Royce’s day off and sometimes Pat would tell me to go and have a game with the Vets. I would go off in the first group then rush in to get ready for the first few wanting drinks. It was very nice but a bit of a rush so I did not do it very often. Pat was a delightful woman who was wonderful to work with and a great asset to the Club. I think she also made Royce look good for the amount of work she did on his behalf.

The seasons slipped by, one year much the same as the last. The wages did improve but the work seemed to get harder and harder. Perhaps I just got older and older. I wish I had kept a day-to-day diary of all the things that happened. It is very hard to recall the sequence of events but I did enjoy the job because of all the good people I met and worked with over those years’.

Those who knew Arnold and his little Morris van would empathise with his description of this manoeuvre. Arnold and the van were both small of stature and you can be sure the task would have challenged much bigger men with more suitable transport. There was a fascinating incident involving this van and a blackbird, if something extending over a period of months could be called an incident. Arnold’s van had a mirror mounted on the front right hand wing as was common at that time and he would park the van where the bar manager still parks at the back of the clubhouse.  One particular blackbird would perch every day on the wing and look at himself in the mirror. Of course he did not recognise himself but saw a rival in the mirror and would hop around the back to remonstrate with that rival. Finding nothing he would come to the front again. He would continue this for an hour or more and for day after day eventually wearing a ring of paint off the van right around that mirror.

title: Personal experiences · p. 210
text:
DAVID MOWAT REMEMBERS

My earliest memories of the Club are of hunting for golf balls in the hydrangeas that fronted the clubhouse where it faced the 18th green. My brother Robert and I would be waiting for our father as he enjoyed the after match conviviality with his friends in the old wooden cottage that served as clubhouse. As children we were not permitted within its hallowed walls. Sometimes we would go further afield in search of balls and tees, the latter being quite common near the men’s tees but rare indeed near the ladies’. Strange that. At home we would use our finds in company with a couple of old irons to hit balls around our paddocks which now make up the Girls’ College at Gate Pa.

When I was about twelve my parents signed me up as a junior member though I was far more interested in cricket, tennis, rugby and yachting at that stage. In any event juniors were not made very welcome at that time and not for quite a few years into the future. My father, the first professional to the club but then back in the amateur ranks, was keen to see a change in that attitude which is why he signed me up. I caddied for my father or one of his friends on occasion. This was before the days of trundlers and we were especially called upon for tournament days when carrying your bag through 36 holes was a daunting prospect.

My first real commitment to the game came in 1957 when I took a year off university in the belief that

I needed to reawaken my enthusiasm for study. A vacancy arose as assistant to Grant Silvester on the green keeping staff and I gained the position through the influence of my father. Grant had been our neighbour at Gate Pa for many years and my father some years previously had suggested to Grant that he would be ideally suited to the green keeping role. Grant and the committee concurred and so began a significant era in the development of the course. I recall working with Grant with a good deal of pleasure. Grant could be a hard task master but very fair and patient, in passing his knowledge and skills on to me and to others. Though Grant had come to the job with little in the way of the special knowledge required of the modern green keeper he was practical, adaptable, and a ready learner. He, along with Charlie Leach of Taupo, was to become instrumental in raising the standards of green keeping throughout the Bay of Plenty. While accompanying Grant to meetings of the BOP Green Keepers’ Association it was soon apparent to me that the other members paid a great deal of respect to the views of these two men.

The machinery we had to work with was minimal compared to the specialised and sophisticated machinery operated by our present-day staff. An old Ferguson tractor hauled a set of three gang mowers that I would use four days a week to mow the course from boundary to boundary during the active growth season. There was virtually no rough. For two days I would mow length wise up and down the fairways, then crosswise for another two days. This was necessary to combat the Paspalum stalks that would otherwise have turned the fairways into hay paddocks in appearance. I remember some summers when the stalks did get away and Jimmy Paterson would be ashamed to charge visitors green fees to play the course. These days it is difficult to find Paspalum anywhere in the fairways and the old local rule allowing Paspalum stalks to be plucked has long since gone from our card. I was very happy doing my mowing job when the sun was shining. On those days I would sing all the popular songs of the day, tunelessly but enthusiastically, as I drove the faithful Fergie around the fairways.

title: Personal experiences · p. 211
text:
On Tuesdays and Fridays Grant would change from his big work boots to his sand shoes or “running shoes” as he called them and mow the greens with the Overgreen mower which he had to walk behind. This would take virtually the full day so was done only in preparation for Ladies’ day on the Wednesday and for the men on Saturdays. There was no possibility of mowing the morning of competition. For a few weeks leading up to the Spalding Masters, and later the PGA, the greens would be mown daily and members would certainly notice the very significant improvement in speed and trueness. While professionals such as Bob Charles claimed these greens were as good as anything in the country it should be remembered that they played them in January when the greens would clearly have been much better than in the winter months when the local season was in full swing. We always found it ironic that the course was virtually deserted from November to March, the period in which the greens and fairways were at their best.

The bunkers were filled with fine pumice sand that we dug from a pit located at the back of the fourth tee. This we did by loading the old Model T Ford shovel by shovel full. On Wednesdays the ladies would not realise we were up in the pit behind them as they teed off and we would hear some rather unladylike language if their shots did not go to plan. The gully was of course notorious for the problems it caused, especially to those trying to earn their handicaps. There was no automatic handicap allotted to women at that time. Unlike men who were given a 24 handicap at the outset whether they could play

to it or not, the women had to earn their initial handicap by playing to 36 or better. Until they achieved that women players would be in a state of limbo and many an attempt to qualify foundered in the gully or in the bunkers surrounding the green. The pumice in the bunkers was light and fluffy and good to play out of when dry but when wet it packed down like cement. We would then plough it up with the little Gravely tractor and in doing so a bit of clay would be added to the pumice with the result that the next time it rained the cementing effect would be even worse. We needed to add new sand fairly frequently and it was hard work.

The Gravely was a marvellously versatile workhorse. We used it with a variety of attachments to stir up the bunkers, to mow the heavy rough in places such as the bottom of the gully, to rotary hoe the ground in new tee and green construction, and to pull a small coring machine. Grant was an ingenious man and he developed a rotary broom, driven off the Gravely, for sweeping corings into rows for easier removal. Another machine he came up with was a groover that he made by adapting a Morrison reel mower for the purpose. It worked very well, though labour intensive. At that time we would groove the greens twice a year then over sow them with the standard 3:1 Brown Top/Chewings Fescue Mix. With improvement in the science of turf management, led by the newly established New Zealand Institute of Turf Culture based at Palmerston North, and the installation of an effective greens irrigation system the need for reseeding gradually disappeared. The new watering system must have been a great relief to Grant who had been in the habit of driving back to the course at night to shift sprinklers.

Another machine I recall was a vicious looking spiking machine. This was developed in conjunction with Edward’s Engineering, a local company run by prominent member Roy Edwards. His widow Joyce is a Life Member of the Club and a wonderful example of how the game of golf can keep you young in spirit.

title: Personal experiences · p. 212
text:
The spiking machine consisted of large, heavy, octagonal shaped steel wheels with ten-inch knives bolted to the corners of each wheel. This was dragged across the greens and the design was such that the knives penetrated deeply then ‘kicked’ back as they emerged. This was effective in breaking up the compaction that develops under the greens as a result of the pressure exerted by people and machinery passing across them.

The professional at that time was J A (Jimmy) Paterson. His business would be very slow over the summer and he would join us from time to time when we had extra work. Jimmy had a truly likeable personality and got on really well with Grant and I but he had virtually no confidence in using machinery of any kind. It was not wise to ask Jim to back the trailer down to the rubbish tip at the top of the gully below the implement shed unless you were prepared to haul the trailer back out of the pit later! Other than this occasional assistance from Jim green keeping was a two-man job for many years. There is no doubt the course was less well cared for than it is today. We simply did not have the manpower, the machinery, or the financial resources to facilitate something better. None the less I am confident the membership got the very best that the circumstances of the time allowed, just as they do today. It is interesting to note that I was paid about £11 in 1957, the same as a senior subscription for a year so it required 50 members to cover my salary as the assistant green keeper. The same would be very nearly true today, the senior assistant’s salary being covered by some 50 members. Of course there are more

assistants today so the cost of maintaining the course is relatively much higher.

There were many memorable moments in my time working on the course. Perhaps the most memorable involved a lesson in the unexpected dangers of smoking. In those pre-OSH days life was a little less regulated. When we needed to remove a row of trees along the left of the 14th fairway Grant came up with the novel idea that we would dynamite them out of the ground. He would use an auger to drill a hole down below the bole of the tree, place a stick of dynamite and a fuse then move on to the next tree. I would then light the fuse, retreat a safe distance to observe the result, then tow the tree away to the dump. By the time I returned the next fuse would be ready to light. Everything worked beautifully for the first few trees, the timing was good and each tree came easily from the ground. Then, returning from the tip once again, I noticed Grant move away from the next tree in line so I bent down, matches in hand. Boom! The tree was blasted out of the ground inches in front of me before I could touch a match to the fuse. Grant, who was often prone to pause in his work to roll and light a cigarette, had done just that after setting the charge and had then automatically touched the match to the fuse before moving away. Fortunately I was not hurt, only severely shaken. We were able to see the comic book humour of it a little later.

On Friday afternoons Noel Hockin, then Club Secretary, would come out from town with our pay packets and Noel, Grant, Arthur Towsey and I would spend a pleasant hour or two sitting on beer crates inside the little bar discussing all manner of things. This made for a very pleasant end to the working week. Those three people had a huge impact on the development of both the club and the course over a long period and I count it as a privilege to have had the opportunity to gain from their collective knowledge and understanding of so many aspects of club and course management. A year or two later after the clubhouse had been upgraded some members complained regarding the Green Keeper coming

title: Personal experiences · p. 213
text:
into the clubhouse on a Friday with his working clothes and boots on. Though there was no mud on the boots and the clothes were tidy working gear these few complainants obviously felt his presence was inappropriate. Although officialdom never told Grant to stay away he did hear there had been a complaint and he reacted by moving his Friday evening custom to the Greerton Hotel down the road. This was all a bit sad and perhaps a sign that things would never be quite the same again.

The story of Commander John Harris, Alan Davidson and his plastic models, and Grant’s endeavour to replicate these on the ground has been told elsewhere. As a member of the Greens Committee I was able to participate from the sidelines in much of this development. While I regret not being present when Commander Harris walked the course I did gain significant insight into course design and construction from being involved, as a member of the Greens Committee, in the follow up over the succeeding months. Grant and Alan were assisted greatly by the experience and skills of local earth moving contractor Garth Renner. Garth had an empathy with them and could interpret what they wanted very readily and he was genuine in his wish to achieve exactly the effect they were looking for. It was a real team effort with a result that would, I am sure, have pleased John Harris though I don’t think he saw the final outcome. The majority of holes underwent some degree of change. Some bunkers disappeared, others were introduced, mounds appeared in strategic places and greens were extended to provide extra depth. In the opinion of some excellent judges the developments transformed Tauranga into one of the more interesting courses in the country. We simply do not hear complaints from members or from visitors that the course is boring to play as does happen with regard to quite a number of New Zealand courses. The manager of an Auckland representative team once commented to me: “I wonder if your members fully appreciate the course you have here. Tauranga is really three courses in one. Those first six holes take us down into the valley and out again. They are full of variety, both of terrain and design. The middle six offer a variety of challenges while the final six represent more typical flat country golf”. To add to that description Michael Nicholson, Tauranga’s outstanding amateur, put it this way: “Those final six holes have a way of sorting the men from the boys”. How prescient that comment was can readily be understood by those who had the privilege of watching Michael in the final stages of many of his championship matches, or in watching another outstanding club member in Eddie Burgess come from behind to win another under 23 stroke play title over those last few holes.

Next time you tee up on the second hole take a look at the three Kauri trees on the right front. Back in 1957 the tee was very different from the way it is now. The tee was in two narrow terraces with tall bracken covering much of the area. One day Grant directed me to clear the bracken away from the

Kauris to “release them”. I had barely realised they were there, hidden as they were by the bracken. From the moment of their release from the shade and competition provided by the bracken they began to thrive and we can now see what 50 years of unrestricted growth does for Kauris. Apparently they had been hidden under the bracken for some 20 years since Keith Lusk planted them in the Thirties. Incidentally the women’s tee was then sited on top of the ridge between the first and second fairways some distance forward and to the right of the present position.
