The outline of the tee can still be seen. Close to that tee was a large blue gum and if you drove up to, or beyond, that tree when playing the first you had achieved a notable feat. Today such a drive would be considered less than adequate by many men club players and perhaps by a few women as well. Such has been the advancement made

title: Personal experiences · p. 214
text:
in equipment. Whether that is for better or for worse remains a matter of debate.

At the beginning of the following year I headed back to University and it was not until three years later that I found myself back in Tauranga at something of a loose end. While deciding where my future lay I was asked to fill in once again on the course as the assistant had resigned and Grant needed some help. I was happy to do so for a short time though it turned out to be for most of the year. At some stage in the year Garth Sim, Principal of Tauranga Boys’ College and husband of Life Member Nen Sim, was playing on the course with my old First XV coach Pat Keenan. Spotting me they stopped and wanted to know what I was doing mowing grass when they were short of Science and Mathematics teachers. They would be happy to recommend me to the recruiting officer who was to be in town the following week. I found out the money was not too bad so much to my surprise I soon found myself studying at Christchurch Training College. I had never had any inclination to be a teacher prior to that time and yet I signed on under Garth the following year and spent the next 31 years at the College. So ended my green keeping career but certainly not my interest in all things relating to the great game of golf.

A regular Friday afternoon four made up of three Businessmen and the Club Professional were inclined to play for a dollar or three. One of the Businessmen, who had something of a reputation for absentmindedness, was busy totting up the state of his financial obligations as the others teed off on the 15th. When they prepared to play their second strokes two balls were located on the 16th fairway, the Pro’s was well up the middle, while our man’s was nowhere to be seen. He was adamant that his tee shot had been ‘straight down the middle’. After some time of searching under leaves that had accumulated in the fairway he put his hand in his pocket and there was his ball. ‘What the hell is going on here’ he said as he strode back to the tee. On another occasion a group were following the same gentleman and were about to play to the third green when they realised there was no flag to play to. Eventually someone spotted the flag being carried in the ‘slope arms’ position up the path leading to the fourth tee.

title: Personal experiences · p. 215
text:
MEMORIES OF TAURANGA GOLF CLUB FROM

BRIAN DUCKER My father Norm Ducker was a schoolteacher and a keen sportsman. In April 1949 when I was six years old we shifted from Thornton to Tauriko where Dad was to be their new headmaster. He had been a member of the Whakatane Golf Club where he had won the Championship in 1947. He joined up with Tauranga in that first year of 1949, playing off a handicap of four throughout most of the following six years.

There was no such thing as organised golf for children of Primary School age at that time and as a consequence I spent a large amount of time on Saturdays, and an occasional Sunday, caddying for my father. Once or twice a week I would play the back nine as the Tauriko School House was only a couple of miles from the course. There was a rule that sons could play with their father members for free on days other than competition days and I played for years with just a cut down jigger which was a hickory shafted club with the approximate loft of a three iron. The course lay out closely approximated that of the present day though changes were always envisaged. The fifth hole was always a problem and changes were constantly made to try and improve the situation. When we first arrived the tee was at ground level to the left of the fourth green while the hole ran along the boundary fence to a small green that was barely visible and surrounded by Toitoi clumps that often trapped a wayward ball. Later a long narrow green was constructed more or less where the present green lies. The pin was still invisible even when a new raised tee was installed further to the left and well back in the corner. The remaining holes are still in the same place but one has to think hard to recall the many subtle changes these holes have undergone. The greens were all smaller and there were very few bunkers in 1950. Now most holes have them. Virtually all the greens have been built up and enlarged while the back portions have been raised and extended. The 2nd, 4th, and 8th greens in particular were small

and steeply borrowed. Now they are cut into the hill resulting in helpful upward sloping backs to those greens. The base of the pin on the Knoll was invisible from the tee as the green was flatter and thus much easier to putt on than is the case now. The bunker in front was installed in Dad’s day. The turf was cut away at the top exposing a pumice “bullnose” face and balls rolled down it to a flat shelf at the bottom. Dad, not always the most confident of bunker players, would sometimes take a putter and bang the ball into the bank and up onto the green. At that time the Knoll green was relaid to provide a larger, lower, surface. For months the substitute hole was a very short par three played with a chip from the front of the 7th tee to the putting green. The cards were not changed and the score made there was recorded as the score for the 12th.

The 3rd green was another to be significantly altered with the bank on the right being built up to prevent the automatic roll around onto the green, and to provide some space for bags and the trundlers that were just beginning to make their appearance.

In 1950 there was a wasteland of scrub, gorse, and blackberry all the way down the left of the 7th fairway from the tractor shed to the bottom of the gully. A shank or severe slice from the 4th tee would

title: Personal experiences · p. 216
text:
disappear into impenetrable jungle. The 4th tee was well below its current position and the shot was played uphill to a pin of which you could only see the top half. The path to the green dipped down to swamp level before sloping upward to the green. Great was the delight when this path was built up a little to ease this climb back out of the gully. It has been further built up on at least two further occasions.

The 18th green was quite different in shape then. It was essentially square with a false front and a slope at the back running up towards the old clubhouse. The holes were all named and though I remember most of them to this day you never hear them identified this way any more. I feel that is really a pity. Sixty years ago most members referred to many of the holes by name rather than number. Today this applies to the Knoll, and perhaps the Gully and The Crescent. I wonder how many members today would recognise the 15th as Kaharoa. That hole was then played as a par five. It was later reduced to a par 4 and by memory was then made the number one stroke hole. Dad always maintained the feature tree for which the 18th is named was not a Moreton Bay fig at all but I fear the Australians may disagree with this view.

The scorecards always carried the handicap allowances on the back. From memory you were allowed three quarters of your handicap in Par (then Bogey) and Stableford competition and five eighths of the difference in handicap match play. This later became three quarters in line with the other competitions. As 24 was the maximum handicap for male golfers no one ever got more than a stroke a hole in Stableford competition. The very idea of anyone getting two shots on a hole would really have upset the old timers. Strokes were owed on different holes in the two forms of play so the card featured two different handicap allocations. Handicaps were based on the two lowest rounds over the previous six months and it seemed handicaps hardly ever went outwards. Playing to your handicap (36 points) was a real achievement and everyone congratulated you on the merit of such a performance.

On Race Days the course was essentially closed to allow for parking on the fairways and for safety reasons as many holes ran adjacent to areas where horses were stabled, loaded into floats, or saddled. I do remember Dad playing on one race day though.  We were on the 13th when the horses thundered past. Clods of earth flew everywhere but even more impressive than that to a ten year old brought up very strictly by a father who did not swear was the sound of non-stop, very loud, cursing by the jockeys as they positioned themselves for the run home. Large wooden observation stands were sited on the fence around the crescent and these required a local rule to clarify the relief available.

I remember as a kid finding an earlier scorecard with different names such as Alpha and Omega for the 1st and 18th. There were other fascinating hints of earlier times. I recall someone telling a story of long ago before the Club owned a tractor. The tee boxes were filled with sand as the wooden golf tee had not then been invented and players teed the ball on a small pile of sand. The tee boxes were battery cases or similar that sat on the ground. Someone made a bet on the 14th tee that he could hit his ball from the top of the sand in the box and reach the green. The result was one box virtually destroyed which the green keeper had to replace by wheeling a new one in his wheelbarrow all the way down to that very distant tee. The following week, or so the story went, another group were discussing the incident and inevitably another wager was made. The result was the same and the long suffering greenkeeper was

title: Personal experiences · p. 217
text:
once again required to trundle that long distance with a second replacement box.

The rules of the game are under constant revision and there have been dramatic changes over the years. The elimination of the Stymie is well known. Less well known is that prior to the early Fifties the penalty for a lost or out of bounds ball was only that you had to put another ball into play (count the stroke only).  My Dad and others found it very hard to accept that you now had to penalise yourself both stroke and distance. They considered this a very harsh penalty for a poorly played stroke.

I recall Peter Thomson playing an exhibition match around 1953. He was the new British Open Champion and his opponent that day was Alex Murray. Thomson had a long, upright, elegant swing and he played some glorious shots though he was no match for Murray that day. On the 8th Murray found trouble on the left and had to chip out just past Thomson’s drive. Thomson then played a short iron close to the pin only to see Murray hole his 3rd stroke and win the hole when Thomson could not sink the birdie putt. At the 13th Thomson’s drive was longer than anyone could recall seeing. He then hit a three iron across the corner to the edge of the green, an achievement unheard of in those days. I remember Dad dropping a pine cone beside the fence to mark the distance the drive had travelled. The most remarkable memory I have is of an event on the 15th. Thomson drove into the edge of the Lawsoniana trees that then lined the left boundary. His ball lay in some longer grass right by the edge. As he went to chip sideways his club slid down a low branch he had apparently not seen and he completely missed the ball. His comical look of total amazement was matched a minute later with one of sheepish embarrassment when, after successfully chipping out, he had to go to Murray and confess he now lay three. At the speeches later Thomson praised the course as being the best groomed in all of New Zealand. I was impressed but my father said that he probably said that of all the courses he visited in order to please the locals. Peter Thomson went on to claim further British Open titles and become recognised as a great champion. From our point of view, if not from their’s, it is sad that the super stars of the game no longer have to tour the small clubs of the World in order to cash in on their success.

I saw Thomson again in the late Sixties when he played in the PGA Championship at the Mount. He had filled out somewhat with age and his swing was more round arm in the style of Mike Souchak. I was playing too but I did not have the nerve to approach him and ask him if he remembered the exhibition match at Tauranga and especially that air shot!

I witnessed two holes in one while caddying for Dad. Mick Cambie achieved the feat into a gale on

the 14th one Sunday afternoon. Mick was a big wide shouldered bloke who thrashed at the ball with tremendous power. On the tee he addressed the ball by lifting the club head a foot or so off the ground then tapping down behind the ball before making a series of such taps, each about half the height of the previous lift. When these taps finally ceased he would freeze for an age before launching with all his might at the ball. The distance achieved was often spectacular, the direction frequently wayward. For the hole in one he played a three iron under windy conditions that were such as to leave other players short when playing the driver.

(Editor’s note – Mick had other eccentricities on the golf course. I recall him once dribbling a ball off

title: Personal experiences · p. 218
text:
the 18th tee. Before it had even stopped rolling he had another ball out of his pocket. This he tossed a few feet in front and, charging forward, he cracked it on the half volley an enormous distance towards the green.)

The other hole in one came during the final of the Senior Four-Ball when Dad’s partner Cary Arneil holed out at the Knoll during the afternoon round. As I have said the base of the pin was not visible from the tee in those days and when I suggested the ball might have gone in the hole I was ignored. Nor was there any acknowledgement of my good guess when the ball was found in the hole. My pair went on to win the match just one up and, back in the clubhouse, Billy Castell, one of the opposing pair, announced that he had scored a two only to lose the hole. I remembered that he had actually holed out in the alternate hole only a couple of feet from where his ball settled. Of course I said nothing (I would have had my ear clipped for butting in) as Billy’s version made a good story. One outcome of their win was that Cary, handicap 2, and Dad, handicap 4, were selected to represent the Club in the BOP Champion of Champions Foursomes which they duly won.

On another occasion I heard that Ron Parkes, a gentle man and a fine golfer, had made an ace at the Gully. I got excited but Dad explained that Ron had duffed his first shot into the swamp before holing his next for a three – a result known as a busted eagle. This was just subsequent to the rule change that imposed a penalty stroke in addition to counting the original stroke and his fellow competitors were disappointed that Ron’s perfect shot had not earned him a deserved birdie as would have been the case a month or two before.

During those years when I caddied regularly Fred Ward was the Club’s best player and always the man to beat in the championship. Fred was the manager of McKenzies Department Store in town and had been a pilot in the Air Force where Dad had also served so they got on very well. At the time Fred did not play a lot of golf and I seem to remember he got married about that time when he was probably in his late thirties. He seemed an old man to my young eyes. One year Fred went off and played in the New Zealand Open finishing 19th. He came back with a centre shafted Schenectady putter that he had been awarded as a result of his placing amongst the amateurs in the field. The putter aroused much discussion, especially with regard to its legality, though Fred, like everyone else, continued to use his old blade putter.

In the first qualifying round of the1952 Championship Dad shot his best ever score, a 70, to lie equal

with Fred. Unfortunately Dad was ten strokes worse the following week but still qualified second. He went on to meet Fred in the final where he went down 3/2. On the day before that final Dad had played in the 36 hole final of the Aquilla Cup where he lost to Billy Castell. Dad was very disappointed to have lost two thirty six hole finals in the one weekend despite scoring birdies on eleven of the fifteen par five holes played.

I remember Fred once hitting his ball into the top of the bank above the swamp at the Gully. We eventually found the ball embedded in the muddy bank. Fred worked the toe of his club behind it before flicking it out and, while it was still airborne, hitting it onto the green. Worriedly I asked my father if that

title: Personal experiences · p. 219
text:
was legal to which Fred responded saying “they probably wouldn’t approve of that at The Masters”. I need not have fussed, Fred was always unfazed and simply accepted the good with the bad. It was typical of him that he had not bothered with taking a drop and trying for a miracle shot to rescue a point.

Another example of Fred’s equanimity that has remained with me happened at the final hole during a Labour Weekend Tournament. At the time important events on the Club calendar such as the Labour weekend Tournament were eagerly anticipated, intensely contested, thoroughly discussed and dissected for months afterwards. In the annals of the Tournament the epic battles between Fred Ward and Andy Fletcher were legendary. A J Fletcher was a talented golfer, a long hitter and a fierce competitor. Regardless of the quality of the field it seemed that Fred and Andy always met in the final at Labour Weekend. The Honours Board reveals that Fred usually prevailed. One year they reached the 18th all square and both made the front right of the green with their second strokes. Both longish putts finished close to the hole and the gallery anticipated concessions and a move to the first tee to continue the contest. Fred knocked Andy’s ball back to him but Andy made no move to reciprocate whereupon Fred made a quick stroke, and laughed before holding out his hand to congratulate Andy as the ball slipped by the hole. I was horrified that such a mighty encounter could end like that but it was typical of Fred to take defeat in that manner. On another occasion the pair went to the 3rd extra hole before Fred secured another title when Andy duffed several successive strokes in the gathering gloom.

The veteran golfers of the time were my friends and many gave me welcome encouragement. If we were playing on a Sunday they would often allow me to drop a ball and play the last couple of holes. Dick Phelan was one of those men. Dick had established the Tauranga Rimu Company and had thus been responsible for giving Tauriko its name for you won’t find that word in any Maori dictionary. Harry Smith and Maurice Bradmore were always there with an encouraging word and they let me have a hit when the opportunity arose. Ron Galloway was a very good single figure player. He had a new maroon

Vanguard motorcar while George Thorne had an identical car, even to the colour. There was a story of the two of them racing them up Waihi Road on their way home from golf but stories like that were not for a boy’s ears and I heard no more. Alan Davidson was a young man at the time and regarded as a promising player who was just starting to make his mark in Club affairs. He too took an interest in me at a time when most players would have known who I was but chose to ignore my presence as I dragged my father’s heavy home made trundler around the course. Lew Gamman was an exception, always friendly and chatty. Visits to town were not complete without a visit to the Sports Depot in Wharf Street where Alan McBride or, more likely, Lew would sell me a small piece of Meccano while chatting to Dad.

Other players I remember include Paul O’Brien who played off a six handicap and had a very smooth swing and Toby Green, then the longest hitter in the Club. I recall Toby driving the 10th green, an unheard of feat at the time. George Harrison and Dave Cambie used to have chipping competitions down at the end of Grace Road where they lived. They would chip across the road, round and even over the houses, and out onto the harbour. George was a keen fisherman and he would go around to the newly reclaimed swamp that is now Memorial Park in order to practise his casting. Once George gave us some nylon line, the first we had ever seen. Jack Lloyd, dapper, swashbuckling and cigar smoking was a confident and able 6/7 handicapper who competed keenly with Dad before deciding to play his golf at

title: Personal experiences · p. 220
text:
The Mount. Jack probably set a record for continuous appearances in the Labour Weekend tournament – he competed over forty times I believe. In a world where only a favoured few had a post-war car Harry Smith stood out. He was the proud owner of a Ford “Fortyniner”, one of only two in the town. Harry’s business partner Tui Harvey was a prodigious, if erratic, hitter. One day someone bet Tui he could not drive a ball from the 13th tee into the newly installed bunker between the 13th and 17th fairways. At the time I had not seen it done, nor heard of anyone having achieved the feat but Tui lined the ball up and proceeded to carry it into that bunker on the fly.

Ten years later I returned to the area and joined the Mount Maunganui Golf Club. It gave me great pleasure to meet again with George Harrison, Jack Lloyd, and others from those earlier days, and to play with them regularly. Later Paul O’Brien shifted across to play at the Mount and he and I still form part of a regular Tuesday four.

Bert Hart was the greenkeeper and another friend. One weekday afternoon, while Dad and I were playing a few holes, Bert drove up on the old Massey Ferguson tractor and stopped for a word with Dad. Apparently there had been a complaint made that I was putting with a five iron. I am sure I never as much as scratched the surface of a green while putting with my old jigger but Dad suggested I had better use a putter from then on so a hickory shafted putter was added to double my club numbers. When I was about 14 I was allowed to use my mother’s clubs that had lain idle for a decade or more. These included a spoon, a three iron and a mashie with very thin blades. There was also a Man’s eight iron with about as much bounce and loft as a modern sand wedge. There was even an ancient leather carry bag. I was in golfing heaven and my scores began to improve. At age 12 in what proved to be my last round at Tauranga during that period I went around the course in 81 strokes with the help of just those six clubs.

During my years at Tauranga I was largely unaware of there being any other junior players. I was the only son regularly caddying and there was no organised programme for juniors. When I got to college I found there were a few boys who played regularly, notably Michael Cambie, Robert Mowat, and Dick Wilson. These boys were a year or two ahead of me at school so our paths did not really cross. It was a few years later that I began to meet them at tournaments where they showed they had developed into fine golfers.

In the early Fifties the Club instituted an open Professional and Amateur 72 hole Stroke Play Tournament.

This was an innovative move as prior to that the only tournaments available to amateurs were three- day events featuring two qualifying rounds on a Saturday followed by four rounds of Match play. The Professionals had even fewer opportunities to compete against their peers. The tournament was held in autumn and every effort was made to attract a quality field, with leading players from Auckland and the Waikato being regular participants. I was about ten when these began and Dad allowed me to make my caddying services available to these golfers. This was great as far as I was concerned for they paid me 2/6 a round as opposed to my father’s occasional bottle of lemonade at the end of the day. I caddied for G. L. Taylor from Hamilton, and then W. W. Smith from Auckland for a couple of years. The tournaments were very successful and attracted considerable interest in the town. It was regrettable

title: Personal experiences · p. 221
text:
that they lapsed some years later.

Opening and Closing days were important as few people played over summer and there were no competitions over those months. I recall one closing day when a variety of competitions were held after the day’s play. There was a long driving contest where participants teed off from the top of the bank behind the 18th green. Dad was most surprised to be given a ball for being the only participant to land both his drives in the targeted area between the 11th and 18th fairways. There followed a short iron contest from somewhere near the ladies’ 7th tee to the 6th green. All those who made a two played again and I recall Dr. Mark winning with his second two. He was a long handicapper and was absolutely delighted to have out-gunned all those lower handicapped players who had fancied their chances. Everyone then repaired to the clubhouse to enjoy High Tea followed by speeches and the presentation of the year’s major trophies.

For the Labour Weekend Tournament of 1953 I was allowed to earn myself some cash by caddying for someone other than my father so I was not privileged to witness the deed that highlighted my father’s golfing career. The details though are forever imprinted upon my mind. On the 6th, a par five of 507 yards, my father made an albatross two. The stand of Californian Redwoods on the hill between the 6th and 7th were then represented by a couple of newly planted saplings so, when Dad drove rather too much to the right past the large gum tree that once dominated the area, he found himself on a clear lie on a little flat terrace. His way forward was blocked by the stand of pines beside the Ladies’ 7th tee but he had in his bag a four wood that he could rely on to produce a hook even when it was not desired. On this occasion he played up the 7th fairway and the club behaved as he wished it to, the ball drawing nicely around the trees and heading in the general direction of the green. The four did the usual searching and muttering until someone in desperation looked in the hole and there the ball nestled. Dad was not considered a long hitter and never before or since did he make the 6th green in two strokes. To celebrate this previously unheard of feat the Club presented Dad with a pewter tankard that I have to this day.

In those earlier days Information about the wider world of golf was very sparse. The NZ Herald certainly covered New Zealand golf and British events such as the Open Championship but the United States PGA Tour was unknown to me. We had seen the film “Follow the Sun” starring Glen Ford as Ben Hogan and later I recall reading a detailed account of Hogan’s win in the Open at Carnoustie in 1953, the only time Hogan played in the Open Championship. He had been told he would not be considered one of the greats unless, or until, he added that title to his list of successes. Consequently Fred Ward’s reference to “The Masters” that day at the Gully had no meaning to me at the time. Even golf played elsewhere in the Bay of Plenty was somewhat remote. I think the only local golfer to make the Bay teams at that time was Harry Dale from the Mount Club though Fred Ward and Jack Bateman had been members of Bay teams earlier. Ivan Deadman was one regular Bay representative who often played in tournaments at Tauranga. I also remember a young Don Boone playing in a four with Dad during a Labour Weekend tournament. That was at the beginning of Don’s long and illustrious career in Bay golf. I will never forget an incident I witnessed in Don’s first round match that year. On the 7th hole Don’s opponent hooked his tee shot into the gorse to the left while Don was long down the middle. When we could not find

title: Personal experiences · p. 222
text:
the ball Don played a good second just short and to the right of the green. As we moved on the other fellow shouted that he had found the ball. He took a bit of time and a couple of shots to get it back to the fairway, then another couple to get within range of the green where we were waiting. What was perhaps his sixth shot sailed to the right where it struck Don’s bag as he waited to play his third. Under the rules of the game at that time Don had to concede that he had lost the hole. My father, as usual, let the incident be a lesson to me as he lectured me on the importance of keeping my gear and myself well out of the way of an opponent’s wayward stroke. I did this religiously for some time though I still got caught out a couple of years later at Middlemore when an opponent shanked a short chip through a bunker onto my cart that was parked safely, I thought, beside the next tee.

The Club did not at first have a resident professional. Bronco Branch gave occasional lessons but was committed to his business in the town. Later Jim Paterson was appointed resident professional. I remember the first time Dad played in a four with Jim he was disappointed that Jim showed no apparent interest in anyone else’s golf. I don’t quite know what Dad expected. I know it must have been very hard going for Jim as paying for golf lessons would have seemed unimaginable extravagance to most members.

Jimmy Mowat had been the Professional before the Second World War and had regained his amateur status after it. He was a Scotsman of the old school who was strict on the rules of the game as well as those of the Club. Late in 1954 my father went on a teaching exchange to the USA, leaving his family home for the year. Before going he said he would pay my subscription for the year, six pounds, if I should make golf my chosen sport.  As it was I was eager to get to College and play cricket and hockey so the subscription was not paid. Early the following year I had a round with a friend and his father, shooting that 81 referred to earlier. That evening my mother got a ring from Jimmy to say that if I was not playing with my father I was not eligible to play on the course so that was the end of my golf for the year. Rules are rules I guess and the rule was that sons of members could play with their fathers, not with other members, but perhaps a bit of flexibility would have done no harm in the circumstances. Towards the end of the year Dad returned from America and soon after was appointed Headmaster at Clevedon School near Papakura so our time at the Tauranga Golf Club came to an end though I have enjoyed playing the course in tournaments and pennant competition on many a subsequent occasion.

title: Personal experiences · p. 223
text:
COURSE RECORDS

One afternoon in May 2002 Club member Eddie Burgess, a New Zealand representative at both Junior and Senior level, joined the Thursday afternoon ‘Ball in the Bucket’ brigade. Club auditor Neville Grey must have been pleased to become Eddie’s partner by dint of the ball toss but little did he know what was in store. Opening with a birdie at the first Eddie followed with further birdies at the third, fourth, sixth, seventh, and ninth to be out in 29. He

then birdied ten, eleven, fifteen, sixteen, and seventeen to be home in 31, so bettering the 61s of Kel Nagle, David Good, Bill Brask, and Michael Nicholson. Michael’s 61 was scored on Waitangi Day 1991, his final six holes reading 4, 2, 3, 4, 3, 3. This would surely be the best ever played over those demanding holes. Later Kevin Smith equalled Eddie’s score of 60. While it may be true that the course was not set up for Tournament play when Eddie, Kevin, and Michael played their rounds we can be confident that it represented a true challenge. The month of May is not the middle of winter nor does it offer the long fairway roll of summer when the four 61s were recorded. It is impossible to compare the conditions under which these rounds were played. Regardless of the conditions Eddie’s and Kevin’s stood as the best rounds ever recorded on the course at that time and deserved recognition as course records. The 59 posted by Richard Lee during the 2010 Carrus Open relegated these earlier records to history though Eddie and Kevin could still lay claim to the record score accredited to an amateur or to a Club member.

title: The Ward dynasty · p. 224
text:
CHAPTER NINETEEN

THE WARD DYNASTY

title: The Ward dynasty · p. 225
text:
Few families, if any, have had such a long and fruitful association with the Tauranga Golf club as has the Ward family. It began in 1947 when F W (Fred) Ward was appointed manager of the Tauranga Branch of Mackenzie’s and he and his wife, Olwyn, moved to the Town. At that time Mackenzie’s and Woolworth’s were intense chain store rivals located in just about every New Zealand town of any size. They sold general merchandise at reasonable prices and perhaps were equivalent to the “Five and Ten Cent” stores of the USA. Woolworth’s was an American company while Mackenzie’s was an all New Zealand  enterprise established by Mr R A McKenzie. Fred began caddying at the Hokowhitu course of the Manawatu Golf Club at the tender age of seven. Fortunately bags were not the heavier bags of today as trundlers had not then been introduced. Fred must have been well regarded by his employers as he rose rapidly through the caddy ranks to earn the badge awarded to the number one caddy, a badge he was very proud to have been presented with. Like a lot of top professional and amateur players of those earlier times Fred learnt the skills and etiquette of the game by observing the actions of the best players he caddied for. Throughout his long career Fred never had a lesson, his smooth, rhythmical swing being developed as the result of emulating the best of what he observed. That remains a great way to develop a sound swing and young players should take every opportunity to watch the best players, amateur or professional, male or female, whenever they get the chance.

Fred was successful in winning the Senior Championship at Hokowhitu before moving to Tauranga where he immediately demonstrated his class by winning the Senior Championship in that first year of 1947. He was to win it on another six occasions between 1950 and 1956, his seven victories being second only to those of Michael Nicholson who won the Championship twelve times between 1970 and 1991. In addition to his Club Championship successes Fred won the Tauranga Open Championship four years in a row from 1947, and again in 1953 and 1958. These six victories place him ahead of D K (Don) Boone, of Springfield, who won the title on five occasions between 1956 and 1963. The Tauranga Open Championship was the premier event at the annual Labour Weekend Tournament that was first played in 1934.  Apart from the War years of 1941 to 1945 when no tournament was held this extremely popular event attracted top players from Auckland, the Waikato, together with those from the Bay of Plenty and further afield. Sadly it fell victim to a new era where players are reluctant to travel away from their home clubs for tournaments such as this and it was discontinued following the 1999 event. At its peak the tournament attracted full fields of 112 divided into seven groups of sixteen for match play.

At Inter-Provincial level Fred represented the Bay of Plenty with distinction in four Freyberg Rose Bowl Tournaments. This tournament has gone by a number of names since, depending on the company sponsoring it. The Freyberg Rose Bowl has now taken a new role as the trophy attached to the “Masters” Inter-Provincial Tournament for the stars of an earlier age.  Fred’s lowest handicap was +1, though he did feel the handicapper was a bit harsh in making him give the course that one stroke.

In 1949 Fred encouraged Olwyn to join the Club and they were active and popular members until 1962 when Fred was promoted to Hastings where he joined the Hastings Golf Club at Bridge Pa. This was the home of Stuart Jones who left no room for any pretender to his throne thus ending Fred’s championship winning run.

title: The Ward dynasty · p. 226
text:
Probably the first sub 70 round at Gate Pa

Playing in the annual Schoolboy Tournament of 1978 Kevin Ward, then a 17 year-old playing off a 24 handicap, aced the Knoll on the Wednesday using an eight Iron. Upon seeing Kevin on the course the following day Club member Peter Pollett congratulated Kevin and then asked in jocular fashion if he had scored any more aces that day. The nonchalant reply was: “Well yes, I got one on the fifth”. And so indeed he had, using a 4 Iron this time. Kevin is a younger brother of John and Errol, members of this family that has been so much a part of the Tauranga Golf Club for more than sixty years.

Fred’s knowledge of the game and his organisational skills were recognised very soon after he joined Tauranga and he was prevailed upon to serve as Club Captain from 1948 to 1951, and again in 1953/54. Olwyn also took a full role in Club affairs, serving on the Ladies’ committee for four years and reaching a handicap of 12. Their son Mark was a junior member from 1958 until 1962.

title: The Ward dynasty · p. 227
text:
Left:  Fred Ward demonstrates his strong address position

Below:  Fred Ward and Andy Fletch er (Te Aroha) had a number of stir ring matches in the annual Labour Weekend tournament.

title: The Ward dynasty · p. 228
text:
Fred’s departure very nearly coincided with the arrival in Tauranga of his brothers, Allen and Claude who were quick to join the Club. The latter would be much more readily recognised by the name of Buster. Like Fred they learned their golf in the Manawatu and each showed much of the family golfing ability. Allen made his mark early by winning the Palmerston North Club Championship in 1938 at the precocious age of 16. He played to a low of 3, while Buster did even better to reach as low as 1. Allen joined in 1961 and remained active until his premature death in 1979. He became a committee member in 1971 and proved to be an extremely influential and wise chairman of the Greens Committee, a position he held at the time of his death. Allen also found time to manage the Bay of Plenty Junior team, a reflection of his interest in the progress in the game of his sons and their peers.

Buster joined in 1962 and remained a member until his death in 2005. He was active almost to the end, being widely recognised as the Patriarch of the Ward Clan who made such an impact with the size of their group at Friday Night Twilight Tournaments throughout many a summer.

J W (John) Ward joined as a junior member in 1967. At Intermediate school he and his friend Noel Johnson had been encouraged to get seriously involved in the game through the influence of Una Wickham who taught at the school. Both eventually went on to represent the Bay of Plenty at Freyberg Rose Bowl level. John represented the Bay from 1972 until 1982 including appearances in the Freyberg team in 1975, 76, 77, and again in 1982. John won the Tauranga Club Senior Stroke play Championship in 1980, 83, and 86, and the Labour weekend Open Championship in 1978. His lowest round at Tauranga was a 66, one better than Uncle Fred’s best. At his peak John reached a handicap of 1. Errol Ward, John’s older brother, first joined in 1976, remaining a member for three years. When he returned to the game in 1993 he became more involved, so much so that he was elected to the committee in 1998 before serving as Club captain in 1999 and 2000. Errol has successfully tendered for a number of renovation building projects at the Club. Younger brother Kevin was a member for just two years but made a lasting name for himself by scoring holes in one on successive days on 17/18 May 1978 when just 17 years old. These were at the 12th and 5th holes respectively. Vivienne Phelps, sister to Errol, John, and Kevin, has been a member since 1997 while her husband, Owen, has been a member since 1990. Later recruits to the Club include Annette Bainbridge and her husband Dennis, and Owen Teague. Annette and Owen are the children of Dorothy who was a sister to Fred, Allen, and Buster. The dynasty continues. Many of the above, plus other family and friends, made up the “Ward Mafia”, a group of up to 25 who patronised the Friday Twilight tournaments in the Eighties and Nineties when they were in full swing. Their ages ranged from that of Buster in his eighties to third generation juniors in their teens.

title: The professionals come to play · p. 229
text:
CHAPTER TWENTY

THE PROFESSIONALS

COME TO PLAY

title: The professionals come to play · p. 230
text:
The committee of 1952/53 sought ways to promote the club to the rest of the country in order to attract green fee visitors and to encourage membership applications from residents and newcomers alike. The age of closed membership had not yet arrived and increased membership together with greater returns from green fee paying visitors were seen as the path to prosperity at club level. The committee reasoned that a prestigious tournament featuring leading professional and amateur players from throughout New Zealand would have a good chance of achieving these aims. They were also cognisant of the fact that professionals in particular lacked opportunities to showcase their skills to the public and it would be beneficial to all parties if the professional game were to be encouraged. Consequently the committee contacted the NZPGA and, with their full support, settled on a 54 hole Stroke Play Tournament to be staged on a weekend in June 1953.

That first tournament was judged to be a great success and the club has since continued to promote itself and the game on a wider stage by involving itself in the hosting of professional tournaments whenever the opportunity has arisen. In that first Invitation Tournament a field of 18 professionals competed for prize money of £200 while 42 invited amateurs made up a quality field. F X (Frank) Buckler, then of Auckland, averaged one over par through the three rounds to comfortably lead the professional field on 216, four strokes clear of Alex Murray, also of Auckland and no stranger to the course as he acted as adviser to the club on course design and development. J A (James) Paterson, then of Wanganui but soon to fill the vacant professional position at Tauranga, finished third. Scoring by the first few professionals was steady if unspectacular, the best rounds being par 71s by the two leaders.

New Zealand Maori champion T P (Tori) Jones of Taumarunui matched these par rounds in his final round to head off tournament favourite A J (Andy) Fletcher by a single stroke. Amateurs P G F (Pax) Smith and W W Smith, each of Titirangi, returned the only sub par rounds, each one under the card.

President Syd Randell in his comments at the prize ceremony admitted the promotion had been an ambitious one for the club but the support of the players and spectators had made the effort well worthwhile. “We are proud of our course and this tournament will have done much to popularise it and make it known in other parts of the North Island and New Zealand generally”. Mr Randell went on to say that the tournament had been staged with the dual objectives of showing players what a good course Tauranga was and to provide young players with the opportunity to see the best New Zealand golfers in action. Both objectives had been achieved.

On the Tuesday following the tournament the BOP Times published a number of comments by participants. These included: Frank Buckler: “A beautiful course in excellent order. The only fault that could be found is that it might be short. Otherwise it is up to New Zealand championship standard. Compared to Auckland courses at this time of the year the condition of fairways and greens is simply amazing. The hazards are good and well laid out”.

title: The professionals come to play · p. 231
text:
Alex Murray: “The course was 100% in all respects. The fact that not one golfer in the field broke 70 showed the course is neither too short nor too easy. Conditions were ideal, no wind nor rain, yet the best 54 hole total was three over par. The green keepers are to be congratulated on excellent presentation and I believe the course would be ideal for a National championship”.

Bob Jackson: “The best conditioned course I have ever played on. The bunkers too are the best conditioned I have seen in New Zealand. Their condition does not put a player in a hopeless position yet they do test his skill”.

Editor’s note: At the time of the 1953 tournament the sand in the bunkers was pumice sand that was dug from a pit on what is now the back of the fourth tee. When dry and stirred up to a fluffy state this material provided an excellent medium from which to play the old-fashioned explosion shot favoured by players of the time. After rain however it became hard packed and difficult from which to gain much control over recovery shots even for talented players. It was not until 1963 that Papamoa sand was tried on the course and today players are fortunate to have bunkers filled with quality river sand. While players now may complain of bad lies and insufficient sand in bunkers I doubt they would appreciate a return to the pumice sand of those years. The heavier sand does require a different technique and the modern club player might be better rewarded by learning to use the correct approach rather than complaining about the state of the bunkers. All in all though it is worth remembering that bunkers are supposed to be hazards irrespective of what we see on our television screens.

TS Galloway (President NZPGA): “I saw the course first in 1924 and again in 1939. It has improved out of all sight. It is in my opinion one of the best country courses I have seen. The short fourth is a gem and the fifteenth one of the best par fours I have experienced”.

Basil Smith Jnr: “I have not seen a course more perfectly grassed. I have not heard one adverse comment regarding the course nor any part of the tournament. The Club is to be congratulated not only on the fine course, which is well up to National Championship standard, but also on a very fine tournament”.

TP Jones: “It is a grand course in every respect and, having won, I think it is just perfect. It is my first visit but I will be back”.

From the above comments it is clear that the staff and administrators of the time were getting many things right and the professionals appreciated the effort made to offer them an opportunity to play for a prize purse and for the opportunity to meet with their colleagues in convivial surroundings.

ALEX SHATTERS THE COURSE RECORD

The 1954 staging of the Invitation Tournament was notable for a brilliant round of 64, or seven under par, played by Alex Murray on the opening day of the tournament. The previous record stood at 68, a record shared by perennial club champion F W (Fred) Ward and the great Australian P W (Peter)

title: The professionals come to play · p. 232
text:
Thomson. Murray scored birdies at the 1st, 2nd, 5th, 7th, 10th, 12th, and 14th holes with not a single blemish on the card. One who witnessed the round remarked that Murray had seldom been on his own fairway but the quality of his iron play was such that he almost always reached the green in regulation. At the time the trees were 50 years younger and did not present quite the difficulties experienced today but, given the equipment of the time, this round compares very favourably with any that have followed since. Alex Murray, born in Scotland, was the son of a professional golfer and, so steeped in golf was the family, that no fewer than eleven uncles were also professionals. Murray showed his quality in winning three New Zealand Opens and would have won another but for his famous error in idly tapping his ball with his putter while waiting to putt during the final round at St. Andrews in Hamilton in 1937.

Despite shooting 69s in the first and final rounds Ernie Southerden of Napier finished two strokes behind Murray while Jim Paterson, now of Tauranga, repeated his third placing of the year before. Further down the field could be seen the name A E (Alf) Guy, a player renowned for his long hitting though his best days were now behind him. The BOP Times recorded that Alf thrilled the gallery by almost driving the 299 yard second hole. As Alf Guy was still one of the longest drivers in the game this gives some indication of the advancement made in ball and club technology as such drives as he achieved are now well within the range of a good number of club players

BUCKLER PREVAILS AGAIN IN 1955

Playing the most consistent golf seen to this time at Tauranga Frank Buckler left a quality field far in his wake following rounds of 72, 67, and 67. While not faultless his play was such as to leave the large gallery greatly impressed with the accuracy of his iron play and the quality of his putting. Regular place getters Ernie Southerden and Jim Paterson followed Buckler thanks to each scoring a 69 in one of their three rounds. The Akarana amateur Neville Dowden also scored a 69 in annexing the amateur section.

1956 THE EMPEROR PAYS A VISIT

In 1956 the reigning amateur champion of New Zealand, S G (Stuart) Jones of Hastings, was attracted to the tournament and he did not let the gallery or his reputation down. With rounds of 70, 73, and a superb final round of 66 “The Emperor”, as he became widely known during his long and illustrious career, outplayed the professional and amateur fields alike by many strokes. This was not to be the last time that Jones demonstrated to the professionals that it was perhaps fortuitous for them that he preferred to remain within the amateur ranks.

Popular winner amongst the professional division was local man J A (Jimmy) Paterson. A true gentleman of the links Jim learnt his trade in England and was one of the finest iron players one could hope to emulate. His well-struck iron shots seemed to fly quite low off the club then, as they slowed, they would rise so as to drop gently onto the green. It was a great pity that Jimmy’s nervous system did not allow him to consistently play the brand of golf of which he was so obviously capable. On this occasion he held his nerve well enough to finish on 217, four over par and two clear of Jack Kelly of Auckland.

Bob Jackson, on this occasion, thanked the club on behalf of the professionals. He commented there

title: The professionals come to play · p. 233
text:
was a special atmosphere in particular clubs and that at Tauranga was one of being “at home”. The Professionals looked forward to coming to the club and to the town each year as a result of this special feeling.

1957 - BIG TED ENTERS THE SCENE

E J (Ted) McDougall, then of Pukekohe, was to become a regular visitor to Tauranga over many years, both as an amateur and as a professional. He was just 19 when he won the Lionel Smith Rose Bowl as leading amateur in the 1957 tournament. Born in Scotland Ted was to become an outstanding competitor at every level of New Zealand golf. Following his Tauranga victory he went on to win the National amateur championship later in the season. As Jones had done the previous Invitation Tournament McDougall put the professionals in the shade as he improved on each of his rounds carding 73, 71, and a final 67 to lead Ross Newdick, later to win a PGA title at Mt Maunganui, by five strokes. Ernie Southerden headed the Professional field one stroke behind Newdick with Buckler another stroke adrift. Stuart Jones honoured his pledge of the year before to return to Tauranga but an uncharacteristic 81 in his opening round put paid to any chance of him successfully defending his title. In accepting his prize from club president Warwick Nicoll Mr McDougall congratulated the committee on the course. The greens, he said, were much superior to any in Auckland.

BUCKLER AGAIN IN 1958

The 1958 tournament was notable for Frank Buckler’s third win in the six tournaments staged to that date and for the victory of W W Smith in the amateur section. WW had played in each tournament since inception without winning the Lionel Smith Rose Bowl, the major trophy for amateurs. Scoring was not up to the standard set in earlier years with Smith averaging 72s and Buckler one stroke worse on 217.

The 16 year-old Aucklander W J (Walter) Godfrey impressed many in the gallery. The BOP Times sports reporter of the day wrote in his tournament coverage that Godfrey’s easy swing indicated he would produce fine golf as he developed physically. How right his prophecy proved to be.

McDOUGALL REPEATS IN 1959 Now a member of the professional ranks Ted McDougall thrilled a large gallery in his first round by scoring a 67 after which he was never threatened, finishing nine strokes clear of veteran Alf Guy with a further stroke back to Frank Buckler in third position. In spite of this success so early in his professional life McDougall rejoined the amateur ranks less than two years later and went on to have a distinguished

career there, a second victory in the New Zealand amateur championship coming in 1970.

A C (Alf) Relph of Rotorua was a very popular winner of the Lionel Smith Rose Bowl finishing seven strokes clear of R A Court of New Plymouth. Alf Relph was a wonderful servant of Rotorua and Bay of Plenty Golf for many years representing each as a player and as an administrator. He is one of only four men to be honoured with Life Membership of the Bay of Plenty District Golf Association. Our own Jim Reid, who served as Captain and later President of our Club in the sixties, was one of the other three. Following the amalgamation of the administration of men’s golf with that of women the BOPDGA has now been re-incorporated as GolfBOP. In 2009 Dan Dougherty, President of our Club from 1991 to

title: The professionals come to play · p. 234
text:
1993, was honoured with Life Membership of the new organisation.

AMATEURS SHOW THE WAY IN 1960

Alf Relph was again successful in the tournament of 1960. This event began in atrocious conditions under which most courses would have been virtually unplayable. Despite persistent heavy rain and gusty northerly winds Relph returned a remarkable score of just one over par. Bay of Plenty team mate D K (Don) Boone of Springfield was only one stroke behind. Sunday brought much more favourable conditions and a good sized gallery saw Relph drop only one further stroke over the two rounds to finish on 215. Boone also maintained form to finish a clear second on 218. Professional winner John Kelly of Auckland finished some distance behind these two but he did improve markedly on the 77 returned under the trying conditions of the previous day.

PROFESSIONAL PRIDE RESTORED IN 1961

Auckland professional, and regular participant, Bob Jackson led a quartet of professionals who relegated the amateurs to the lower spots on the Leader Board in the 1961 renewal of the event. The tournament attracted a strong field of 16 professionals and 56 amateurs. Jackson highlighted the weekend with a hole in one at the fourth hole, “The Gully”, on the Sunday afternoon. It has long been said that if you play the par threes well at Tauranga you will have a good round. This may be self-evident from the very fact that there are five of them here while most courses have only the standard four. The adage was surely true of Jackson on that afternoon for his aggregate of 12, or three under par, on the par threes led to a three under round of 68. With earlier rounds of 72 and 73 Bob won by four strokes from Noel Hayden, a good friend of Tauranga golf and a man who did a great deal for Junior Golf, first from his base in Rotorua and later in Auckland. It was good to see Bob Jackson succeeding as he had been a strong supporter of the tournament from the first staging.

Eldon Carswell of Rotorua who had almost certainly been one to benefit from Noel Hayden’s interest in juniors, led the amateurs with a rather uninspired total of 13 over par for the 54 holes. Carswell himself was heard to say he would have been much happier had he shot three seventies and finished second. Another prominent BOP representative in Ivan Deadman of Rotorua finished one stroke behind Carswell with Don Boone making it a Rotorua trifecta a further stroke back.

1962 - THE WOMEN ARE INVITED

Always willing to be innovative the organising committee decided to invite women (though they were

still called lady golfers at the time) to the tournament. This was believed to be the first time women had been invited to participate in an open tournament of this nature in New Zealand. The initiative was very warmly received by the low handicap women invited. In the event itself local champion Miss Una Wickham had to bow to Mrs Jean Mangan of Palmerston North. The two were separated by a single stroke, Miss Wickham uncharacteristically missing a short putt at the last hole that would have tied the pair. Both women were New Zealand representatives so the aim of the promoters to provide competition for these women prior to the Tasman Cup series proved to be successful.

Meanwhile New Zealand Men’s Representative Walter Godfrey burnt off a strong amateur field with an

title: The professionals come to play · p. 235
text:
excellent closing round of 67. Apart from a sponsored tournament held earlier in the season at Akarana the amateur field assembled at Tauranga was said to be the best assembled in New Zealand that year. Appearing on the leader board were regular supporters of Tauranga tournaments including Peter Maude (Otorohanga), Terry Leech (Taupo), Ross Newdick (Auckland), Trevor Ormsby (Otorohanga), and Frank Cullen (Matamata).

In the professional division the two regular placegetters, Ernie Southerden and Jim Paterson, along with Irishman Eddie Fennell of Gisborne, fought out a close contest with Southerden edging home by a stroke from the other two. Paterson should have won in a canter but for an uncharacteristic 82 in the middle round. No player, amateur or professional, came close to emulating Godfrey’s tournament total or his best round of 67.

In an unusual and much appreciated gesture Frank Buckler, now president of the NZPGA, presented trophies on behalf of the PGA to the Men’s and Women’s club captains of the Tauranga Golf Club “in appreciation of what the Club is doing, and trying to do, for golf in New Zealand”.

BUCKLER WINS AGAIN IN 1963

Frank Buckler crossed the Kaimai ranges once again to annexe his fourth Tauranga Invitational on what must surely be his favourite course. The Canada Cup representative finished four under the card this time playing consistently good rounds of 69, 72, and 68. On this occasion no one amongst Buckler’s professional colleagues could mount a serious challenge with only the long hitting amateur Peter Maude lying close after the first round. Maude held on to win the amateur title in spite of relatively poor rounds of 75 and 73 on the Sunday. Ross Newdick finished two strokes behind Maude.

The gap between Tauranga’s best and those from elsewhere in New Zealand was demonstrated when Tauranga’s leading competitor, D K (Doug) Furrie, finished eleven strokes shy of Peter Maude’s total while another four local players were much further adrift. It was to be many years before Tauranga men began to make their mark at National level. In the case of the women however the club had seen much stronger representation and local star Una Wickham was a popular winner of the Women’s division despite scoring rather more poorly than was her norm. Six strokes behind Una Sally Turvey, the 16 year old from Rotorua, threw out an indication of the future of the game as young players gradually came to the fore. Another youngster from Rotorua, Jane Butler, also gave an indication of her potential, only a poor middle round preventing her from challenging for the lead. Jane went on to a very successful

career in golf and is now better known as Jane Little. In common with many quality players Jane’s father was a Green Keeper so she was in touch with the game from a very early age.

RECORDS APLENTY IN 1964

As the result of some changes to the course that really had little impact on its playing difficulty the course record of 64 set by Alex Murray ten years earlier was no longer recognised as applying to “the new course”. Consequently new records in both the Amateur and the Professional sections were recognised as the result of scores posted in the 1964 tournament. Walter Godfrey, now a professional, set the pace all the way with rounds of 69, 67 (recognised as the new record), and 72. Godfrey dropped

title: The professionals come to play · p. 236
text:
Don Stevenson one morning bought a new ball at the Pro Shop when Jim Paterson was the incumbent. Don teed up and promptly toed his new ball back into the shop, breaking a large window on the way. Many will remember Don’s wife Sylvie who was an active and very popular member over at least forty years commencing in the early sixties.

only one stroke during his record round, that being at the relatively easy tenth thus illustrating there are no easy holes in golf. Good as it was Godfrey’s record was to last only as long as it took Terry Leech of Taupo to complete his afternoon round. Leech (son of legendary Taupo Green Keeper Charley Leech) had played the first two rounds very well in 70 and 72 to trail Ted McDougall by four strokes in the Amateur section of the tournament. Heavy overnight rain resulted in the greens playing slow and the fairways long on the Sunday. To add to these conditions drizzly rain fell throughout the afternoon. In spite of this Terry Leech played some of the greatest golf ever seen on the course during his round of 65. His outward nine of 34, thanks to a birdie at the long seventh, did not suggest what was to follow on the final, more difficult, second nine. Birdies at the 10th, 11th, 13th, and 15th, together with an eagle three on the short par five 17th were offset by a shot dropped at the par three 14th. To annex the Amateur prize Leech needed this score or better as McDougall continued his good form with a one- under-par round of 70 to finish just one stroke back.

Jane Butler, now representing the North Shore Club, won the Women’s section on count back from Miss P Harrison on the strength of a final round of 77, three better than her rival. Incidentally this result would have been reversed had the committee adopted an alternative count back method that gives priority to the lowest round of the tournament. It is obviously important to have all tournament conditions published before the event. An indication of the strength of women’s golf at our own Club was given by the placing of both Olga Johnson and Pat Kidd in the top ten, while Una Wickham was not a competitor that year.

WALTER WINS AGAIN IN 1965

Although he was not able to reproduce the brilliance of the previous year Walter Godfrey again won the Professional section. Commencing with a 72 he improved a stroke in each round to defeat evergreen Ernie Southerden by three strokes. Interestingly the pair showed the same scoring pattern with Ernie starting one stroke higher on 73. In similar vein Terry Leech played steadily without the extra inspiration of the previous year and his four-over-par total of 217 was not good enough to hold out rising star Brian Boys of Hamilton who sandwiched a 75 between two 69s. Tauranga’s Keith Dawkins claimed fourth place, the best performance by a local man in the history of the event, still nine strokes off the pace.

Thanks to an opening round of 71 Miss Natalie White of Auckland, a New Zealand representative, headed Miss Wickham by 10 strokes after the first 18 holes. Using all her experience and wealth of

local knowledge to close the gap Una failed to do so by three strokes. Mrs Olga Johnson, another

local, was two strokes back in third place.

title: The professionals come to play · p. 237
text: Action on the sixth green during the 1962 Invitation Tournament. Ted MacDougall (back to camera) shows why he was known as “Big Ted”.

title: The professionals come to play · p. 238
text: Scenes from the 1962 Invitation Tournament courtesy Photo News. Corrections:  Ernie Southerden is called Sutherland in first photo caption.   It is Terry Leech not Tony. Roy Bathgate - Club Captain - checks a competitor’s card.

title: The professionals come to play · p. 239
The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 240
text:
CHAPTER TWENTYONE

THE SPALDING

MASTERS AND THE NZPGA CHAMPIONSHIP

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 241
text:
The 1965 Tournament proved to be the last of the Invitation Tournaments to be held at Tauranga but by no means did it herald the end of quality Professional and Amateur tournaments at the club. We were soon to see even bigger and brighter stars on show thanks to the initiative of local businessman R A (Bob) Owens; later Sir Bob. In 1965 Mr Owens had been instrumental in establishing the NZPGA Championship at Mount Maunganui. Prior to that time the Professional Championship of New Zealand was run by the New Zealand Golf Association in conjunction with their Open Championship and, like the Amateur Championship, it was a match play event following the Open. The Professional Championship was not played in 1964 and Mr Owens saw the opportunity to promote the Tauranga area, his company, and the game of golf. Once he settled upon a course of action Mr Owens was the type of man who made certain that a positive outcome ensued and the first STARS Travel (Stevedores Travel and Reservation Service) NZPGA Championship was held before enthusiastic, beach dressed, galleries at the height of summer in January 1965.

During these years a fledgling New Zealand Golf Circuit had developed with sponsored events being played at courses throughout the country. The committee at Tauranga felt it would be wise to drop the June/July Invitation Tournament and concentrate their efforts on becoming part of that circuit by promoting an event in January while visiting Professionals from New Zealand and Overseas were in the district. It was therefore fortuitous that in April 1967 the Spalding Company, then possibly the most important sporting goods company serving New Zealand, approached Tauranga with a view to staging the Spalding Masters as a pre-curser to the NZPGA at the Mount. The initiative Tauranga had shown in offering competition and prize money for the Professionals in earlier years when very little was provided for them undoubtedly had much to do with the approach now being made. As was to be expected Tauranga enthusiastically accepted the Spalding offer and the Tournament was scheduled for the 8th/9th of January 1968 over 54 holes for prize money of £1000. The Spalding Company put up £750 while the club decided to put in a further £250 so as to make the purse appear so much more attractive. This was considered an excellent purse at the time especially as the Professional purse for the Invitation Tournament had been only £200. Prior to the tournament New Zealand adopted decimal currency so the field ultimately played for total prize money of $2000. This was sufficient to attract a quality field headed by reigning PGA champion of Australia E W (Billy) Dunk.

The first day of the tournament saw a spate of sub par scoring which resulted in the accepted course record of 67 set by Walter Godfrey in 1964 being bettered no less than five times during the day before the 20 year old John Lister of Timaru settled the issue with a 64 towards the end of the day. There will always be debate about what constitutes a course record and many will feel as I do that this 64 only equalled the 64 scored by Alex Murray fourteen years previously. In the intervening period the course had been altered by siting the tee at the par three fifth to the South so the hole paralleled the seventh fairway and was some 30 metres longer. How much more difficult this made the course is impossible to measure, but since 64 was to be bettered within twelve months the question did not remain relevant for very long. On the more general question of course records it could be argued that they belong in the same genera as the fastest times in Marathons. There is no record for a Marathon as courses differ so much from one to another. In the same way Golf Courses do not offer the same conditions from one day to the next. Pin positions, tee positions, weather conditions, and condition of greens, fairways and

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 242
text:
rough all change on a daily basis. Provided a round is played in accordance with the Rules of Golf and the course is set up from the normal teeing grounds then the lowest score ever recorded gets my vote as the ‘course record’.

On that first day in 1968 six under par rounds of 65 were scored by Billy Dunk and Denis Sullivan (North Shore), 66s from Bob Stanton (NSW), Walter Godfrey (Auckland) and John Croskery (Remuera), and 67s from Len Thomas (Western Australia) and Terry Kendall (Manor Park). Sullivan’s round included an Out of Bounds penalty at the thirteenth so a 63 had certainly been a possibility. The long hitting Dutchman, Martin Roesink, who had attracted very large galleries during the first two rounds was well down the field with rounds of 72 and 71. As a result the fans had deserted him when he embarked on his third and final round. That was unfortunate as they would have been treated to some wonderful entertainment. Roesink showed his true ability with a faultless 63, four under on each nine, to wrest the record from John Lister. It was claimed that Roesink drove the third green during this round but only his playing companions and their caddies were witness to the feat.  Driving the third green was unheard of at that time yet today a number of club players drive across the trees in the direction of the green and occasionally one will reach it. Martin Roesink was later to try his luck in the United States where at least one Golf magazine claimed he was the longest hitter on the circuit. Unfortunately the rest of his game seldom reached the standard of his driving, perhaps because in his own words he “kept looking around to see who was on the course”. The handsome Dutchman was certainly popular with female spectators and it may be understandable that his concentration was sometimes less than 100% on his game. A further example of his hitting ability was in evidence one day when he drove into the seventh fairway when playing the sixth. From there he lofted a nine iron over the pines and into the heart of the green. This was before the advent of the one-piece ball and metal drivers and, no, the pines were no less lofty than they are today.

In spite of missing a ‘tiddler’ on the 54th and final green Billy Dunk, a man renowned for setting course records in Australia, completed immaculate rounds of 65, 66, and 67 to defeat Tasmanian Bob Shaw whose closing 64 left him two strokes in arrears. Ted McDougall was an impressive winner of the Amateur division with rounds of 69, 66, and 66. In all 24 competitors aggregated par or better through the 54 holes.

MORE FIRSTS IN THE 1969 SPALDING MASTERS

The organising committee were delighted to accept the offer of the Spalding Company to have the great American Professional Miss Marilynn Smith play in the 1969 tournament scheduled to be played over 72 holes for the first time. It was no accident that Miss Smith was drawn to play in a dream grouping with New Zealand’s best Amateur and Professional, Stuart Jones and Bob Charles respectively. This was the first occasion that a woman had played in men’s company in any Open Tournament in New Zealand and proved extremely popular with the crowds that thronged the course. Playing before a gallery estimated at 600 these three all played excellent golf. Charles showed his class with a 66, Jones shot a 69, and Marilynn Smith a 74. Miss Smith expressed the opinion that New Zealand women’s

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 243
text:
golf would be greatly stimulated if New Zealand women were to join the USA Professional Tour. She believed that Tauranga’s Una Wickham and Natalie White of Auckland “could fare well on the circuit though would have to be helped initially through considerable financial backing”. Twentyfour players bettered par while 19-year old Jim Lancaster of the host club returned an excellent 70 in his first tournament at this level.

Teeing off in the second round Charles led by just one stroke from Guy Wolstenholme of England and Ted Ball of NSW. He soon showed he meant business with a superb round of 62 featuring eight birdies and no dropped shots,  par having been dropped to 70 with the 17th hole now correctly identified as a par four. Charles commented after the round that he “holed every putt within ten feet except one on the 14th, but my only really good birdie putt was on the seventh”. Ted Ball, of the lightning fast swing trailed by seven strokes and was heard to comment: “There is only one man who can stop Charles on this course. That’s Kel Nagle and he’s in Australia”. How prophetic those words were to prove as Charles compiled rounds of 69 and 63 in the final rounds to finish on 260, twenty under par and ten strokes clear of John Lister in second place.

Meanwhile Marilynn Smith demonstrated that women playing off the back tees on a course set to test the best men would always have difficulty competing against them. Never the less the quality of her ball striking and general play impressed the spectators, both male and female, who were privileged to see her in action. Her best round was a 73.

Paul Hart, an unheralded NSW professional, matched Charles’ record 62 during his third round, a feat witnessed by a mere handful of spectators until word of his deeds spread late in the day. With his other three rounds including a pair of 69s and a 71 Hart tied for third with Bob Shaw and Brian Boys. Stuart Jones made no contest of the Amateur division with a seven under aggregate including a fine 65 in the second round.

When asked by the BOP Times reporter for comment following the tournament the following were representative of the replies received: Bob Charles: “The finest greens in New Zealand”. Dennis Sullivan: “That seventeenth green would grace any course in the World”. Guy Wolstenholme: “They have really worked hard on the course and the greens have been prepared by someone knowledgeable and are as good as anything in New Zealand”. Bob Shaw - recently returned from playing in Europe and the USA. “The only bad green is the 15th. The rest would compare favourably with anything I have played on”. Jess Vaughn (USA): “The course is as good as any I played on in England, the United States, or Australia, and would be on a par with many competition courses in the United States”. Marilynn Smith: “I found the course very much the same as Overseas, the greens being very true with no hidden tricks”. Editor’s note: With respect to the comments above it should be noted that, at the time of this tournament, the 15th green had been struck by an as then unrecognised fungal infection while the 17th had not yet

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 244
text:
been relocated to its present position.)

1970 - THE EMPEROR RULES

Otago Professional Alistair Palmer led with a 65 on the first day but a crowd of Australians, led by then five times British Open Champion Peter Thomson, loomed in his wake. This threat soon became reality as Thomson added a 66 to his opening 68. Another seven Australians were within two strokes of his lead. Three strokes further back Stuart Jones and Aucklander Bob Gillespie, who had aced the gully during his opening round, headed the Amateurs. During his round American Jesse Vaughn scored what must rank as one of the more spectacular eagles to have been recorded on the course. Playing the sixth hole Vaughn’s tee shot found the fairway bunker that used to feature some twenty metres short of the tenth green. From there a magnificent stroke sent the ball to the heart of the sixth green where a five-metre putt completed an unlikely eagle. Many years later local man Josh Geary, runner up to Gavin Smillie in our Senior Championship final when just a schoolboy, went one better by holing out with a three iron from another now defunct fairway bunker for an albatross two on our 13th hole during the annual under-23 age group tournament held on the course.

Surprisingly Peter Thomson, after his strong start, dropped away in the third round leaving three other Australians, Vic Bennets, Paul Morgan, and Barry Coxon, as the main contenders moving into the afternoon’s final round.  No one was picking Stuart Jones to pose a threat to the leaders despite his steady rounds of 68, 71 and 70. While it is now unheard of for Professionals to be required to play two rounds on the final day of a tournament it was common practice in earlier years and the fourth round would fully test the mental and physical resources of all the contestants during a hot Tauranga day in January.

Jones, playing in a threesome with Coxon and Wolstenholme, birdied the two long holes on the front nine to be out in 33 making up just one of the three strokes by which he trailed Coxon. Meanwhile Wolstenholme overtook them both only to fall away on the more difficult second nine holes as many another has done before and since. It was not to be until the 16th that Jones was able to draw level with Coxon and, with Bennets also fading over the closing holes, it was down to these two to fight out the finish. To the delight of the gallery it was the Amateur who prevailed, his closing 66 being too good for Coxon’s even par 70. By the end of this round some players were suffering quite markedly from heat exhaustion or possible sunstroke and it was considered unlikely that competitors would ever again be scheduled to play 36 holes in one day under these conditions. The difficult conditions seemingly did not adversely trouble Australian David Graham who climbed many places up the leader board with a closing 64. Graham went on to join the PGA Tour in the USA where he won the USPGA Championship in 1979 and their Open Championship two years later. He later became known as “the club maker to the pros” designing and fitting clubs to suit each individual.

SNAPE SETS THE PACE IN 1971

Transplanted Australian Alan Snape, who had recently qualified as a member of the NZPGA and was later to become resident Professional at the Tauranga Club, led a quality field through the first two

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 245
text:
rounds at eight under par. Unfortunately Alan was destined to strike disaster in the third round and thus drop from contention as more favoured contenders such as Charles, Marsh, Wolstenholme and Lister made their way up the leader board. This year the tournament had drawn the usual contingent of Australian and New Zealand Professionals but was made more International by the presence of a strong group of Americans headed by PGA Tour winner Larry Ziegler who was at that time 37th on their money list. Included in the American contingent were three young men who arrived in the belief that they were entered in this tournament and in the PGA Championship at the Mount. It transpired they had been let down by their New Zealand contact and organisers here had not heard of them.
