Fortunately the NZPGA and local organisers were flexible enough to allow their late entries and they were included in both fields. One member of this group, Jim Albus, responded by heading the first day leader board with a grand 64, six under par, a score he maintained to the end of the tournament to finish in eighth place. Years later Albus was to feature prominently on the Seniors Tour in America over a number of seasons. Fellow American Ziegler may well have won the tournament but for a poor round of 74 sandwiched between a 67 and a final pair of 65s.

Bob Charles and Graham Marsh, brother of Australian wicket keeper Rodney, were paired in a Trans Tasman battle that enthralled the large gallery that accompanied them throughout the afternoon in spite of rain that fell midway through the round. The contest became a virtual singles match between the pair

until Wolstenholme, playing three holes ahead, looked likely to upset that scenario as he rose to the top of the leader board with just five holes to play. His bad hole came at the par three 14th but he held his game together over the closing holes to post a twelve under par total of 268. At that stage Charles and Marsh were also twelve under and playing the 16th. Marsh birdied that hole to move into the lead. Uncharacteristically Charles missed a putt of little more than a metre on the 17th to yield second place to Wolstenholme while Marsh gave the gallery a final thrill by playing a great iron shot to the 18th green. He made no mistake with the resultant two metre putt to round out a convincing victory. His total of 266 was made up of two 67s followed by two 66s, consistent excellence by a grand sportsman.

While the long 13th hole, “The Crescent”, proves the undoing of many a player Graham Marsh rated it his favourite hole. He commented: “I had two eagles, a birdie and a par there. It seems a simple hole but it does not allow you to get away with much”. Most club players would agree with him, at least in regard to the second sentiment.

An interesting incident occurred on the fourth hole during this round when Marsh’s tee shot struck the lip of the front bunker and fell back in. On reaching the green Marsh walked along the green above the bunker and pointed his club at the spot where the ball had struck. In doing so he disturbed a grain or two of sand. On reporting this to Charles the pair became concerned that a rule may have been infringed so the Rules Committee were called upon. After consulting with eye witnesses the committee ruled no advantage had been gained by the inadvertent disturbance of a few grains of sand and no testing of the condition of the hazard had resulted so no penalty would be imposed. Both Charles, and obviously Marsh, were happy with this decision. Later Larry Ziegler, on hearing of the incident commented: “The committee made the sensible and wise decision. However had it happened on the PGA Tour at home a penalty would have been imposed”.

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 246
text:
Scoring in the 1971 event was remarkably good throughout the field with 64 rounds under the par of 70 being recorded while five players were under par in every round. Fifteen players bettered the 72-hole par of 280 including Amateur winner Ted McDougall.

1972 - TO CHARLES THE GLORY, TO MACKLIN THE SPOILS

The 1972 staging of the Spalding Masters, which also proved to be the last, featured a $3000 prize for a hole in one on the fourteenth hole. Murray Macklin, born in Tauranga but resident of Masterton, took the prize with a four iron shot during his second round. Under PGA rules Macklin, as a Probationary Professional, was unable to receive prize money from the tournament but special prizes such as those for holes in one were exempt from this policy so he was free to take the $3000. Later Bob Charles commented tongue in cheek: “I get only $1000 for playing 54 holes. Murray plays one shot and pockets $3000. Is that fair”? In reality of course Bob was only too happy for Murray, especially as he came from Bob’s hometown of Masterton.

While the field included some interesting newcomers, plus the usual representation from New Zealand and Australia, the leader board featured old rivals Bob Charles and Guy Wolstenholme from the first day. These two matched one another stroke for stroke with identical totals of 67 and 68 before Charles pulled clear with 65 against Wolstenholme’s 67 in the final round. Terry Kendall was a further four

strokes back in third place while locals were delighted with the performance of their star junior, 18 year old Michael Nicholson, who annexed Amateur honours with grand rounds of 72, 69, and 69. An excellent photographic study of the two winners can be seen hanging in the clubhouse. Top honours to Michael in this tournament contributed to a great month for him which included a tie for leading Amateur in the City of Auckland Open at the Grange and a win in the New Zealand under 23 Championship played at Bridge Pa, Hastings. A closing 66 in that event emphasised the quality of Michael’s play.

A deluge during play of the third round of the 1972 Spalding which flooded many of the greens eventually forced the organisers to abandon that round and reduce the tournament to 54 holes. Though some players who were in the last stages of their rounds, including one who was reputedly seven under after the 14th, were very upset at the decision the committee had no choice. While greens on the final few holes were playable and the complaining players could have comfortably completed their rounds those on the front of the course had no chance of doing so. With the NZPGA Tournament scheduled to commence at The Mount there were no spare days available to complete a fourth round.

Following his victory at Tauranga Bob Charles was poised to become the first player to win $10 000 in a New Zealand season. Finishing in the top four places at Mount Maunganui would achieve that milestone.

TAURANGA STAGES 1974 NZPGA CHAMPIONSHIP

Sadly the 1972 staging brought down the curtain on the five year show that had seen the Spalding Masters attract quality golfers to Tauranga from many parts of the world. Those players had provided appreciative galleries with competitive, exciting golf. Fortunately the fans would not have to wait long for

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 247
text:
the show to return to Gate Pa but the Spalding Masters itself was now confined to history. Tauranga’s next opportunity to stage a major tournament came through the misfortunes of the Mount Maunganui club. Subsequent to the staging of the 1973 NZPGA Championship on the course the greens there were struck by disease to such an extent that they had to be completely worked up and resown. As a result Tauranga was asked to stand by in case the Mount was not ready in time for the 1974 tournament. This proved to be the case and Tauranga staged its first NZPGA tournament in January 1974. The loss of their greens proved to be a blessing in disguise for the Mount Club as the new Pencross greens proved to be a great success earning high praise when the Club later hosted a number of prestigious tournaments including two Men’s Inter Provincial Teams events, the most recent in 2008 being won by the Bay of Plenty.

The 1974 PGA Championship brought Ted Ball’s comments of 1969 into sharp relief. That great gentleman of Australian golf, Kel Nagle, came to Tauranga and quickly demonstrated his talents. He showed he meant business even in the more relaxed atmosphere of the Pro/Am traditionally played the day before the tournament proper. On that day the American, Jerry Breaux, matched the score of 62 set by Charles and Hart in 1969 only to see Nagle better this by a stroke within the hour. Nagle’s 61 was free of blemish and contained seven birdies and an eagle three at the seventh. The latter helped him to a 29 outward nine. Breaux’ round was even more spectacular with eagles at the sixth, seventh and tenth holes to go with five birdies. Dropped shots at the second, fifth, and seventeenth holes negated these to deny the American the chance to break 60. Perhaps to show that the Gate Pa course is not as benign as some are tempted to believe Breaux shot a 75 in the opening round of the tournament proper. Many a club golfer could empathise with this 13-stroke disparity between one round and the next. Breaux demonstrated his professionalism by shooting 7 under over the remaining three rounds to finish in a tie for fifteenth, a placing shared with Michael Nicholson, the leading Amateur. Michael’s final three rounds were all sub par following an opening 73, another meritorious tournament for the young star.

New Zealand World Cup representative Dennis Clark of Palmerston North led the field with a 64 in the first round while players of the calibre of Lindsay Sharp, Kel Nagle and John Lister lay within three strokes of him. Nagle indicated his desire to win his sixth NZPGA title with a second round 64, three under on each nine, while Sharp kept in touch with a 66. Stewart Ginn, the popular and very fashionable Australian, was the prime mover with a 64 to add to his opening 69. Sharp would have been confident of closing the gap to Nagle following his third round 64 but it was not to be with Nagle also home in

64. The New Zealand Professional Walter Godfrey, a young man of enormous potential, made the strongest move, his 63 taking him to 13 under and just two strokes down on Nagle. In the final round it was Godfrey, playing with Nagle, who kept the pressure on the leader as others fell away. None the less the gap had increased to four by the time they teed up at the long 13th. Here Godfrey was long and straight while Nagle pushed his drive to the right. An attempt to cut a five iron around the big pine that once stood on that corner instead produced a draw and a visit to the racecourse. Even the greats get it wrong sometimes. Godfrey’s two-putt birdie reduced the deficit to one and a real contest was on for the run home. The next three holes were halved in pars but Nagle bunkered at the 17th, came out too strongly, and they were square playing the 18th hole. This Nagle played to perfection. A long straight

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 248
text:
drive presaged an immaculate iron to within 3 metres of the hole. A confident putt found the centre of the hole to ensure there was to be no further entertainment for the large gallery that day.

In an aside to the day’s play Terry Kendall, having just made the cut for the final round, was drawn to play in a twosome at the head of the field. He and his fellow competitor completed their 18 holes in 2 hours 15 minutes with Terry shooting 67 to show it is possible to play quickly and still score well. It must be said neither player was too concerned about their position in the tournament so it was a very relaxed round. On the same subject long serving Greens Superintendent Grant Silvester was interviewed at this tournament on a number of aspects of play and he did comment that he had noticed a significant increase in the time taken to play a round of golf. “Five years ago a four could get around in little more than three hours and 3 1/2 hours was considered slow”. Grant’s view had some veracity as he was in a position to observe more rounds than practically anyone else over many years. Courses are more crowded these days so it is not realistic to expect to match the times of another age yet it does appear that there is a lot of room for improvement in the way modern club players manage their way around the course. Leaving your clubs in the right place, being ready to play when it is your turn, filling in the card while others are teeing off, saving social gossip for the clubhouse. These are all ways to save time and thus add to the enjoyment of everyone. Simple course management is perhaps something of a lost art. Four-hour rounds are now perhaps realistic and acceptable, much longer and they cause unnecessary frustration to the majority of the field. It is also apparent that there is now an unwritten law, at least on our course that: “Thou shalt let no other group play through even if you have lost two fairways and are searching for a ball”.  This is all really a little sad.

THE JUBILEE NZPGA CHAMPIONSHIP OF 1976

The legendary A J Shaw was a special guest at the 50th Jubilee Tournament staged at Tauranga in January 1976. Andy Shaw won seven New Zealand Open Championships between 1926 and 1936 together with seven Professional titles, the last of these in 1946. Born in Scotland he was a superb striker of the ball and, given the financial opportunity, was considered to have had the game to succeed on the American Tour. In exhibition matches in New Zealand he defeated both Gene Sarazen and Walter Hagen.

Californian visitor Bill Brask enlivened an unusually rainy January day when he equalled Kel Nagle’s record 61 in the opening round. Eagles at 6 and 7 followed by birdies at each of the next three holes took Brask to nine under and the record looked there for the taking with eight holes left to play. Unfortunately

fate, in the form of the weather, played a hand, the round being suspended for an hour as some greens became flooded. When play resumed Brask drove under the Lawsoniana to the right of the eleventh fairway to drop his first stroke. Birdies at 13 and 15 made it ten under but he was only able to score a five on the par 4 seventeenth as the rain poured down and when a birdie putt slipped by on 18 the record was equalled, not broken.

In spite of the conditions sixteen players beat the par of 70 with John Lister, Bob Charles, and Simon Owen all close enough to catch Brask should he falter. The second round will be remembered as the day Kel Nagle took seven strokes to complete “The Knoll”, the infamous, seemingly innocuous, par-

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 249
text:
three 12th hole that has ruined many a lesser player’s day. While Nagle was effectively eliminating himself from contention fellow Australian David Good scored 61 to match the record held by Nagle and Brask. Good’s ten birdies included twos at four of the five par threes, his one dropped shot coming from a five at the seventeenth. The course at the time these 61s were recorded measured 5602m, only 15m short of the course as measured from the blue tees today. Good led Brask by a stroke with another two strokes back to Lister commencing the third round and the three put even more distance on the rest of the field with the first pair scoring 65s and Lister a 67. Good was the first to fade in the final round, his four bogeys in the middle of the round leading to a 72 and a third place finish earning him $1800 from the $20 000 prize pool, a very large purse at the time. Brask made the early move with a birdie at the second followed by an eagle and two more birdies in the next five holes. He looked all over the winner even when Lister started his own birdie barrage with four in succession starting with a two at the fifth. Following a spectacular shot from the now defunct fairway bunker to the heart of the 13th green Lister’s eagle putt lipped out, the birdie leaving him still three behind with only five to play. To the disbelief of the gallery, and no doubt to his own, Brask bogeyed each of the final three holes to allow Lister to draw level at 17 under par. The stage was set for a dramatic play off made more pressured by the need for Brask to catch a plane for home. The playoff started at the 16th hole as only the latter part of the course was set up for TV coverage. The crowd that flocked there to follow the outcome was such that it enclosed the par four hole from tee to green two and three deep in places. The sight from the tee was impressive. The 16th was halved in pars before the pair moved on to the 17th where Lister launched an 8 iron from the centre of the fairway to within a metre of the pin to ensure the championship was his. A memorable occasion in the history of competitive golf in Tauranga, both for the pleasure derived from a New Zealand victory, and for the play and deportment of the man who had set the standard from the first moments of the tournament, Bill Brask.

A number of Professionals from New Zealand and Australia were sponsored by Air New Zealand at that time to act as ambassadors to the company. As part of the deal they were required to assist in putting on clinics for interested juniors at tournaments such as this. John Lister was one such and his input to the clinic held in Tauranga was outstanding. His clear demonstrations and explanations were of exceptional value to those attending and anyone fortunate to be present during his explanation of the correct way to handle bunker shots would be unlikely to have had much problem with those since.

THE NZPGA CHAMPIONSHIP OF 1978

Scoring during the opening day that year was surely the poorest for any major tournament held on the course. Among the few to break par was the popular Anglo Australian Guy Wolstenholme, a great supporter of New Zealand tournaments over those years. Scores improved on the second day with Wolstenholme heading New Zealand amateur representative Geoff Clarke of St. Clair by a stroke with Bob Charles best of the rest on even par. In spite of tournament best cards of 64 from Simon Owen and Stuart Reese in the third round the tournament looked to be Wolstenholme’s for the taking following his second successive 67. This gave him a four-stroke lead at 7 under starting the final day.

Wolstenholme may have had a portent of things to come when he commented: “I’m in good shape for

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 250
text:
tomorrow as long as the trees don’t get in the way. The trees can make this course a bit tricky. You can be lucky or stone dead”. This was prior to the “skirts” of the trees being raised off the ground as they now are and indeed one could be stone dead under many of them. The final day developed into a contest between Wolstenholme and Owen, though not head to head as Owen was two or three holes ahead in the field. Owen made some ground over the early holes before Wolstenholme regained his four-stroke lead with an eagle on the 7th. When Owen hit out of bounds at the 10th and then compounded the error by three putting the green his challenge was seemingly over. To his credit he did not allow the mistake to ruin his round, scoring three birdies in the final eight holes to post a 67. As Owen walked the 18th fairway he was still four behind Wolstenholme who was then playing the 16th. When they completed those holes the margin was down to a single stroke, Owen holing a four metre birdie putt while his rival struck tree trouble, then three putted for a double bogey six. Incredibly another double bogey followed at the 17th for the man who had made virtually no error in  sixty nine previous holes. Thus Simon Owen, the man who was later to battle the great Jack Nicklaus right to the final hole of the British Open, found himself a surprise winner of the 1978 NZPGA Championship of New Zealand.

CHARLES’ PUTTER FAILS TO DELIVER IN 1980

An air shot on the 15th hole when his swing encountered a small branch on his downswing cost Roger Davis, the man with his name on his socks, sole custody of the lead after round one of the 1980 NZPGA Championship. His 66 matched that of Kim Southerden, son of Ernie who was a three-time winner of the New Zealand Professional Championship during its earlier match play era. Ominously poised behind the leaders were Simon Owen and Bob Charles on 67 along with Rick Barker, later to become resident professional at Tauranga. American Mike Krantz and Billy Dunk scored 68s.

Charles put a break on the field with a second round 63 that featured eight birdies. Owen and Southerden held on three strokes back while Davis, Krantz, and Barker were still well in contention. Charles increased the lead with a third round 64 that might well have been even better. Playing partner Mike Krantz was quoted as saying: “I think Charles could beat the world on this course”. Record books were being consulted to see if anyone had bettered 16 under par after three rounds and to see what Charles might need to do in the final round to better existing 72 hole records. Charles’ putting, for which he was renowned throughout the golfing world, was on target during these three rounds and he needed just one further birdie in the final two holes of that third round to join Brask, Nagle, and Good as record holders on 61. To the disappointment of the large gallery, and probably his own, though he showed no outward sign of that, Charles failed to find the green at either hole to drop strokes at each. His 64 still

left him five strokes clear of Davis (65) and seven clear of Krantz (66) and Owen (68). Barker continued his strong run with a third sub-par round taking him to seven under with a round to go.

Starting the final round Charles had two goals: To break Mike Souchak’s best ever 72 hole total of 257, and to win a tournament in the fourth decade in which he had played Championship golf, his first success having come in the 1954 New Zealand Open at Heretaunga. Birdies at the two opening holes suggested both goals could well be achieved but it was not to be. Another two birdies and a single dropped shot made up a 67, a good closing round in most circumstances but disappointing on this particular day. Somehow the putts, that had seemed mystically drawn to the centre of the cup from all

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 251
text:
distances on previous days, now slid past the edges. Charles’ final 19 under par total of 261 comprised 21 birdies, a single eagle, and a meagre four bogeys, ensuring that the second goal was never in doubt.

An intriguing battle developed for second place worth a healthy $3560. Roger Davis prevailed, his 68 giving him a total of 267 that would have been good enough to win many a tournament. A pair of 65s in the final rounds catapulted Billy Dunk up the leader board for a share of third place with Simon Owen. John Lister went one better over those final rounds with a 65 and a 64. Rick Barker dropped a couple of strokes but still completed a very strong tournament at five under.

Gillian Bannan, now a full member of the NZPGA, achieved a notable first by completing four rounds playing off the same tees as the men. Her total of 34 over par reflected the difficulty women would always face in competing against men on equal terms.

THE 1981 NZPGA CHAMPIONSHIP

That year the Tournament attracted a field of 144 drawn from Australia (47), The United States (22), The United Kingdom (5), Japan (3), Canada (2), and New Zealand. Prize Money had now increased to $50 000 with a top prize of $9000. Though one $5000 sponsor failed to “hole out” the prizemoney and the total entry both represented records for a PGA Tournament in New Zealand. The change from the traditional New Year dates to late November to tie in with the NZ Open at Titirangi would have had much to do with the superb field attracted to the tournament.

The Pro/Am on the Wednesday gave a good indication of the sort of scoring that was to follow. Terry Gale of Australia led with a 63, three others shot 64, and four made 65s.  As an indication of the quality of the field 25 players were on 68 or better.

While Terry Hulls, a 23 year old from Australia, replicated his Countryman’s 63 of the previous day, the first round highlight was credited to a young New Zealand professional from North Shore, John Reid. Reid ended the day on what would prove to be a very ordinary score of 70, but he came away the proud owner of a sparkling new Honda Civic valued at $13 200, compliments of his hole in one at the 14th hole. John used a nine iron for this perfect stroke.  Such a club choice would be more in keeping with the modern game as now seen on the USPGA Tour rather than that of 1981. This was but one of an unprecedented string of aces scored during the week. Barry Vivian set the trend during the Pro/Am by acing the Knoll, while on Saturday Bob Charles went into the lead when acing the fifth. Moments later Terry Gale completed the quartet when his tee shot found the cup at the ninth hole.

Terry Hull’s 63 included an eagle and seven birdies while New Zealand hopes, Bob Charles and John Lister, were well placed on 65. The hot scoring continued on the Friday with the cut being made at one over par 141. Notable players to miss the cut included Simon Owen, Jack Newton and Wayne Grady, a further indication of the quality of the field. John Lister scored successive 65s yet complained of a bad break at the Knoll (who hasn’t on occasion?). His nine iron landed well up on the green, or so he claimed, before “sinking back” into the bunker. Ted Ball, the Australian credited with the fastest swing in golf, matched Lister’s paired 65s, while Charles was just one stroke off the pace. Roger Davis (66, 66),

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 252
text:
Eamon Darcy (68, 64), Terry Gale (66, 67), Peter Croker (65, 68) and Ian Stanley (65, 68) were in close attendance. New Zealand’s Bob Charles looked to have his fourth NZPGA Championship safely under control when he scored another 65 on the third day. This left him a comfortable three strokes clear of Ted Ball and Roger Davis, and five clear of Terry Gale and Kel Nagle. Canadian Jerry Anderson was one stroke ahead of the latter two and thus four behind the leader. The only question in the mind of most spectators seemed to be by how many strokes would Charles win. Alas the putter that had served Charles so well throughout his career decided to go cold that day. Three putts were required at the fifth, a hole that had yielded an ace the day before. Another three-putt followed at the ninth. In spite of these blemishes Charles teed off on the penultimate hole with a lead of two strokes over Gale who was then in the clubhouse and resigned to finishing a stroke or two short of the win. Surprisingly Charles missed from less than two metres at the seventeenth for his third three-putt, and third bogey, of the day leaving him just one stroke clear playing the final hole. There his tee shot was hooked to finish just short of a tree on the right of the fairway. A good recovery was drawn around the tree to finish in the mouth of the green from where he failed to get down with a chip and putt so a play off was required.

The sudden death play off commenced at the sixteenth where both drives were well placed in the fairway. Charles made the green with his second but was at least 15 metres away while Gale failed to make the green at all. His chip was weak finishing three metres short. Uncharacteristically Charles putted some 1.5 metres beyond the hole only to see Gale roll his longish putt home. The crowd who had braved miserable weather featuring rain and a blustery wind throughout the day were stunned to see Charles pressure putt slide well wide of the hole for his third successive bogey. Gentleman and sportsman as always Charles was quick to congratulate Gale, his sincerity obvious to all in spite of the disappointment he must have felt. At the start of the day many players had an opportunity to challenge for the title but all, other than the ultimate champion, fell away. Perhaps the weather conditions, so much in contrast to those earlier in the week, may have accounted for the fact that only seven players bettered par. Round of the day went to Peter Crocker whose 66 included four birdies and an eagle. No one else managed an eagle on the day. Amongst those expected to challenge for the title Ball blew his chance by taking three to find the green at the knoll, Davis lost interest rather early dropping shots at the second, fourth and fifth, while Lister, like Davis, shot 69. Nagle played well enough to be a serious threat but for once the Tauranga course failed to yield much in the way of birdies to the popular Australian. The Canadian Anderson launched the most threatening challenge to Charles and Gale when he birdied the ninth and tenth but bogeys at the 16th and 17th ended his run.

Tauranga Club professional Rick Barker performed well in the Tournament making the cut comfortably with rounds of 68 and 70. Rick finished mid field with a three over par total of 283.

Sadly this 1981 staging of the NZPGA Championship was to prove to be the last held at the Tauranga course. The Championship went into recess for a lengthy period before being resurrected at the Clearwater course in Canterbury in the new Century. It was to be another 25 years before Tauranga again saw a quality field of Amateurs and Professionals contest an Open Championship.

title: The Spalding Masters and the NZPGA Championship · p. 253
text: Bob Charles (now Sir Bob) and Michael Nicholson.  Proud recipients of the Spalding Masters Trophy and Lionel Smith Rosebowl as professional and amateur champions in the 1972 tournament.

title: Exhibition matches · p. 254
text:
EXHIBITION MATCHES

CHAPTER TWENTYTWO

title: Exhibition matches · p. 255
text:
Tauranga has long sort ways to bring top golf to the district and though the likes of Gene Sarazen and Bobby Locke, who each toured the country in their prime, could not be attracted to the club other options were pursued. In 1960 Kel Nagle played Jim Paterson, the match finishing all square with Nagle scoring 68, Paterson 69. For their pains Nagle was paid £75, Paterson £25, while the club lost £25 on the day and felt it was money well spent.

Another popular Australian, Peter Thomson, participated in an exhibition match with Fred Ward when that fine player was at the peak of form. Some who were present recall Thomson hooking his drive under the hedge that ran the entire length of the boundary to the left of the fifteenth fairway. This Lawsoniana hedge was wide and the branches reached the ground. Anyone who attempted to play from inside the hedge, as Thomson did, was virtually invisible. The ball emerged followed by the player who quickly advised his opponent and the gallery that he had played an “air shot” when his club struck branches on his downswing. That would have been a rare event in the life of one of the greatest of British Open Champions.

In the year following the Nagle exhibition Bob Charles played a match against Jimmy Paterson. Once again the local Professional gave a good account of himself against outstanding opposition. On this occasion Charles was the winner by two and one following an excellent display by both men before a large and appreciative gallery.

The fifteenth hole has been the subject of some interesting observations. Though little longer than the sixteenth it always seems to play much longer.  It is well within the recognised length for a par four for men and just above the upper limit for women. It is rated par five on the women’s card. The competitors in the top 16 in the Una Wickham Memorial Tournament

played off the blue tees while the remainder played off the yellow. For many years during that tournament the yellow tees were placed on the back of the fifteenth tee, the blues on the front. This happened on no other tee. When asked why this was done the official response was that the hole was played as a par four for the top group, a par five for the rest. When asked what importance this had in a tournament that was entirely Match Play the enquirer met only with a perplexed look. It was many years before it was realised that the top players should be offered the greatest challenge at every hole. It was even more perplexing to see the reigning New Zealand Women’s Stroke Play Champion arrive at the fifteenth tee to find no yellow blocks. This was during the Carrus Tournament when the women were playing from yellow, the men from blue tees. It soon transpired that the blocks were about fifty metres ahead in the fairway where they had been placed by the Tournament Director who was an outside ‘expert’ supposedly well steeped in golfing lore though perhaps not in common sense!  We can only presume the young star needed the head start in order to have a chance to play the hole in four strokes to match the men she was no longer competing against. To add to the quandary this young lady was the only woman to survive the 36-hole cut thus displacing a male player who had played off quite different tees.

title: Exhibition matches · p. 256
text:
In 1967 Tauranga staged a match between four of the International Professionals competing in the PGA at Mount Maunganui. A large gallery saw Martin Roesink (Holland) and Tony Jacklin (England) defeat Billy Dunk (Australia) and Resident Professional Jim Paterson two up. The three overseas stars all scored 66s while Paterson was also under par. While Roesink thrilled the crowd with the power of his driving it was Jacklin who particularly impressed for the all round quality of his game. His pure swing and clean struck iron shots had many an astute judge claiming we would hear much more of him in the future. This proved to be accurate as Jacklin went on to win the NZPGA at Mt. Maunganui that week in an 18-hole play off with Roesink. Far more importantly Tony Jacklin was to restore British golfing pride with victories in both the British and US Opens the following year. He then went on to enjoy a successful career that culminated in appointment to Captaincy of the European Ryder Cup Team.

The exhibition that afternoon began with a clinic on the first tee. Bob MacDonald, a popular Professional from Wellington acted as Master of Ceremonies in between amusing the large audience with his comic imitations of well known golfing identities. His show, in itself, would have made the afternoon worthwhile.

Martin Roesink demonstrated his driving ability by playing a number of drives. His first two were slightly faded and finished at the base of the second tee. The next was pin high to the left of the first green, the last three were all through the back of the green. It was a spectacular demonstration of power hitting. This was with a wooden headed, steel shafted driver, and using the rubber-wound ball. It is difficult to imagine where these drives would have reached had he been using equipment equivalent to that available today.

THE BILLY CASPER SHOW

When Billy Casper visited New Zealand in 1969 Tauranga had the opportunity to invite one of the World’s very best players to demonstrate his talents to our members and to interested members of the public. Casper, along with Bob Charles, was recognised as one of the great putters of all time, yet he was very much more than that. During his career he registered 51 Professional victories including three majors, the 1970 Masters at Augusta complementing his two United States Opens. He appeared in eight Ryder Cup teams registering more points than any other player and was described by Johnny Miller as being the “most underrated golfer of all time, hands down”. It is difficult to see why he was so underrated as he competed extremely successfully in an era during which Ben Hogan was still active while stars such as Arnold Palmer and Gary Player were enjoying their best years.

For his visit to Tauranga Casper was scheduled to put on an exhibition clinic before Lunch then play an 18-hole match partnering the newly crowned Club Champion Jim Lancaster against Club professional Jim Paterson and Noel Hayden of Rotorua. Lancaster, at that stage the youngest winner of our championship aged 19, was given the honour of partnering Casper against the two club Professionals. Defeated championship finalist John McLeod was invited to caddy for the American and advise him on features of the golf course, as Casper had no prior knowledge of any of the holes.

No one who was privileged to be present at the exhibition will forget the occasion. Billy Casper was a

title: Exhibition matches · p. 257
text:
little taken aback when invited to play his demonstration shots from the upper level of the putting green but, on being reassured by Greens Superintendent Grant Silvester that he would be only too happy to repair all the damage later, Casper held nothing back as he played a great variety of strokes including many that took considerable divots. The choice of the putting green as a stage for the show was perfect in allowing the big crowd to get an excellent view of the action. While Casper was not known as an especially long hitter his driving down the seventh fairway certainly impressed those present with both its length and its accuracy. He had a caddie stand at the top of the hill while he drove balls almost to his feet. He would then wave the caddie back twenty yards or so and repeat the process. This he did once or twice more with the caddie barely moving to retrieve the balls. To have such control over the longest club in the bag was remarkable and his control of the iron clubs was equally impressive. A truly wonderful clinic staged by a great personality. For a description of the exhibition match that followed we are indebted to a first hand account from the man closest to the action, Jim Lancaster.

THE DAY I PARTNERED BILLY CASPER

I had only been playing golf for four years at the time when I was fortunate to win the Club Championship and thus gain the right to partner Billy Casper in the exhibition match. To be honest I had not read a lot about the top Professional players so was not as over-awed at the prospect of partnering a player of such fame as I may otherwise have been. I have since learned that Billy was the leading money winner on the PGA Tour in two of the previous three years, a five-times winner of the Vardon Trophy for the lowest scoring average on Tour, and winner of 68 Professional Tournaments, including 51 PGA Titles. This places him at 7th on the all-time list of tour winners. He also won three majors.

At the time of the exhibition Billy was staying on a sheep station at Taupo during a holiday in New Zealand and consequently was very relaxed. Perhaps that was his nature anyway. I recall the exhibition clearly. The shots he demonstrated were amazing to me and I would think to all those present. Prior to hitting each shot Billy would explain what he intended to do. The caddie hardly moved as sliced shots, drawn shots, and even straight ones, landed at his feet even when he was up to 280 yards away. This was achieved using clubs with steel shafts and wooden heads. Also the old wound ball then in use flew considerably less in distance than does the modern one-piece ball. Throughout the exhibition, and during the subsequent round, Billy was friendly, jovial, and talkative. I was surprised that he invited members of the gallery to take photographs and ask questions about any aspect of the game they wished.

I had not considered myself to be a nervous player but since I started bogey, triple bogey, double bogey, I must have been nervous without being fully aware of it. Poor Billy must have wondered what he had done to deserve such a partner. With his encouragement I settled down and played three under over the remaining holes to complete a respectable 74. It was a giant relief to redeem myself in the eyes of my partner and those of the large gallery that accompanied us throughout the day. We were matched against local Professional Jim Paterson and his colleague Noel Hayden. With Billy breezing around the course in a bogey-free 67, we won comfortably. Billy had never seen the course before the round

title: Exhibition matches · p. 258
text:
so his score was especially commendable. He talked all the way round, commented on shots played by myself and the other two, and freely answered questions from members of the 1000 strong gallery. I got the impression he knew just where each of his shots would land and how far it would run. With the small heads typical of woods of that time he was able to work the ball in any desired direction. He never looked in serious danger of dropping a shot and on the only couple of times I recall his missing a fairway he was able to play a great recovery shot.

I recall him enquiring where the third green was and, after receiving conflicting advice on his best approach to the hole he decided to take the trees on. His tee shot finished just 40 yards short of the front of the green. On the 7th he played a seven iron for his second contrary to the advice of his caddie who wanted him to take more club. As a consequence he finished short and failed to gain the birdie his drive deserved. He did birdie the 9th, his five-iron finishing about 10 ft. from the hole. Another birdie followed at the 10th to reward a drive of some 280 yards. At the time I had the confidence of youth on the putting green and had the habit of walking forward ready to retrieve my ball from the hole following putts of ten feet or so. I did this again at the 11th only to have Billy tell me to “Let the ball get to the hole before you pick it up”. It was holed on this occasion or I would have looked a little silly.

Billy had a good sense of humour. I had a set of Kangaroo head covers and dropped the one from my driver beside the 17th tee. Billy immediately gave it a thump with his driver as he said, “what’s that critter. Quick, get it”.

Over the years I have been privileged to play in Tournaments such as the Spalding Masters and the PGA Championship where I have been paired with some outstanding Professionals from New Zealand and Overseas. None of these were of the calibre of Billy Casper who played with, and defeated, many greats of the game including Ben Hogan, Arnold Palmer, and Byron Nelson. In 2000 the United States Golf Digest ranked Billy as the 15th greatest golfer of all time. While, at the time of the exhibition, I was unaware of Billy’s true standing in the history of the game I have since come to realise how fortunate I was to have been one of a very few New Zealanders to have played with Billy Casper, a great golfer, a true gentleman, and a man who was patient enough to put a novice like myself at ease throughout the day.

At the end of the round the Club presented Billy with a book featuring the scenery of New Zealand. I received an inlaid wooden box suitably engraved as a memento of my experience. I treasured that box for 37 years until, sadly, it was stolen from my home in 2007.

title: Professional golf returns to Tauranga · p. 259
text:
PROFESSIONAL GOLF

RETURNS TO TAURANGA

CHAPTER TWENTYTHREE

title: Professional golf returns to Tauranga · p. 260
text:
When well performed New Zealand Professional Greg Turner promoted a series of tournaments to provide opportunities for budding young players in New Zealand the Tauranga Club was quick to volunteer to be one of the host clubs. Paul and Sheryl Adams of Carrus Corporation, a local company involved in sub-division developments, became the name sponsor. Many other local companies became involved to ensure that the first tournament was able to attract a quality field including leading Amateurs together with the best of the Country’s Professionals.

THE 2006 CARRUS TAURANGA OPEN CHAMPIONSHIP

The tournament proved to be an outstanding success, not least because of the runaway success of local Amateur Josh Geary. While Josh was best known as a member of the Mt. Maunganui Golf Club as a boy he was also a member both of Otumoetai and of Tauranga. In 2001, still a schoolboy, he featured in the final of our senior championship where he went down narrowly to the experienced Gavin Smillie. Geary played superlative golf throughout the Carrus Open apart from one hole during the third round when he struck all sorts of trouble on the long 7th hole to record a ten, his first double figure score since his first tournament start as an eleven year old. Cruising well clear of Tauranga’s Kevin Smith prior to this Geary yielded no less than seven strokes of his lead as Smith eagled the same hole. It was a mark of Geary’s temperament and the quality of his game that he was still able to complete the round in 70. With par surprisingly retained at 71 for the event Geary completed the tournament a nominal 22 shots under par. (Traditionally the 17th hole, never a genuine par 5, is reclassified as a par 4 during Professional events). None-the-less rounds of 63, 63, 70, and 66 represented golf of the highest quality.

After nine holes of the final round Smith and Geary were locked together at 16 under, well clear of the Professionals headed by Grant Moorhead, Doug Holloway and Tony Christie. While the others went

BIRDS

One evening I was walking home in the gathering darkness when I saw what appeared to be one of those long-necked driver covers lying on the fifteenth fairway. As I bent to pick it up it moved away. It was the Golden Amhurst pheasant that lived on the course for a number of years, a very beautiful bird and a pleasure to see. The unusual blackbirds with white markings that are seen near the clubhouse have been with us for many ‘bird generations’. The rare genetic sport causing this has not been in evidence elsewhere to my knowledge. Another bird that attracted attention briefly was ‘Morrie Minor’, a very friendly mynah bird that was soon captured and sent off to an aviary somewhere. This was rather sad as he was becoming quite a character on the course. Members welcome the annual visit by many Tuis that enjoy the nectar from Japanese flowering cherries. Unfortunately those same trees are becoming a serious weed in the countryside as the tuis spread the seed far from the original trees..

title: Professional golf returns to Tauranga · p. 261
text:
backwards Geary picked up another six shots to finish seven clear of Smith with the leading pair of Professionals, Moorhead and Holloway, a further six strokes away. Geary made the decisive move by holing out from the greenside bunker at the tenth for an eagle two. Birdies followed at the 9th, 12th, 13th, 14th, and 17th. Moorhead, a member of New Zealand’s only successful Eisenhower Trophy winning team, fired a grand 64 to catch Holloway who scored a 66, the pair each taking away a very welcome $6400. Moorhead birdied the last four holes to bypass a number of his fellow Professionals.

THE 2007 CARRUS TAURANGA OPEN CHAMPIONSHIP

With Josh Geary not able to return to Tauranga to defend his title it was left to Auckland Amateur Leighton James and Taihape Professional Hamish Robertson to emulate his opening round 63 of the previous year. Amateurs Josh Munn (a 16 yr old from the Manawatu), Sean Roach (Arrowtown), and Mike Wilson (ex BOP team member) all shot 65s, a total matched by Professional Brad Shilton.

James and Robertson continued to set the pace when each shot 67 in the second round while Mark Purser, a Waikato Professional, came into contention with a magnificent 61. This included two eagles, six birdies, and a single bogey. This year the 17th was correctly rated as a par four so par was set at a more realistic 70. This round elevated Purser to equal third with local man Jared Pender, later to

be selected to represent New Zealand at the Eisenhower Tournament. Jared’s scores of 67 and 65 represented his best form at this level.

A second 63 from Leighton James appeared to have put the Championship out of reach of the others with the final round to come. While a pair of Amateurs again led the field the question of who would take the money was yet to be decided. Purser was not prepared to allow James the title without a fight and, in a dogged pursuit he finally got his nose in front to win by a single stroke. To achieve this he had

to shoot a seven under par 63 while James slipped to a one over 71. Kevin Smith, such a prominent contender the year before, headed all but one of the Professionals to finish third. An inexplicable four- putt at the 15th ended his challenge though his third round 61 ranked with Purser’s earlier 61 as the rounds of the tournament. Robertson was 12 strokes worse than that in his third round to lose any chance he had of heading the field. Purser and James were level with two holes to play but Purser stole the initiative at the 17th when he hit a wedge from 128m and canned the resultant 3m putt. James could only par the final two holes to finish a valiant second.

THE 2008 CARRUS TAURANGA OPEN CHAMPIONSHIP

Sublime conditions, immaculate fairways, and fast greens presented a quality field with a matchless opportunity to create records on the opening day of the championship. While many threatened to do so none succeeded. Kevin Chun, seven under with four to play, Michael Hendry, his score spoilt by one double bogey, and Amateur Scott Johnson all shot 65s to set the pace. A trio of Amateurs including 2007 runner-up Leighton James came in at five under. 13-year-old Cecilia Cho led the women on even par 71. Hendry held his form through the second round to establish a three-stroke advantage over the field.

title: Professional golf returns to Tauranga · p. 262
text:
Grant Moorhead of Eisenhower Trophy fame moved into second place with an excellent 66. Josh Geary, not especially comfortable with his game, still managed to shoot 68-67 to share fourth place. Local New Zealand representative Jared Pender improved five strokes on his opening round of 71 to make the top ten. After three rounds Hendry, Moorhead, and Brad Shilton led by one stroke from Geary with many others poised to make a serious challenge for the title. A brilliant final round 64 looked to have ensured Geary of his first victory as a Professional as others fell by the wayside. Eventually only Moorhead looked to have a chance to match Geary’s 14 under total. This possibility increased dramatically when he holed a 5m putt on the tough par four 17th, a hole where Geary earlier had dropped his only stroke of the round after his second had ended with the ball wrapped in a fallen branch to the left of the green. Courageously Josh had elected to play the ball as it lay rather than pay the penalty for deeming it unplayable. The two-stroke swing on this penultimate hole sent the pair into a play-off when Grant failed to birdie the final hole. In deference to the large crowd estimated at fifteen hundred that clustered about the 18th green the players returned to that tee to settle the issue. Both missed birdie opportunities as had been the case when playing the hole as the 72nd so back to the tee they went. This time Geary thrilled the crowd by firing his wedge second to within 30cms of the hole to ensure victory.

Fellow local Jared Pender shot the low round of the tournament, a brilliant 63, to elevate himself to fourth place overall and leading Amateur one stroke clear of Gary John Hill. This showing may well have cemented Jared’s claim to a spot on the Eisenhower team.

THE 2009 CARRUS TAURANGA OPEN CHAMPIONSHIP

Peter Fowler, the Auckland based Australian Professional, may well have been the favourite to win the 2009 Carrus Tauranga Open and his opening 65 did nothing to dent public confidence. Blair Shaw,

of Hastings, matched Fowler’s score while another eight players lay within two strokes of the lead. These included local Amateur Brad Kendall of Mt Maunganui and Jared Pender, now a member of the Professional ranks. Shaw’s round featured an ace on the difficult par three fifth hole, the ball pitching just 15cms from the cup before finding the bottom of the hole.

Fowler scored a second 65 to open up a three-stroke lead over Pender whose 66 left him one stroke clear of three other rookie Professionals in Troy Ropiha, Blair Shaw, and Hamish Robertson. Cecilia Cho followed her opening 72 with a brilliant round of 67 to take a decisive lead into the final round of the Women’s section.

Peter Fowler carried his wonderful form into the third with an excellent 66 to leave him in a seemingly impregnable position three strokes clear of his nearest pursuer. Michael Hendry and Hamish Robertson shot 65s to inch closer to that lead, while Pender’s nine under total suggested a high finish was well within his grasp on his home course.

Fowler lowered his guard early on the final day, dropping two strokes in the first eight holes after dropping only one over the preceding 54 holes. The putts that previously found their way unerringly

title: Professional golf returns to Tauranga · p. 263
text:
into the cup now slid frustratingly by to allow the chasing pack to get within range. With just four holes to play any one of six front-runners looked capable of taking the title. It was Michael Hendry who best held his nerve to draw level with Fowler at 12 under and so force a play-off for the second successive year. This time only one traverse of the 18th was required to settle the tie before Hendry holed a pressure-filled three metre putt to nullify the many disappointments he had suffered through a run of close finishes in previous tournaments.

Hamish Robertson and Richard Lee failed by just one stroke to join the play-off while Pender disappointed his local fans by shooting a closing 73 to fall back into 11th place. Omokoroa teenager Andrew Stewart shot the round of the day, a 66, to annex the Amateur title while Cecilia Cho had made no race of the Women’s contest that concluded the previous day.

THE 2010 CARRUS TAURANGA OPEN CHAMPIONSHIP

Wellington Professional Andrew Green set the 2010 renewal of the Carrus alight with a sizzling 62 in glorious conditions on the opening day. Andrew may well have believed this would give him a substantial lead going into the second round but that was not to be. Southland Amateur Cody Harper (63), and Wellington Professional Brenden Stuart (64) had other ideas.

The Women’s field featured World long-drive champion Phillis Meti who thrilled the gallery with some prodigious driving. Sadly her short game was not of the standard to allow her to take advantage of the opportunities these drives provided.

Andrew Green followed his 62 with a superb 63 and yet this wonderful start was over-shadowed by Japanese based professional Richard Lee who established a new course record with a spectacular 59, the first time a sub-sixty total had been recorded in a New Zealand tournament. As word of this

There are many stories of the par threes at Tauranga. It is notable that David Good, during his record round of 61 in 1976, scored four twos and one three. Club member Eddie Schwartfeger bettered this total of 11 for the par threes in rather dramatic fashion. Playing a Club competition round in June 1982 Eddie scored two pars, a birdie two, and an ace at each of the 9th and 14th holes. Some felt the feat of two aces in the one round may have been a first, and perhaps it was for New Zealand, but a little research discovered that the feat had been achieved over 300 times in America (where else?) the previous year alone.

While no written record has been discovered old time members claim that Jack Bateman, four times Senior Champion and our first BOP Champion of Champions, also bettered David Good by scoring all five par threes in two during a handicap singles match in the early fifties. Jack’s opponent that day would have felt a little shell-shocked.

title: Professional golf returns to Tauranga · p. 264
text:
possibility spread about the course a large crowd was drawn to the tenth green in the hope of seeing history made. They were not disappointed as Richard took up the challenge of attempting to drive this short par four only to see the ball roll into the bunker alongside the green. A solid bunker shot left the ball within two metres of the hole from where Richard appeared to hole it calmly enough though he later confessed his hands were not as steady as may have appeared. In spite of this remarkable round Richard still trailed the leader by three strokes. Wellington Amateur Nick Gillespie matched Green’s 63 to lie level with Lee at 12 under. Unnoticed in all the excitement Masterton Amateur Ben Campbell quietly went about his business to compile rounds of 66 and 65 to trail by six strokes together with Cody Harper. The third day was something of a comedy of errors, the leaders appearing to vie with one another to see who would self-destruct next. First Nick Gillespie (65, 63) appeared to destroy his round by firing three balls into the orchard beyond the Norris residence to the left of the eighth fairway. Playing partner Andrew Green followed by recording a 9 at the par three ninth. He followed an out of bounds tee shot by firing his second tee shot into the bunker alongside the green. Andrew then incurred a two-stroke penalty when his caddie (his father) raked the bunker while Andrew’s ball lay within it.

Meanwhile Campbell took advantage of the situation as he added a 64 to establish a three-stroke lead over Green (73), with a further two strokes back to Hendry (66) and Lee (72). Ryan Fox, son of legendary All Black Grant, produced his best Tauranga performance to date, three successive 67s leaving him a further stroke back.

Ben Campbell gave no one else a chance on the final day, shooting a 66 to win by four from Hendry who shot 65. Fox improved on his 67s with a 66 to edge Jared Pender, who closed with a 64 to add to his third round 63. This enabled Jared to collect his best cheque as a Professional with his second placing behind Hendry. Richard Lee, perhaps still somewhat shell-shocked from his 59, self-destructed at the 13th by firing a succession of drives into the racecourse to record a double-digit hole score and a final round 77. It may be hard to believe that a Professional could show a spread of 18 strokes between any two rounds of a tournament but it did happen.

PAST CHAMPIONS

title: Professional golf returns to Tauranga · p. 265
text:
Caroline Bon of Northland made no race of the Women’s section, firing three sub-par rounds to finish 15 strokes clear of what has to be said was a rather mediocre field. This in no way detracted from the merit of Caroline’s performance, sub-par rounds being hardly commonplace in New Zealand Women’s Golf.

THE 2011 CARRUS TAURANGA OPEN CHAMPIONSHIP

Unheralded Waikato Professional Jim Cusdin won the 2011 Carrus Open in fine style in spite of his claim at the final day presentation that he had not been confident at the start as he had not played the course well on previous visits. Tournament favourite and clear first day leader Michael Hendry expressed very different sentiments in relation to the course. Said Hendry: “I love this course. It really suits my game. It is a course where you feel you can attack every hole but the key is not to push too hard. I did that on the 8th hole on day one and paid the price. The key is patience.” Hendry set the pace in round one, posting a five under par 65 in very windy conditions, one stroke ahead of local star Jared Pender and Te Anau Professional David Klein. Co-favourite Gareth Paddison followed on 67. Hendry’s round included six birdies and a sole bogey on that 8th hole.

Gareth Paddison, showing the value of the experience he has gained from appearances on the PGA Tours of both the USA and of Europe over the previous season or two, scored an impressive 64 in favourable conditions to lead by three strokes over Dominic Barson (also 64) and Pieter Zwart after the second round. Michael Hendry dropped back with an even par 70, while Pender (67), and amateur Ryan Fox (67) remained well in contention. Starting at the 11th Fox four putted the Knoll, an experience not unknown to local members though they seldom play the green when it is running as fast as it was that day. Despite that set back Fox later birdied each hole from the second to the eighth with the exception of the par three Fifth. Six birdies in seven holes demonstrated the true quality of golf of which

this talented New Zealand representative is capable.

The women competed over 54 holes so their competition finished on the Saturday afternoon with NZ representative Emily Perry of Waikato firing a final round of 72 to finish five under par and four strokes clear of Charlotte Thomas.

title: Professional golf returns to Tauranga · p. 266
text: Cusdin and Fox staged an epic battle over the final round on an uncharacteristically wet Tauranga Sunday afternoon. The day was so wet that play had to be suspended for two hours in mid afternoon as the greens became unplayable. This was in spite of the dedicated efforts of a large number of officials and volunteers who worked the squeegees vigorously in an attempt to keep the play flowing. In spite of the conditions and the frustration of suspended play this pair played impressive golf over that final round. Cusdin appeared to have set up a winning lead when he birdied the 14th and 16th only to see it reduced to a single stroke as they teed off the 18th. Jim Cusdin confessed to feeling very nervous as he had never succeeded in winning over 72 holes on any previous occasion.  Ryan Fox reduced the pressure when driving to the right into the area by the advertising signs. When correctly denied free relief from that situation he was forced to chip into the open before firing his third shot to the green. Meanwhile Cusdin played safely to the green to set up a 6m putt that he was greatly relieved to see fall into the hole for a birdie and an excellent winning total of 15 under par. Michael Hendry closed with a 64 but his earlier 70 in round two had effectively left him too far adrift though he continued his run of “Podium finishes” at the Carrus with third placing on 12 under. Paddison followed on 10 under.

title: The Una Wickham Memorial Tournament · p. 267
text:
THE UNA WICKHAM

MEMORIAL TOURNAMENT

CHAPTER TWENTYFOUR

title: The Una Wickham Memorial Tournament · p. 268
text:
The Club lost its greatest woman player with the untimely death of Una Wickham in 1983. The Women’s Committee decided to institute a tournament in her honour and endeavour to develop it into a truly prestigious event on the Northern Golfing Calendar. This became a reality with the tournament soon attracting the best players from Whangarei to Taupo and sometimes beyond. For some years it served as a trial for the Northern Inter Provincial teams but sadly lost support as other priorities commanded the attention of the top players. It is unfortunate that we no longer have the opportunity to see outstanding women players of the quality of Brenda Ormsby, Jan Arnold, Tina Howard, Gina Scott, our own Joanne Brooks, and many others. These women inspired local players, both men and women, to endeavour to raise their own standards. It is to be hoped that one day the top women players from around the country will again grace our links in honour of our greatest woman player. A year by year history of the tournament, and its predecessor the Tauranga Women’s Open Match Play Tournament follows.

1976 Shirley Johnson of Rotorua won the final of this, the inaugural staging of the tournament, defeating Una Wickham 6/4 in a surprisingly one-sided final. Earlier Shirley had defeated a youthful Brenda Ormsby of Te Puke in another easy victory. Shirley was then playing number one in the Bay of Plenty representative team, a position she clearly warranted on these performances.

1977 Shirley Johnson successfully defended the title she had won the previous year, easily holding out the challenge of Penny MacDougall in the final. Earlier in the tournament Tauranga’s Mary Parkinson had provided Shirley with much stronger opposition before losing one down.

1978 Alison Eather of Auckland won the Championship after a series of tight matches. She was three down with five to play versus Tauranga’s Peg Copestake yet got home at the 20th. 1977 finalist Penny MacDougall was five up at one stage yet lost to Alison at the 18th. Playing Avis Osborne (Mt Maunganui) in the final Eather was two down with two to play yet again won on the 20th. Such a series of fighting come backs must seldom have been matched in this or any tournament. The semi-final against Cushla Hickey of Opotiki was the antithesis of the other three matches, Miss Hickey being five down after twelve holes only to come back strongly before losing by just one hole.

1979 Jocelyn Glanfield (North Shore) became the new champion, defeating Sue Bunt (Titirangi) one up in the final after accounting for the defending champion Alison Hasey (Nee Eather) two up in the semi- final. Sue Bunt went on to a distinguished career in Golf Administration where her work over a number of years did much to further Golf in Auckland and in New Zealand.

1980 The tournament continued to be seen as a trial for the Bay of Plenty Russell Grace team while the Auckland and Waikato selectors were also very interested in the form displayed by potential team members. As a result the tournament attracted strong entries from these regions. New Zealand representatives Cherry Kingham (Grange), Jan Arnold (Morrinsville), and Brenda Rhodes (Nee Ormsby) highlighted another strong field in 1980. In the final it was Jan Arnold who prevailed 4/3 over Kingham who never recovered from Arnold’s sizzling outward 32. Earlier Kingham had scored a surprisingly easy victory over Rhodes.

title: The Una Wickham Memorial Tournament · p. 269
text:
1981 In spite of two New Zealand representatives being involved the final was a disappointing match. Neither Kingham nor Rhodes was able to show the form expected of them. It could be said, probably unkindly, that Kingham made fewer mistakes to prevail 2/1.

1982 The final featured the finalists from the previous year in Cherry Kingham and Brenda Rhodes. These two could now lay claim to being the best two women golfers in the country. Rhodes, who had held the National Championship for the previous two years, was again frustrated in her ambition to win this tournament. The match featured superb tee to green play by Rhodes in particular but some tentative putting by her allowed Kingham to stay in touch before finally taking control to win 2/1. Despite the excellence of much of the iron play only one birdie was scored in the entire match.

1983 Ruth Middleton (Matamata), now in the veteran class, was able to show the youngsters she still had plenty of quality to her game and probably caused provincial selectors some perturbation as she defeated three potential Bay of Plenty representatives on her way to the final against Jocelyn Queenan (Nee Glanfield). Ruth, a long time supporter of Tauranga tournaments, was a very popular winner of the final.

1984 This was the year that the tournament was first played under the title of The Una Wickham Open Match Play Tournament in memory of the Club’s greatest woman player. Former New Zealand Champion, Jan Arnold, won the tournament. defeating eighteen-year old Jan Cooke of Western Bay, now Omokoroa Golf Club, who played very well to be beaten just two down. Jan Cooke might well have been considered a prodigy of Miss Wickham as she had been pulled from relative obscurity by Una to fill the number five spot in the winning BOP Russell Grace team of 1983. A win by either finalist would have seemed a fitting tribute to the late Miss Wickham. On the way to the final Miss Cooke had defeated two previous winners in Jocelyn Queenan and Alison Hasey to demonstrate her form and her potential.

1985 The tournament this year again featured Jan Arnold and Brenda Ormsby, the latter having reverted to her maiden name. This time the two came fresh from finishing second to the USA in the World Team Championship. Mary Laugerson (ex Wanganui) who was widely recognised as one of New Zealand’s most knowledgeable golf authorities claimed the two finalists to be the best New Zealand had ever produced. While other candidates for such an honour will spring to many a mind it has to be true that these two names would rank very highly in a New Zealand Golfing Hall of fame.

The dominance these two held over a quality field was amply demonstrated in the semi- finals where Arnold beat the Auckland number one, Karrin Duckworth 7/6, while Ormsby beat Bay of Plenty number one, Jane Little, 6/5.

The final featured quality golf with many birdie opportunities, a pleasing number of which were converted. Successive birdies at the fifth and sixth edged Arnold ahead and, although Ormsby squared the match a number of times, Arnold was never behind before winning just one up after Ormsby missed the final green with her approach. The winner was an approximate two under par at the close.

title: The Una Wickham Memorial Tournament · p. 270
text:
Once again Brenda had fallen just short in her desire to win this tournament, a desire even stronger now that the tournament had been dedicated to the memory of a woman whose golf had been an inspiration to her.

A highlight of the tournament from a local aspect was the hole in one scored by Noeline Grant at the fifth hole during Sunday play.

1986 The quality that has for so long been displayed in this tournament was emphasised this year when the semi-finals featured four of the very best players in the country. The Auckland pair of Karrin Duckworth and Marnie Maguire were shortly off to Asia to represent New Zealand in the Queen Sirikit Tournament, while Bay of Plenty’s Jan Cooke was named non-travelling reserve for that team. Brenda Ormsby, now back in the Bay and based at Springfield, made up the semi-final group. Jan Cooke looked all over the winner against Duckworth only to lose the lead late in the day to go down at the 19th. Meanwhile Brenda Ormsby took an early 3 up lead against 16-year old Maguire and, though Maguire was able to square the match immediately after the turn, Ormsby pulled ahead again for a comfortable 2/1 victory to leave her poised to win her first Tauranga Una Wickham Open Championship. Alas for Ormsby it was to be another defeat in her fourth final. It was Duckworth’s exceptional play on, and around, the greens that made the difference in the final. Four down at the turn it looked all over for Ormsby but she came back strongly to square the match with three holes to play only to see her opponent win two of those final three holes for an entertaining two up victory.

1987 There was a new look to the field this year with many of the name players of previous tournaments missing for one reason or another. The final had a real Hawkes Bay flavour to it with Karen de Lautour (ex H Bay, now Remuera) defeating Ingrid van Steenbergen (ex Tauranga, now Hawkes Bay) 3/2 after van Steenbergen had set the early pace. Prior to this tournament van Steenbergen, previously apprenticed to the Greens Staff at Tauranga, had been appointed Head Green Keeper at the Flaxmere course in Hawkes Bay. She was probably the first woman to be appointed to such a position in New Zealand.

1988 Ingrid van Steenbergen returned to have another attempt at the title that had eluded her the previous year. Her quest was successful when, in a close fought final, she defeated former National trialist Jan Malcolm (Lochiel) at the 19th. Local teenager Catherine Rodgers proved something of a giant killer as she eliminated Gay McMillan (Paeroa) and Jan Cooke (now Tauranga) on the way to a

semi-final loss to Jan Malcolm.

1989 Jan Higgens (nee Cooke), now of Manakau, defeated defending champion Ingrid van Steenbergen at the 19th, the same hole where van Steenbergen had won her title one year before. Both finalists had previously been members at Tauranga and both had represented New Zealand at Overseas tournaments in 1988 so there was a lot of local interest in the final. The crowd were not disappointed as the pair fought out a close match where not more than one hole separated them as they each played the course in not more than one over par, this from the blue tees as was always the case for the Championship group. The power these women bring to their game was exemplified by Higgen’s play of

title: The Una Wickham Memorial Tournament · p. 271
text:
the 13th hole where her second shot finished pin high and just to the right of the green.

1990 One can imagine the delight experienced by Brenda Ormsby when her long quest for success in this tournament was rewarded with a 3/2 win over Otago’s Jan Scandrett in the final. Brenda played in the first Tauranga Match Play Open in 1976 and in most of those held since. Runner up on four occasions Brenda had missed the previous two tournaments. This year she may have been in more relaxed mood as she defeated Gina Scott, Sheree Higgens (now married to successful New Zealand professional David Smail), and Ingrid van Steenbergen on her way to the final.

The promising young Tauranga player Anne Rodgers, sister to Catherine, did very well to defeat three very well performed players, including Lynnette Brooky (Grange), in winning the Championship Plate after bowing to van Steenbergen in the first round. Earlier in the tournament Brooky had aced the fifth hole and almost repeated the feat at the fourth in her match with Rodgers, the ball finishing just centimetres from the hole after almost completing a ‘slam dunk’.

1991 The tournament this year was recognised as an official New Zealand trial. This guaranteed an exceptional field including the entire National squad of nine players. Ultimately the two top ranked entrants met in the final after relatively straight forward wins in the preliminary matches. Left hander Lisa Aldridge (Paraparaumu), playing in her first Una Wickham Tournament defeated four time finalist and previous winner Ingrid van Steenbergen at the 19th hole by sinking a 2m. birdie putt. Ironically this putt was almost identical to the putt holed by van Steenbergen at the first hole of the match for birdie. It was Ingrid’s third visit to the 19th hole in her four finals. Of these she had won just that once in 1988.

1992 Brenda Ormsby had a lot less work to do in winning her second Una Wickham Match Play Title than had been the case when winning her first two years previously. In grand form throughout the tournament Brenda needed only 57 holes to dispose of her four opponents, only Sandra Carey of Putaruru getting close when going down 2/1. Anne Familton (Grange) went down 5/3 in a final where Brenda’s consistency left few opportunities for her opponent to win a hole.

1993 Two of New Zealand’s most talented young players, Gina Scott (Kawhia) and Shelley Duncan (Otago) reached the final following preliminary play that featured many close contests. These two were the only New Zealand squad members competing this year and fittingly came through to meet in the final where Scott prevailed two up in a very entertaining final. Gina Scott in particular thrilled the gallery

with the length of her drives. These were consistently around the 230 - 240m mark. As an example of her power she was able to reach the 17th green with a seven iron second following her drive from the blue tees. When just 20 years old Scott had won the Waikato Champion of Champions title in 1991. Later she was to play in the Professional ranks in Europe.

This 1993 Una Wickham Tournament introduced an eleven year old from Whitianga to the Tauranga public. Julia Kraschinski started golf as a nine year old and qualified for this tournament when she reduced to a twelve handicap. Playing in the fourth sixteen she defeated four much older players in winning the group. It must have been quite unnerving to be outplayed by one so small and so young.

title: The Una Wickham Memorial Tournament · p. 272
text:
Julia came to be much admired as she returned to the tournament over the following years. Julia and her sister Miriam, who contested the tournament a little later, were born in Germany before the family moved to New Zealand.

1994 This year the tournament was designated as an official trial for both the Bay of Plenty/Thames Valley and Waikato/King Country teams thus ensuring all prospective team members in those regions were entered. Top seed and recently crowned World Left Handed Champion Lisa Aldridge staved off the challenge of the Northern stars, defeating Brenda Ormsby in the final.

1995 This year saw the emergence of Tina Howard of Taupo who was to have a significant presence in the Una Wickham Championship over the following years. Barely qualifying for the Championship flight in 14th spot the teenager defeated Ingrid van Steenbergen, Sandra Carey, and Robyn Pellow (Ngaruawahia) on her way to meeting the 1992 champion Gina Scott in the final. In that match Howard surged to a five-hole lead after seven holes and looked certain to bring off a huge upset when still four up with just five to play. It has long been claimed that whoever wins the 14th at Tauranga wins the match and Scott must have been aware of this as she birdied the par three to start her come-back. Pars over the testing 15th, 16th, and 17th holes and a birdie three at the 18th brought Scott level before she won the title with a further birdie at the first extra hole. After dropping seven strokes over the first six holes Scott was level with par over the final twelve.

Thirteen year old Julia Kranschinski distinguished herself by reaching the semi-finals where she bowed to the ultimate champion by 3/ 2.

1996 The Auckland, Waikato, and Bay of Plenty selectors all designated the tournament this year as an official trial again ensuring a quality field faced the starter. Tina Howard defeated Joanne Croskery, Catherine Knight, and Annette Stott on the way to another showdown against Gina Scott in the final. Gina had made it to the final by defeating three members of the BOP/TV representative team in Joanne Henderson, Julia Kraschinski, and Brenda Ormsby. As in the 1995 final between these two Tina began with a rush to be five up after just eight holes and though she three putted the ninth she still made the turn one under the card and four up. Unlike in the previous year she did not allow Gina back into the match and won comfortably.

1997 Kaye Carroll returned to the tournament after an absence of twelve years during which she

produced a family of four children.  Kaye (nee Johnson) had been an unknown teenage golfer from Opotiki when Una Wickham, realising the potential of the youngster, plucked her from comparative obscurity to join her in the Bay of Plenty team. Together they enjoyed a number of Russell Grace successes. Thus it was not difficult to see why Kaye had long harboured an ambition to win the Una Wickham Memorial since her first appearance in the event. In the final Kaye Carroll defeated Wendy Hawkes one up after an exciting match. On the way Carroll had defeated ex Tauranga player Joanne Brooks (Grange) in round one and Eleanor Hodgson (New Plymouth) in the Semi-final. Eleanor had caused a big surprise in defeating top seeded Julia Kraschinski at the 19th in the second round while Wendy, besides beating her twin sister Angela in round two, had

title: The Una Wickham Memorial Tournament · p. 273
text:
caused perhaps an even bigger upset by ousting tournament favourite Tina Howard in their semi-final.

1998 Twin sisters Angela and Wendy Hawkes of Titirangi met in the second round, one of many times these two were to meet in important tournaments. An excellent match went to the 20th before Angela prevailed. Angela then defeated International René Fowler 3/2 in the semi-final and defending champion Tina Howard 2/1 in the final. Angela’s victory was well received by the gallery as Wendy and Angela had been loyal and popular supporters of the tournament

1999 Responding to changes in the National Diary of Events the organising committee opted for a change from the traditional February dates to a weekend in August. Whether or not this was a wise decision is open to debate but it does appear to have heralded a decline in the quality of the field and the prestige of the tournament. While this year the tournament attracted most members of the Bay of Plenty team selected for the Inter Provincial Championships there were few quality players from elsewhere.
