In a rather ordinary final, which perhaps was indicative of the quality of the field, Sandra Baxendine (Matamata) defeated Sue Bassett (Te Puke) one up. Local interest centred on the performance of Chelsea Cox, daughter of Vanessa Barker, wife of Club Professional Rick Barker. Chelsea must have caused some concern to the Bay selectors as she defeated two of their team before losing a close semi-final match with Baxendine one down.

2000 The tournament date was changed to June. That suited Tina Howard, now a member of the New Zealand National Team and on a Golf Scholarship to the Louisiana State University. Home for a break Tina won her second Una Wickham title by defeating Robyn Pellow (Ngaruawahia) 2/1 in the final. This meant Tina had made the final in all four of her appearances in the tournament, winning two of those.

2001 That year the tournament regained status as an official trial for the Waikato and Bay of Plenty teams. Brenda Ormsby on plus 3 and Tina Howard on plus 1 were the highest ranked players while thirteen of the Championship flight contenders were on handicaps of 3 or better. Jan Storey of Waiterimu was in giant killing form, disposing of Penny Newbrook (Springfield), Wendy Hawkes (Arrowtown) at the 21st, and Brenda Ormsby (Te Puke) at the 19th. Tina Howard had a much easier passage to the final winning her matches comfortably. Storey continued her form into the final to reach the end of the regulation 18 holes all-square. Down the 19th in gathering gloom went the pair only to halve that hole. Recognising that the gloom would make the 2nd hole virtually unplayable the referee obtained the consent of the committee to play the 18th as the 20th hole. Though Tina raised an objection play

resumed on the 18th where enterprising Club members lined up their cars to cast some light on the green and approaches. Again the hole was halved and the players, now facing almost total darkness agreed to share the title - a bizarre ending to an entertaining final.

2002 Wendy and Angela Hawkes were probably the best performed women in the field and they met in the semi-final where Wendy prevailed 3/2. It was unfortunate that these two seemed destined to meet before the final in so many tournaments. It would have been interesting to see them meet in a final. Wendy continued on her winning way to score a 2/1 victory over Akane Iijima of Pakuranga in a final that was closely contested throughout.

title: The Una Wickham Memorial Tournament · p. 274
text:
2003 While the 2002 final featured a player of Asian descent the 2003 tournament could be considered the real beginning of the trend that saw Asian women rising to the top of women’s golf in New Zealand. Five of the Championship flight were this year of Asian descent. The failure of one of these to arrive from Auckland infuriated Tournament organisers especially as they were not advised of the non-appearance until 15 minutes before tee off. Worse, the player was seeded number one for the tournament. Tournament officials were equally upset upon learning that a National training camp had been scheduled in Wellington for the same dates. Remarkably Women’s Golf NZ claimed to be “unaware of the status of the Una Wickham event”. Sixteen top players were in Wellington for the camp. Women’s Golf NZ did adjust their calendar to avoid a clash in the future.

The final featured two young Asian women with 16 yr. old Bo Bae Kim defeating 12 yr. old Sharon Ahn one up. The power generated by these young players was evidenced on many occasions with drives of 250m and more being a regular feature of their play. The 15th hole that is normally played as a par five by women club players was reached by Ahn with a drive and five iron. Many a man could watch these young women and learn that hitting it long does not necessarily require brute strength. The feature that stands out is the co-ordinated rotation of the upper body with little apparent movement of the legs and knees.

2004 Stacey Tate (Huapai), a young player of genuine potential, defeated Mi Kyung Kim (Pupuke) 3/1 in the final after defeating the top seed, Tina Howard, in the semi-final. The final was notable for the over enthusiastic behaviour of Kim’s father who caddied for his daughter. At the sixth hole the referee ruled that Kim had conceded Tate a short putt for a half based on something she had said that caused Tate to pick up her ball.  While Kim made no protest her father began to rage at the referee for “not being fair to his daughter” though it was difficult to understand what he was concerned about. When he started to protest again at the eighth tee the referee suggested it might be better if he ceased caddying and left his daughter to get on with the game. He then handed the bag to another family member and the match continued in a better atmosphere. It sometimes seems that young players, especially those of Asian descent, would do better if their parents left them to find their own way in the game.

2005 Perhaps the most interesting match of this tournament took place during the second round on the Saturday afternoon. 13 yr. old Zoe Beth Brake (Kawerau) and Penny Newbrook, a former New Zealand number one, finished all square at the end of regulation play. At that stage darkness had set in so the pair set out virtually at dawn the following morning with Brake securing the win at the first extra hole.

Brake later claimed that she had looked up to Penny as her idol from the time she, Brake, had begun to play as a six yr. old so she had mixed feelings following her win.

The final featured two Asian women with Jackie Shin defeating last year’s runner up Mi Kyung Kim one up. Shin played the first nine in two under par to turn four up before her short game began to falter. Just one up with three to play a win at the sixteenth gave Shin just enough breathing space to hold out her rival.

title: The Una Wickham Memorial Tournament · p. 275
text:
2006 Preparations were made for the tournament in the usual manner that year but, sadly, the entries were not sufficient to make it viable to continue. The tournament appears to have been a victim of the times. More women were now committed to full-time work, the appeal of tournaments away from home was on the wane, and economic conditions seemed to have become more difficult for many potential participants. The women were not alone in these problems. The long established and previously highly popular Labour Weekend Tournament for men, featuring the Tauranga Open Title, had struggled to survive in the same era before finally fading into history. The sad realities of a more pressured world were exerting their influence over a multitude of activities. Golf, including the social aspects of our game, was to be no exception to the trend. The demise of these tournaments could in no way be attributed to those charged with their organisation. Everything that could reasonably have been done to ensure their popularity and consequent continuation was done. The world had simply moved on.

THE RUSSELL GRACE TOURNAMENT

The most important Women’s tournament ever staged at Tauranga has been the 1973 Inter-Provincial Championship then known as the Russell Grace Inter-Provincials just as the equivalent Men’s tournament was known as the Freyberg. These tournaments actually involve competition between

teams representing the District Golf Associations rather than Provinces but what’s in a name? While sponsorship has led to the demise of these old respected names this has been a small price to pay for the very welcome benefits that sponsors have brought to the Championships.

Anna Brabyn has given us information relating to the history of the tournament and the Russell Grace Cup. Mrs Nancy Young donated the cup to the NZLGU in memory of her mother, Mrs Russell Grace, who was a talented Wanganui representative golfer and long time member of the LGU. It had been Wanganui that first suggested that a National Inter-Provincial Championship be held. Originally the teams competed on a Regional basis, the first final being held at Invercargill in 1949 when Auckland became the first name engraved on the cup. All Districts competed at the one venue for the first time at the Ngamotu course in New Plymouth in 1963. Auckland was again successful though they had not dominated in the intervening years, this being their third victory. Bay of Plenty and Canterbury had been equally successful. Bay of Plenty/Thames Valley were again successful in 1983 at Heretaunga when the cup was awarded for the last time prior to the Tournament becoming known as the Stylemaster Inter-Provincial Championship. The Russell Grace Cup that somewhat incongruously had started life as a trophy awarded to the winner of a prestigious race at the Wanganui Racing Club was finally retired to a supposedly permanent home at the Wanganui Golf Club. The name and the cup were however resurrected to serve the New Zealand Masters Inter-Provincial Tournament first held at Methven in 1992. Many competitors in that first tournament would have been well aware of the proud history of the trophy.

The 1973 Russell Grace Tournament was held in perfect autumn weather at our Gate Pa course. It has often been said that our course is at its best in the Autumn months and, with the extra work put into course preparation for the tournament, this certainly proved to be the case.

title: The Una Wickham Memorial Tournament · p. 276
text:
Una Wickham, so often a major contributor to Bay of Plenty successes turned her talents to a spot of soothsaying prior to the start of tournament play. She predicted that the Waikato/King Country combination could well prove to be the dark horse of the tournament. Waikato number one Ruth Middleton indicated her intention to prove this prediction to be justified when she recorded six birdies in leading her team to a shock opening round victory over defending champions Auckland. This was Miss Middleton’s seventeenth Russell Grace and seldom had she played better golf. Four birdies in the first nine holes had the talented Gillian Bannan tottering yet Ruth had to birdie the 15th and 16th in order to prevail 3 and 2. This match set the standard for much high quality play leading to many a hard fought match throughout the tournament.

Two Tauranga players, Miss Wickham and Mrs Kath Johnston were included in the BOP/TV team. The formidable Wellingtonians were despatched that first morning but the highly favoured Manawatu/ Wanganui team proved too strong in the afternoon thus diminishing hopes of a local victory. The BOP/ TV team finally finished a very credible fifth.

Miss Middleton led from the front in becoming the only number one to remain unbeaten throughout the tournament as her team continued on its winning way. On the final day Canterbury, the most likely team to deny Waikato/King Country victory, was locked in an exciting battle with BOP/TV. Una Wickham, playing her best golf of the tournament, defeated Canterbury number one Sue Boag but it was not enough as Canterbury scraped home by three matches to two.  Canterbury could then only sit back and hope that their neighbours, South Canterbury, could topple Waikato/King Country. That was not to be and Waikato/ King Country had their name on the cup for the first time in their history. They thoroughly deserved what was very much a team success. Each individual member had wins when they were needed and though Canterbury scored more individual wins by a margin of four Waikato took the title by eleven team points to ten.

The organization of the tournament had been excellent, the fine weather played its part, the course was in as good a condition as any player could wish, and much of the golf had been of a standard to entertain the most discerning of spectators. The only occurrence to cast a gloom over the tournament came at the end of the final day. An excellent gallery had followed the last few holes as the tension mounted to see which of the two leading teams would prevail. As a result a large gallery was assembled around the 18th green in the gathering gloom and there they remained in the expectation that the ceremonial presentation of the cup would follow very soon after the final putt was holed.  Alas it was not to be. The organisers representing the Club were ready, the Press was waiting, the spectators were expectant. Where were the LGU representatives? Finally someone tracked them down. For some reason known only to themselves they had found that particular time to be the most appropriate hour to cloister themselves in the privacy of the Ladies’ locker room to deliberate on the selection of teams for something known as the ‘Home Internationals’! By the time they emerged the crowd had departed for warmer destinations.

title: The second one hundred years, 2014–2114 · p. 277
text:
THE SECOND

ONE HUNDRED YEARS

2014 - 2114

CHAPTER TWENTYFIVE

title: The second one hundred years, 2014–2114 · p. 278
text:
In this chapter I will attempt to look into the future to see how the Club and Course will develop during the next 100 years. The chapter will read as though written by someone looking back over the second century of Golf at Gate Pa. Sadly I will not know how perceptive these predictions prove to be.

THE SHORTCOURSE FACILITY

The second 100 years of our Club really started with the establishment of the new short course facility to the left of the second fairway.  Suitable practice facilities, or the lack thereof, had long been a problem for the Club, restricted as it had been from the beginning by the lack of space upon which to expand.  The available acreage was barely adequate to establish 18 holes of sufficient length to provide a realistic challenge, let alone allow for practice facilities.  The problem became even more evident as advances in technology, particularly in ball technology, reached a peak in the early years of the new Century.

The land the new facility occupies was part of a block purchased by Jack Grant’s Grandfather over 100 years ago.  Jack and his wife, well known, long standing, Club member Sybil Grant, farmed the land for many years.  Older members will recall Jack and Sybil making hay on the area then transporting it across the second fairway to link with the driveway to Cameron Road.

The Tauranga City Council recently purchased the land, and some perceptive members of our Club saw the potential offered by the relatively flat area adjoining the second fairway.  The legal expertise of Board member Michael J Smith overcame any possible obstacles and satisfactory lease terms were negotiated with the Council.  The Short Course team then investigated the available products and made the decision to use synthetic materials to establish permanent, low maintenance, tees and greens.  Field Turf NZ were the preferred product supplier and they were contracted to supply and install three greens together with the associated tees, a large practice mat, and an additional large green to be known as the High Performace area.  Our own staff established Windsor Green fairways using material harvested from our established fairways.

2013 Club Champion Dave Cooke, in tandem with Club Professional Jay Carter, designed the course to serve a wide variety of purposes for a wide variety of people.  The course can be used as a short six-hole Pitch and Putt course, a practice area for anything from chipping to medium iron play, or as a versatile teaching facility where individuals or large groups might be accommodated.  There is even a bunker where members can develop those skills so frequently required during most rounds.  This particular feature, as with others, is the first of its kind in New Zealand.  A product named Bunker Matrix was laid in the base of the bunker, this asphalt derived product encapsulates the clay base so as to keep contamination of the sand to a minimum.  The porous nature of the matrix allows water to flow through the sand and out through aggregate material and strategically placed pipes.  All this ensures

title: The second one hundred years, 2014–2114 · p. 279
text:
the sand remains in good condition and very little maintenance is required. None of this development would have been possible had it not been for a grant from the Lion Foundation arranged by Club Manager Michelle Towersey and BOP Golf Chief Executive Chris McAlpine.  This grant covered all direct costs so the only cost to our Club was through the use of our staff to establish Windsor Green turf throughout the area.

The promoters of the Short Course Facility envisage a wide variety of activities taking place on the area over the coming years.  Time will tell how much of this comes to pass.  Whatever the final usage the facility should prove a valuable adjunct to the main course limited only by the imagination of those who use it and promote it.

title: The second one hundred years, 2014–2114 · p. 280
text:
The most important debate of the first two decades of the 21st century was related to Global warming. The question was not as to whether it was a reality, but whether it was caused by the activities of humans or was a purely natural phenomenon that had been recurrent throughout the history of the planet. By the year 2020 the vast majority of people had come to accept that anthropogenic activity was clearly the major cause. In light of all the evidence presented to the public and to politicians by scientists it became increasingly difficult to argue that a century and more of intensive livestock farming, forest clearance, fossil fuel use in transport, energy production, and other applications, together with the associated generation of waste products had had little, if any, influence on the state of the atmosphere and the consequent health of the Planet. The academic debate receded into history as people everywhere realised that fighting the problem, not debating the cause, was essential if a path to a sustainable future was to be found.  The dangerous upward trend in Global temperature was finally stopped in the decade of the Forties, but not reversed until much later in the Century.

The Bay of Plenty had been blessed with a climate that was the envy of those in other parts of the Country, and indeed in much of the World. While summer droughts had been an occasional problem in the region they became much more frequent and more intense as the Century progressed. Consequently the decision of the Board back in the Nineties to establish Windsor Green fairways throughout the course proved to be a great investment for the future. These Cynodon fairways continued to thrive and provide a good playing surface in both summer and winter without the need to install fairway watering. Extensive irrigation would not have proved a viable option in any event as legislators were forced to severely restrict water usage as water became an increasingly scarce resource.

By 2020 the Board had reacted to the restrictions on the use of irrigation water by converting all the tees and fairways to Windsor Green and to investigating the availability of a suitable strain of Cynodon for use on the greens should the need to convert them arise. In 2030 the decision was made to go ahead with converting the existing predominately Brown top greens to a very fine leaved Cynodon developed by the New Zealand Institute of Turf Management. While these measures added to the requirement for a greater level of mechanical treatment to greens, fairways, and tees, they allowed members to enjoy a high standard of course presentation even in the driest years.

Throughout its early years the Tauranga course had been considered short by National or International standards. There was little that could be done to change that though the reduced run on the Cynodon fairways certainly increased the effective playing length by a significant margin. The possibility of

developing some additional holes in the Kopurererua Valley had been in mind since late in the 20th Century but the cost and other problems associated with this meant no decision to go ahead had been made by 2020. At that time modern equipment, especially advances in ball technology, had contributed to the relative shortening of all golf courses. Many quite ordinary club golfers were driving the ball far in excess of the distances reached by top professionals in the years when the PGA Championship was held on the Tauranga course some fifty years previously. Fortunately the International administrators of Golf, the Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews (R and A) and the USGA, finally recognised that technological developments were simply making the game more and more expensive as existing courses proved too short for even the average player. The solution they settled upon was to restrict the

title: The second one hundred years, 2014–2114 · p. 281
text:
Continuing the story of early tribulations suffered by Junior Boys we recall an incident from the Sixties. Two juniors, Wayne Holden and Brent Sutherland, both still at College, were playing the quarter final of the Club Senior Championship. All square after 18 holes they set off to the 19th tee. When the Captain informed the men waiting to tee off at the first hole for their afternoon round that the boys would need to play through the

comments of some of those men waiting to tee off were to the effect that “we are not standing aside for a couple of juniors”. The Captain made it very clear that that was exactly what they were required to do. After this distressing confrontation, the boys were clearly uncomfortable playing the hole, and from memory, scored a five and six to complete the match.

In Michael Nicholson’s junior days the Clubhouse was divided into two distinct areas,

the linoleum covered dining area and the carpeted lounge. The rule was that juniors were not permitted on the carpeted area. This was presumably to protect them from the evils of the Bar or perhaps the risqué stories and language of the senior members. By dint of his ability and behaviour Michael had been invited to join the playing category termed Boys’ A, thus enabling him to play on Saturday afternoon with the men. As Michael was still not permitted on the carpeted area the three men playing with him each week would position a table such that they could sit on the carpeted area while Michael’s chair sat on the linoleum. Thus the rule was complied with.

How times have changed. Juniors today are given every encouragement to develop their game and to participate fully in Club activities. They qualify for our representative Pennant teams, including at senior level where they often excel. It is to be hoped they will appreciate that the privileges they now enjoy were hard earned by their predecessors and by those adult members who recognised the need to change the culture that had long treated junior members as deserving of little in the way of encouragement

distance the ball would travel when driven by “Iron Byron” the mechanical driving machine owned by the USGA. This was achieved by softening the ball so that drives in excess of 250m by professionals and top amateurs became the exception rather than the rule. Few players could reach a hole of 450m or more in two strokes. This regulation was introduced in 2020 though the manufacturers challenged it all the way through the courts, ultimately without success. Golf ball manufacturers were understandably reluctant to see any restriction on ball design as they had so much invested in research and development. The Callaway Company alone spent 170 million $US in developing their first ball termed the Rule 35 ball. To compete with one another to produce a ball that is fast and low spinning off the drive, yet has a high spin rate when struck with a short iron, the competing companies employed people who previously worked as aerospace engineers or polymer and rubber chemists. Many employees held PhDs in these areas or in physics or applied mathematics. The humble golf ball had become a product of Space Age

title: The second one hundred years, 2014–2114 · p. 282
text:
technology.  The golf ball market is highly lucrative and long dominated by Acushnet, manufacturer of Titleist, Pinnacle, and Cobra brands. Other companies had been determined to challenge Acushnet’s dominance and research funding seemed to be no problem. Even following the Court decision in favour of Golf Administration the research continued as companies vied to produce “the better ball” within the new regulations. Spin rates, dimple pattern, and cover properties were all fertile areas for further experimentation. Never the less an effective cap had been placed on distance, and club administrators could confidently expect that future course policy would not need to plan for ever increasing driving distances.

For the Tauranga Golf Club, and for Clubs World-wide, the successful introduction of the softer ball had far reaching consequences. The need to lengthen courses was no longer apparent while new courses could be developed on relatively small areas. This was important in an age when suitable available land had become increasingly scarce and expensive. The Tauranga course once again became sufficiently challenging to test the best players, both men and women, while offering fair competition to Club members at all levels of ability.

Though legislation to restrict the flight of the golf ball achieved the desired result Club officials were still interested in making changes, both major and minor, to course design. Three major weaknesses that had long been identified were successive par threes at the fourth and fifth holes, the fact that there were five par threes in all, and the lack of practice facilities. During the decade of the 2030s funds were found to develop two holes in Kopurererua Valley. The third hole was now played as a dog leg to the left, the drive being essentially the same as previously, the hole then turning in a south-westerly direction to a green requiring a mid to long iron second stroke from a drive of average length. A new par four fourth hole was developed requiring a drive and a short iron to a green to the left of, and slightly beyond the present third green. This green was well bunkered to penalise a wayward short iron. These two holes were developed without any inconvenience to play as the existing third and fourth holes remained in play until the third was no longer required. The existing fourth, an excellent par three, became the fifth hole while the existing fifth was incorporated into extended practice facilities linked to the driving range. The abandonment of the existing fifth also enabled extensive contouring of the seventh fairway to provide a better landing area for the second stroke, a long sought improvement to that hole.

A number of other changes were made in the first half of the 21st Century. These included:

Hole 1 The green was moved back and tucked slightly to the right so that the tee shot needed to be played towards the left side of the fairway in order to gain the best approach to the pin. Hole 2 The Casuarinas to the right were removed and replaced by a cluster of fairway bunkers. Hole 6 A new bunker was installed to guard the left front of the green. Hole 7 A new green was developed to the right of the existing green to provide a more accessible target for

title: The second one hundred years, 2014–2114 · p. 283
text:
the third stroke. When allied with the newly contoured landing area for the second stroke the new hole provided a fairer yet adequate challenge to all players. Few lamented the demise of the green that had been developed in the early years of the new millennium. Hole 8 The fairway bunker on the right was eliminated and replaced 30m forward of the original position. Its partner on the left was enlarged by extending it towards the green. These bunkers now tended to penalise the better player’s poorer stroke rather than the average player’s best effort, a much more desirable aim on a club course. Hole 11 The bunker to the right and short of the green was reinstated but reconstructed so as to allow for easier maintenance. It had long been felt the hole had lost much of its character when removal of the original bunker had opened up the right hand side of the green. Hole 14 The shrubbery in the Southeast corner was brought back into bounds. Hole 15 The Casuarina hedge along the first half of the fairway was removed after replacement groves of trees had been grown behind them. Fairway bunkers supported these groves in order to encourage play away from the left side of the fairway. The Out of Bounds line reverted to the boundary fence. Greenside bunkers were installed to the front left of the green to further encourage play away from the left side. Hole 17 One of the bunkers in front of the green was eliminated in order to provide an opening to the green. It was considered unfair to expect an average to poorer player to be capable of playing a shot from one bunker across another to reach the pin. For men the hole was re-rated to play as a par four, its length being well within the recommended range, even now that driving distances had been constrained. As a corollary to these course changes the men’s committee had another look at stroke allocation and analysed stroke play cards returned by their own members over a three-month period including the 72 Hole Stroke Play Championships. As a result of this analysis serious anomalies that had arisen earlier in the millennium were rectified. The review included the re-rating of holes two and twelve in particular. Now no par three hole rated ahead of any par four or five hole. The revised allocation closely resembled that which had existed throughout most of the previous sixty years. While the analysis showed the 17th hole deserved to be the third stroke hole this was considered to be too late in the round for that allocation as match players might very well lose their match before being able to exercise their right to use the stroke. In all respects the new allocation exactly followed the recommendations contained in

both the USGA and the NZGolf handbooks. The long-standing controversy associated with this topic was finally put to rest to the satisfaction of the majority of players following an awareness campaign to familiarise those interested in the aforementioned recommendations. As a result of the information made available the women’s committee came to realise that the par of a hole has no bearing on fair allocation of strokes for match play and their fifteenth hole was re-rated as the 5th stroke hole.

The New Zealand economy enjoyed a protracted period of growth beginning in the late 2020s leading to a significant rise in the living standards of the majority of the population. This growth was based upon the forward thinking of the Government, or in spite of their actions, depending upon your political

title: The second one hundred years, 2014–2114 · p. 284
text:
persuasion. In truth the stimulus arose in the desire of young, educated New Zealanders to make the best future for themselves and for their country. Many of these young people were those returning from Overseas in search of a more relaxed life style while highly qualified immigrants from a wide variety of countries added significantly to the pool of talent.  The aspirations of these people led the country away from its traditional dependence on the production of meat, milk, wool, wine, wood and fruit. This eventually led to New Zealand becoming a World leader in Biotechnology. This was especially true of applications in genetic engineering related to the Agricultural, Horticultural, and Medical Sciences. Developments in healthcare, environmentally friendly energy production, and other innovations in science and engineering contributed to significant advances in the wealth and living standards of the population.

With improved economic conditions golf enjoyed an upsurge of interest and the Tauranga Club was again forced to operate a waiting list. The four-day working week had become a reality for many people even though it was not made a constitutional requirement. This put further pressure upon courses as players made greater use of the facilities seven days a week. The population of Tauranga and the Western Bay of Plenty continued to grow and new courses were developed at Papamoa (opened 2026), and at Tauriko (opened 2035).

With more people enjoying a high standard of living and greater leisure time open Match Play tournaments of various formats began to be promoted by Clubs across the Country. The reinstatement of the once popular Five Day Veteran Golfers’ Match Play tournaments across the Country was in the forefront of this trend. In 2030 Tauranga became one of the first clubs to restage such an event. A year later the Club reinstated the Annual Labour Weekend Tournament in the original format that incorporated the Tauranga Open Championship last held in 1999. Full fields were attracted to both events with many participants coming from outside Clubs.

For much of its history the Tauranga Golf Club had struggled to maintain subscriptions at sufficiently high levels to ensure they covered annual running costs while allowing reserves to be put aside for future capital needs. For too long the Club had relied on sponsorship from City Businesses and on grants from those who controlled the distribution of profits from Poker machines. Sponsorships had always proved difficult to obtain while grants from Gaming Machines now tended to be channelled towards genuine charities rather than to Sporting Clubs. The growth of the city population, allied to higher living standards, meant that members were better able to meet the true costs of their sport. In addition the advantageous siting of the course well within City boundaries meant there was never a shortage of people keen to join a Club that offered excellent playing conditions all year round together with Clubhouse facilities of a very high standard. The future promised to be at least as rewarding as had been the past.

On arrival in New Zealand he farmed at Mangaweka for some years before moving to Auckland where he established a successful business producing and distributing agricultural chemicals. Later he moved to Tauranga where he resided for many years. Ken took a keen interest in young people and donated the cup to encourage Junior Boys to work hard at the game. Members were pleased to accept an offer from Keith Frith to fill the breach for a further term.

Up until 1996 the Captain, together with other executive members, had been elected by the full senior membership (men and women). This person was effectively the Men’s Captain and his chief function was as Chairman of the Men’s Match Committee that was known simply as the Match Committee. There was irony in the situation where the women members could, in theory, decide who should be in charge of men’s competitive golf. In 1996 a new position of Club Captain was constituted distinct from that of Men’s Captain. The new appointee was to be a member of the Board and would chair the Player’s Committee that was introduced to oversee and coordinate all golf played on the course. As a corollary the men would now elect their own Captain and Match Committee just as the women had done since 1937.

CLUB TROPHIES

A full photographic record of all trophies has been compiled and a copy kept in the Club office. Consequently a full list of them will not be provided here. There are some trophies that warrant an explanation of their origins and others where it is important to acknowledge those people who donated them. In many cases the trophy donors were responsible for establishing a competition where none existed prior to their initiative. In most instances the donors have been notable figures in our history and their contributions to the development of the Club have been recorded elsewhere in this publication. This is especially true of the trophies involved in Veteran’s competitions, both Men and Women’s.

MEN’S TROPHIES

One of the earliest trophies to be contested was the Cameron Cup. Senior players compete for this over 36 holes of Stroke Play. Surprisingly the Cameron name is not derived from our main thoroughfare or from one of the Cameron families of the district. Miss Mae Cameron of Auckland was a regular visitor to Tauranga and enjoyed her visits so much that in 1924 she decided to present this cup to the club as a mark of her appreciation. The first of the two rounds of this competition serves as the qualifying round for the Aquila Cup. This is a senior handicap Match Play event.

The origin of the Aquila Cup has been lost with the passage of time. There was a coastal steamer by that name that made regular trips between Auckland and Tauranga and it is likely that some of the men manning her enjoyed a game of golf when in port. Perhaps the Captain or some of the men decided to express their appreciation for hospitality extended to them. I would like to think that this was the case.

The Waitemata Cup contested by Intermediate members in parallel with the Cameron Cup for senior players is an example of trophies that were presented to the Club in appreciation of the support given by the Club to the suppliers of certain products. Waitemata was a brand of beer produced by Dominion Breweries and supplied to the Club through Guiness Brothers who ran their business from premises at the Northern end of The Strand. Brownie and Joyce Carnachan, Colin and Betty Johnstone, were prominent Club members associated with the business, Betty and Joyce each being members of the

Guiness family. Those Intermediates qualifying for Match Play as a result of their performance in round one of the Waitemata Cup went forward to contest the Geo Wilcock Junior Cup, more commonly known simply as the Wilcock Cup. Life Member and Past President George Wilcock presented this trophy in an era when only two competition grades were recognised, Senior and Junior. When the Intermediate grade was instituted in 1946 it was felt appropriate that the Wilcock Cup should be contested by players at that level rather than by players in the newly defined junior grade. The committee provided the Junior Cup to be contested in parallel with the Cameron and Waitemata Cups while Norman Green presented the Green Cup that is now awarded to the winner of the junior

handicap Match Play event. This was originally awarded to the winner of the ‘C Grade Championship’ that was contested by longer handicap players prior to the introduction of the three grades we now recognise.

Match Play events have always been popular with Club players. The Occupational Four Ball was an early introduction to the programme and was open to all members, the only restriction as to who could team together being that implied by the title. This event drew very large fields often requiring elimination matches to be played in order to allow pairs to advance to the main draw of 64. Eventually the competition was discontinued and replaced by the Senior/Junior Four Ball and the associated trophy transferred to the new event.

The Winter Four Balls are contested in three grades. Norman Robson and Paul O’Brien, well-known Club members who ran Businesses on The Strand, presented the cups awarded to the senior winners. Bob Eaton and Keith Frith presented the cups contested by the Intermediate pairs while the committee provided those for the juniors.

The most important Match Play events are those for the Club Championships. Several of the trophies associated with these are of very long standing. Bill Darley who was Secretary to the Club when it first moved to the present course in 1914 presented the W M Darley Cup. It is awarded to the player recording the best gross score over the two qualifying rounds. The Passmore Trophy goes to the best nett qualifier. Like the Waitemata Cup this is a trophy presented to the Club by a grateful supplier. CS Passmore was a liquor wholesaler based in Auckland. In the first few years after this trophy was presented the winner also received two bottles of the best of the Passmore range. The first player to find this tradition had been discontinued was a very disappointed man.

Mr E T Baker, one of our earliest Life Members presented the Senior Championship Cup.

Stroke Play Championships were established in 1980. These were originally played over 72 holes as stand alone competitions not associated with the Match Play Championships. More recently they have been reduced to 54 holes and qualification for the Match Play Championships is based on rounds played in these competitions. Some consider that the staging of the two championships in tandem has reduced the importance of the Stroke Play Championship. The practise of allowing the best two of the three rounds to count for qualifying purposes also causes problems for purists and/or traditionalists.

Whether these innovations continue into the future remains to be seen.

David N Coleman, a prominent Tauranga Share Broker, presented the cups awarded to both the Senior and the Intermediate Stroke Play Champions while the Juniors play for the ANZ Bank Cup. The Alan Ward Memorial Trophy is awarded to the player scoring the best Nett over the first two rounds of the Stroke Play Championships. Alan was a member of the Ward family featured in Chapter Nineteen. Details of Alan’s service to the Club are given there. The James Mowat Memorial Trophy has gone through a number of transformations. Jame’s widow Margaret presented the trophy and, following the advice of the then Match Committee, it was originally

presented to the player recording the best aggregate gross score over any five rounds throughout the season. This proved difficult to administer in the pre-computer era and for some years it was contested as a Match Play event open to all members whatever their handicap. This led to some interesting singles matches involving senior players having to give a stroke a hole, and sometimes more. That is very difficult to do. The Mowat family provided vouchers that the recipients could use to subsidise purchases of their own choice. The sight of Reg Carter one year proudly donning a Club jacket that he had decided was the ideal prize to commemorate his win lives vividly in the memory.  Following a period when it was awarded for the best aggregate nett score over the Stroke Play Championships the trophy reverted to its original role, computers having now made record keeping much simpler.

The Pinto Fruit Juice Company donated The Pinto Cup for Foursomes competition. Past president Dan Dougherty was manager of the company at a time when the company was a major supplier to the Club.

Other important trophies are the Alan Bradmore Memorial Cup and the Nicoll Cup. Harry Bradmore presented the former in memory of his son Alan who was killed in the Second World War. It is contested over two rounds of Stableford competition. Harry and his son Maurice have been acknowledged earlier in relation to their invaluable work in relation to the trees on the course. Life Member Warwick Nicoll presented the latter Cup and it is contested over two rounds of Par competition.
